en: Preface to the Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra,
written by the Meritorious Subject for Promoting Sincerity and Preserving Virtue, Acting Minister of the Ministry of Punishment,
Commissioner for the Capital Region, Director of the River Administration, and Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture.
The Duke of Kaiguo of Jiuyang Commandery, with an enfeoffment of five thousand three hundred households, who speaks well of the Buddha—how could he fail to speak of its Way?
Is it not the spirit of boundless goodness? Profoundly still, eternally refined, perfectly full, and impartial: one may seek it, yet see no head.
Following it, its end cannot be seen. It is born again and again yet does not arise; it transforms again and again yet does not change. It envelops all existence and contains the ten directions;
it provides the beginning for all conditions and fulfills all practices. Its radiance shines secretly yet is not form; its empty penetration operates latently yet is not void.
While worlds shift and change, it does not move; while mountains and peaks turn and collapse, it remains eternally still.
Those who are deluded by what is manifest before them fail to discern it; those who are confused in their daily lives do not know it. The *I Ching* says:
"Tranquil and unmoving, yet responding and thereby penetrating all. Laozi says: "Standing alone and unchanging, circulating everywhere without weariness.
Is this not what is called one's nature? Since beginningless kalpas, all sentient beings have clung to external objects and forgotten their original mind, thereby becoming divided.

The four entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) fold into the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*); they race forth as deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), congeal into obscuring veils, aggregate into afflictions (*kleśa*), and flow into birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
These burden my true source and cause me to enter the various realms of existence in vain. Out of compassion for them, the Tathāgata composed the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
Because sentient beings suffer from their frantic flight, he expounded the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) for them; yet they remain stuck in form (*rūpa*).
Because of [the clinging to] marks, he pointed out the "eight returns. Because of the mistaken identification of the faculties and objects, he distinguished the "six entrances.

Because of false calculations regarding causes and conditions, he discoursed on the "seven elements. As for bending his golden arm and knotting the flower-towel, these were the most skillful of metaphors, used to sweep away subtle delusions and cause those who gaze upon the jewel-light to know that the essence of seeing does not waver, and to listen to the bell... [and so forth].
Regarding "Sound": it is the awakening to the ever-present nature of hearing. When fundamental luminosity turns back upon itself, still wisdom arises.
One then mounts the supreme jewel vehicle and roams the boundless ocean of nature. One regards the form-body as a mote of dust and views the great void as a mere speck of cloud.
Therein lies no root for the cycle of rebirth, nor any views of inversion held for billions of kalpas, nor the false attachments of self and person, nor the [grasping at] longevity.
The floating thoughts of life are like a flame from glowing coals consuming a tuft of swan’s down, or the morning dew being dried by the scorching sun;
they dissolve of their own accord without even waiting for deliberate contemplation. How great is the wondrous perfection of Bodhi! It is pure and tranquil from the very beginning.

Since the true essence is free from the cataracts of delusive illusions, how could there be a body or mind subject to birth and death? When the water is clear and the sediment has been removed, the outflows are exhausted and all phenomena are eliminated. Thus, the myriad practices...
Without cultivation, it is spontaneously perfected; the six supernatural powers are realized without seeking. Is one who anticipates this not truly divine?

Nevertheless, this scripture distills the essential core of the Eight Collections (Aṣṭapiṭaka) and exhausts the source of the myriad transformations. The translator prioritized brevity, while the reviser favored ornate diction;
because some have thus become mired in detailed study and fixated on the parsing of phrases, there is the monk Kedu [who has written this].

The annotations of this work distinguish between the detailed and the concise with systematic order, encompassing both the Chinese and the Sanskrit traditions. As the cycle of the years completes its second revolution, my labors are finally concluded.

Those who observe it hereafter should reverse the karmic conditions of their dreams and fantasies, abandon the habitual causes within their minds and eyes, realize the fundamental essence of consciousness, and return to the source of solitary wondrousness.
When the clouds disperse, the moon’s movement ceases; when the wood is exhausted, the ashes fly away.
Furthermore, even illusory phenomena vanish; not even a hair’s breadth remains. True reality is naturally profound and dark.
Those who seek the untainted, supreme understanding of the Buddhas should fortunately apply themselves with diligence to this.
Preface on the first day of the second month in the fourth year of the Jingyou era,
to the *Śrī-mahā-buddhôtta-ma-tejo-ratna-śikhara-sūtra-tathāgata-rahasya-hetu-bhāvanā-sākṣāt-kriyā-nītārtha-sarva-bodhisattva*... [text continues]
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on All Practices, Scroll One (Part One of Two).
Translated by the Indian *śramaṇa* Prajñāmitra;
translated into Chinese by the *śramaṇa* from Udyāna, Moksagupta.
Recorded by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Fang Rong;
classified by the Śramaṇa Weiqu from Daxingfu Monastery in the Western Capital;
annotated by Keduo, the Great Master of Śūraṅgama in the Early Song Dynasty.
Great. First, the explanation of the title of the scripture is divided into six sections. First, the pairing of the Dharma and the metaphor. The commentary states:

"In Sanskrit it is *mahā*, in Chinese it is 'Great' (*dà*). 'Great' refers to the Dharma that is expounded; its essence is complete, harmonious, and fused, and its principle is ultimate and non-dual."

It is "square" (fang) because it does not correspond to the small; it receives its name from its own essence. Thus, the subsequent passage says: "I now establish for you the great banner of the Dharma.
Among the two types of expression, this is subsumed under direct expression (biao-quan).

"Buddha. The commentary states: "In the language of India, *buddha* means 'the Awakened One' (*jùzhě*); in the language of China, it is translated as 'the Awakened One. In this sutra, only the character 'Buddha' is retained without the other characters.

This is because the people of the Qin state favored brevity, and furthermore, it was done to accommodate the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings in this land, so that upon hearing [it], they might..."
The Buddha contemplates the good and gives rise to superior understanding; therefore, this term is not translated.
Regarding "Ding" (頂), the commentary states: the Sanskrit term is *uṣṇīṣa*, and the Chinese term is "Ding. It is a metaphor. This refers to the *Śūraṅgama* [Samādhi]...
The elucidation of this principle is unfathomable even to Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages. It is likened to the Buddha’s crown protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*), which is beyond the realm of visibility;

the World-Honored One himself does not see it, signifying that it is free from self-characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*). No Bodhisattva, however pervasive their presence, can see it, signifying that it is free from other-characteristics (*para-lakṣaṇa*).
Among the sixty-two metaphors, this is the foremost metaphor of the "Crown Protrusion" which cannot be seen.
*Tathāgata*. Second, clarifying the cause by means of the fruit. The commentary states: *Tathāgata* in Sanskrit; in the Chinese language, "Thus Come One" (*Rúlái*).

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "There is nowhere from which he comes, nor anywhere to which he goes; therefore he is named Tathāgata. This is in reference to the *dharmakāya*. Furthermore, all...
The Master explains: "Riding the path of suchness" refers to returning to the source of original enlightenment from the perspective of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
"Arriving to achieve perfect enlightenment" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, Master Kuò says: "Tathāgata" is a profound designation that accords with the fundamental [nature].
This is an explanation based on the meaning of the fundamental and the initial.
"Secret" (*mi*).
The commentary states: The Sanskrit term is *vākya*, which in the Chinese language means "secret. It signifies firmness and density, as well as concealment.
Although there are worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), there has never been any leakage [of the essence].

"Causes. The commentary states: *hetu* in Sanskrit; "cause" (*yin*) in the Chinese language. "Cause" carries the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*). It is the fundamental nature of sentient beings and the source of the Tathāgata’s awakening.
Because it remains unmanifest while within the toils of worldly affliction, it is provisionally designated as a "cause. Thus says the Tathāgata.
"Result" (*phala*) is the designation for the fruit; "cause" (*hetu*) is the name for the secret cause;

and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the practice. Regarding the correspondence between cultivation and realization, the commentary states: the Sanskrit term *kṣata* translates into Chinese as "cultivation" (*xiū*). Cultivation means...
To advance in cultivation. However, all Bodhisattvas give rise to the mind of awakening; they take non-action as their subtle power for cultivation and realization.

The commentary states: "The Sanskrit term is *sādhana*, which in the Chinese language means 'realization' (*zhèng*). This refers to the realization of the fruit, wherein one personally attains perfect clarity."

The essence is realized through the perfection of the means of realization; therefore, the subsequent text states: "Having attained the primordial, luminous awareness, which possesses the nature of neither arising nor ceasing, one takes this as the mind of the causal stage, and thereafter fully accomplishes the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage."
*Nītārtha* (Definitive Meaning).
Fourth, the two expressions of the ultimate intent are presented in parallel. The commentary states: *Sakha* in Sanskrit; "definitive meaning" (*liao-yi*) in Chinese.
"Definitive" (*liao*) means manifest and clear; it points directly to the true source. This sutra is called "definitive" because it definitively expounds the truth. [The sound...]
Name, phrase, and syllable take these four dharmas as their essence. The subsequent text states: "I have now already explained the dharma of true cultivation.

Here, "meaning" (*yi*) refers to principle (*li*). This indicates that the ultimate principle elucidated by this Śūraṅgama is beyond investigation and deliberation, where speech and discourse are cut off.
The subsequent text further states: "The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, transcending all names and characteristics."
"Various.

Regarding the five pairs of the agent and the object of action: the commentary states that the Sanskrit term is *sarva*, which in the Chinese language means "various," signifying that they are not one.
"Bodhisattva.
The commentary states: The Sanskrit term *bodhisattva* translates into Chinese as "Awakened Being" (*jué yǒuqíng*). "Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation.

To inspire wholesome thoughts in those who hear it, one does not say "Awakened Being," yet one may still be called a "Bodhisattva. This refers to one who is capable of seeking and capable of practicing.
This refers to one who possesses the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.

Regarding "myriad practices" (*wanxing*): the commentary states that *ca-li* (拶哩) is the Sanskrit term, which in the Chinese language means "myriad practices. "Myriad" (*wan*) has the sense of number; "practices" (*xing*) refers to meritorious deeds. However...
All bodhisattvas, while on the path of causes, practice the myriad deeds of the six perfections to enable them to seek realization of the source; this must be discussed in terms of their conduct.

As the subsequent text states: "The King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi is fully endowed with the myriad practices. This first indicates the person who seeks, and subsequently clarifies the practices to be performed.

Śūraṅgama. This refers to the profound principle and the profound teaching of the sixth [chapter]. The commentary states: "The Sanskrit term is *śūraṅgamā*; what is now called 'Shoulengyan' is an abbreviation.
Taken as a whole, it is translated as 'the ultimate culmination of all phenomena.'"
Sūtra. The commentary states: The Sanskrit term is *sūtra*. Translated according to its meaning, it signifies "scripture"; it is also translated as "thread.
In the ancient Sanskrit, it is called *yukti-sūtra*, or also *sūtra*. This is translated as "conformity," meaning conformity with principle and conformity with the capacities [of sentient beings].
Therefore, in the current period, the sūtras and śāstras mostly use the new term *sūtra* (in Sanskrit), rather than *sūtra* or *sūtṛu*.

They speak only of "sūtra" and not of "thread. This refers to the principle that, like the Five Classics and Nine Classics of this land, they shall be practiced for ten thousand generations and remain unchanged through a hundred reigns.
The fundamental essence of this sūtra takes the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama as its primary tenet, [teaching] sudden enlightenment.
Cultivation through gradual stages serves as the path. Thus it is.
In order to explain this sutra, there are broadly three sections; the beginning and end are as follows. Down to the point of receiving the holy instructions, it is called [the section on]...
This constitutes the Introduction (*nidāna*). Next, from the words "The Buddha said" up to the eighth section below, titled "False Contemplation," constitutes the Main Body (*śarīra*).
Finally, from "At that time" up to "paid homage and departed" below constitutes the Dissemination (*pariṇāmana*). Furthermore, the text of the initial Introduction is divided into two parts:

first, the General Introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*); second, the Specific Introduction (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*). The text of the General Introduction has six sections; the first indicates the Dharma that was heard. [End of] Commentary.
"Yun" (Cloud) means: the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) realized by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. "Shi" (Is) means:
that which has been spoken by our Buddha, the World-Honored One, opening his golden mouth and moving his red lotus tongue.
"I have heard.

This next section describes the person capable of hearing. The commentary states: "The faculty of the ear gives rise to the auditory consciousness, which takes as its object the stainless sound of the World-Honored One.
Now, setting aside the ear and the mental faculty, one speaks of 'I have heard' by abandoning the specific for the general. Furthermore, it is thus regarding the five secrets."
Regarding the three causes for realization—the true cause and the true fruit—I, the Venerable Ānanda, have personally heard the account from the Buddha himself.

It is said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Venerable Ānanda was compiling the Dharma-piṭaka among the Saptaparṇa Cave, his body manifested all the marks and signs of a Buddha; then, upon descending from his seat, he returned to his original form.
At that time, the assembly had three doubts: first, they doubted that the Buddha, out of great compassion, had arisen from the realm of *nirvāṇa* to further preach the wondrous Dharma;
second, they doubted that another Buddha had come from another direction to preach the Dharma here;

third, they doubted that Ānanda, having transformed his consciousness to become a Buddha, was preaching the Dharma for the assembly. It was then that Ānanda recited in verse: "Thus have I heard. The great assembly—
The three doubts were instantly extinguished.

At one time, when the teachings were expounded for the third time. The commentary states: "This does not refer to a single day, nor to the twelve periods or six periods [of the day]; it refers only to the assembly."

The conditions for the roots of goodness have matured; there is a profound resonance with the Buddha-mind. As the matters of principle and phenomena are about to conclude, a provisional designation of "one time" is established.
Furthermore, since the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is timeless, it is called "one time."
"Buddha.
Regarding the four characters [of his title], "Zhuchi" (垂□主) is annotated as follows: The Sanskrit term is *Buddha*; the Chinese translation is "The Awakened One" (*Juezhe*).
This preserves the original Sanskrit sound for the purpose of generating wholesome roots in sentient beings. Two thousand years ago, the sixteen-foot-tall teaching lord Śākyamuni was this very one.
In the city of Śrāvastī, there are five sites where the Dharma was proclaimed. The commentary states: the Sanskrit name is Śrāvastī; the old Chinese transliteration "Shewei" (舍衛) is a corruption.
In Chinese, it means: 1. City of Abundant Virtue; 2. Abundance of Wealth; 3. Realm of Desired Objects; 4. Abundance of Learning; 5. [The fifth site].
"Abundant Liberation. Possessing these four virtues, it is called "Abundant Virtue," which refers to the kingdom of Central India.
Regarding the Jetavana Monastery, the commentary states:
it is also called *Jetṛ*, which is the old Sanskrit; the new [transliteration] is *Jetavana*. In the language of China, this means "Victorious in Battle. Thus, the *Pā*... [text truncated]
When Prince Siṇika was born, a neighboring hostile kingdom arrived; he defeated them in battle, and thus he was named "Victorious in Battle" (Saṅgama).
This tree was planted by the prince, and this vihāra was built by Sudatta. In the old [translation], he was called Sudatta; in the new, Sūdattra.
In the language of the Flower [China], it means "Good Giver" (Śubhadatta), or also "Giver of Orphans" (Anāthapiṇḍada). As for "Good Giver," he was benevolent and...
Rui (Prasenajit) accumulated wealth and was able to distribute it; he provided relief to the poor and destitute and showed compassion for the orphaned and the elderly.
People of the time praised his virtue and called him the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver of Alms to the Destitute). He was a minister of King Prasenajit (formerly called Po-si-ni in Chinese;
here both the sovereign and the subject are mentioned together), hence the name Jetavana Vihāra. "Jetavana" refers to the king, and "Vihāra" refers to the monastery.
The minister then asked: "The merit of Sudatta in scattering gold was great; why does he rank behind? The Prince Jeta’s merit in relinquishing the grove was small;
why does he rank ahead? He replied: "Although the merit of relinquishing the grove was small, as the sovereign, it is logically appropriate for him to take precedence.
Although the merit of scattering gold was great, as a subject, it is right by principle that he should occupy the subsequent position."

"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus. This is the sixth section, describing the assembly that heard the teaching. The text is divided into three parts; the first concerns the śrāvakas. This section has four parts. The first is the designation of their category. The commentary states:

"Accompanied by" (yǔ) carries the sense of inclusion or conjunction; it refers to the collective mention of both teacher and disciples. "Great" (dà) is a title for those of great transformative power (*mahopāya*). Regarding the six stages...
This refers to the Arhat liberated through both wisdom and concentration (*prajñā-vimukti*). The Sanskrit term *bhikṣu* translates into Chinese as "beggar" (*qǐshì*).
Above, he seeks the Buddhas, begging for the Dharma to nourish his spirit; below, he seeks from donors, begging for food to sustain his life.

Among the five reasons for not translating, this is an instance where multiple meanings are retained without translation. When there are three or more individuals, they all obtain the title of "Assembly" (*saṃgha*).
"Accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
Next, the *Jian* (Commentary) states: "The compiler of the sutra asks how many followers were present at that time; the verse explains the teaching, saying... and so forth.
The Vinaya and the Sūtra on Cause and Effect state that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he first delivered the five men, including Kauṇḍinya;
next, he delivered the three Kāśyapa brothers along with their one thousand disciples; next, he delivered Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others along with their two hundred disciples;
and next, he delivered fifty people, including Yaśas, the son of an elder—altogether totaling one... [thousand].
"One thousand two hundred and fifty-five people. The commentary states: "According to this assembly, Kauṇḍinya is present again.

Since he was not included in the previous count, there is no doubt that five were added. Alternatively, the sutra may cite the total number, as in the case of the 'ten categories' [of beings]. 'Together' (俱) means that their locations are not separated."
All are great Arhats free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

This section on praising their virtues consists of two parts. First, the general summary. The commentary states: "Question: What virtues and moral attainments do these one thousand two hundred and fifty people possess?

The verse provides the answer as follows... The term *jie* (皆) signifies "all" or "entirely. The term *shi* (是) indicates the sense of "referring to" or "identifying. *Lou* (漏) refers to the outflows.
These are synonyms for afflictions (*kleśa*), such as "leaking from a house" or "leaking from a boat," and are deeply loathsome and to be renounced.

The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) has sixty-one factors as its essence; the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) has ninety-two factors as its essence; and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) has fifteen factors as its essence.
Because these three outflows do not exist now, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Sixth, regarding the six stages (*ṣat-sthāna*): [the text continues].

This refers to the stage of immovability (*akopya*). There are six types: first, the one of the nature of retrogression (*parihāṇadharman*); second, the one of the nature of reflection (*cetana-dharman*); third, the one of the nature of protection (*anurakṣaṇādharman*);

fourth, the one of the nature of abiding (*sthitākampya-dharman*); fifth, the one of the nature of being capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*); and sixth, the one of the nature of immovability (*akopyadharman*). The Sanskrit term for *arhat* is translated into Chinese as "one who is worthy" (*ying*).

It possesses three meanings of worthiness: they are worthy of destroying the thieves of afflictions; they are worthy of not receiving a future body of existence; and they are worthy of receiving the offerings of gods and humans.

"Buddha-sons who maintain the teachings" is a separate section. The commentary states: Because they are the sons of the Buddha, they are called "Buddha-sons. Question: Only those who are Bodhisattvas are called Buddha-sons;
why then are Śrāvakas also named Buddha-sons? Answer: The Buddha possesses great compassion, and thus all three vehicles [are his children].

"Abiding" (zu) means abiding in the untainted (anāsrava). "Sustaining" (chi) means sustaining so as not to lose it; it sustains the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and nirvāṇa, ensuring they are not lost.
This refers to one dharma of concentration (samādhi).
"Skillfully transcending all modes of existence.

The commentary states: "Mu" (目) refers to liberation. "Transcending" (*chao*) means to surpass or go beyond. "All modes of existence" (*zhū yǒu*) refers to the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the existence of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the existence of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Within these, there are the afflictions of discrimination in the existence of desire, and the innate afflictions in the existence of formlessness; alternatively, it may refer to the twenty-five modes of existence.
As a verse says: "The four continents, the four evil destinies, the Brahma kings, the six heavens of desire, the non-conceptual beings and the Pure Abodes,
the four formless realms and the four dhyānas—
[the Tathāgata] is able to manifest majestic deportment throughout these lands."
The commentary states: Having untied one's own bonds, one no longer fears saṃsāra; thus, one is able to manifest in the lands of the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings.

This refers to the meaning of "accomplishment" and "perfection. That which possesses awe-inspiring power is called *wei* (majesty); that which possesses a model for imitation is called *yi* (dignity).
Furthermore, it is said that *wei* resides in the countenance, while *yi* resides in the person. It is one dharma within the wisdom of the eyes.
"Transmitting from the Buddha like a turning wheel.
The commentary states: "It is like the bhikṣu Aśvajit, who received the Dharma from the Buddha and taught it to Śāriputra;
Śāriputra, having attained the Dharma, in turn taught it to Maudgalyāyana. Thus it flows and turns without ceasing, just as a wheel can crush and grind all things."
Free from the afflictions of ignorance, he was further able to turn others away from error and toward the correct path, and was himself eloquent in debate.

He was profoundly worthy of being entrusted with the final instructions. The annotation states: "The term 'wisdom' (*jñāna*) refers to the measure of wisdom; it is deep, secret, and subtle, and is thus fit to be used for entrusting the bequeathed Dharma to [others]."
"Other [texts] speak of the 'Purification of the Vinaya.

The commentary states: *Vinaya* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China (*Hua-yen*), it means 'Subduing' (*Diao-fu*). 'Subduing' (*Diao*) refers to the refinement of the three karmas; 'Subduing' (*Fu*) refers to the restraint [of them]."
I prostrate and repent for my transgressions. It is said that the Śrāvakas are able to strictly maintain the purity of the World-Honored One’s two hundred and fifty precepts;
as jade-like and ice-cold in their clarity, these constitute the Vinaya Piṭaka, which elucidates the study of ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā).
"Expanding the model for the three realms.
The Commentary states: "Hong (弘) means great; fan (範) means law. This refers to being able to expand the Great Law within the three realms to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings."
The response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is immeasurable.

The commentary states: When a *śrāvaka* wishes to transform sentient beings, they first enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to observe the faculties and capacities of others, and subsequently provide transformation according to those capacities without limit. This person lacks the Mahāyāna response-body of the fruit-stage; this, then—

The body of responsive resonance manifested eighteen transformations and other such feats within the void. Regarding the single dharma of "Eye of Compassion," it delivers and liberates sentient beings.
The commentary states: it causes all sentient beings to depart from the bonds of affliction and not undergo rebirth within the three realms.

"Rescuing and delivering those of the future. The commentary states: "To 'extract' (bá) means to pull out; 'to deliver' (jì) refers to crossing over [to liberation]. During the first millennium of the True Dharma (Saddharma), the Buddha propagated his transformative teachings.

During the first millennium of the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka), the four types of *śrāmaṇeras* (*catvāraḥ śramaṇerāḥ*) appeared. During the Final Dharma (Śāsanānta), more than ten thousand *śrāvakas* emerged. This is the object of my sorrow."
"To transcend all worldly dust and burdens.
The commentary states: "To transcend" means to go beyond. "All" (zhū) signifies multiplicity. "Dust" (chén) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). "Burdens" (lèi) refers to the accumulation of karma.
To transcend one's own defilements is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); to transcend the defilements of others is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Just as these present fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms are both transcendent, [the Buddha] universally extols his eye, precepts, wisdom, eloquence, liberation, compassion, and knowledge.
Their names are as follows:
[The names of] the four rows. The commentary states: It asks, "What are the names of the great arhats?
It answers: "Sages have no names; these names are established by force upon the nameless essence."
"Mahāprajñā Śāriputra. The commentary states:
"In the Sanskrit language, Śāriputra; in the Chinese language, 'Spring Warbler' (Chūnyīng). It is also called 'Cuckoo' (Qúlù). Putrā means 'son' in the Chinese language.
He was the son of that Spring Warbler, and his name was established after his mother. Thus he is now called Śāriputra."
This is an abbreviation. Before his mother conceived him, her speech was inadequate;
whenever she debated with her younger brother Mahākoṣṭhila, she was always inferior to him. However, since conceiving him, her responses have been sharp and brilliant, surpassing even her brother.
Because the mother possessed such great eloquence—likened to that of a spring oriole—the son was named after her. He once...
Maudgalyāyana was his companion. Together they served the non-Buddhist teacher Śreṇika. Among the ten great disciples, he was foremost in great wisdom and was designated as the leader;
for among all the Buddhas of the ten directions, wisdom is always held as the primary attribute.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The commentary states:
This is a corruption of the old Sanskrit term. In the new [translation], it is called Mahā-maudgalyāyana.
In the Chinese language, this means "Great Mung-bean Clan" (Dà Cǎishǔshì). *Mahā* means "great. *Maudgalyāyana* means "of the Mung-bean Clan. *Śu* (菽) is a general term for beans.
Name: In ancient times, there was an immortal who cultivated the Way in the mountains, subsisting solely on bean sprouts. This Venerable One is his descendant;
among the ten great disciples, he is foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Mahākauṣṭhila. The commentary states:
"The Venerable One with Large Knees," so called because his kneecaps were large.
He was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and the son of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
The commentary states: This is a corruption of the Sanskrit. The correct Sanskrit should be *Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra*. In the Chinese language, this means "Son of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇī.
*Pūrṇa* is his personal name; *Maitrāyaṇī* refers to the maternal lineage. Before her pregnancy, the mother’s disposition was largely harsh and ill-tempered.

After she conceived the child, her nature became exceedingly compassionate. This child was either obtained by her from the God of the Manmang River (Pūrṇa-nadī-devatā), and thus named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra;
or "Pūrṇa" and "Maitrī" were both names for the mother, and he was therefore called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Subhūti. The commentary states:
He is also named Subhūti; in the language of China, this means "Good Appearance" (Śubhavyūha) or "Empty-Born" (Kūṭastha).
This is because when this Venerable One was born, all the vessels within his household suddenly became empty. An interpreter of physiognomy observed him and said:
"If this son leaves the household life, he shall understand the empty nature of all phenomena, with Upānanda as his chief. The commentary states:
"It is also called *upaniṣad*. In the language of the Flower [China], it means 'a small portion near. *Upa* is 'near'."

This is but a small portion. However, when this Venerable One first practiced contemplation, he took a single hair from his body and, using the sword of conceptual wisdom, vertically divided it into four parts.
From among these four parts, he took one part and divided it into sixteen parts. From among these sixteen parts, he took one part and divided it into twenty-five parts. Twenty-five...

Take one part from among these divisions and split it into a hundred parts. From among those hundred parts, take one part and split it into a thousand parts, continuing until the point where it can no longer be split.
This final portion, which is about to enter into emptiness, is called a *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal particle). It is so named because it is adjacent to empty space;
once more, the blade cannot be applied—were the blade applied even slightly, it would immediately dissolve into emptiness. This single remaining part is what is preserved.
It gathers the mental factors of a single aggregate so that they do not dissipate. The term "etc. refers to the aforementioned five types of persons, who remain the most eminent leaders.
Among these venerable ones, those who practice the contemplation of analyzing form to clarify emptiness are the foremost. Furthermore, among the five aggregates, the analysis of form is primary.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable [beings]:

the two types of pratyekabuddhas along with those at the initial stage of the mind. The commentary states: "Furthermore" (fu) means "repeatedly. "There are" (you) carries the sense of "not being non-existent.
"Immeasurable" (wuliang) refers to a number so vast that it is difficult to describe.
The Pratyekabuddha who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The commentary states: *Pratyekabuddha* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Solitary Realizer" (*dujue*), also called "Rhinoceros-like.

Such a person severs their own afflictions and realizes the *nirvāṇa* of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). They cultivate the contemplation of seventy-seven knowledges (*jñāna*) and the contemplation of forty-four knowledges.

Contemplating ignorance as emptiness, one realizes that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without volitional action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). There are two types [of practitioners]. First, those of sharp faculties:
having emerged from the seeds of the increasing eon (*vivartakalpa*) where there was no cause for a Buddha, they become Buddhas in a world without a Buddha.

Just as the final flame of a lamp is barely seen when a Buddha appears in the world, so too does the light of great compassion shine forth. Śatadru, seeing this light, thought the eon was in decline; he then proceeded toward the Paṇḍaka Rock.
The fire of internalized wisdom incinerates the body; body and wisdom are simultaneously cast away without remainder, becoming identical with great empty space.

Second, as for those of dull faculties: they possess the cause for Buddhahood and appear in the world of a Buddha. Being practitioners of this school, they act according to its categories—whether fifty or a hundred [in number].
This passage cites those of dull faculties who, being non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), realize the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*).

This excludes those śrāvakas who abide in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), including those at the initial stage of their resolve, as they have all come to the Buddha’s presence. The commentary states:

"Some have given rise to the initial resolve for the Mahāyāna; this refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Others have given rise to the initial resolve for the pratyekabuddha path; 'pratyaya' (condition) refers to..."
Forty-five years later, he preached this *Uṣṇīṣa-samādhi* dharma. On two occasions he arrived at the Jeta Grove with great haste and addressed the bhikṣus, followed by a listing of the bodhisattvas.
The text has three parts; first, the initial seeking of the Dharma. The commentary states: "Addressed" (*shǔ*) means "encountered" or "met."
*Xiūxià zìzī* (The Summer Retreat’s Self-Indulgence).

The commentary states: "Xiūxià" refers to the sixteenth day of the seventh month. When the summer retreat of the monastic community in the Western lands has concluded, if there are any offenses regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected, one must not conceal one's shortcomings before the assembly but allow others freely to point out one's transgressions.
"Bodhisattvas of the ten directions inquire to resolve their doubts.

The commentary states: "Sentient beings of great resolve from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below petition the World-Honored One to provide for them a definitive discernment.
To be hesitant and unable to decide is called 'doubt' (*vicikitsā*). If one speaks in terms of the person who is a bodhisattva, they have no doubt; doubt belongs only to [others]."

Discrimination (*vikalpa*) has already been severed upon entering the gateway of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Nevertheless, although this person lacks such discrimination, afflictions (*kleśa*) still remain;

because a portion of the dharma-attachment (*dharmagrāha*) within the seventh consciousness has not yet been forgotten, it is metaphorically termed "doubt" (*vicikitsā*). Alternatively, it may be that the lower stages do not comprehend the higher stages.
"Respectfully receiving the Compassionate and Austere.
The commentary states: "Respectfully" (qin) means to hold in reverence; "receiving" (feng) means to honor. The Buddha possesses the capacity to instruct his children;
thus, while he is compassionate, he is also stern.
"Seeking the secret meaning.
The commentary states: "Jiang (將) means 'should'; qiu (求) means 'to seek. This refers to the intention to seek the profound and secret principle of the World-Honored One.
Below, the five secrets and the threefold cultivation and realization are explained."
Thereupon, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in tranquil repose.
Next, he fulfilled the invitation so that all might be universally moistened. The commentary states: "Ji (即)" has the meaning of "not abandoning.
When the multitude requested that the profound meaning be sought, "Ru" (如) refers to the principle of suchness. Wisdom arises and accords with this principle; therefore, it is called "Ru."
He comes; this is the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata. He prepares the Dharma seat, majestic and grand, dwelling in tranquil stillness and composure.

This is the essence of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the great meditative concentration of the Dharma-realm. It is also like the entry into the Samādhi of the Place of Immeasurable Meanings as described in the Lotus Sūtra.
Alternatively, it may be said that he spreads his *niṣīdana* and sits in quiet repose; the meaning is the same.
For the sake of those in the assembly, he proclaimed and revealed the profound depths.
[The] Commentary states: Venerable Ānanda recited this in verse. Having spread his seat and settled into ease, he declared:
"This is the Buddha’s proclamation and revelation of the most profound and secret principles."
The pure assembly at the Dharma banquet attained what they had never experienced before.

The commentary states: "In this single assembly, there were thirty-six classes of beings—Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and various Arhats—along with the measurable and pure multitude, all of whom obtained extraordinary benefits. Yet, forty-five years later, [the Buddha] preached this *Buddhoṣṇīṣa*..."
Obscure. Not shared by other assemblies.
The *kalaviṅka*’s celestial voice pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
The commentary states: *Kalaviṅka* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means the "co-life bird" (*gòngmìng niǎo*). Its sixty-four tones are uniquely sublime.
It is sound. The voice of this bird is soft, clear, resonant, and elegantly mournful, comparable to the voice of a Buddha.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gather at the site of enlightenment.
The names of the leaders are listed below. The commentary states: The Sanskrit term is Gaṅgā, also called the Ganges River;
in the language of China, it means "River Come from Heaven. This refers to the fact that the source of this river is so distant that it is as if it has come from heaven.
It is forty *li* in circumference, and the sand within it is as fine as flour, flowing mixed with the water. Bodhisattvas are as numerous as the grains of sand in this river. Bodhi...
"Bodhi" refers to awakening; this signifies seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above. "Sattva" refers to *sattva*, which means sentient beings;
this signifies delivering sentient beings below. All have come from the ten directions and gathered at the site of attaining the Way within a single assembly in Jeta Grove.
"Way" (*mārga*) refers to the path realized; "site" (*pada*) refers to the field of quiescent extinction.
[The assembly] was headed by Mañjuśrī. The commentary states:
"The scribe of the sutra asks, 'It is not yet clear who is the leader. The verse then provides the explanation, etc. In the Sanskrit language, Mañjuśrī [is the name].
Mañjuśrī is also called Mañjuśrī; in the language of China, this means "Wondrous Auspiciousness.

When this Bodhisattva was born, there were ten kinds of auspicious signs, and he was named after them. He is the crown prince of King Brahmadatta in the north. This concludes the general introduction.

At that time, King Prasenajit—from this point concerning King Prasenajit down to his receiving the holy instructions—constitutes the separate introduction (*nidāna*). There are ten sections in the text.
The first clarifies how King Prasenajit prepared offerings and invited the Tathāgata. The commentary states: "The preceding general introduction applies universally to all teachings."

There are six kinds of meanings of accomplishment. This is the separate introduction at the end; it is distinct because this teaching alone is treated separately. As for "time," it refers to the time when the request was granted.
"Vatsa" (Bosiriji) is a corrupted abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; in full, it should be *Prasenajit*. In the language of China, it means "Victorious Army.
[The fourfold army consists of: first, the elephant army; second, the chariot army; third, ... [the cavalry army]; fourth, the infantry army.
The cavalry. The four divisions of the infantry. Because all four armies were victorious, people from the ten thousand regions came to him for refuge, calling him "King" (*rājan*).
He established a fast (*upavāsa*) on the anniversary of his father king’s death.
The commentary states: "For" (*wei*) means "to give to"; "his" (*qi*) is a term referring to what follows; "father king" refers to the former emperor. This speaks of the former emperor.
It was precisely on the sixteenth day of the seventh month that he passed away; today is the morning of his memorial service, for which I have prepared these offerings for the vegetarian feast.
Regarding "memorial" (jì) and "avoidance" (huì): "memorial" refers to refraining from performing auspicious matters, while "avoidance" refers to shunning the mention of his name.
He requested the Buddha from the inner palace to come forth personally to welcome the Tathāgata.

The commentary states: "The room within a house is called a *shì* (chamber); the chamber within that room is called a *gōng* (palace); the two courtyards outside the palace are called the *yè* (flanks).
On the sixteenth day, the King himself went out of the city to the Jeta Grove to welcome the Buddha; alternatively, he may have welcomed him at three locations. First—
1. Proceeding to the Jeta Grove; 2. On the way; 3. Exiting the palace gate.
He extensively prepared rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors.
The commentary states: "Extensively laid out rare and exquisite offerings. *Xiū* (delicacies) refers to cooked food. The king established a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*). 1.
All subtle and exquisite foods have nothing that can surpass them; when they are in the mouth, they are called "flavors. Such food possesses three virtues:
first, it is light and soft; second, it is pure and clean; third, it is in accordance with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, he personally invited the various great Bodhisattvas.

The commentary states: "Jian (兼) means 'together with'; fu (復) is a particle used for emphasis. This asks whether it was only the Buddha who was invited, or if he also separately commanded the various great Bodhisattvas;
the author of the scripture answers as follows.
Furthermore, there were elder householders (*gṛhapati*) within the city.

Since the two luminaries had invited many people together, they ordered their followers to divide the offerings accordingly. The commentary states: "Furthermore" means "also. "City" means "flourishing."
It is said that because they accommodate all people, these are those who are long-lived, aged, wealthy, and of profound virtue;
those who are honored and esteemed for their domestic life, who govern their households, and who cultivate the Way and harmonize the spirit.
"At the same time, they feed the monks, awaiting the arrival of the Buddha to respond.

The commentary states: "On the sixteenth day of the seventh month, at the time of the summer retreat's conclusion, every household feeds the monks, waiting for our Buddha, the World-Honored One, to come and provide for them in response."
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the bodhisattvas and arhats to attend to the various hosts of donors. The commentary states:
"The words spoken by the World-Honored One are called 'commands' (*chì*). Since the Buddha has accepted what the king requests, he must not disregard the king’s pleasure;
therefore, he commands Mañjuśrī to lead the various sentient beings of great resolve and the three classes of noble ones."
"O Śāriputra, there was a meal at the house of an elder and householder within the city of Vaiśālī. Because he was providing for his long-term field of merit, only Ānanda was present;
having previously accepted a separate invitation, he had traveled far and had not yet returned, so he could not wait in the order of the Saṃgha."
Third, Ānanda invited [the Buddha] separately; having no offerings, he returned alone. The commentary states: "Only" (*wei*) has the meaning of exclusion or restriction.

"Having" (*you*) has the meaning of not being provided with. "Huang" (遑) means "to manage to reach" or "to have time for. *Ānanda* in Sanskrit is translated into Chinese as "Joyous Celebration" (*Qingxi*).
On the day the World-Honored One first attained enlightenment, the court announced to King Śuddhodana that Prince Siddhārtha had already achieved Buddhahood.
The inner palace again reported that King Śuddhodana had given birth to a prince; because this was celebrated with joy, he was named "Joyful Celebration" (Pramudita).
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, [the Buddha] had previously accepted an invitation from a separate donor and traveled far away, not yet having returned.
Since he had not yet returned, he was unable to attend the two assemblies of monks.
Since there was neither an elder (*sthavira*) nor an *ācārya*, he returned alone along the way. On that day, there were no offerings. The commentary states:
"One who sits at the head of others is called an elder (*sthavira*). *Ācārya* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China (*Huayan*), it means "Model Teacher" (*guifanshi*).
It is also called "One Who Delights the Assembly. Ānanda returned alone along the way, and on that day, furthermore, there were no subsequent offerings.
He suspended [the bowl] to give it to another.
At that moment, Ānanda took up his alms-bowl and, while traveling through the city, went from house to house seeking food, practicing equanimity.
The commentary states: "This means that during the fast, he did not wait for his turn in the monastic assembly."
At that time, he held the World-Honored One’s bowl of appropriate measure, for it was suited to the measure of his body and mind.
As for the aforementioned Ānanda, who was fully capable of traveling, the city was the destination of his journey.

"He begs in successive order. The commentary states: "Successive" means following in sequence. From one household to the next, he proceeds in accordance with the teaching to eliminate the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*):

first, "looking upward," such as observing the stars and constellations; second, "looking downward," such as engaging in farming and planting; third, "looking to the sides," [such as engaging in commerce]; and fourth, "looking straight ahead," [such as seeking gain through flattery].
He causes [the teachings] to be transmitted. With four sharp mouths, he harmonizes medicines; he regards begging for food alone as supreme.
Alternatively, he may circulate among various households to beg for food everywhere.
In his mind, he first sought the final donor to serve as the host of the vegetarian feast.
The commentary states: "The sixth consciousness reflects upon seeking first the donor who gives, the donor who gives last, and the donor who fills the bowl—all of these are the hosts of the feast.
In Sanskrit, this is called *dāna-pāramitā*; in Chinese, it is called "generosity" (*bǔshī*). Having thus practiced...

Having practiced giving, one then transcends this shore of birth and death and reaches the other shore of bodhi; this is called "transcending. Here, both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together.
Whether one is from a pure or impure realm, whether of the noble Kṣatriya caste or a Caṇḍāla, it makes no difference.
The commentary states: In the Western Heaven (India), there are Brahmins of pure conduct and Brahmins of defiled conduct.
*Kṣatriya* in Sanskrit means "Lord of the Fields" (*tiánzhǔ*) in Chinese; they are the lineage of kings. In the western lands, there are four castes, and this is the highest caste.
*Caṇḍāla* in Sanskrit means "one of fierce and evil karma" in Chinese; they are also called those of "improper discipline," such as hunters.

Fishermen, hunters, butchers, and the like—Ānanda is just like them now. Without distinguishing between the pure and the defiled, he always begs for alms with a mind free from acceptance or rejection;
only then does he practice impartial compassion, not discriminating against those who are lowly or base, so that his resolve may be perfectly fulfilled.
The commentary states: "Fang" (方) means "to compare. This refers to the World-Honored One practicing the compassion of equality, or perhaps expedient action.
This compassion of equality does not discriminate against those who are lowly, inferior, poor, or humble; it initiates the mind and brings it to full completion, thereby practicing equality.
"All sentient beings possess immeasurable merit.
The commentary states: "Since the mind of the person who seeks [to give] is immeasurable, the blessings of that which is bestowed shall likewise be immeasurable."
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa;
with five intentions surpassing the dual intentions and his robes properly adjusted, he entered the city. The commentary states: "Yi" (已) means "already"; "he" (呵) means "to rebuke.

"Tathāgata" is a title modeled after the tracks of former [Buddhas]; "World-Honored One" is a title for one who is uniquely honored in the world. In the Sanskrit language, Kāśyapa; in the Chinese language...
Regarding the name Kāśyapa: in ancient times there was a rishi whose body possessed such radiance that it eclipsed the light of the sun and moon;
Kāśyapa is of his lineage. Subhūti begs from the wealthy, whereas Kāśyapa begs from the poor.
"Regarding the statement that 'the minds of the Arhats were not impartial,' the commentary states:
'Regarding' means 'it is so. 'Equilibrium' (均等) refers to equality. The World-Honored One once rebuked these two individuals, saying:
'These three are superior persons (上士), yet they lack a mind of equanimity; all of them engage in grasping and rejecting.'"
"Reverently admiring the Tathāgata, he opens and expounds without obstruction.
The commentary states: "To reverently admire and emulate the Buddha; to open up and propagate [the Dharma] without any hindrance.
'Without obstruction' (wuché) means not discriminating between enemies and kin; it carries the sense of impartial benefit."
"Crossing over all doubt and slander.
The commentary states: "To cross over" means to deliver [beings] across. "Doubt" refers to the doubting minds of all ordinary worldlings that give rise to ridicule and suspicion.
"Slander" refers to the need to avoid non-Buddhists who give rise to defamation.
He passed through the moat of that city and walked slowly through its outer gate.

The commentary states: "To pass through" means to traverse. That which has water is called a *chí* (moat/pool); that which lacks water is called a *huáng* (ditch). It is a place where people take earth [to build the walls].
He paced his steps slowly. Regarding the gates of the city walls: "guo" (郭) is synonymous with "kuo" (廓), meaning that which is situated outside in a vast expanse.
Thus, he maintained a solemn and orderly demeanor, observing the rites of purity with reverent gravity.

The commentary states: "To solemnly adjust one’s deportment so that it is grave and harmonious, and to be reverent and cautious regarding the rules of the fast—this is indeed what the eighth fascicle of the two sutras says:
'There are six places where one should not go for alms: first, one should not go to a place with vicious dogs;

second, one should not go to a place where a calf has recently been born; third, one should not stay in a place inhabited by evil kinds of people; fourth, [one should not go to a place where there are]..."
One should go to places where men and women give rise to afflictions; one should not go to places where people harbor reproach and suspicion;
one should not go to the dwellings of non-Buddhists.
At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and encountered a great illusionist.
Sixth, encountering adverse conditions that destroy the practice of *śīla*. The commentary states: "To encounter" means to meet with.

At the time of begging for alms, while holding his bowl during the course of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), he passed through a chamber tainted by a foul wind and encountered a great, delusive magical artifice;
this was a spell of the former Brahmā-devas.
The Mātangī girl, by means of the *sāvikāra* mantra of the former Brahmā, was drawn into the chamber of lust. The commentary states:
"In the language of China, her original surname was An; this is thus a specific name for the woman. It is used [in the sense of] *sāvikāra*. *Sāvikāra*: [Sanskrit term].
In the language of China, he is called the "Yellow-Headed Immortal" (*pīśācaka*), also known as the "Yellow-Red Immortal. This refers to the fact that his beard and hair are yellowish-red in color.
By reciting mantras and performing ritual acts—dragging flowers and anointing the altar—he summoned Ānanda and brought him into that brothel.
The lecherous man stroked [Ānanda] with his body, intending to destroy the essence of his precepts.
The commentary states: "Intending" means "about to. "Stroking" (fǔmó) refers to that which is done with the hands; it means being touched by the woman's hands and body.

This was intended to damage Ānanda’s essence of the precepts, constituting a violation of the rule against physical contact. Among the eighty thousand practices, he violated only this single precept. He committed [the offense].
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, one may attain purification by confessing them before a community of twenty monks. However, if one commits a root offense (*mūlāpatti*), it cannot be confessed;
it is like a needle with a broken eye that can never be used again, or like a *tāla* tree that has been cut down.
It cannot be brought back to life; it is like severing a person’s head, after which they do not live again, or like splitting a stone, after which it can never be rejoined.
Question: What constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of the precepts? Answer: Some say that non-manifest volition (*avijñapti-cetanā*) is the essence of the precepts, but this is incorrect.

For how could mere non-manifest volition possibly prevent one from violating them? Now, we shall simply take the essence of receiving the precepts as it pertains to the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Below...
The Sūtra says: "Observance and violation merely bind the body; without the body, there is nothing to bind.
When the Tathāgata knew that the arts of seduction had been employed against him, he finished his fast and returned.
The seven great ones perceived this and returned to the Jeta Grove. The commentary states: "Jiā (加)" means "to encounter" or "to be subjected to"; "bì (畢)" means "to conclude" or "to cease."
"Xuán" means "to return. This refers to the Buddha, by means of his correct and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha-jñāna*), knowing that Ānanda had been ensnared by the illusory arts of others;
having finished his midday meal, he returned to the Jeta Grove.
The king, along with his great ministers, elders, and householders, all came to follow the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
The commentary states: "Along with" (*ji*) carries the sense of "together with. The king is King Prasenajit; the great ministers are the various officials of the court.
The Commentary states: "In accordance with the previous account of returning from the royal palace, there were elder householders and others who pointed to this passage.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness."
"Entering Transformation to Expound the True Mantra: An Imperial Edict for the Assembly of Tiqū. The commentary states:

At that time, at the very moment of a sudden flash, there was none who surpassed him in his crown-robes. Upon the uṣṇīṣa of his head were the hundred jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth—which signify fearlessness and sovereign mastery.
From within the light, a thousand-petaled precious lotus flower emerges.

The commentary states: "Light is emitted from the aperture at the crown of the head; from within this light, a single precious lotus flower appears with five thousand petals, symbolizing the descent of the thousand Buddhas of the future."
There is a transformation body of a Buddha, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), proclaiming a divine mantra.
The commentary states: Furthermore, within the precious lotus, he manifests a small transformation Buddha. "Jia" (in *jiajia*) means to cross [the legs].

If the left foot presses upon the right, it is called the "conquering Māra" posture (*vajraparyaṅka*); if the right foot presses upon the left, it is called the "auspicious" posture (*bhadrāsana*). As for the present [posture], it is not so.
These two types constitute the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), with the two legs crossed and both heels placed upward.
The divine mantra is the *Sitātapatrā-hṛdaya*, consisting of forty thousand and twenty-six phrases.
The Imperial Edict says: "I command Mañjuśrī to take this mantra and go to protect him.

Let the evil mantras be extinguished. The Commentary states: The True Buddha commands that this mantra be taken to that place to rescue and protect Ānanda, causing his evil mantras to be extinguished;
as light arrives, darkness departs; as wisdom arises, delusion vanishes.
He exhorted Ānanda and the daughter of Mātanga to return to the place where the Buddha was.

The commentary states: He uplifted, encouraged, and urged the Joyful One (Ānanda) and the woman by her original surname to return together to the place where the Buddha was preaching the Dharma at that time.
Ānanda saw the Buddha and prostrated himself, weeping with grief.
Nine times he reproached himself with earnest lamentation, seeking the wondrous gateway of the Buddha. The commentary states:
Having returned from the chamber of Mātanga to the assembly at Jetavana, Ānanda beheld the World-Honored One and, with his highest crown, paid homage to the Buddha until it touched his feet.
This humble writing is sufficient to express my profound respect. To have sound but no tears is called *bei* (sorrow); to have tears but no sound is called *qi* (weeping).
I regret that from the beginningless past, I have been devoted solely to extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) without fully perfecting the power of the Way (*mārgabala*).

The commentary states: It is regrettable that from time immemorial, since the era of the Buddha Vairocana (the Empty-King Buddha), you have consistently taken extensive learning as your nature, upholding the untainted teachings of all Buddhas.

Yet, despite this vast learning, it could not counteract the dry wisdom of karma; thus, you have not escaped the wheel of suffering. Since you can hear and uphold the Buddhas through others, why do you not hear what is heard within yourself?
Furthermore, as their wisdom increases over time, they fail to realize the true nature of reality and have not yet fully mastered the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
"Power" (bala) carries the meaning of subduing; since they have not yet fully attained that power, they are consequently seized by false teachings.
He earnestly entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the attainment of Bodhi.
The commentary states: "Earnestly" refers to the words used when requesting the Dharma repeatedly; "Bodhi" is a conditioned fruit that encompasses the unconditioned fruit within it.
Exquisite *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*: the initial skillful means. The commentary states:
