these four being the internal organs— the commentary states that adding the lungs makes five viscera. Even if you do not perceive their subtle characteristics, [they are nonetheless present].
The nails grow and the hair lengthens; the tendons turn and the vessels quiver. This is truly evident and clear; how can one not know it?
Beyond the five reproaches for not knowing these external phenomena, the commentary states: "Why do you not perceive such coarse signs as the growth of nails and hair?"
One certainly does not know the internal. How, then, can one know the external?

The sixth [point] refutes both the internal and the external. The commentary states: "How does one know the coarse characteristics of the external? By using the internal as an analogy, both are refuted."
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which perceives and cognizes dwells within the body—is impossible.
This fourth point establishes that your attachment is empty and false.
The second [point] is the external search for the essence, which is like "smearing fat" and then "threatening. The commentary states:
"Thus, Ānanda had previously maintained that the mind resides within, but this was already refuted by the World-Honored One. He then proceeded to maintain that the mind resides without;

therefore, the Master of the Sub-commentary says: 'Ānanda, having been interrogated, lost his reasoning regarding its internal location, and skillfully cited the light of a lamp to establish its residence without.'"

How is this known? Therefore, the Sūtra says: Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and said to the Buddha, "When I heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I realized that my mind truly resides outside the body. He then spoke the analogy of a lamp kept outside a room, saying:
"For example, if a lamp were lit outside a room, that lamp would certainly be able to illuminate the interior of the room. From its..."
The door of the room, its interior, and the courtyard outside—within all these, sentient beings do not see what is inside their own bodies, but see only what is outside.
It is just as if a lamp were placed outside a room; it cannot illuminate the interior. The Buddha then used the remainder of a single meal as a metaphor for this.
To refute Ānanda’s attachment to the view that the mind resides outside [the body], the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī, begging for alms-food and returning to the Jeta Grove. I have already finished my meal. Observe, Ānanda:
when one bhikṣu eats, are all the others satiated? Ānanda then replied in a manner that was inconsistent with the facts and contrary to reason.
[The interlocutor] falls into the error of grasping at an external mind. He replies, "No, World-Honored One. [The Buddha] then questions him: "For what reason?
Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their physical bodies and lives are distinct. How could one person cause the multitude to be satiated?
The World-Honored One again raises his hand to point toward the mind and asks Ānanda, "I am now showing you this tūla-cotton."
[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, when you see with your eyes, does your mind discern [the object]? Ānanda replied that it does discern. The Sūtra says this. The World-Honored One then refuted it, saying:
'If they are mutually cognizant, how can [the mind] be outside? He then refuted [the position] in its entirety.
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which is aware and capable of cognition dwells outside the body—is impossible. Above.
The refutation of the external [self] concludes.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body."

Second, the miraculous ointment returns the signs of intimidation. This has two parts. First, the establishment [of the argument]. This has three parts. First, the mind that gives rise to present calculations by removing old attachments due to causes of delusion.
The commentary states: "I have heard the preceding sounds of the Dharma teaching which refute the notion that the mind does not abide within."
Having realized and understood that this mind truly resides outside of these five aggregates (pañca-skandha), the text then provides the analogy of a lamp placed outside a room. Why is this?
For example, if a lamp is lit within a room, that lamp will necessarily first illuminate the interior of the room.

From the door of the room, extending to the edge of the courtyard, he subsequently composed the *Zhenglilue* (Examination of Established Doctrines) and the *Fuchengxinli* (Attachment to New Principles). His commentary states: "If the light of a lamp is within a room, it is like the mind being within the body;
one ought then to see the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach first, and only thereafter see the mountains, rivers, and the great earth. This is as if...
The lamp illuminates the room; thereafter, from the door of that room, it reaches the courtyard.
All sentient beings do not see within their own bodies, but see only outside their bodies, as if the light of the lamp were situated outside the room.
"It cannot illuminate the room.
The Commentary states: "The mind abides outside the body; thus it does not see what is within the body. It is just as a lamp’s light, situated outside the room, cannot illuminate the room."
This meaning must be clarified so that there shall be no delusion; it shall accord with the Buddha’s definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), lest it be erroneous.
The subsequent statement, "there will be no delusion," is likely a modest expression of humility. The commentary states: "This" refers to this [meaning]; "shall" means "will.
It says that this meaning will certainly be clear and distinct, and that one shall have no doubts or confusion. The phrase "lest it be erroneous" is a word used to caution against suspicion.
Thus it was said. The Buddha told Ānanda: "These various mounds [were] just now coming from my city of Śrāvastī.

This section consists of two parts: first, the implicit refutation based on facts; this has three sub-sections. First, the inquiry regarding one meal and the remainder being sufficient. [Commentary: *Jian* (annotation).

"Yun" means "from the past. This refers to the time prior to the preaching of the Dharma, when these twelve hundred arhats and others had collectively come while wandering through the city to beg for food.
"Alms-gathering by collecting morsels.

The commentary states: "In ancient editions, this was translated as 'morsel-food' (piṇḍa-bhojana). This is because in the Western Regions, when food is offered to monks, it is mostly given by hand in morsels.
However, this method does not exhaust all possibilities, as for liquids, drinks, or moist substances, they cannot be formed into morsels. Later, Xuanzang... [text continues].
"Dharma" is translated as "segmented food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because food consists of distinct portions or segments. Furthermore, food has four constituent factors as its essence:
visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
"Return to the Jeta Grove.

The commentary states: "Return to the Jetavana Vihāra. The sub-commentary (*śū*) says: "You and the bhikṣus, return to the Jeta Grove," which serves as proof that this is not different [from the aforementioned location]; it refers to this very passage.
"I have already observed the fast for the previous night.
[The commentary] states: "Having received an invitation on the preceding day, the Buddha—the Great Teacher of the Three Realms—for those who plant the seeds of merit, all invite the Tathāgata.
You should observe: when one bhikṣu eats, are all people satiated?"

The commentary states: When one person has finished eating, as for the others—whether they are satiated or not—if Ānanda says they are satiated, then the previous position that the mind exists externally would be established.
Ānanda replied, “No, World-Honored One.
He then answered that differing forms contradict reason.
Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are arhats, their physical bodies and life spans differ; how then could one person [accomplish it]?
He caused the multitude to be satiated.
Later, when questioned regarding this matter of contradiction, he annotated: "Ānanda himself was caught in the fray of arrows and spears;
how then could he say, 'How can one person cause the multitude to be satiated? This is the point of Śrīmitra."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind that perceives, cognizes, knows, and sees were actually located outside the body," [the following refutation follows].
This section consists of four parts; first is the testing of the claim regarding cotton wool. The first part restates the position. The commentary states:
"If your mind that is capable of perceiving, cognizing, knowing, and seeing—that is, the sixth consciousness—definitively resides outside the body."
Body and mind are external to one another; they do not interfere with each other.
Second, a general summary. The Commentary states: "The mind is outside the body, and the body is outside the mind.
Body and mind do not interfere with one another, just as water and fire are entirely unrelated. Furthermore, this is a provisional hypothesis.
Thus, what is known by the mind cannot be perceived by the body;

these three mutually manifest their mutual separation. The text has two parts: first, it cites the mind to demonstrate the body’s separation—what is sensed at the boundaries of the body cannot be known by the mind.

The subsequent section marks the form and clarifies that [the mind] is external to the nature. The commentary states: When awareness is at the boundary of the body, the mind is likewise unable to know the body;
since awareness is said to be outside, it is subsequently refuted below.
"I now show you my tūla-cotton hand.
[This passage] has four parts that mark the object and exhaust the mind. Section one: "The Initial Address to Another to Manifest the Pointing. The commentary states:
The Buddha takes his own hand as the object to fix Ānanda’s attention upon another.
"When you see with your eyes, does the mind discriminate?

Later, he asks this to examine the mind. The commentary states: "If one says there is no discrimination, the previous attachment [to the view] that the mind exists externally is saved, and that position is established."
Ānanda replied, "So it is, World-Honored One. [The commentary notes:
These two correct responses differ according to the specific context; Ānanda, not knowing [the answer], replied, "So it is.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If they are mutually cognizant, why are they outside?"

"Third, the refutation of the mind being outside the body. The commentary states: "To claim it is clearly within [the body] is to recognize the error of its being separated from its essential substance and characteristics.
Therefore, you should know that your assertion—that the cognizing mind which is capable of awareness resides outside the body—is impossible."

The fourth section concludes the refutation of the attachment [to the heart being outside]. The third [section] was a hidden probe to re-examine the matter; it is like a "golden needle" for those below. The commentary states:

Previously, Ānanda held the view that the mind is located outside, which has already been demolished by the World-Honored One. Herein, he again shifts his calculation and clings to the idea that the mind resides within the hidden sense organs.
Therefore, the metaphor of the lapis lazuli bowl covering the eyes is spoken: "It is as if there were a person who takes a lapis lazuli bowl and places it over both eyes.
Although something covers them, there is no obstruction; indeed, there is no hindrance at all, because it is hidden within the sense organ.
The World-Honored One then questioned Ānanda, saying: "That person would have his eyes covered by a lapis lazuli bowl."
"When one sees mountains and rivers, does one see lapis lazuli? Ānanda said, "If I say that I see it, what fault would there be?
If I say that I do not see it, what fault would there be? Therefore, for the time being, I say that I see it. "It is so, World-Honored One.
This person would indeed see the lapis lazuli with their eyes covered by a lapis lazuli cage. The Buddha then refuted him, saying, "If your mind were the same [as your eyes]..."
"If one sees mountains and rivers through a crystal vessel, why does one not see the eye itself? This is yet another fault: the eye would then be identical to its object.
If you say that it is not seen, what further fault would there be? The Buddha said:

"If it cannot be seen, how can you claim that this discerning mind resides within the sense organ like a crystal vessel? This is yet another instance of perceiving the distant while being deluded regarding the near."
[The opponent] objects. Then, [the author] refutes it in general, saying: "Therefore, one should know that your statement that 'awakened realization reaches the non-existent' is impossible.
The Commentary says: "Ānanda cited the analogy of the Vaiḍūrya gem, considering only the aspect of non-obstruction; the Dharma King refuted this from within."
This eye does not see objects in a uniform manner. [The preceding section] concludes the refutation of the theory that the faculty is hidden within.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, according to what the Buddha has said—that because it does not see internally, it does not reside within the body;
and because the body and mind know each other and are not separate from one another, it does not exist outside the body—I now reflect and know that it must reside in a single location."

The third section treats the symptoms of internal obstructions. It has two parts. The first is the establishment [of the doctrine], which has five sections. The first is the inclusive description of the mind’s abode.
The commentary states: "To know that it resides in one place" means that Ānanda was merely grasping at the hut as his dwelling.
The Buddha asked, "Where does it reside now?
Ānanda replied, "It resides in the principle of certainty.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, this cognizing mind neither knows what is within yet is able to see what is without. According to my contemplation, it is hidden..."
Lying within the sheaths of the sense organs.

Thirdly, here I present a detailed analysis. The commentary states: "This consciousness that cognizes, since it does not know what is internal—reiterating the prior point that it cannot see the heart, liver, and so forth—yet is able to see what is external, and furthermore clearly perceives external objects, I now seek [to understand this]."
He reflects and contemplates that [the consciousness] lies hidden and concealed within the faculty of the eye. To illustrate this, he employs the metaphor of a crystal bowl placed over the eyes:
it is as if someone were to take a crystal bowl and cover both eyes; although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct or hinder [vision].
Those faculties follow what is seen; as soon as it is seen, they immediately engage in discrimination.
Four analogies are raised to demonstrate this. The commentary states: "Among the seven treasures, there is the substance of lapis lazuli (vaidūrya).
This is like a person taking a lapis lazuli bowl and placing it over both eyes; although objects are in contact with them, they are not obstructed or hindered."
Furthermore, while the object of perception appears externally and my mind resides within the sense faculties, the ability to see the external is likewise so.
Let us take lapis lazuli as a metaphor for the eye, and the eye as a metaphor for the mind. That eye perceives as it encounters an object, and immediately follows with conceptualization.
Once the eye has seen, the mind then performs the discrimination.

However, as for this mind of mine that awakens and knows: its not seeing the internal is because it resides within the sense organs; its clearly beholding the external without obstruction is because it penetrates into the interior of the organs.
The five fetters lay hidden within the principle.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said, that which is hidden within the faculties is like lapis lazuli. Suppose that person were to place a lapis lazuli screen over their eyes;
they would see the mountains and rivers, but would they see the lapis lazuli?"

The subsequent refutation consists of six sections. The first section, "Doubly Collecting and Singly Interrogating," includes a commentary stating: "As you have said" is a restatement of the opponent's position.
When that person uses a lapis lazuli cage to cover their eyes, they should see the mountains and rivers; yet they still see the lapis lazuli.
One does not see the lapis lazuli. Ānanda, if you say that you see it, you commit the error of the seeing faculty being identical to its object;
if you say that you do not see it, you further commit the error of seeing what is distant while being confused about what is near.
"Thus it is, World-Honored One. This person would see the lapis lazuli as truly being lapis lazuli through eyes covered by a lapis lazuli cage;
both the subject and the object would gaze upon it together. The commentary states: "Ānanda did not understand how one could say 'I see' in such a manner. The Buddha then rebuked him, saying:
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind were joined with the lapis lazuli as one, you should see the mountains and rivers;

why do you not see the eye? This is the third reprimand for failing to observe the sense organ (*indriya*). The commentary states: "The eye is likened to the mind, and the lapis lazuli is likened to the eye.
Since the eye sees both the lapis lazuli and the mountains and rivers, why does the mind not see the eye? Whether it is said that it sees or that it does not see," [the fault remains].
All [these positions] result in fallacies; neither can be saved.
If one were to see the eye, the eye would then be identical to its object, and thus it could not function as a "concomitant" (anuvartin).
This refutes the primary sense organ and its secondary objects. The Commentary states: "In reality, there is no seeing. Even if one were to concede that the eye is seen, the eye..."
If the sense organ were identical to its object, it could not function as a "follower" [of the object]. Your body would then become an external object;
once it has become an external object, what would serve as your eye? Thus, there is the fault of the object being unable to follow [the subject].
If it cannot be seen, how can one say that this cognizing mind is latent within the sense-faculties like a piece of lapis lazuli?
These five objections show that the logic is inconsistent. The commentary states: "If it cannot be seen, then the dharma (the subject) and the metaphor are not congruent.
Previously, one spoke of seeing the lapis lazuli; here, one ought to see the eye."
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious cognition dwells hidden within the sense organs like a piece of lapis lazuli—is untenable;
the six arguments for this are irrational. The commentary states: "In this case, both the doctrine and the analogy are refuted."
The fourth [point] concerns searching through darkness as if adding fire to a torch. The commentary states:

Thus, Ānanda had previously held the view that the mind resides within the hidden sense organs, which has already been refuted by the World-Honored One. Furthermore, he now holds the view that the mind resides within the internal viscera, and thus says:
"I am now facing the Buddha; when I open my eyes and see light, this is called seeing the external; when I close my eyes..."
"Seeing darkness is called 'seeing internally. What is the meaning of this? It is intended to resolve the two faults regarding the internal and external previously mentioned.
Therefore, the World-Honored One asked: 'When you close your eyes and see darkness, is this realm of darkness facing the eye, or is it not facing the eye?
If it faces the eye, then the darkness is in front of the eyes; how can it be established as internal? This directly refutes [the opponent's position]."
If seeing were established internally, then while staying in a dark room where there is no sun, moon, or lamp, that entire dark room would be your own internal viscera.

Even if the external space were broken open, if it did not face [the organ], how could seeing be established? Only when it is actually broken open does there exist something outside the physical form.

The refutation of "abiding within" [is as follows]: the refutation through the confusion of self and other; the refutation through knowing both Buddhas simultaneously; the refutation through the dual mind, and so forth. Then, the general refutation states:
"Therefore, one should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called 'seeing within' is untenable. Thus, the Master of the Commentary (the Sū-shu-chu) says:
"Suddenly considering the stratagem of the 'aperture-treasury,' he proceeds to describe the principle of the obscurity and clarity. This constitutes the first section.
Having finished reading the cryptic text, Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected as follows:

within the bodies of these sentient beings, the internal organs and viscera reside inside while the cavities and apertures are situated on the outside. Where there is a solid organ, there is darkness; where there is a hollow aperture, there is light. I wish to open [this] before the Buddha."
When one opens the eyes and sees light, it is called "seeing the external. When one closes the eyes and sees darkness, it is called "seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?

In the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya), in the second section on the initial establishment [of the categories], the sub-commentary states: "The 'organs' (*fu*) refer to the three *jiao* and the six *fu*."
The "storehouses" (kośa) refer to the five viscera. They reside within the body. The body has nine orifices: two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils—these make six; adding the mouth makes seven;
and the two secret organs, front and back, complete the nine. When the heart, liver, and other five viscera are inside, it is dark;
when there are orifices on the outside, there is light. Ānanda calculated both ways and said: "When the eyes are open, one sees the light before one."
If the proposition that "the object is called seeing the external" is established, then the previous position that the mind exists outside can be rescued.
When one closes both eyes and sees darkness, this is called "seeing the internal. If this proposition is established, then the previous position that the mind exists inside can be rescued.
[The Master] asked: "What do you say to this? [The Opponent replied: "The Buddha’s meaning here is not intended to be definitive."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye, or does it not face the eye?

The subsequent analysis consists of two parts. The first part follows the text and has two sub-sections. The first is the dual inquiry regarding whether it faces [the eye] or not. The commentary states: "This realm of darkness..."
Regarding the elements (*dhātu*): do they face the eye or not face the eye? This is a double question posed to Ānanda concerning that which comes from outside.
If you say they face it, what fault is there? If you say they do not face it, what fault is there?
There are faults in both cases. What are these faults?
If it were in opposition to the eye, and darkness were situated before the eyes, how could it be established as "internal"?

Next follows the refutation by means of a specific lateral analysis; the text has two parts. First, the refutation of the opponent's position in accordance with the text, which has two sections. First, the refutation based on darkness residing outside the body. The commentary states:
If one says it is in opposition to the eye, the Buddha then restates that opponent’s calculation, saying: "If it is in opposition to the eye, it is like an object [situated before it]."
Facing one another like this, you are still outside; how can you be considered inside? To refute this directly:
if you were truly inside, then when you are in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps, that entire dark room would be nothing but your own internal organs.
"Later, the external [elements] become empty and the viscera are destroyed. The commentary states:

"If the dark objects before one were formed within, then while residing inside a dark room at a time when the three lights of sun, moon, and lamp are absent, this dark room would at that very moment become your three *jiao* (burners) and six *fu* (viscera).
Now, if you simply say they do not correspond, what fault is there? Below follows..."
[The Master] restates: "If [the object] does not face [the eye], how can it constitute seeing?
Later, he does not respond. The *Jian* (Commentary) says: "If a dark object does not face the eye, how, furthermore, can it constitute seeing?"
Now, as for "seeing," one must have an object present before the eyes to speak of seeing. Without an object, what is there to see? Thus, there is no fault of dualistic opposition.
If one departs from external seeing, it is established through internal correspondence.
The subsequent refutation consists of six sections. The first is the refutation based on the inability to look back and see one's own face; this section has three parts.

The first is a concessive argument (*yadyapi*). The commentary states: "If, setting aside the case of opening the eyes to see light as 'seeing the external,' and closing the eyes to see darkness as 'seeing the internal,' this is the restatement of [your] position."
When you close your eyes and see darkness, it is called being "within the body. When you open your eyes and see light, why do you not see your own face?
The commentary further rebukes: "When you close your eyes and look back at the internal darkness, I will grant that you see within;
yet when you open both eyes and see the light, why do you not see your own face?"
If one does not see the face, the internal confrontation is not established;

it is finalized later. The commentary states: "When the eyes are open and one sees light, it is as if seeing the face; when the eyes are closed and one gazes into darkness, the internal meaning is established."
When opening the eyes, one sees light but does not see the face; when closing the eyes, one gazes into darkness and it is not formed.

If seeing the face were formed, it could not exist externally as two distinct substances, nor could it abide internally, which would lead to contradiction. This passage has three parts. First is the concession. The commentary states: "Suppose, for a moment, that the face were seen."
Furthermore, how could it be logical for this to be seen? Even granting that one sees the light, one would also see one's own face;
thus, this cognizing mind and the faculty of the eye would both reside in empty space.

Next, [the argument for] establishment. The commentary states: This sixth consciousness, which is capable of discerning and cognizing, as well as the eye faculty, must be suspended in space before it can function;
how then could it be established within?
[This is] subsequently refuted. The commentary states: "Since it is outside, how can it constitute the 'internal'? This is the error of the mind’s eye residing in emptiness.

If it were in empty space, it would be refuted by the three [arguments of] the confusion between self and other. The text has two parts; first, the formal proposition. The commentary states: "In reality, it does not reside in emptiness; for now..."
Even if it were other, it would not be your own substance.
The subsequent refutation of the text has two parts. First, the refutation by citing the established nature of "otherness. The commentary states: "It is said that this is not your own house."
"The body" refers to another person's body; this is the fallacy of [the self] being constituted by the substance of another.
It follows that when the Tathāgata now beholds your face, that too must be your body.
This subsequently refutes the argument that another constitutes the self. The commentary states: "It would follow that the Buddha’s current beholding of your face is also you."
Regarding one's own body: Ānanda came forward and said, "My mind is in space," and he also saw his own face.
Since this is so, your body has become another's body, and another's body has likewise become yours. Thus, even the Teacher, the Tathāgata, would necessarily be you, Ānanda;
this results in the error of making another's body identical to oneself.
"You have already understood this with your eyes.

This refutes the position that the four bodies and the eye do not combine to produce cognition. The text has two parts; first, the formal proposition. The commentary states: "Furthermore, it turns back to refute [the claim] that 'you have already understood this with your eyes.'"
"The body is conjoined [with consciousness] but is not itself conscious.

This is refuted later. The commentary states: "If your eye already possesses conscious awareness while situated in empty space, then this body of yours, composed of the four great elements, must be identical to lifeless objects such as withered wood or stones; yet now it again possesses conscious awareness."

If you insist on asserting that there are two cognitions—the body and the eye—this is refuted by the "Five, Two, Knowledge, Two Buddhas, and Dual Minds. This passage has three parts; first is the fixed assertion. The commentary states: "Bi" (必) means "fixedly" (定).
I [say]: Let it simply be said that there is one cognition in the body and one cognition in the eye. Then, to address this directly:
"Ānanda, you insist that the eye exists in empty space and possesses one cognitive awareness, and that the body likewise possesses one cognitive awareness;
thus, you fall into the error of dividing the mind between body and eye. This conceptualization is here refuted.
"There ought to be two cognitions.

[The Master] then set them side by side. The commentary states: "Ought" means "should be so. If there were one cognition for the eyes and one cognition for the body, then this single body of yours would have to become two Buddhas.
This is refuted later. The commentary states: "If you, Ānanda, were to sever the obstructions of one body and realize the principle, you would necessarily become two Buddhas.
This would contradict worldly propriety and constitute the fault of having two natures within a single body."
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that seeing darkness is called "seeing within"—is untenable.
The six knots have been untied;
the fifth has been thoroughly investigated and treated with the efficacious mantra. The commentary states: "However, as for Ānanda who had previously come forward..."
The attachment of the mind within the internal organs has already been shattered by the World-Honored One.

Furthermore, regarding the attachment to the seventh consciousness (*manas*) therein, it is said that "wherever [the object] is joined with, the mind follows and exists there. The seventh consciousness has constant and deliberative reflection as its essence.
The Sub-commentator says: "According to principle, there are six; according to the text, there may be seven. As for this refutation, it concerns the sixth, the fifth, and the eighth."
[Ānanda] replied, "I understand. The Sūtra says: "As I now reflect, this very essence of reflection is truly my own mind-nature.

The World-Honored One refuted this with the phrase "both existent and non-existent. The World-Honored One then asked whether it conforms to the presence of an essence or conforms to the absence of an essence;
this was a dual interrogation. Thereafter, he refuted it individually. Ānanda said, "If there were both an essence and a non-essence, what fault would there be? Now...

Furthermore, when it was stated that there is no substance [to contact], the Buddha refuted this by saying: "If there were no substance yet they could still combine, then the nineteen elements would combine with the seven objects.
The outsider asked: "Ānanda maintains that there is no combination; why do you refute him with something that is non-existent? [The Buddha] replied:
"That substance does not exist inherently is itself the calculation of non-existence. To insist verbally that it exists—what fault is there in that? Worldly...
The World-Honored One then refuted this, saying: "If there were such a substance, it would be like your own hand touching its own body.
As for the mind that you know, does it emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerged from within, you should see what is inside your own body;

if it came from without, you should first see the face [of the person speaking]. Ānanda then rose and posed a challenge to the World-Honored One, saying: "Seeing is the function of the eyes; as for the mind..."

To know that it is not the eye that sees is to realize that [the opponent's] position is meaningless. The World-Honored One compared the door to the eye to demonstrate that the dead have no perception;
he used this weighty analogy to dispel their attachment. He then asked: "If it is the eye that sees, when you are inside a room, can the door see?
He further asked: "Then all those who are already dead still possess eyes; should they not all see objects? The Master of the Commentary (*Ṭīkākāra*) says: "For now, let us consider the door..."
The principle is thus clear: it is evident that death is without perception, and that the mind is the sovereign master.

Only then can one further refute [the views of] finitude, oneness, multiplicity, omnipresence, non-omnipresence, and so forth. The preceding exposition concludes the refutation of the "conformity with combination" (anuvāda).
Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all various phenomena arise.
The five divine mantras whip and subdue the wraiths. This text has two parts. The first part establishes the framework and has three sections. The first section recounts the past exposition.

The commentary states: 'Kai' (open) refers to awakening; 'shi' (reveal) refers to entry. Thus, it is 'opening, revealing, awakening, and entering. 'You' (by/through) means cause; it points to the initial stage of the eight consciousnesses."

Delusion regarding the truth gives rise to the two inversions; that is, a single thought-moment deviates from Suchness (*tathatā*), and the signs of weariness appear. Thereupon, there arise the three subtle consciousnesses of karma, transformation, and manifestation.
This manifesting consciousness is the substance of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which serves as the support for all phenomena.

However, both their establishment and their experience arise from the eight consciousnesses; the eight consciousnesses are the producers, while the phenomena consist of the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world.
Regarding the realms and so forth:
because they arise from dharmas, various types of consciousness are produced.
The commentary states: "Because they arise due to the images of dharma-objects (dharmāyatana), the sixth consciousness then exists, relying upon dharma-objects."
The sixth consciousness arises based on birth, abiding, change, and cessation. It is like a sick person who cannot walk without a staff;
thus, the subsequent passage states: "Objects are not permanent. When they undergo transformation and cease, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
This consciousness cannot arise unless it is moved by the activity of objective objects. Why, then, does [the text] not instead cite the seventh consciousness? It says: "Citing..."
The sixth consciousness takes the seventh consciousness as its object of calculation; or perhaps Ānanda has retained the seventh consciousness as his object of calculation.
When I now contemplate, that which is the very essence of contemplation is truly my own mind-nature.
Next, he clarifies their respective modes of examination. The commentary states: The seventh consciousness has constant and investigative deliberation (*nitya-santīraṇa-manasikāra*) as its nature.
The eighth is constantly non-investigative. The seventh is both constant and investigative. The sixth is neither investigative nor constant. The fifth is neither constant nor investigative.

The essence of volitional thought (*manana*) is precisely the seventh consciousness; it constantly examines internally and cannot take external objects as its conditions. This refers to this very seventh [consciousness].
Consciousness is, in truth, the nature of my mind.
Wherever it conjoins, the mind exists accordingly; yet it is not located in any of the three places—internal, external, or intermediate.

The subsequent passage points to its manifestation according to conditions. The commentary states: "Consciousness conjoins with objects. If one speaks of 'conjoining according to [conditions],' this refers to the sixth consciousness."
Nor is it internal or external; it is that which was previously described as internal and external. Question: Why is it mentioned here when one has not yet reached the intermediate state? Answer:
Ānanda intends to calculate the intermediate state below, and thus it is raised here for this purpose.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various minds are produced—the subsequent refutation of this passage consists of four parts.

First is the dual refutation of existence and non-existence, which has two sections. First is the refutation of non-existence, which has two sections. First is the restatement of the position followed by the formal refutation, which has three sections.
First is the citation of the opponent's view. The Commentary states: 'Various minds are produced' refers to the six consciousnesses; this is raised as an example."
The sixth [consciousness] leads to the seventh conception.
Regarding the phrase "wherever it conjoins, the mind follows existence," this is established next.
The commentary states: "This is a restatement of the conception; this too is the sixth consciousness."
This mind has no substance.

The subsequent refutation consists of two parts. First, the determination of the position. The commentary states: "Is it said that they combine because there is substance, or is it said that they combine because there is no substance?
Ānanda merely says 'it has no substance. How then can you cite [his words] by saying, 'this mind has no substance'?"
"Then there is nothing with which to unite.

This is followed by a refutation. The commentary states: "The refutation says, 'then there is nothing with which to unite. Now, for things to unite, there must be two; only then can one speak of union.

Although there are now three names [for these states] in this harmonious reconciliation, they are all but a single deluded consciousness. It is not yet clear whether there is no union or whether there is an object."
Furthermore, it is restated below:

"If there were no substantial entity yet they could still combine," then even if one subsequently establishes that this is ultimately untenable, the text has three parts; first, the establishment of the concession.
Thus, there are nineteen realms. This is due to the conjunction of seven particles.

Next, an analogy is cited; the commentary states: "If it is already established that the non-existent can be joined with the existent, then it must also follow that the non-existent can be joined with the non-existent."
The claim that there is no conjunction and no meaning is not established; however, the claim that there is conjunction and there is meaning contradicts worldly convention.

There are only eighteen realms: six sense organs (*indriya*), six objects (*viṣaya*), and six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). These three sets of six constitute the eighteen realms. To speak of nineteen is incorrect, as one [of these]—the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)—does not exist apart from the mind.
Furthermore, there are only six objects: form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharmas*). To speak of seven is also incorrect, as one [of these], the unmanifest, does not exist.
The claim that the manifested object is non-existent is incorrect;
this point will be refuted later. The commentary states: "As for your assertion that they combine, this is not the case. Where would there be no substance?"
And yet, it would conjoin with the object; thus, there would likely be no fault in the conjunction.

If it possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there are four textual passages for subsequently refuting that existence. First, the fixed adherence: the commentary states, "I shall now merely state that the possession of an intrinsic nature is untenable. Furthermore—
"How so? [The Master] refutes by citing the following:
"It is like you using your own hand to touch your own body.
This second citation uses the sensation of touch to manifest the nature of the body. The commentary states: "It is as when you, Ānanda, use your hand to touch your own body."
"Body. As for this mind that you know, does it emerge from within, or does it enter from without?

This constitutes the three pairs of interrogations. The Commentary states: "The 'mind that you know' refers to the seventh consciousness, which constantly knows internally; [the question is] whether it emerges from within..."
"Go out! Since you have entered from the outside, how is it when you go out from within? The following text reiterates this:
"If you again go out from within, you will still see the heart and liver within your own body.
The commentary states: "If you again go out from within, you will still see the heart and liver within your own body."
The thirty-six items, etc., are as previously recorded in the internal text.
If [the Buddha] had come from outside, one would first have seen his face. The commentary states: "The Buddha’s Way... came from... First...
"I must see your own head and face; this is the error of being deluded regarding both the internal and the external.
Ānanda said, "Seeing is the function of the eyes; it is the mind that knows, not the eyes. Therefore, seeing is not the meaning [of the eyes]."
"The Two Vehicles contradict the second rescue. The commentary states: Ānanda countered with a rescue, saying, "I previously saw the text within my internal organs.

The World-Honored One refuted this, saying, "When opening one's eyes, one sees light; why then do you not see my face? Now, within this passage concerning the union of the faculties, the mind knows that it is not the eye.
Why does the World-Honored One suppress [the distinction] and compel one to see the face, taking what the mind knows as the eye? This is seeing what is not.
This is its meaning. However, Ānanda was a person of great expedient power and possessed no such attachment;
rather, this salvific text was composed because ordinary beings cling to the notion that the eye can see. It is fortunate that the Buddha refuted this.
The Buddha said: "If it is the eye that can see, then when you are inside a room, can the door see?

This consists of three parts: first, refuting the opponent's reliance on the literal text; second, suppressing the notion that the door can see; third, [the subsequent argument]. The commentary states:
[The opponent] firmly adheres to the view that the eye alone can see. To refute this, [the Buddha] asks: "When you are within a house or room, can the door see? Ānanda, if he says—
If it were able to see, then the eye would indeed be able to see; since the door cannot see, the argument that the eye can see is untenable.

With the eye being like a door and the person being like the mind, the general intent is to refute the claim that the eye cannot see, establishing instead that seeing is solely the function of the mind.
If that were so, then all those who have already died would still possess eyes and should therefore see objects.

Next, [the opponent] attempts to observe this by means of the eyes of the deceased. The commentary states: "When a person dies, they lack consciousness; yet their eyes remain. They ought to see objects.
Why do they not see? I shall now simply ask: even if they did see objects, what of it? Below follows the refutation.
If one perceives objects, how can it be called death?
Even if one subsequently observes [the absence of objects], it is not death. [The Commentary] states: If death were to perceive objects, it would not be called death.
Ānanda, furthermore, if this mind of yours that is conscious and capable of knowing must have a substantial body, [then...]
The fourth section refutes the existence of limits; it consists of three parts. First is the general inquiry, which has two sub-parts. First is the formal proposition.
The commentary states: "If" (*ruo*) means "as if"; "must" (*bi*) means "certainly. This refers to the claim that there must necessarily be a substantial entity (*tǐ*).
Is it a single entity? Or are there many entities? Is it currently within your body? Or does it pervade the entire body?
This is the subsequent inquiry. The commentary states: "As for the question 'How can it be a single entity?'—the following text restates this."
If it were a single entity, then when you prick one limb with your hand, all four limbs should feel it.
Next, the refutation is divided into four parts; the first part refutes the notion of oneness. This section has three sub-parts. First, the formal refutation. The Commentary states:
"If you claim that consciousness is a single entity and thus pervades the entire body, then when you use your left hand to touch the right hand, [the four limbs should likewise feel it]."
The limbs must be perceived simultaneously. If one says that all four limbs are perceived as a whole, then it is established that the meaning of "a single body" is achieved.

If, however, one touches a single limb and the other three limbs are not perceived, then one commits the fault of failing to perceive the remaining limbs. These four limbs refer to the two hands and two feet.
Now, how is it that you say they are "all perceived"? [The following section] restates this point.
If [the body] were perceived as a whole, there would be no specific location for the prick.
Next, he proceeds to refute this further. The commentary states: "If it were perceived all at once, which limb would receive the prick? Therefore, the prick has no location;
this commits the fault of 'knowing the same' while losing the perception of touch. Now, he simply asks: "Even if one says the prick has a specific location, what of it? Below, he restates the point.
If it were pointed out as having a specific location, then your "single entity" could not be established.
This concludes the refutation. The commentary states: If it were pointed out as having a location, then it would have distinct boundaries;
thus, the principle of your previously asserted "single entity" would again fail. If it had a location, then when [the hand] touches it, the foot would not know [it]. Why?

If they were named as a single entity, one would incur the fault of claiming there is no transgression when receiving a blow; but what if they are said to be many entities? [The text] below cites this:
"If they were many entities, then they would constitute many persons. Which entity would be 'you'?"
2. Refuting the Multiplicity [of Consciousness]. The Commentary states: If one asserts that consciousness has multiple entities, it follows that there must be multiple persons.

Since there would be multiple persons, their entities would be distinct; thus, one must determine which body belongs to you, Ānanda. This commits the fallacy of attributing multiple minds to a single substance.
Now, as for the statement that it "pervades the entire body," how is this so? The following section cites [the opponent's position]:
"If it pervades the entire body, it is the same as what was previously refuted.

This is the second refutation of pervasion. The commentary states: "If consciousness were to have a pervasive essence, it would again be identical to the previous attachment to a single entity; it is merely..."
If the Way is not all-pervasive, how so? [The text] below provides the formal citation:
"If it were not all-pervasive, when you touch your head, it would also touch your feet; while the head has sensation, the feet would be without cognition."

Fourth, the refutation of non-pervasiveness. The commentary states: If you claim that the substance of consciousness does not pervade the entire body, then when you reach your head with your hand and also touch your foot, the head ought to have sensation while the foot should be without cognition. Why is it that both the head and the foot are aware?
This commits the fallacy of both the head and the foot being cognizant simultaneously.
Now you are not so; your subsequent conclusion is incorrect.

This section has two parts. First is the general reprimand. The commentary states: To assert that [the self] is both a single entity and multiple entities, or both pervasive and non-pervasive, is in both cases untenable.
Therefore, you should know that wherever the mind is joined with something, it exists there; it is impossible for it to be elsewhere.

[The Master] concludes this refutation. Sixth: "Both internal and external are simultaneously dispelled; a sharp blade splits the brain. The commentary states: Ānanda previously maintained that the mind resides in...
This has already been refuted by the World-Honored One within the discussion on "conformity. Furthermore, regarding this point, you maintain that the mind resides in between;
this is the sixth consciousness. Ānanda then maintained: "As I contemplate it, there is nothing seen internally, yet there is no mutual cognition externally.
To reside within is not established, for the body and mind would then cognize each other; to reside outside is illogical. Now, because they do mutually cognize one another, it must be internal..."
"There is no seeing; it must be in between. The World-Honored One refuted this with the phrases "existence" and "non-existence," then asked Ānanda:
"You speak of 'in between. That which is in between must not be confused; it cannot be without a location. Now, as you investigate this 'in between,' where does it reside?
Does it reside in space, or does it reside in the body? Having thus questioned him regarding both locations, he then refuted [the position]. Ānanda...

[Ānanda] spoke with difficulty: "If I were to say it is within the body, what fault would there be? The World-Honored One refuted this, saying: "If it were within the body, it would be at the periphery and not in the center;
yet it would also shift to being in the center. He further refuted this, saying: "To be in the center is the same as being internal; thus the meaning of 'body' is not established. Ānanda said:
"If it is located in a place, how would that be? [The Buddha] refuted this, saying: "If it were located in a place, would it be something indicated, or..."
There is nothing manifested. Since non-manifestation (avijñapti) is likewise non-existent, manifestation (vijñapti) would lack fixedness. Why is this?

For example, when a person has a manifested form, at the moment that form is being manifested, looking from the east it is west, and observing from the south it becomes north. Since the substance of the manifestation is thus confused, the mind should likewise be disordered.

The meaning of its location is not established. Ānanda further attempts to defend his position, saying: "That which I speak of is neither of these two; it must exist between the sense organ and the object.
The Buddha refutes this by examining whether it encompasses both or neither. The above concludes the refutation of the intermediate position.
The Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll One, Part One.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, the Cultivation and Realization of the Ultimate Meaning, and the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have also heard when the Buddha was conversing with Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma Princes about the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), that the World-Honored One likewise said: 'The mind is neither within nor without.'"
Six: The Golden Knife that Splits the Brain. Four sections. Part One: Establishing the Text. Three subsections. First, recounting what was previously heard.

The Commentary states: "I once, forty-five years ago, within the gradual teachings of the Mahāyāna, also heard the Buddha [teach] for Mañjuśrī and other Bodhisattvas—namely, Avalokiteśvara and the various Dharma-Princes such as Xian—who succeeded and glorified the Buddha-sun, filling its place..."
He dwells in the position of supreme honor; he is the Son of the Buddha. "Talk" (tan) here means "to speak. When he speaks of the signless as being without signs, this is the time of the true mark.
The World-Honored One also said that the mind does not exist externally; this was intended to reveal that his true mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Ānanda came forward previously, and the Buddha shattered his notions of internal and external; now we know that the Buddha has likewise [done so].
To speak of it:
as I contemplate, there is nothing perceived within, nor is anything mutually known without.
Next, I examine the preceding principle. The commentary states: "As I personally contemplate and deliberate with my own mind, I do not perceive a mind within."
The liver and other organs do not currently know one another externally; yet I now claim they know one another internally.
Since there is no cognition within them, they cannot be established as being internal. If the body and mind were to cognize one another, it would be illogical for them to be external.
The commentary states: "This refers to the underlying principle. It then proceeds to state: "To claim that the principle resides within the body is untenable;
yet when one raises the hand to point toward the mind, there is still further conceptual differentiation. To claim it resides outside the body is likewise irrational."
"Because they are combined and mutually cognizant.

The commentary states: "It was not previously combined and mutually cognizant; now it is combined and mutually cognizant. This citation does not appear in external versions. There is a manuscript that reads 'now mutually cognizant,' which is also acceptable."
Furthermore, there is no seeing within.
The commentary states: "If there were seeing within, yet there is no seeing, then it is established that seeing does not reside within;
it must therefore exist in between."

The subsequent section describes the place of cessation. The commentary states: "It contains an account of the mind's abode; this calculation falls within the 'middle. It is not yet clear what is meant by 'the middle' in this calculation;
it refers to the location where the body arises."
The Buddha said: "Regarding what you call 'the middle,' that which is in the middle must not be deluded;

it is not that there is no location for it. This section consists of two parts: first, the general inquiry. This part has two sub-sections: first, the general inquiry. The commentary states: "Regarding what you call 'the middle.'"
"You must certainly not be deluded; you must also have some basis upon which to rely. [The Master] then poses a challenge:
"Now, as you search for the 'middle,' where does this middle reside?
He further questions him by distinguishing it. The commentary states: "Now, Ānanda, as you investigate and seek its center, where exactly is that center located? It should be...
"In what place? Does it reside in a location, or does it reside in the body?
The commentary states: "Does it reside in a location—that is, in the midst of the five sense-objects (pañca-viṣaya): form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch?"
Furthermore, [if you say it] resides within your body, then the body consists of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. But tell me, how can it be "within" the body?
The following text cites and refutes this:
"If it were in the body, it would be at the periphery, not in the center."
This is subsequently refuted separately. The text has two parts. First, regarding the body, there are again two sections. The first relies on the "extremes. The commentary states:

"The person of the East and the person of the West each have their bodies situated at one extreme. How can [the center] be between them? Thus, you commit the error of calling the extremes 'the center.
Furthermore, if you further argue that the interior of the body constitutes the center, this is immediately refuted below."
"Within" (*zhōng*) is the same as "internal" (*nèi*).
Later it is translated as "internal. The commentary states: "If one says 'within the body,' this is identical to the previous textual attachment to 'internal';
it commits the error of taking what is internal to be 'middle. But how can it be said that [the Dharma] resides in a location? The following text reiterates this point.
If it exists in a location, does it have something indicated, or does it have nothing indicated?
Regarding the subsequent discussion of "location," the text has two parts. First, there is a dual interrogation regarding existence and non-existence. The commentary states: "The dual inquiry asks:
'Does it further have something indicated, or does it have nothing indicated? When both locations are questioned, they are vast, desolate, and boundless. Now, one specific location is established."

This serves as the middle [section]. One must establish a marker. But if one simply says there is no manifest action (*vijñapti*), how can that be? The following text refutes this. The refutation of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is the same as that for non-existence;

it is refuted separately later. The text has two parts. First, regarding non-existence: the commentary states, "If one says there is no manifest action, it is again the same as non-existence. This establishes the middle [position].
The meaning is not established. Now, in establishing the Middle Way, there must be some defining characteristic. Since you have no such characteristic, by what means will you establish the Middle?

You commit the fault of failing to manifest an infinite number of errors. But if you simply say that there *is* a characteristic, how can that be? [This] is the citation of the subsequent [objection].
The manifestation is not fixed;
there is a subsequent existence. This passage has four parts. First, it demonstrates that [the manifestation] is not fixed. Why is this?
Second, the investigation of the indeterminate cause:
for example, when a person uses a marker to designate a center, looking from the east it is west, and observing from the south it becomes north.
Third, the description of the characteristics of indeterminacy: the commentary states that it is like using an object to mark the center of a room; as a person from the east looks...
When one faces west, those to the south perceive it as north.
Since the manifested forms are thus confused, the mind should likewise be disordered.
Regarding the fourth instance of "manifesting" (*biao*): the commentary states that since these manifested locations are intermingled, the manifesting mind is likewise [confused].
"Confused and disordered; sometimes to the east, sometimes to the west—it is uncertain.
Ānanda said, "Among what I have spoken, it is neither of these two kinds.
[The commentary on] the three rescuing passages has three parts. First, it rebukes the empty adversary. The sub-commentary says: "Ā-zá comes forward to contend with the World-Honored One."
He said: "In what I have taught, it is not these two kinds. These two kinds refer to the extremes of the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and the extremes of views regarding limits (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi).
As the Blessed One said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.'"

Next, the *Chuo yin ming tan* (Discourse on Citing and Explaining) provides a commentary, stating: "The Buddha, within the framework of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) school, has arranged it thus:

the eye is the supporting object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), while form (*rūpa*) is the condition that draws forth the mind. The eye and form acting as conditions constitute the conjunction of the sense organ (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*)."
Thereafter, visual consciousness arises. Consciousness is that which discerns conditions; since there are already the sense organ and the object, there is then the mind of consciousness.
Only through the conjunction of these three is the "seeing-portion" (darśana-bhāga) established.
The eye possesses discrimination; the dust of form is without cognition. When consciousness arises between them, then the mind is present.
Later, he points to the center and says the mind is there. The commentary states: "The eye possesses discrimination" means the eye has sentience;
"the dust of form is without cognition" means form is insentient. This arising of the mind-consciousness within these faculties and objects constitutes what is called "my mind."
[This refers to] where [the mind] resides. Below, this further refutes the text regarding the root (organ) and the object.
The Buddha said: "If your mind were located between the organ and the object, would the essence of this mind encompass both, or would it not encompass both?"
Section Four: A Second Refutation of the Text, in Two Parts. First, the dual interrogation. The Commentary states:

"If your mind were within the faculties and objects," this restates the opponent's previous position; it then interrogates: "As for the substance of this mind, does it encompass both the faculties and the objects?"
Furthermore, [the object] does not simultaneously involve both the sense organ and the object-field. As for how it could be said to involve both, the text below restates the position:
"If it involved both, the substance of the entity would be confused.

This is subsequently refuted in three parts. First is the refutation of the simultaneous involvement. The Commentary states: "If it involved both, this is the formal restatement of the position. The refutation says: [as follows].
"Objects are disordered. "Objects" refers to the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Since the faculties are internal, why are they called "objects"?

However, the faculties are also indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and thus likewise "objects. "Entity" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). As for "disordered," it means that consciousness is disordered in its association with the faculties and their objects.
This constitutes the fault of "the substance being identical while the objects are mixed.
It is known that the object is not the substance.

The commentary states: "The object refers to the sense-faculties and their sensory data, which lack cognition; the substance refers to consciousness, which possesses cognition. This thus commits the fault of "confusing categories with objects."
To claim there is no fault is to establish two opposing sides. How, then, can this be the Middle? To attempt to encompass both is likewise untenable.

The Commentary states: "Opposing" means to stand in opposition. One half belongs to the sense faculty (*indriya*), and one half belongs to the object (*viṣaya*); thus, they stand as two. Since [each] is but a half...

When the sense faculties and their objects are taken as such, they constitute extremes; thus, the meaning of the Middle Way is not established. To attempt to combine both is impossible, as it commits the error of positing two entities within a single substance.
This is neither knowing nor not knowing.
Next, the refutation of "not being inclusive. The commentary states: There is one sentence missing in this passage. It should read:

"If it were not inclusive, then it would neither be knowing nor non-knowing; consciousness would likewise not be inclusive of the faculties (*indriya*), nor would it be inclusive of the objects (*viṣaya*).

Since it is not inclusive of either faculty or object, it would neither know the faculty nor the object. Therefore, it is said that if it does not know, it is not a faculty of cognition; if it does not perceive, it does not perceive the object."
It would then have no essential nature (*svabhāva*).

What, then, would constitute its characteristic as the "middle"? The commentary states: "Since one does not know the sense-faculties and their objects, there is no essential nature for consciousness. Since consciousness is absent, what can be designated as the 'middle'?
This would incur the fault of failing to encompass [the factors] while losing the essential nature. Furthermore, this passage is missing one phrase at the end; it should read: "No..."
Furthermore, it cannot be established.
Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for [the contact] to exist in the interval between them.
This concludes the refutation. The commentary states: To say that it exists in the interval between the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) is impossible.
"Seventh, the subsequent inquiry regarding non-attachment: 'If one treats withered bones,' the commentary states:
Previously, Ānanda held the mind to be located in the middle [of the body], and this was completely refuted by the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, when the World-Honored One refuted his persistent attachment to this [corpse]—just as when Bian Que’s acupuncture caused a dead man to return to life—he insisted, saying: '[... "
"Non-attachment is what we call 'mind. Is it not the case, then, that my non-attachment is also called 'mind'? Ānanda clung to the notion that the mind is non-attached;
