"Six: Describing the Use of the Pupils. The Commentary says: "I and the thirty-six classes of beings all employ the faculty that perceives through the eyes."
He sees the eye, which is a floating root composed of the four sensory objects.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Now you answer me, the Tathāgata. I shall bend my fingers into a radiant fist to illuminate your eyes and mind."
The fourth section, "Examining the Text," has two parts. First, "Distinguishing the Headings and Examining the Mind. The commentary states: "You now stand before me, the Tathāgata;
I have bent my fingers into a 'luminous fist' to illuminate both your mind and your eyes. This is the formal citation (*nirdeśa*).
"You can see it with your own eyes; what do you take to be the mind? [The Master] then held up his fist and said, "When my fist shines forth, what is it that perceives this?
The commentary states: This was to interrogate him as to what he considers to be his mind when my fist is shining forth.
Ānanda said, "The Tathāgata is now investigating the location of the mind.
Later, the text states, "He is able to investigate and infer [its nature]. The commentary notes: "The Tathāgata is at this very moment thoroughly investigating the location of my mind."
"And yet, when I use my mind to investigate, exhaustively search, and pursue [the nature of things], that which performs this investigation—I take that to be the mind.

The commentary states: "And yet, when I employ my mind to examine, scrutinize, seek out, and pursue—this very thing that is daily luminous and alert, which clings to conditions and chases after objects—is precisely it. This demonstrates that the deluded capacity for investigation is itself the root."
Regarding the eighth consciousness, the Buddha said: "Ho! Ānanda, this is not your mind.

The subsequent passage on the "seizure" consists of four parts; the first rebukes the presentation of the false root. The commentary states: It is inappropriate for the Buddha to both withhold and concede [the point], yet he nonetheless utters the exclamation "Ho! (du).
[The Buddha] rebuked him, saying, "This is not your mind.
Ānanda was startled; he left his seat, joined his palms, stood up, and addressed the Buddha: "This is not my mind. What should it be called?"

"Second, 'agitated, lost, startled, and distressed. The commentary states: 'Jue' (矍) describes an appearance of alarm and fear. To leave one's seat means to shift the body to the side or retreat backward.
This is not my own mind; I simply accept it as it is. Under what name should this be designated? I beg you to clarify the term that does not apply."

The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is the false appearance and conceptualization of the external objects before you; it deludes your true nature. (3) This clarifies how it deludes the source of truth. The Commentary states:

"This refers to the external objects," which generally indicates the objects of perception. "False appearance and conceptualization" refers to the arising of conceptualization based on appearances; this encompasses their fundamental origin.

By stating that these appearances and conceptualizations are [the cause], it identifies the preceding as the object and the succeeding as the subject. Thus, it is said that these appearances and conceptualizations are...
The eighth consciousness deludes you regarding the fundamental nature of your original *tathatā*. You commit the transgression of grasping at the false as true.
From beginningless time until your present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son, thereby losing your original constancy and undergoing the cycle of rebirth.

Fourth, "Injuring and Retaining the Robber Child. The commentary states: Because of you, from beginningless time until today, you have mistaken the robber for a child and lost the originally true and constant mind;
therefore, you undergo the cycle of rebirth. If one recognizes the true mind as the mind, there will be a time when one attains Buddhahood;
if one clings to that which performs the investigation as the mind, how is this any different from mistaking a robber for a child?
As for the son: all his dharma-wealth and merit were stolen away at once, after which he could not avoid the cycle of birth and death.
The tenth [section], "Discerning the Rest from the Sand," the commentary states: this indicates the purpose of the preceding passage; that is to say, Ānanda has come forward.

He clung to that which performs the act of deliberation as being the mind. Even after being rebuked by the World-Honored One, he still grasped and begrudged this mind, refusing to let it go, and said:

"Why should my mind alone make offerings to the Tathāgata? It shall even travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving all Buddhas and spiritual friends, giving rise to great valor, and performing all manner of difficult dharmic deeds. All of these...
"Using this mind, even if this illumination were not the mind, I would then be without a mind and identical to earth and wood.
Therefore, World-Honored One, you invited Ānanda to set aside external objects and recognize the true nature of discernment, saying:
'I am not commanding you to grasp it as being non-mind; rather, you must subtly examine and investigate this mind yourself.'"

"If there were a nature of discrimination that existed apart from the external objects before you, it would indeed be your true mind. Having thus explained the metaphor of sifting sand to point out [the mind], Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha; because my heart loves the Buddha, he caused me to leave the household life."
Part Two: Ten Verses on Striking Gold from Ore; Sub-section One: A Solemn Petition in Ten Sections. First:
Relying on the Buddha to Decline Honor. Commentary: It says, "I am the younger brother whom the Tathāgata cherishes.
Previously, having beheld the Buddha’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics—so supremely wondrous and extraordinary—I immediately resolved to leave the household life."
He has a rounded crown and wears a square-cut robe;
this is my heart’s intent. Why should I offer worship only to the Tathāgata?
[The two Śākyas] personally attended him. The commentary states: "Du" means "only. "Offering" refers to the four requisites; "nurturing" refers to personal service and care.
I say that my mind does not merely offer worship to the Tathāgata, the Teacher;
rather, it shall travel throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving all Buddhas and spiritual friends.
"Three times throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust. The commentary states: This refers to traveling extensively through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

"Serving and attending all sages of the various fruition stages who are spiritual friends" means to skillfully accord with the teachings of the Tathāgata, knowing causes and recognizing fruits, and knowing illnesses and identifying the appropriate medicines.
One gives rise to great courage and vigor, and performs all difficult practices and dharmic deeds, employing this very mind in each case.

Regarding the "fourfold efficacy in practicing what is difficult," the commentary states: one gives rise to a mind of great fortitude, vigor, and sharpness, relinquishing one’s head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, children, and so forth—all of which is accomplished by means of this very mind. This indicates excellence.
"Even if one were to slander the Dharma and forever lose their roots of goodness, it is still due to this mind.
Regarding the "five types of icchantikas who slander the Dharma," the commentary states: "Even if I were to destroy and slander the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings..."
For those who are icchantikas and lack faith, they commit the transgression of the two roots and fall away from unsurpassed bodhi;
this is also due to my own mind, which marks this as unwholesome.
If this "manifestation" were not the mind, then the sixth consciousness would collectively present both types of karma.
The commentary states: "Manifestation" refers to daily攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to conditions) and 逐境 (zhú-jìng—pursuing objects), giving rise to delusions and creating karma.
If the eighth consciousness were not my own mind, [how could this be so?].
I am indeed without mind, identical to earth and wood; apart from this awareness and cognition, there is nothing else.
"The seven categories are like clods of earth. The commentary states: "Earth" refers to clods of soil, and "wood" refers to plants and trees—insentient things.
This means that outside of this awareness and cognition, there is no separate mind whatsoever.
"How is it that the Tathāgata says this is not the mind?
The eighth [question] is "The Tathāgata’s empty denial. The commentary states: "When the Buddha previously said, 'This is not your mind,' I was truly struck with alarm and fear;
including this great assembly, there were none who did not harbor doubts."
9. Clarifying that his own assembly shared the same doubt. The commentary states: "Indeed, there was a state of alarm and terror;
not only I, but the entire great assembly as well, seeing the Buddha take away this mind of ours, were at once hesitant and unable to decide."
"May you deign to bestow great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened.
Ten times he requested that the Buddha proclaim this so that they might awaken. The commentary states: The Buddha possesses great compassion of the same essence;

this compassion is able to uproot suffering and provide opening, guidance, and instruction. [The disciple] says: "I myself am merely one who has not yet awakened; I request the Buddha to provide instruction for me."

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed and taught for Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
This consists of two parts: first, the consolation; second, the discernment of the dual mind. The first part, describing the source upon which delusion relies, contains seven sections.

The first clarifies the secret operation of encompassing compassion. The commentary states: "Opening" refers to gathering [beings] toward awakening, while "revealing" refers to causing them to enter. As previously stated: "There is none among this great assembly who is not..."
Doubt. Herein, that which is shown and declared as "non-arising" is the principle of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two emptinesses.
Non-arising is also non-ceasing. "Dharma-patience" (*dharma-kṣānti*) is the wisdom of the true suchness of the two emptinesses. "Dharma" (*dharma*) has the meaning of an object of apprehension;

"patience" (*kṣānti*) has the meaning of sealing and recognizing. This means that one gives rise to wisdom to seal and recognize the aforementioned principle of the true suchness of the two emptinesses.
At the lion throne, he rubbed Ānanda’s crown;
twice he rubbed his crown to settle his mind. The commentary states: facing the lion throne symbolizes fearlessness.
By rubbing Ānanda’s heart and crown, he causes him to realize the method of the *Śūraṅgama-śikhara* (the Summit of Heroic Power), and furthermore, he comforts him.
He addressed them, saying: "The Tathāgata has constantly taught that all phenomena which arise are manifested solely by the mind.
This points to the source of the myriad dharmas. The commentary states: "All phenomena" refers collectively to all internal bodies, external environments, and so forth.
"Manifested solely by the mind" specifically excludes the existence of anything outside the mind; it means they are manifestations of consciousness and mind, while their true essence is non-existent.
Manifestation is like a jewel appearing as various objects; yet the nature of the jewel is without arising, its essence being eternally perfect and pure.

It manifests in response to all sentient beings through the ripening of the karmic fruits created by their own actions. Nevertheless, a portion of true nature has never undergone change. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Both the establishment [of the world] and its enjoyment arise from the eight consciousnesses. And as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All that exists within the three realms..."
Dharma: All things are created solely by the mind; they arise upon the appearances of consciousness (*vijñapti-lakṣaṇa*), yet these are not yet the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-tathatā*).
If one awakens to the nature of consciousness, then appearance and nature are of one essence—just as waves and water share the same moisture.
All causes and effects, and even the minute dust motes of the world, take form through the mind.
(4) This clarifies the essence of the cause of birth. The commentary states: "Cause" means dependence.

It says that among all classes of sentient beings, good causes lead to rebirth in the good realms, while evil causes lead to falling into hell (*niraya*). These constitute internal inversion and external inversion; thus, [it refers to] the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
The elements, the four great constituents, and so forth—whether internal or external—all arise through delusion based upon the nature of the one true reality.
They all take their substance by depending on the true mind, and they all manifest as transformations within the characteristics of consciousness-only; not a single dharma exists apart from the mind.
Ānanda, if in all worlds there were anything whatsoever— even down to a blade of grass, a leaf, or a thread— were one to trace back its origin,
they would all possess a substantial nature.

Fifth, regarding the nature of luminosity as it arises from what is produced. The commentary states: "Whether it be a single blade of grass or a leaf, a single flower or a fruit, if one exhaustively traces their root source, they are none other than the origin of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is by depending upon these four great elements that they are able to grow and develop."
"Even though space is void, it nonetheless possesses name and appearance;

the characteristic of emptiness is manifested by its six fingers. The commentary states: "This says that space has a name and appearance, taking non-obstruction, emptiness, and permanence as its essence."
How much more so for the pure, wondrously pure, and luminous mind, whose nature is that of all minds, yet which itself has no substance.
(7) This reveals the perfect basis of original enlightenment. The commentary states: How much more so for the fundamentally pure, subtle, tranquil, and perfectly luminous mind-nature;
this true nature is the source of all minds, while these [other] minds are delusive. Yet delusion is established in dependence upon the True. It is like...
The waves exist because of the water; however, when one speaks of the reality, it is not that the true mind lacks its own substance, for even all grasses and trees possess their own essential nature.

If you maintain that the nature of what is cognized by the discernment of vitarka (initial application) and vicāra (sustained application) must necessarily be the mind, then we shall subsequently examine this regarding the objects [of cognition].
This section has four parts; first, the formal proposition. The commentary states: "Bi" (必) means "certainly"; "wei" (為) means "to act as.

To "cling" (執) is to guard against delusion without wavering; to "be stingy" (恡) is to secretly resist its removal. "Discernment" (分別) consists of six types: *vitarka* (覺) is seeking, and *vicāra* (觀) is investigating.
The nature of that which is cognized pertains to all eight [consciousnesses]. Eye-consciousness cognizes the objective realm of visible forms;
ear-consciousness cognizes the objective realm of sounds, and so forth; the sixth consciousness cognizes the seventh; the seventh consciousness cognizes the eighth;

and the eighth consciousness cognizes its own objects, such as the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world (the environment). This "cognition" refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness. As the Sūtra says: "Discrimination is the eighth..."

Sixth: This refers to the case where others stubbornly cling to this mind and will not let go. For the time being, we shall concede that they take this deluded mind to be the true mind; later, it will be refuted.
This mind should immediately be separated from all things: colors, fragrances, tastes, touches, and all sensory objects and activities.

This consists of two parts of the commentary. First is the general exclusion. The sub-commentary states: "Jiēn" (jié) means "immediately" or "it should be. "This mind" refers to the mind of attachment and grasping;
it says that this mind should immediately be separated from all things. Colors, fragrances, and so forth refer to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
All objects (*viṣaya*) depend upon the seventh consciousness as their sixth support. What is undertaken is called "matter" (*vastu*); the accomplishment of matter is called "action" (*karman*).
These refer to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses respectively. Alternatively, "matter" refers to the seventh consciousness, which takes constant and deliberative reflection as its matter;
"action" refers to the eighth consciousness, wherein the seeds of good and evil acquired through momentary perfuming fall, and subsequently [the seventh] constructs [its objects].
One attains the collective and individual retributive karma of the three realms;
separately, there is the complete nature.
The commentary states: "If one sets aside the preceding eight consciousnesses and seeks a portion of the nature externally, it does not follow the objective fields (*viṣaya*)."
When it falls away and ceases, I grant that this is your mind’s complete nature; it is a spiritual discernment that is uniquely intrinsic and does not arise dependent upon objects.

This is because it is true. As stated in the following passage: "It does not, by means of external sensory objects, give rise to cognition and vision. If one were separated from the five preceding objects...
To discriminate that there is no nature externally is merely the deluded mind; this is a general refutation.
Furthermore, when teaching others to leave behind objects and recognize their own nature—as you do now, listening to my Dharma—this is discrimination arising from sound.

Thereafter, there are two separate excerpts from the Wen. The first concerns sound (*śabda*). The commentary states: "For now, taking the sense-object of sound as our point of departure, when one receives [it] through hearing, the ear-faculty gives rise to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*); 'receiving' refers to the act of listening and perceiving."

"Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, they would subsequently accord with the Dharma. The commentary states: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing—that is, the eye; hearing—that is, the ear;
sensing—that is, the body; and cognizing—that is, the tongue and nose—they would no longer share the same objects as these five [senses]."
"Internally maintaining stillness in the profound and secluded.

The Commentary says: Although the five sense-faculties do not engage with the five objects, the eighth consciousness still internally engages with mental objects (*dharmas*). "Profound" means deep and remote;
although it is "secluded," it has not attained complete seclusion, as it is merely a semblance of engaging with the secluded. This refers to the Śrāvaka who has suppressed [the afflictions].
The sixth consciousness does not share the same objects as the five [sensory] consciousnesses. Although it does not externally perceive objects, it perceives internally;
like grass pressed down by a stone, it temporarily fails to grow, yet it will inevitably sprout when spring arrives. This is because it has not yet attained complete stillness.
"This is still merely a matter of conceptualizing shadows within the dust of mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*).
The Commentary states: "The inner mind conditions phenomena without ceasing for even a single moment. If one does not reflect upon the past, one immediately leaps ahead to calculate the future.
These 'shadow-matters' pertain to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses; as long as there are only shadow-matters, this is not yet the truth."
"I do not command you to hold [this] as non-mind.
This section on examining the text has two parts. First, not contradicting the prior position. The *Jian* (Commentary) states: "Command (*chì*) means correctness.

This refers to the previous refutation of the "other mind" (*tācitta*), which was strict. This examination of the text says, "I do not command you," which is compassionate. The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "The Buddha possesses..."
Out of the compassion with which he instructs his sons, he thus borrows the title "Compassionate yet Stern.
When he says, "I am not commanding you," his meaning is that there is no true mind existing apart from the delusions; for there are no waves apart from water, and no gold apart from the vessel.
However, you must subtly examine and scrutinize the mind. The commentary states:
"Examine and discern the two minds in detail; through repeated contemplation and observation, you will find there is no separate entity."
If there were a nature of discrimination that existed apart from the external objects before one, that would truly be your mind.

The commentary states: This teaches others merely to abandon the deluded mind that conditions objects through the eight consciousnesses—from the visual consciousness conditioning the object of form, up to the eighth consciousness conditioning the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world. All of these are the false phenomena of external objects; they are merely...
Apart from the external objects before you, there is a portion of luminous, discerning nature that is not conditioned by perfuming;
it does not perish along with those external objects, but remains solemnly and alone—this is truly your mind. As the subsequent text states: "It appears as if it were the objects before you;

yet if one were to remove those external objects, this luminous, discerning nature that is not conditioned by perfuming would not exist. This, then, is the deluded mind, not the true mind. The commentary says:

Regarding the discernment of the two types of mind: that which is free from objects and possesses intrinsic nature is the true mind; that which is free from objects and lacks intrinsic nature is the deluded mind.
As for the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature), it has no substance when separated from objects.

The fourth [section] consists of three parts, while the first [section] points out that [the imagined nature] lacks substance in accordance with its objects. This section has two parts; the first clarifies that it lacks substance apart from its objects.
The Commentary states: "If the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva) is separated from the preceding eight consciousnesses, it then lacks substance."
"This refers to the reflected images of the discriminations of the preceding sense-objects (*pūrvadhātu-viṣaya*).
The subsequent phrase "pointing to the presently manifest deluded mind" is annotated as follows: "This refers to the five preceding sense-objects;

'discrimination' is the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*), which forcibly generates discrimination; 'reflected image' is the seventh [consciousness], which clings to the objective aspect (*viṣayabhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as its own self."
The eighth matter is the matter of the fruition of karma. This deluded mind is not the true mind. Objects (*viṣaya*) are not permanent;

next, it clarifies that when objects perish, they vanish accordingly. The text has three parts: first, the designation that the nature of objects is impermanent. The commentary states: "Regarding the words 'before'..."
The nature of sensory objects (dharmas) cannot abide eternally.
When they undergo transformation and perish, the following clarifies the limit of their cessation. The commentary states: "At the time when the preceding sensory objects transform and perish..."
This mind would then be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.

The subsequent metaphor [of the hair and horns] is identical to the permanent extinction of external objects (*dharmas*). The commentary states: "The hair of a tortoise and the horns of a rabbit are among the five types of non-existence;

they are absolute non-existents. If you cling to this discriminating mind directed toward external objects as being the true mind, then when those external objects undergo transformation and extinction..."
At that time, if this mind were to suddenly fall away and cease to exist absolutely, then your Dharmakāya would be identical to annihilation.

Thereafter, there would be no cause by which to realize the ultimate fruit, nor would there be the primary causal factor for the initial realization. [The] Commentary states: "The Dharmakāya is not said [to be annihilated]."
Annihilation. You refute the attachment of others who take these eight consciousnesses—the deluded mind that perceives objects—to be the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).

When objects cease and the mind perishes, the *dharmakāya* must likewise become annihilated. This is because you maintain that the deluded mind is the true mind; thus, the true mind must be annihilated.
Once the true mind is annihilated, the *dharmakāya* is thereby known [to be so]. The true mind is itself the *dharmakāya*.
It is the body.
Who could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Later, one will surely realize the supportless. The commentary states: Since the Dharma-body has already been severed and extinguished, [the text] further instructs Ānanda.
Cultivation consists of severing hindrances and realizing principle. "Cultivation" refers to the wisdom that practices; "Dharma-patience" (dharmakṣānti) refers to the object of that practice.
The preceding exposition on the destruction of false consciousness and its emptiness is hereby concluded.
The latter passage refers generally to the secret cause. Regarding the "pointing with the hand" mentioned at the beginning, the commentary states: "This indicates the underlying intent.

It means that in the previous section on 'picking sand' and 'pointing,' it was pointed out that Ānanda’s true nature—if it exists apart from external objects and possesses a discerning nature—is precisely your own mind.
Because Ānanda and the others did not recognize the path leading back to the truth, they remained silent."

[This was] lost. Therefore, the World-Honored One declared: "Among all those in the world who practice and study, even if they have attained the nine successive meditative concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) before their eyes, they cannot exhaust their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) to become Arhats.

This is entirely because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistakenly taking them for reality. Ānanda then rose and requested: "Since I followed the Buddha and resolved my mind toward renunciation..."
The Householder relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and constantly thought to himself, "There is no need for me to practice.
When his Dharma-eye was opened, he then raised his hand and spoke to Ānanda, saying: "For example, my fist—if there were no hand, there would be no fist;
if there were no eyes for you, your seeing would not be established. By means of your faculty of sight..."
For example, regarding my fist: is its meaning the same [as yours]? Ānanda replied, "Indeed so, World-Honored One. Since there is no 'self-eye,' 'self-view' is not established;
it is like the Tathāgata’s fist, as the facts and meanings are analogous. The World-Honored One then rebuked him, saying:
"Your statement that they are analogous is incorrect. Why is this? For instance, if a person has no hands, the fist is ultimately extinguished. That...
"One without eyes" does not mean that seeing is entirely non-existent. Why is this? You should try asking a blind person on the road, "What do you see?
Viewed through this principle, the objects before one are naturally dark; what deficiency is there in the faculty of seeing? Therefore, the Commentary says:
"Ānanda, by acquiescing to this, was about to conform to the profound model; why did he side with the Sage’s intention and thus invite himself to fall into defeat? [End of] Upper Section.
The section on the analogy of seeing the hand’s characteristics by pointing has concluded.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent and lost in self-reflection.

Following this, the sixth section, "Extensively Pointing to the Secret Cause," begins. Within this, the first part, "The Analogy of Seeing the Hand’s Characteristics by Pointing," consists of six sub-sections; the first of these is "The Disciples’ Loss."
The meaning is as follows. The Sub-commentary says: This refers to the Buddha coming forward and again taking it away, saying, "This is not your mind.
Within this, he further points it out, saying, "I am not commanding you to grasp it as being non-mind.

If one acknowledges the Buddha's act of taking it away, yet if one does not acknowledge the Buddha's pointing it out, one is thus constrained whether advancing or retreating. One can only remain silent and lose oneself, returning to the True.
The Commentary states: "A hound of Han leads a beast; here, it is as if the beast has run into its den.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All those people in the world who practice and study..."
Second, the Tathāgata’s correction of errors, consisting of five parts. First, the general mention of those who practice. The commentary states:
This refers generally to all persons who study and practice the Dharma;
although they may have currently attained the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

Second, the explanation of the stages and sequence of cultivation. The commentary states: "The arrangement follows a systematic order; proceeding from the lower to the higher according to their proper sequence is called 'successive order' (*anupūrva*).
The nine concentrations are: the first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, and fourth dhyāna—these belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);

and the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

These are the eight. To these, add one more: the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). It extinguishes the six [consciousnesses] while simultaneously exhausting the seventh; it is also called the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*) and the "mindless attainment" (*acittakasamāpatti*).
"One cannot exhaust the outflows and become an Arhat;
with three fingers not ascending to the true fruit. The commentary states: It should read, "One cannot exhaust the outflows and thus become an Arhat."

This passage appears to be inverted. This excludes those who have not realized the body (kāyasākṣin). Nāgasena attained only the eight dhyānas but had not yet attained the cessation attainment (nirodhasamāpatti).
Had he attained this attainment, his outflows would have been exhausted and he would have become an Arhat. "Realizing the body" means direct realization.
Why did he not attain it? The following text states:
All this arises from clinging to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistakenly taking them to be real.
Fourth, it reveals the error of guarding what is fundamentally delusive. The commentary states:

This refers to how, due to clinging generally to these deluded thoughts of birth and death—the mind of the eighth consciousness that perceives objects—one is deceived into mistaking them for the true nature. The following text then introduces the subsequent section.
Regarding others:
for this reason, although you have now attained much learning (*bahuśruta*), you have not realized the fruit of a noble one (*āryaphala*).
Fifth, *Sacejja* (Exhortation), Ānanda: the commentary states that although he has attained much learning, he maintains the words of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Regarding the Teaching: A sutra states, "One who hears and upholds [the Dharma] shall become a Buddha. If so, why does the Buddha not hear it himself? Furthermore, it says, "Much hearing increases wisdom.
This implies that one who does not know the true nature (dharmatā) cannot attain the four fruits of arhatship.
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with deep sorrow.

He entreated [the Buddha] three times. Part II: The Text of the Entreaty, which has three sections. Section I: The Text of the Entreaty, which has five parts. Part A: The Text of Self-Reproach for Lacking Wisdom in Others. This has five parts.
The initial account describes the profound sense of grief upon receiving the admonition. The commentary states:
"Ānanda had previously returned from the chamber of the Mātanga woman and wept bitterly once; now he weeps again here, which is why it is called 'repeated'."
He prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, knelt for a long time with palms joined.

"Five: Describing the realization of cessation through one's own person. The commentary states: "The Buddha is the Dharma-body; he does not substitute for my body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

I have lost my original mind.

It is like a person who speaks of food but can never satisfy their hunger;

World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles.

This is truly because they do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.

The Commentary states: "Truly" (liáng) means "to believe"; "because of" (yóu) means "due to. This says that because one does not awaken to the truth—that the quiescent, perfect, and eternal mind is the original nature of the mind, the fundamental essence—the following request is made.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on me, who am destitute and exposed.

At that moment, from the *svastika* on the Tathāgata’s chest, precious light surged forth.

This light is brilliantly radiant, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors.

Simultaneously pervading the Buddha-worlds as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, it shone brilliantly across threefold realms.
The commentary states: "This is because there is nowhere that its radiance does not illuminate."
It universally irrigates the crowns of all Tathāgatas throughout the precious lands (*ratnakṣetra*) of the ten directions.

[The text says] "fourfold irrigation of the crowns of all Buddhas. The commentary states: "The precious lands of the ten directions are the 'supported' (*niśraya*), which is the retributive environment (*bhogya-niṣyanda*);

The essence of birth and birth is one. Furthermore, this expresses the teaching of the *Cūḍā-samādhi* directed toward this [state], and it also expresses that this sutra is inconceivable;

"Seventh, 'Proclaiming the Establishment of the Dharma Banner. The commentary states: A banner signifies height and prominence; it symbolizes that this sutra is the standard and pinnacle among all teachings.

This one volume, consisting of five sections on the causes and threefold cultivation and realization of the Five Mysteries, is established as a great Dharma banner. Because the Great Dharma is like a banner, it is called a "Dharma Banner.

Mun. He bends these five fingers and clenches them into a fist; thus, there is this mark of the fist.

Section Six: Text on Citing Examples to Point to the Mind (Seven Parts). Part One: Admonishing for Understanding. The Commentary states:

Ānanda, it is like my fist: if there were no hand of mine, my fist would not be formed.

"Fourth, the charges are unequal. The Commentary states: "This meaning is not so.

Just as for a handless person, the fist is ultimately extinguished; so too, for one who lacks eyes, it is not that seeing is entirely non-existent.

As will be explained later, seeing persists even in the absence of eyes. The commentary states: "The fist is ultimately extinguished" indicates that the *nimittabhāga* (the objective aspect) is entirely absent;

"it is not that seeing is entirely non-existent" indicates that the *darśanabhāga* (the subjective aspect of seeing) is not non-existent. This means that although the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) may be obscured by darkness, the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) constantly persists.
Why is this so? Section Six, "Seeking and Attaining," consists of three parts. First is the narration that the blind possess sight. The commentary states: "For what reason?
(so yì hé guǒ).

The "Seven Knots" refers to the mind. The commentary states: Using the aforementioned principle for observation, the external objects are inherently dark;

therein, the Buddha invited Ānanda, saying, "Try now, on the road, to ask a blind person: 'What do you see? He...
"O blind men, you will surely come to answer me that you see only darkness and such things. Therefore, the World-Honored One pointed this out, saying:
'Observe by this principle that the external objects themselves are dark; what deficiency is there in the seeing? Consequently, Ānanda raised a doubt within this context, asking:
'If the eyes of the blind see only darkness, how can it be called seeing? Thereupon, the World-Honored One..."

Second, the use of a lamp-light to clarify the pointing. This section has three parts. First, questioning the previous [argument] and rejecting the pointing.

The two types of black are distinct; are they not distinct?

The commentary states: "A person without eyes sees only the black before them, whereas a person with eyes is situated within a dark room. This...
The two who see in the dark: are they distinct from one another, or are they not? Let another explain this.
Thus, World-Honored One, when these people in the darkness are compared with that group of blind men, there is no difference whatsoever between the two types of darkness.

The subsequent response states that when the group of blind men together observe the two types of darkness, there is no difference between them. The commentary notes: "The meaning of Ānanda’s reply is that there is indeed no distinction;
one must know that even those without eyes possess seeing, and it cannot be said that they have no seeing."
Ānanda, if a person who has no eyes sees only total darkness before them, and suddenly regains the light of their eyes so that they see various forms within the external objects before them,

Regarding the subsequent section on inferring the mind through the accomplishment of seeing, there are three parts. First, inferring that the lamp is the same as the eye by suppressing seeing to establish the lamp; this also has three parts.
First, citing the case of a blind person whose cataracts are removed so that their eyes can finally see. The commentary states: "The Buddha further cites this example of a person without eyes."
Suddenly, someone took tweezers and pried open his eyes for him; he could once again see objects such as those before him.

That person in the darkness perceives only the blackness before them; when they suddenly obtain the light of a lamp, they likewise perceive various forms within that same field of objects.

Later, citing the analogy of a person with sight receiving a lamp, it is argued that the lamp constitutes seeing.

[The Master] says: The commentary states: "If you do not name it 'lamp,' the meaning of 'lamp' is not established. Furthermore, if one must establish whether it is sentient or insentient, yet seeing lacks meaning, it is not established.

The subsequent section, which clarifies both visible form and the faculty of seeing to establish that [seeing] is the mind, consists of two parts. First, the lamp is cited to point to the eye. The commentary states:

The eye can manifest color; such is the nature of seeing. This is the mind, not the eye.

Seeing occurs within the mind; thus, it is the mind that sees. If one were to say that the eye can see, then why do dead people, who possess eyes, not see?
Clarity does not follow the sense organs; rather, clarity relies upon the organs to manifest.

The third [section] concerns the pointing-out of departure and remaining, movement and stillness. The commentary states: "Departure" is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*), as they are like guests who do not remain for long.

"Empty. Because it is neither arising nor ceasing. This indicates the intended meaning. However, what was previously held to be the "mind" that performs the investigation was refuted by the World-Honored One.

In the Deer Park, for Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya and the other five bhikṣus.

"Although I have encountered the Buddha, I still harbor doubts.
The second [passage] states: "Though I have met the Righteous One, I still doubt. The commentary says: "This means that although I have now indeed encountered the World-Honored One..."
I am still filled with doubt. The nature of foxes is to be full of suspicion; being suspicious, they hesitate and cannot reach a decision.
I do not know whether these two non-Buddhist practitioners, in making such statements, were actually speaking the truth or not.
"How does one manifest and realize this mind as the stage of neither arising nor ceasing?"—this is the third request for a clear exposition of the true path.
The commentary states: "To 'manifest' (huī) means to employ; 'stage' (dì) refers to the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
[The Bodhisattva] requests the Buddha to employ his power for the sake of others so that they may realize and fully know that this mind neither arises nor ceases."
Now, all those in this great assembly who still possess outflows (āsrava) universally desire to hear [this].
The commentary states: "The fourfold narration is for those of similar capacity who joyfully wish to listen. This excludes those free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Regarding why the King requested [the teaching] again when Ānanda had previously asked and the Buddha had not yet answered, there are three reasons for reconciling these points: first, lest the main text be lost; this...
The meaning of the *Madhyama Āgama* is not complete [in this regard]. Regarding the two kings, they represent the sense of sovereignty (*vaśitā*).

They asked whatever they wished to ask, regardless of whether Ānanda had previously questioned them. Furthermore, these kings had harbored this question for a long time; seeing that Ānanda’s inquiry coincided exactly with their own intentions, they spoke.
He then rose and questioned [the Buddha]. When the Buddha was about to answer, he also answered what Ānanda had asked.
The Buddha told the Great King: "While your body is currently present, I shall certainly demonstrate it later.
This passage has two parts. First, the exclusion of cessation. This has three sections. First, the section on cessation, which has four parts. First, the question. The commentary states:
The Buddha addressed the king, saying: "Your body currently serves as the ruler of Central India. There is a sūtra that employs the character *cun* (存), whose meaning is comprehensive.
Now I ask you again: regarding this physical body of yours—"
The commentary states: It is said that this body of yours, a mass of flesh, is composed of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood;
for thirty-six days within the mother’s womb, it was situated above the stomach and below the large intestine, formed through a provisional combination.
"Is it like the eternal and indestructible state of a vajra, or will it undergo transformation and decay?
The commentary states: "Is it like the eternal body and dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas—unborn and undying—or will it migrate, change, and rot?

The Buddha’s intention was to ask whether he should explain [the nature of things] to others as being unborn and undying; however, he first asked about birth and death in order to address the immediate and superficial concerns [of the interlocutor].
"Extremely profound.
World-Honored One, this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.
Second answer. The commentary states: "It refers to this body of mine, a temporary union of semen and blood, a physical form composed of the four elements that is precarious and fragile. (1)
"In the morning there is no constant death; when the ghost of death arrives, one must inevitably undergo transformation, ruin, and extinction.
The Buddha said, "Great King, you have not yet been extinguished; how then can you know what it is like to be extinguished?"
The third inquiry. The commentary states: The Buddha asked again: "You have not yet realized cessation; this body still exists before you.
How can you know that it will undergo transformation and perish?"
World-Honored One, although this body of mine, subject to impermanence and decay, has not yet perished, I observe before me that from moment to moment it undergoes change and passes away;

it is ever-new and never abides, like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away and dissolving. As this dissolution continues without ceasing, I know for certain that this body must eventually come to total extinction.
The fourth response. The commentary states: "I say that this impermanence of mine cannot endure for long; yet this body of transformation and decay has not ceased even until now.
As I observe what is present before me, from the preceding thought to the succeeding thought, they thus flow on in succession and fall away."
It never pauses for rest. Observe that the preceding thought is new, and the succeeding thought is even newer than the preceding one;
all are being shifted by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It is like a mass of fire that gradually turns to ash;

once it has become ash, it is blown away by the wind, gradually dissolving and perishing without further cessation. You must certainly know that this body must likewise undergo transformation and extinction.
"It is coming to an end.
The Buddha said, "It is so, Great King. Your present age has already reached senescence; how does your appearance compare to that of your youth?"
Next is the section on "Difference. This passage has two parts. First, the question comparing the old to the young. The commentary states: "It asks:
'Regarding your present physical body and its age, you have already reached a state of decay and senility; how does your countenance and appearance compare to when you were a ten-year-old child?'"
“World-Honored One, in my former childhood, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous.

Later, as I grew old and decrepit, they became withered and coarse. [The commentary states: “An infant is called *xing*; at two years of age, one is called *hai*; at three years of age, one is called *ru*.
‘Skin’ (*fu*) refers to the outer layer of the skin; ‘convergences’ (*cou*) refer to the places where the blood vessels meet. [In youth, the skin was] moist, slippery, and radiant.”
When one reaches full maturity, the blood and vital energy become fully developed.
The commentary states: "In successive stages, one reaches adulthood and becomes established; the bones, blood, vital energy, and complexion all become robust, plump, and full.
At the age of twenty, one is still soft and weak, yet begins to wear the cap and grow hair. At thirty, one is strong and enters into family life."
Now, my declining years are pressed by decrepitude and senility.
The commentary states: "Now, my age has fallen into decline; it is as if a crumbling mountain is beset by both cold and heat.

One is driven by the shifting of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), becoming decayed, withered, and senile. At eighty, one is called "decayed" (*śuai*); at ninety, one is called "senile" (*mao*).
The physical form and features are withered and haggard;
the spirit is clouded and dull. The commentary states: "The body and complexion are parched and emaciated; the spirit is dim and consciousness is obscure.
The hair has turned white and the face is wrinkled; one will not last much longer. How can this be compared to the time when one was full of vigor?"
The commentary states: "White-haired and chicken-skin-skinned" means that one has reached [the end]; "will die before long.
The intent is that now that one is old, one must not act like a child.
The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical form and countenance should not have withered all at once, but rather gradually over time.
First, he examined him closely. The commentary states: "This means that your body and facial features should not have suddenly become decrepit from the very first year;
the Buddha’s intention was for the King to describe how he aged through gradual stages."
The King said, "World-Honored One, transformation shifts secretly.

The subsequent answer consists of three parts. First is a general account of the hidden flow. The commentary states: 'Secretly' refers to the secret of desire; 'shifts' refers to alteration and transition.
This means that the growth of hair and nails is the transformation brought about by the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations)."
Truly, I was unaware that as cold and heat have shifted and flowed, I have gradually reached this state.
The Commentary states: "As the sun and moon revolve, there is one cold and one heat;

through these shifting changes and flowing transformations, this body of my four elements has gradually moved from childhood to middle age, and from middle age to old age, aging in successive stages."
For what reason? At twenty years of age, though I was called young, my countenance was already aged compared to when I was ten.
At thirty, I was further declined than at twenty. Now that I am sixty-two, looking back at the time I was fifty, I appear as if I were still in the prime of my strength.

Next, I shall separately state the coarse and easy [aspects]. The commentary states: "At the age of twenty, the year I reached my early manhood (*ruogan*), my appearance was already aged beyond that of a ten-year-old child.
As the years successively increased, at thirty I was in the 'toothed' (*chi*) stage; yet I was even more decrepit than at my early manhood.
At sixty, when one ought to be in the 'ear-harmonious' (*er-shun*) stage, I have exceeded that by double, and moreover surpassed it by two."
It has now reached sixty-two years. When I observe the five aggregates at a single moment, they appear as if perfectly robust and vigorous.
World-Honored One, I perceive their subtle shifting; though this body withers and falls away, [the mind continues].

Later, the details of the transition from Zheng to Qian are described. The Commentary states: "The Book of Documents says that in the 'Yao' chapter, [the term] 'cu' (passed away) is used; we do not take 'beng' (collapse/death), but rather take 'lao shan' (to die a good death).
In the interval between these, there are shifts and changes, and furthermore, it is limited to ten years."
The commentary states: Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the process of flux and transformation is extremely subtle.
Now, speaking in coarse terms, we shall limit it to ten years; twelve years constitute one cycle (*yuga*). Here, taking the full number, we define one instance of aging.
If I were to contemplate this further in minute detail, would its transformation occur only once every *ji* (twelve years) or two *ji*?
The commentary states: "It is not merely that one ages once every twelve years; nor is it merely every two *ji*, which is twenty-four years;
nor is it merely that one undergoes aging once every twenty-four years."
It is truly a transformation of the year; how could it be merely a transformation of the year?
It is also accompanied by a transformation of the month. The commentary states: "Truly, it is a change that occurs once every year. Furthermore, it refutes this by stating:
"It is not only a change that occurs once every year, but is also accompanied by a change that occurs once every month."
"How can it be that they change monthly and, moreover, shift daily?
The commentary states: "Directly" means "only. Furthermore, it is said: "Not only do they undergo transformation once a month, but they also shift their positions once every day."
"Contemplate with deep reflection; moment by moment.
The commentary states: "Reflect subtly and observe with precise clarity. Time is extremely brief, not exceeding a single *kṣaṇa*.
In the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers, there are sixty *kṣaṇas* and nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing."
From moment to moment, there can be no staying still; thus one knows that this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.

The commentary states: Since the preceding thought-moment and the succeeding thought-moment cannot remain stationary, one knows that this physical body of flesh must ultimately undergo change, decay, and destruction.
The Buddha said to the Great King: “You have seen that transformations and shifts occur without ceasing;

now I shall show you what is permanent. This section has three parts. First, the question asking whether he knows this or not, which has two sub-parts. First, restating his previous realization. [The text reads: “Examine yourself to know the truth.
The commentary states: “This restates what the King previously said: ‘Is it only the body that changes? It also includes... (text fragment).
Yunzi Qian said, "In old age, my vital energy has dissipated and my appearance has changed;
I have realized that you are subject to extinction.

The commentary states: "To 'realize' means to understand and know for certain that you are subject to extinction. This reiterates what was previously stated: 'Therefore, I know that my own body will ultimately undergo transformation.'"
"Extinction.
Furthermore, at the time of extinction, do you know that there is anything within the body that does not extinguish?
The commentary states: "Furthermore" means "then. That is to say, at the time when the four great elements undergo transformation and extinction, do you still perceive these four great elements?
Within the body, there exists a portion of the true nature of Śūraṅgama, which cannot be destroyed or decayed.
It is like [the lotus] in mud, which remains unstained even when immersed; it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning, and now, is it not likewise unceasing?
King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "I truly did not know.

Later, he prostrated himself with his forehead to the ground and respectfully consulted [the Buddha], recounting his confusion regarding true nature. The commentary states: "If the King knew, he would have known it thoroughly.
According to the *Sāṭhāgata-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*, King Prasenajit was a Buddha in a past life; it was because two teachers could not coexist that [he appeared as a king].

Manifesting transformation, he displayed the rites and protocols of various kingdoms to illustrate the confusion regarding the True [Dharma]. With a humble heart, he requested further instruction, seeking to understand the Buddha’s descent for the sake of preaching it;
this was intended to cause all sentient beings to know it.
The Buddha said: "I shall now show you the nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
Next, he granted permission for the appropriate demonstration. This section has four parts; the first grants permission to demonstrate the mind. The commentary states:
The Buddha said, "Since you do not yet know it, I shall now show it to you, so that you too may know the nature of this 'not-knowing'—which is neither born nor extinguished."
"Great King, at what age did you first see the waters of the Ganges?
This second section raises the characteristics of the river and consists of four parts. First is the question regarding the time of his observation of the river. The commentary states:
"The waters of this river flow from the Lion’s Mouth of Lake Anavatapta; the circumference of this river is forty *li*."
The sand in the middle is as fine as flour and flows mixed with water; it is also called the River of Gold Sand, because this river contains golden sand.
It is also called the River of Blessings, for when people of the Western Heaven (India) give birth to children, they all bathe them in this river, saying that they thereby obtain blessings.
Located five *li* from the city, outside the southern gate, it is within the range of human vision. When the Buddha preached the Dharma, he frequently used this river as a metaphor.

To illustrate this, the King said: "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīvaka. As we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges."
"Second, she rewarded me when I was a child, being able to understand [my needs]. The commentary states: "The five mothers—these two are the foster mothers.
When I was three years old, the foster mother took me in her arms and went to visit the god Jīva. In the language of China, this means 'the God of Life'; it is a temple.
When people in the Western Regions give birth to a child, they all come to this temple to seek blessings or longevity. He said, "As for me..."
When these three years had passed, he then recognized it as the waters of the Ganges.
The Buddha said, "Great King, it is as you have said: at twenty, one declines from the state of ten, and so on until sixty."
The sun, moon, years, and seasons change and pass from moment to moment. Thus, when you were three years old and saw this river, how was its water when you reached the age of thirteen?
Third, he raises the fundamental point to demand an explanation. The commentary states:

"According to what you have previously asserted—that at twenty years of age one is already declining compared to ten—then it is not only the years that change, but the months as well; and not only the months, but [the days and so forth]."
It also involves daily shifts. Thus, day and month alternate with a year, and further with a season.
When you have seen this Ganges River for three years, and ten more years have passed—reaching the thirteenth season—what will you see of the water?
The King said, "It is exactly as it was when I was three years old; there has been no change until now, even at sixty-two years of age.
Fourth Answer: Water is eternally unchanging. Commentary: The King said that it is as it was at the age of three, and so on through his sixtieth year.
There has been no difference between those two times. Even now, after sixty-two years, this water has likewise undergone no change.
This refers to the absence of transition in the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*); subsequently, it concerns the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).
The Buddha said, "Now you lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled. Your face will certainly be more wrinkled than it was in your youth.

Thus, as you look at this Ganges River now, is there any difference between this vision of the river and the vision you had when you were a child looking at the same river? Is there any distinction between childhood and old age?"

The third section, "Examining the Transition and Persistence of Vision," has two parts. First, it raises the phenomenon of the transition of form to examine that the nature remains identical and appropriate.

The commentary states: "If you were like yourself now, with hair already turning white through grief and the skin of your face inevitably wrinkled, then this visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) at the age of sixty-two would be the same as it was when you were a young child."
[The Buddha] asked, "Is there still a distinction between old and young? Do you mean that at the time of childhood and at the time of old age, the seeing-nature remains without difference?
The King replied, "No, World-Honored One."
The subsequent answer states that the mind is always different from the body and is easily transformed. The commentary says: "The answer is that [the mind] does not age.
The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face has wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never wrinkled in its nature."

Fourth, the manifestation that the mind is eternally quiescent, which is further divided into three parts. First is the analogy. This section has three sub-parts. First is "wrinkles. The commentary states:

"Although your face is wrinkled, the nature of the arising and ceasing of deluded consciousness has never been wrinkled. This refers to the *pratyakṣa* (direct perception) of the eye-consciousness, which is identical to the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This *pratyakṣa* of the eye-consciousness is the immediate objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses; it does not differentiate between the object and the subject.

What is called "semblance direct perception" (*sākṣātkalpa-pratyakṣa*) merely points toward semblance direct perception; through this, true direct perception (*bhūta-pratyakṣa*) is naturally revealed.
When semblance is fully understood, one returns to the real. All of these are the single nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
That which wrinkles is subject to change; that which does not wrinkle is not subject to change.
Next, regarding change:
that which changes undergoes cessation. That which does not change is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
"Subsequently extinguished.
What does this mean? How can one undergo birth and death within that?
Next, "Constant. The commentary states: This asks how, within the *tathāgatagarbha*, there can further arise ever-new [phenomena]. It says:
Birth is the arising [of phenomena], and their falling away moment by moment is called death.
Yet [the Buddha] still cites that Makkhali Gosāla and others, who all claim that after this body dies, there is total annihilation.
Later, he rebukes them. The commentary states: Makkhali Gosāla; his personal name was Makkhali, and his mother’s [name was] Gosālā.
He was named Kauśīlī. Relying on his mother’s name, he was called by it; among the six teachers, he was the second.

He maintained that the Way is fundamentally natural (*svabhāva*), so why rely on cultivation or realization? As a verse says: "Who cleared the thorns and drew the beasts? Who dug the rivers and piled up the high mountains?
When a violent wind suddenly arises, it ceases of its own accord; One should know that all phenomena are naturally so. Thus it is equal [to the other views].
He summoned the six heretical teachers.
When the King heard these words, he later understood their meaning and rejoiced. The commentary states: Before King Prasenajit had encountered the Buddha, he saw this [Kāśyapa]...
Candana and Vairaṭiputra both said, "This body, after death, is called nirvāṇa.

Now, having heard the Buddha point out the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, saying, "Though your face is wrinkled, this essence of seeing has never been wrinkled," and even further, "How could birth and death occur within it? King [Śrīgupta] heard these words from the Buddha.
They came to know with certainty that after death one casts off this life to take up another; together with the great assembly, they leaped for joy and experienced what they had never known before.
The commentary states: "Faith" (śraddhā) refers to faith-understanding; a pure mind is called faith. Faith is like a crystal bead, for it can clarify turbid water.

"Knowing" (jñāna) refers to awakening-knowledge; it is the awakening-knowledge that once this particular retribution has been exhausted, one is born again into another retribution through virtuous causes.

One is born into the good realms; through evil karma, one falls into the hells. Shedding this body composed of the four great elements, one proceeds to birth within the nine stages of the three realms.
To leap for joy and exultation is for the flavor of the Dharma to nourish the spirit; to attain what has never been attained before is to gain a most excellent benefit.

The second [section], "The Appearance Contains the Essence," specifically points to the secret cause. It consists of thirteen passages: first, the commonality of ordinary beings and sages in their suchness;
second, the entire tide of the great ocean; third, observing the moon from a roadside inn; fourth, the entrustment of the eight returns; fifth, the nature being devoid of causal marks.
Sixth, the substance has neither increase nor decrease. Seventh, views are neither one nor different. Eighth, like flowers in the sky and the single moon.

Ninth, refuting spontaneity. Tenth, refuting causes and conditions. Eleventh, realizing that the cataract is not the seeing itself. Twelfth, refuting conjunction. Thirteenth, refuting non-conjunction.
Now, regarding the first point—that both ordinary people and sages are alike as a finger—this is the intended meaning of the "finger. However, it refers to Ānanda’s seeing.
The World-Honored One pointed to King Prasenajit to demonstrate that the faculty of seeing is neither born nor extinguished. Ānanda then asked:
"If this faculty of seeing and hearing is necessarily neither born nor extinguished, why, World-Honored One, do you say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of perversion?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke the parable of hanging down the hands to remove names, answering Ānanda and causing him to understand.
Regarding the body in its upright and inverted states, the Sūtra says: "At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm;
with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda and said, 'Do you now consider my *mudrā* hand to be upright or inverted?
Ānanda replied, 'In the world, sentient beings regard this as inverted, yet I do not know which is upright and which is inverted. The Buddha told Ānanda:"
"If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then by what standard do worldly people determine what is upright?
Ānanda replied, "If the Tathāgata were to extend his arm—his hand as soft as cotton wool—and point it upward toward the sky, that would be called upright.
The Buddha then extended his arm and asked Ānanda, "If this inversion were such that head and tail were swapped, how many times more would worldly people [be confused]?"
[The Buddha] gazed [upon him]. Thereupon, the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda to look toward the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and observe the two designations of "ordinary person" and "sage.
The Sūtra says: "Follow your careful observation of your own body and the Buddha-body: where do the names 'perversion' and 'that which is called perversion' reside?
The preceding section concludes the explanation that ordinary persons and sages are equally identical to Thusness (tathatā).
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt on both knees, and addressed the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, at first, ordinary people and sages were alike, like the finger [pointing]. Section Two: First, the text of the objection, which has four parts. First, the formal expression of inquiry. The commentary states:
Ānanda saw the World-Honored One previously approach and, based upon the present direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), pointed to King Prasenajit.
The King [asked about] the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which exceeds what was previously discussed. Therefore, he immediately rose to raise an objection, saying:
"If this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither arising nor ceasing," thus presenting two points regarding the realization of principle.
The commentary states: "Seeing and hearing are the five consciousnesses of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); they are the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing."
"Nature" (*xing*) must mean "constancy. It has never arisen from the beginning, nor does it cease now. This refers to when the World-Honored One pointed to King Prasenajit and said:
"Though your face is wrinkled, this essence of seeing (*jian-jing*)—its nature—has never been wrinkled; it is fundamentally without arising or ceasing."
"How is it, World-Honored One? You have named us as those who have lost the true nature and act with inverted conduct.
This is stated three times in contradiction [to what was previously said]. The commentary states:

"How can the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, in the preceding passage, name us commoners as having lost our original *tathatā* (Buddha-nature) and acting with inverted, head-downward conduct? Regarding "acting": it refers to not practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
This is correct. It means that when Ānanda previously, while the fingers of Tuōluó were opening and closing, said, "I see the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing;

it is not my seeing-nature that has opening and closing. Furthermore, when [the Buddha] pointed toward the brilliant light of the wheel, he said, "My head is moving, yet my seeing-nature does not even have stillness—what is there to be shaken? This is...
The World-Honored One rebuked him as before, saying: "Why do you now take movement to be the body and movement to be the object?
From beginning to end, thought after thought arises and perishes; you have lost the true nature and act in delusion.

Having received this reprimand from the World-Honored One, Ānanda, at the beginning of the second fascicle of the sutra, requested the Buddha to explain the difference between arising-and-perishing and non-arising-and-perishing.

The two aspects of arising and ceasing clarify the nature; one must therefore subvert delusion to cultivate the real. The Buddha did not yet answer him. King Prasenajit then rose and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha, based upon the immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*) of eye-consciousness, pointed to the *tathāgatagarbha* nature—pointing to the true within the midst of the deluded.
He intended for him to realize that there is no "true" to be grasped and no "deluded" to be abandoned. How could he have known that the intent was profound and the words were pregnant with meaning?

This contradicts what was stated previously. Therefore, Ānanda, being a follower of the Hīnayāna, failed to understand the World-Honored One’s pointing to the Dharma and immediately rose to raise an objection.
I pray that you will bestow compassion and wash away my defilements.
Fourth, the request for a comprehensive resolution. The commentary states: "I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will arise—'arise' meaning to manifest.

His compassion (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness; his pity (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering. With the water of the Dharma, may he wash away the defilements of my deluded mind. That which soils one's own essence is called 'dust' (*rajas*);
that which stains and is difficult to remove is called 'impurity' (*mala*)."
At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm; with his wheel-marked hand pointing downward, he showed it to Ānanda and said:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted?"

The subsequent section clarifies the doubt. It consists of two parts. The first part concerns the lowering of the hand to establish the characteristics; it contains five sub-sections. First, the lowering of the hand and the dual questioning. The commentary states:
*Mudrā* (Mother-dhara) hand is also called the *Auspicious Hand*. When the Buddha’s hand forms the *mudrā* seal, it is the Seal of Certainty (*niścaya-mudrā*).
The hand represents the aspect of form: that which is correct is the True, while that which is inverted is the Delusory. The True is the Sage; the Delusory is the Ordinary being.
Ānanda said, "The sentient beings of the world take this to be inverted; yet I do not know who is upright and who is inverted.
[This is] the second citation of worldly renown. The commentary states: Previously, Ānanda had been rebuked by the Buddha and did not dare to determine for himself.
He therefore said, "Those people in the world who are deluded regarding the Truth and turned away from Awakening take this to be inverted; however, I myself do not know which one..."
"This is correct; that is inverted. Ānanda secretly revealed that there is fundamentally neither correctness nor inversion.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the world consider this to be inverted, then by what standard do these people determine what is correct?"
"Three times he asked about what is upright. The commentary states: "People of the world see my hand hanging down and call it 'upside-down';
they see my hand held upright and call it 'upright. Such are their empty and false discriminations."
Ānanda said, "If the Tathāgata raises his arm, which is as soft as *tūla* cotton, pointing it upward toward the sky, that is called 'correct.
When the four [fingers] of the *tūla*-soft hand point upward,
the Buddha then raised his arm."
The five Tathāgatas, citing [the matter] in turn, addressed Ānanda, saying: "If this inversion were to exchange its beginning and end, the subsequent decree would be the dual name of 'Truth' (di).
This passage has three sections. First, it restates the preceding divergent views. The commentary states: "If" (ruo) means "as" (ru).
This refers to "knowing" as its meaning. All categories of delusion involve incorrect knowledge and vision.
For instance, when the arm is suddenly raised, sentient beings call it "upright," and being upright is then the head;
when the arm is suddenly lowered, sentient beings call it "inverted," and being inverted is then the tail. In this manner, they interchange with one another.
All people of the world gaze at this with a single-minded focus.
The commentary states: To be deluded regarding the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) while relying upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) constitutes one layer of delusion.

Furthermore, upon the characteristics of the dependent nature, they give rise to *parikalpita-agraha* (conceptual construction), distinguishing between the correct and the inverted, and between the true and the false. This, then—
This is to add delusion upon delusion.
Thus one knows that your body, when compared and illuminated alongside the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas, is next contrasted with the different names for ordinary beings and sages.
The commentary states: "Thus one knows that your body is precisely the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), a bubble-like illusion."
The physical body is an inversion; the pure *dharmakāya* is the eternally abiding body, which is the truth. By comparing and contrasting these categories, one gives rise to clear understanding:
the body of the Tathāgata is called "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).

The commentary states: You should simply say that the Tathāgata is right-cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and universal-cognition (*sarva-jñāna*). Right-cognition is fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*), and universal-cognition is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
"Your bodies are termed 'inverted nature. The commentary states:
It is said that this body of mine is an ordinary person's body; its nature alone is luminous clarity, while its characteristics are fundamental ignorance."
"Examine this closely as you wish: your body and the Buddha’s body—wherein do these names 'upside-down' reside that they are called 'upside-down'?
Later, he exhorted them to observe both together to exhaust their distinct characteristics. The commentary states:

"The World-Honored One then instructed Ānanda to give rise to a small measure of wisdom regarding the First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya) and observe: 'Your body is called upside-down; the Buddha’s body..."
"This is the Perfectly Enlightened One; your body is false, while the Buddha-body is true. To speak of truth and falsehood is in both cases a perversion.
What is called "suchness" regarding ordinary beings and sages is all but a dream-word; both "Buddha" and "nirvāṇa" are merely figurative designations.
Consequently, neither ordinary names nor holy names, nor ordinary characteristics nor holy characteristics, can be apprehended at all.
Regarding the second "Great Ocean" (Dàhǎi Quáncháozhǐ), the commentary states: this refers to the underlying intent.

It means that Ānanda did not understand the principle that the ordinary and the holy are one and the same; therefore, together with the great assembly, he stared vacantly at the Buddha, his eyes unblinking.
In an instant, they were unaware of where their own bodies and minds had become inverted.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, giving rise to a heart of great compassion, uttered a voice like the tide of the ocean and addressed Ānanda and the great assembly, saying:

"O sons of good family, I have often said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and all phenomena that serve as objects of perception, are manifested solely by the mind. Your body..."
The mind—these are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence, the wondrous mind. He rebuked them, saying:

"How is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, your jewel-like, luminous, and wondrous nature? He further said: "In a single moment of delusion, you take this as your mind and are certain to be confused, thinking it resides within the physical body.
You do not realize that from the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, [all are manifestations of that mind]."
All these are things within the wondrously luminous true mind. To illustrate this, it is said:

"It is like discarding a hundred thousand vast, clear oceans and recognizing only the substance of a single bubble, taking that bubble to be the entirety of the tide. The preceding passage points to the entire ocean as the tide.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha with unblinking eyes; they were unaware of where their own bodies and minds had become inverted.
[The second section on the two great oceans reaching their full tide has two parts. First, the disciples lose the essential meaning. The commentary states: "At that time..."
In an instant, Ānanda and the great assembly of thirty-six classes fixed their gaze intently upon the Buddha, no longer looking to the side.
"To blink" means to move; it refers to how previously, both ordinary beings and sages were alike like fingers.
Now, the World-Honored One instructs them to turn toward the ultimate meaning and truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to observe: from what do these names of "ordinary being" and "sage" arise? Ānanda—
Those of the Hīnayāna possess a narrow wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons; they fail to recognize the path leading back to the True, and thus lose their essential aim.
Consequently, they do not understand that the body of the five aggregates and the deluded mind of the eight consciousnesses are the locus of inversion—the very place from which delusion arises.
If one knows the source from which delusion arises, one will then flow against the current to return to the origin, turning the hearing inward to hear the self-nature.
It is because of their nature.
The Buddha gave rise to compassion, feeling pity for Ānanda and the great assembly.
