Later, out of profound pity, the Buddha proclaimed it again. The text has three parts. First, explaining how delusion manifests from the True; this section has four parts. First, a detailed exposition of conditions.

"Mark. The commentary states: "It means to arise. Since the World-Honored One saw that Ānanda and the great assembly were staring vacantly at the Buddha, unaware of where their own inverted bodies and minds lay, and that their wisdom-minds were submerged so they could not bring themselves to inquire, the Teacher, the Tathāgata, gave rise to unconditioned compassion. The Buddha took great pity as his power.

Out of compassion and pity for Ānanda, as well as for the fourfold assembly at the Śūraṅgama Sūtra gathering, [the Buddha] uttered the ocean-tide voice and proclaimed it throughout to all the good sons present. The Commentary states:
Among the sixty-four types of sounds, this is the "Warning" (Jiǎngjào) or "Majestic" (Xióng) tone. Since the ocean tide was about to arrive, he first [uttered it].
He utters a majestic sound and awaits those on the shore to gather their stomach-nets and other gear; only then will the tide surely arrive.
According to the Dharma, when the World-Honored One is about to preach the Dharma, he first emits his untainted voice.

The Buddha’s voice is perfect and sudden, warning the great assembly gathered there and fully inspiring in them the resolve to enter the Way, so that they may incline their ears and eyes to receive it with reverence.
Listening to the sounds, one clears away the dust and appreciates the profound elegance.
I have often said: "The various conditions of form and mind. The commentary states:

this describes what is constantly proclaimed. "Form" refers to the forms of the five sense organs and the forms of the five sense objects, as well as that which is subsumed within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

Form and mind refer here to the deluded mind of the eight consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, and so forth. "Various conditions" refers to the inclusion of the four conditions:

first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); third, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); and fourth, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

However, visual consciousness arises from nine conditions; auditory consciousness arises from only eight; material phenomena arise from two conditions; and mental phenomena arise from four conditions.
"And the mental factors (*caitasika*) that act as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). The commentary states: "There are fifty-one mental factors:

five universal (*sarvatraga*), five object-specific (*viniyata*), eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four indeterminate (*aniyata*). 'Latent dispositions' refers to the ten latent afflictions. Five.
The five dull afflictions (*anuśaya*) and the five sharp afflictions constitute fifty-one factors that are termed "afflictions" (*anuśaya*) by their very nature.
All sentient beings are driven by these mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*), just as a master drives his servants.
"All objects of perception. The commentary states:

"This reiterates the preceding objects; that is, it binds together the prior conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), which are manifested solely by the mind."
The commentary states: "Only" (*wei*) has the sense of exclusion and limitation. It excludes and limits [the notion that] outside of the true mind there is not even a single dharma.
The mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is itself the *tathāgatagarbha*. The *tathāgatagarbha* acts as the manifestor, while all objects of cognition act as the manifested.

This is like the body of water manifesting thousands of waves and ten thousand ripples. If one follows the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*), it is held that [all things] arise solely from the eight consciousnesses.
Regarding "manifestation above": the eight consciousnesses act as the manifesting agents, and all objects of perception act as that which is manifested.

This *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* belongs to the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*), representing the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*)—the ultimate and most comprehensive discourse. It maintains that [all things] manifest solely from the True Mind (*tathatā-citta*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All phenomena within the three realms are entirely manifestations of the mind. And as the *Awakening of Faith* says:
The mind does not perceive the mind. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.
Your body and your mind are both the wondrously luminous, true essence—the wondrous mind.

The second section, "Twofold Gathering of the Essential Purport," the commentary states: Whereas the preceding was extensive, the present is concise; it merely cites the two dharmas of body and mind to encompass all phenomena.
The "mind" mentioned previously—that which manifests as all things—is, in its entirety, the subtle, wondrous, perfectly luminous, and exquisite mind.
This is the original true mind. Regarding the objects manifested within it, the commentary states:
"The delusive is the delusion within the true; it is like waves upon water, or as there is no gold outside the vessel. [This concludes the] inclusion.

The vessel returns to gold; the vessel manifests from gold. For what reason, then, do you call it a "thing"? It is because there is no true awakening to illumine it, such that it is no different from an ordinary object.

This rebuke applies to all sentient beings who are deluded regarding the truth and turned away from awakening; they abandon the false in their search for the true, not realizing that the false is itself the true.
Between the two types of causes, this is merely a supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*), not a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
"How is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, this precious and brilliant wondrous nature?
You have thrice abandoned the true source. The commentary states: "How is it that you have lost your original, subtle, wondrous, perfect, and truly luminous mind?
This nature is noble and weighty; it is as real and internally and externally refined and bright as it is."
The first reprimand concerns losing the fundamental true mind;
it refers to recognizing awakening while remaining in delusion.
The fourth reprimand concerns gathering in the deluded consciousness. The commentary states: "To recognize" means to be attached to [something as real]. Awakening is the truth; it is not—
One can recognize the true within the true; however, one may only recognize the delusion within the true. When one is deluded, this is delusion.
This delusion is the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*. Since beginningless time, it has served as the fundamental basis for the internal body and the external world of vessels.
At present, sentient beings cast aside their precious, luminous, and wondrous nature, recognizing only the deluded mind of the eight consciousnesses.
Obscurity becomes emptiness;

next, the appearance of light arises, from which birth proceeds. This section has three parts. First, the description of the characteristics of the arising of delusion. The commentary states: "If one does not describe..."

Regarding the origin of these characteristics, [the opponent] still harbors a divergent view. The World-Honored One now explains the conditions for form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and their causes for arising.

"Obscuration" (*huì*) refers to the state of being dark and obscured; this is the essence of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It means that even a single thought-moment violates Suchness (*tathatā*).

Thereupon, the inherently luminous mind arises. Carrying along its karma, it transforms the two consciousnesses into the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) and the *nimitta-bhāga* (phenomenal aspect).
These three subtle consciousnesses combine to form the first transformative consciousness, the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Because it does not accord with true luminosity, it is "obscured" (*he*).
"Obscured" (*mei*) means dark and dim; this refers to the arising of the seventh consciousness. When the eight consciousnesses exist, there is consequently the seventh consciousness.
Arising, it internally grasps the eight aspects of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) together with the four delusions of self-delusion, self-love, self-view, and self-pride;
externally, it simultaneously brings forth a layer of vast, desolate, and stubborn emptiness. This is what arises through the false mind of all sentient beings.
"Within the dark void.
The commentary states: This reiterates the preceding scripture, concluding that darkness constitutes form (*rūpa*).

The commentary states: "Out of loathing for emptiness and aversion to obscurity, one attempts to restore original clarity; yet through such agitation, the wind of conceptualization arises, eventually resulting in the formation of objective divisions (*nimitta-bhāga*) where form becomes intermingled with false discrimination."

The commentary states: In principle, there is originally no form; now, there is form. Since there are objective dharmas of form as objects of perception, one becomes entangled with the reality that is formless.
This is the mark of false and deluded conceptualization. "Conceptualization" (xiang) means grasping at images. It arises within the internal mind to grasp and cling to external objects of form.
Because the subjective and the objective become intermingled and confused, this occurs.
"Perception and its signs constitute the body.

The commentary states: "Because perception arises from signs, it is called 'perception and its signs' (*saṃjñā-nimitta*). The body is provisionally formed through the father’s perception, the mother’s perception, and the perception of a child;
these three perceptions are received as the embryo, which is the *kalala* during the first seven days. If the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is male, he faces..."
One gives rise to thoughts toward the mother’s body; if the being in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is female, it gives rise to thoughts toward the father’s body.

It gathers its conditions and vibrates within, subsequently grasping and assuming a form. The commentary states: "The sixth consciousness internally surveys the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), constantly racing about without rest."

Quiescence. The sixth [consciousness] constantly examines internally the reflected images of mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*). [Yet it] moves toward external objects with speed, undergoing birth, abiding, change, and cessation. The Commentary states:

"The sixth consciousness shares the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses]; it gives rise to delusions and creates karma, being turbid, clamorous, agitated, and restless as it rushes toward external realms."
Racing and wandering, it is a state of confused turmoil. The commentary states:
"Turbid" means dark and obscured; throughout the day there is turmoil, and through the night there is gloom. This refers to the sixth consciousness. Toward...
At the gates of the six sense organs, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, revolving through the three realms of existence without ever stopping;
this is taken to be the nature of the mind.
The Commentary states: "All sentient beings inherently possess the true nature of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), as stated previously: 'Precious, luminous, and wondrous...'"
This nature does not abide in a location, nor is it separate from a location; yet, by employing the sixth consciousness, one takes the mind to constitute the essential substance of the true mind.
Once deluded, this becomes the [deluded] mind, which is certainly mistaken for being within the physical body.
The commentary states: A single thought that deviates from Suchness results in a determinate retribution that cannot be altered or turned back.

One becomes stubbornly attached, asserting that the mind resides solely within the five aggregates and the physical body; thus, one identifies these five aggregates as the Dharma-body and the eternal body.
Nevertheless, these five aggregates are likewise not separate from the Dharmakāya. As the World-Honored One announced to the great assembly at the site of his parinirvāṇa:

"This present body is itself the eternal body, the Dharmakāya. If one stubbornly clings to the delusory as real, how is this any different from mistaking a pig for an auspicious sign or taking a chicken for a portent?

One does not know the physical body (*rūpakāya*). From within to the external mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—later one is reprimanded for recognizing one while discarding the rest. The commentary states: "The reprimand says:

'You do not know that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the physical body are the internal four great elements; that externally, the mountains and rivers are what is transformed. 'Shan' (山) means production; the vital spirit (*lingqi*) issues forth and gives birth.'"
The "ten thousand things" refers to all phenomena. The "rivers" refers to the great rivers. Space (*ākāśa*) is their support; it takes as its essence the unobstructed, the void, and the eternal.
"Great" means vast and expansive. "Earth" is that which can bear up the ten thousand things.
"All these are objects within the wondrously luminous, true mind.
The commentary states: "All" means "in total. This refers to all things being objects within the fundamental, true mind that is subtle, wondrous, perfect, and bright.
All sentient beings merely cling to this deluded consciousness as residing within the body, not realizing that what they cling to [is actually external] to the body. All phenomena...
All phenomena are manifested solely by this single mind; there is not a single dharma that does not arise from the Truth (Tathatā).
This is like the metaphor of hundreds of thousands of vast, clear oceans.
[The following] consists of three parts: first, the heading. The commentary states: "Cheng" (澄) means "clearly settled" (澄湛), and "qing" (清) means "pure."

"Purified" refers to the vast number of hundreds of thousands; "the ocean is a hundred thousand yojanas wide" is a metaphor for the Dharmatā-body (dharmatākāya) dwelling in the Dharmatā-land, pervading the entire Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) with boundless expanse.
Discarding [the ocean], one recognizes only the substance of a single bubble and designates it as the entire tide, exhausting the vastness of the sea.

This is followed by the second section, "Rebuking Wen," which has two parts. First, rebuking the recognition of the small while neglecting the great. The commentary states: "Violent winds lash and strike, creating waves and foam."
It thus becomes a floating bubble. At present, people merely recognize this as the ocean, as Yingzhou, one of the Ten Islands that are mountains within the sea, or as another name for the Bohai Sea;
they speak of abandoning the great ocean and recognizing only the substance of the floating bubble.
This constitutes the entirety of the tide, exhausting and reaching the ultimate limit.
Yet, it is like all sentient beings discarding their constant body—the *dharmakāya*—and instead identifying this illusory body of the five aggregates as the body of the Buddhas;
it is like discarding the great ocean and identifying a single bubble as the entire tide of the great ocean.
"You all are people who are doubly deluded.
Later, he rebukes them for maintaining dual attachments. The commentary states: "To be doubly deluded means to be further deluded within delusion.
All sentient beings cast aside the Buddhas' eternal body and *dharmakāya*, yet instead identify with this body of the four elements and five aggregates."

Thus, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) constitutes one layer of delusion. When one enters toward this body, giving rise to afflictions and creating karma, and grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises; this constitutes two layers of delusion.
"It is like my hanging down my hand, which is without distinction.
The commentary states: This again cites the previous metaphor; it is as if the preceding [analogy] of ordinary people and sages being identical to the finger was used.
Regarding "hanging down the hand," setting aside the name, if this were inverted and the beginning and end were exchanged, all worldly people would gaze upon it with double the intensity.
The Tathāgata calls them those who are to be pitied.
[The commentary] states: "The Buddha takes great compassion as his power; seeing such people, he feels they are deeply worthy of pity and compassionate concern."
The third section, "Observing the Moon at the Pavilion," the Commentary states: This refers to the time when the entire tide of the great ocean reached its peak;
the Buddha, moved by compassion, gave forth the sound of the ocean tide to universally address all the good sons assembled there, saying: "I have often said..."
All conditions of form and mind, as well as all objects of perception associated with the mental factors, are manifested solely by the mind.
Therefore, Ānanda immediately took the Buddha’s manifested voice preaching the Dharma to be the true mind, saying:

"Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and awakened to this wondrously luminous mind—which is fundamentally perfect and the eternally abiding ground of the heart—I have realized the Buddha's manifestation..."
The sound of the Dharma being preached. You currently manifest this conditioned mind, which is worthy of your veneration;

yet you have merely obtained this mind and dare to claim it as your fundamental, original ground of the mind. Therefore, the World-Honored One asked Ānanda: "You all still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind;
this Dharma is itself also conditioned. He spoke a parable, saying: "It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another; that person, because of [the finger]..."

One should look at the moon by means of the finger. If one instead regards the finger as the substance of the moon, such a person not only loses sight of the lunar orb, but also loses sight of the finger itself.
Why? Because they have taken the pointing finger to be the bright moon. Furthermore, it says:

It is like a traveler who stays overnight at an inn; having rested briefly, he departs and never remains permanently, yet the one who manages the inn never goes anywhere and is thus called the master of the inn.
The preceding passage concludes the analogy of the traveler at the inn observing the moon.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

“Regarding the three stages of the pavilion and the pointing at the moon, the text has two parts. First, the request for a resolution concerning the causal mind; this section has three parts. First, the sorrowful presentation of the realization of the principle.
The commentary states: ‘Having received the Buddha’s great compassion which rescued him from others, [Ānanda] was deeply admonished and instructed,’ as the sutra says.”
"You all are people who are doubly deluded within delusion. Furthermore, it says: "To recognize delusion within awakening is a profound admonition.
Crossing one's hands [in *añjali*] signifies the meaning of respect.
"Although I have received such a wondrous voice from the Buddha," the commentary states:
"As previously pointed out, 'your body and your mind are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence, the wondrous mind.
It was further stated that one does not know that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all [of this same nature]."
It is an object within the wondrously luminous true mind; it is this wondrous sound.
To awaken to the wondrously luminous mind is to realize that which is originally perfect and complete, the eternally abiding ground of the heart.
The commentary states: "I have awakened to this subtle, wondrous, perfect, and luminous true mind, which is originally complete and perfect. This constitutes...

It is the eternally abiding ground of the mind. "Eternally abiding" means immovability; it does not shift or change throughout the three periods of time. "Ground" refers to the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Thus, I have awakened to the Buddha’s manifested preaching of the Dharma-sound.
Next, eliminate the mind that clings to conditions. The commentary states: "I still maintain my own understanding:
while the World-Honored One was present at the assembly in Jeta Grove, he preached the Dharma of the *Śikhara-samādhi* with stainless sounds."
"Presently, by means of the cognizing mind, one truly gazes up [in reverence].

The commentary states: "Truly" (*yǔn*) means "to believe. Presently, by means of the mind that is capable of cognition, one believes in the Buddha’s vocal teachings and gives rise to this gazing-upward in reverence.
Taking this mind that is capable of cognition as being my own mind, I have merely obtained this mind;
I do not yet dare to recognize it as the fundamental ground of the mind. The commentary states:
"Tú (徒) means 'empty' or 'in vain. Although I have empty-attained this mind, I still do not dare to definitively establish this mind [as the true self]."
"This is the original ground of my own mind.

I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim the perfect sound (*paripūrṇa-svara*) so that I may resolve my doubts through this request for clarification. The commentary states: "The 'perfect dharma-realm' refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) sound."
"Uproot the root of my doubt.

The commentary states: "To 'uproot' means to pull out by the hand. I pray that the Buddha, through the power of his untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), shall uproot the firm and stubborn mind of doubt within me, Ānanda, along with its roots and sprouts.
For 'roots' carry the sense of growth and proliferation."
"Returning to the Unsurpassed Way.

The commentary states: This refers to the expressive text; that which follows refers to the principle expressed. It means: "I shall merely eliminate the subject-consciousness (the mind that takes objects as its conditions), and thereby attain the Unsurpassed Way."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and the others still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind; this Dharma is also conditioned.

Thereafter, he provided two further illustrations in response to his teaching. First, pointing at the moon in the vast sky. This section has two parts; first, rebuking the conditioning of vocal teachings.

The commentary states: "You" refers to Ānanda; "etc. includes the great assembly. Even so, they still employ this deluded mind capable of cognition (*ālambaka*) to hear the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) teachings.
Yet, the Buddha’s untainted verbal instructions become, in turn, the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Why is this so?

If one intends to take the deluded mind as the object of cognition and takes the Buddha’s untainted (anāsrava) teachings as the object, these untainted teachings will likewise become objects of cognition.
Where there is a subject capable of cognizing, there must be an object; thus, the characteristics of subject and object arise in mutual dependence.
"One does not attain the nature of dharmas.

The commentary states: "This refers to not attaining the nature of dharmas, but merely attaining the characteristics of dharmas. If it were the nature of dharmas, then for the one who preaches the Dharma, there would be no preaching and no demonstrating;
for the one who listens to the Dharma, there would be no hearing and no attainment."
It is like a person pointing at the moon with their finger to show it to another.

This subsequent section uses analogies to clarify delusion and consists of three parts. The first part, "Pointing Out the Moon," consists of two sections. The first clarifies the presentation of the pointer.
That person, by means of the finger, should look at the moon;
subsequently, they must observe that which it points toward. The commentary states: All sentient beings do not awaken to their true nature.

The Buddha, therefore, through the words of the *neyārtha* (provisional teachings), reveals the *nītārtha* (ultimate) principle they signify. Nevertheless, sentient beings must rely upon the words to awaken to that principle.

If one further regards the finger as being the substance of the moon, the text next investigates the simultaneous loss of both paths. This section has two parts; first, the loss [of the first path], which consists of three sub-sections. First, regarding the finger becoming the moon:
the commentary states, "If this person recognizes the tip of the finger and takes it to be the substance of the bright moon," and below this, the refutation follows.
This person has not only lost the lunar disc, but has also lost his finger;

subsequently, both the finger and the moon are lost. The commentary states: "This person not only fails to recognize the principle that is signified, but also fails to recognize the text that signifies it."
Why is this? It is because that which was pointed out as the finger is taken for the bright moon.
Later, the erroneous observation is examined and restated; the commentary states: "Taking the expressive text to be the expressed principle."
Not only has he lost his finger, but he also fails to distinguish between light and darkness.
This concludes the third section on the confusion regarding the text; first, it reveals the ignorance of one who cannot discern. The commentary states:

"He not only loses the expressive text (*vyañjana*), but also fails to recognize that 'light' refers to the moon, which serves as a metaphor for the expressed principle (*artha*). Its perfect brightness and purity resemble the minds of all sentient beings."
The light is pure and bright, free from any blemish or obscuration. "Darkness" is a metaphor for the expressive words; its substance consists of the four factors of sound, name, phrase, and syllable.
These names and characteristics are dim and obscure.
Why is this? It is because the finger used to point at it is taken as the very nature of the bright moon.

Next, the inquiry describes the point of delusion. The commentary states: Because one takes the words of the expressive teachings as the essence of the expressed principle, the two natures of light and darkness are not clearly discerned.
Later, he concludes with the principle of the "confused pair. The commentary states: "Since this is so, both principle and teaching are not fully understood;
you, too, are like this."

The subsequent section combines metaphors to refute delusion and cause one to recognize error; it consists of three parts. First, the refutation of one's own [delusion] to reveal the mistake. The commentary states:
"Your Ānanda, who clings to the teachings as being the mind, is just like this."
If you take the discriminative consciousness that differentiates the sounds of my Dharma-teachings as your mind, then subsequently, even though phenomena are established as the mind...
[The commentary states: "If one takes the sixth consciousness—the deluded discerning consciousness that acts as the subjective perceiver—as being the mind, this is a restatement of your position."
This mind, by its very nature, should be free from the sounds of conceptualization; yet it possesses a conceptual nature.
Later, when one seeks that which is beyond words and sounds, the true nature is fully revealed. The commentary states: "This mind" refers to this deluded mind.

It naturally ought to be separated from the objects of the external world. Following these objects, it engages in discrimination; while the sense-object of sound possesses a degree of discrimination, the spiritual mirror does not.
The nature of perfuming exists independently and does not arise from external objects; it is therefore called the true mind.

However, if one were to remove the sensory object of sound, this discriminating nature would no longer exist externally; in that case, it would be false and not true. As the preceding text states: "Objects are not permanent.
When they undergo transformation and perish, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit."
It is like a traveler who stays overnight at an inn; having halted briefly, he departs and does not remain permanently.
Later, the host [addresses] the guests and visitors. Part Three: First, the presentation of the analogy. The commentary states:
It is like a merchant who travels by day and halts by night, lodging and staying overnight at an inn. Whether sleeping or eating, once the matters of food and rest are finished, he sets out...

Preparing for the path ahead, he has no leisure to dwell in ease. Fashang [explains] that this deluded mind capable of objectification possesses mental discrimination when hearing sounds, but lacks mental discrimination when there are no sounds.
Others have said that as the sensory objects arise and then fall away, the mind follows them.
Suddenly appearing and suddenly vanishing, yet the person who presides over the pavilion never departs; he is called the "pavilion master.
The commentary states: This is a metaphor for all sentient beings whose true mind listens to the Dharma—neither coming nor going, yet its spiritual discernment alone remains.
When the preceding sensory objects fall away and perish, this portion of true nature remains and does not follow those objects;
this case is likewise so.

Next, the section on reconciling with the text has two parts. First, the cessation of false recognition, which consists of three sub-sections. First, citing the analogy of the mind and the mirror. Commentary:

[The Buddha] said: "What preceded was a metaphor; this is the application of the Dharma. You, Ānanda, have just now manifested a mind that conditions objects, which is indeed worthy of being observed.
Your clinging to this deluded mind that conditions sensory objects is likewise like that of a traveler."
If it were truly your mind, then it would have nowhere to go;
next, it is granted that there is indeed no shifting. The commentary states: "If it were your true mind, then it would not undergo transformation or extinction in accordance with external objects."
What is meant by "separation from sound"? It is the nature of non-discrimination.

Later, [the text] rebukes the nature of the lost mirror. The commentary states: For what reason is there discrimination when objects are present, yet once those external objects are removed, there is again the nature of non-discrimination?
This is not merely a matter of the mind that discriminates sounds.

Second, providing examples to demonstrate the error, which has two parts. First, the example showing that form is the same as sound, which has three sections. The first restates the nature of sound mentioned previously.

The commentary states: "Si" means "this. To speak of "this" implies that there is not only the sound of my preaching the Dharma, but also your own mind of subjective discernment capable of perceiving it;
thus, false thoughts arise, leading into the following passage.
"Distinguishing my own appearance" means being free from all marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) and possessing a non-discriminative nature.

Next, "inverting form to be identical with emptiness. The commentary states: "Distinguishing" refers to the discriminating faculty—the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—which, together with the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), takes as its object "my own appearance," which is that which is distinguished.
This refers to the Buddha’s thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), regarding which Ānanda had previously spoken.
"I saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and therefore sought to leave the household life.

Furthermore, this "gentleman" (zhǐ zhōng shì) refers to one who truly gazes upon and truly listens to the sound of the World-Honored One preaching the Dharma; "gazing upon" means seeing the World-Honored One’s thirty-two marks.
Thus it is said that one discriminates one's own appearance; when this mind possesses the characteristics of form, there is then discrimination.
Nature. When there are no marks of form, there is no nature of discrimination. This consciousness is like a weak person who cannot walk without a staff;
thus it continues until discrimination is entirely absent.

Later, the critique regarding the object of cognition as being devoid of characteristics will address improper conceptualizations. The commentary states: All eight consciousnesses possess discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The visual consciousness discriminates the objective realm of visible forms; the auditory consciousness discriminates the objective realm of sounds;

and so on, up to the sixth [consciousness] discriminating the seventh, the seventh discriminating the eighth, and the eighth discriminating the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), and so forth. As it is now with the eight...
Consciousness does not, at one time, take its own constituent parts as an object. The eye is separated from form; the eighth consciousness is separated from the eye;
and the mind that discriminates the body and the vessel-world has for the most part fallen away.
"Neither form nor emptiness.
The commentary states: "Neither form" means one does not perceive the source of the nature of form, but merely clings to the mind being signless.

"Nor emptiness" means one does not perceive the principle of true emptiness, but merely clings to the capacity of the nature to reflect as it follows objects. Form is itself wondrous existence; wondrous existence is...
The existence that exhausts emptiness is the emptiness that exhausts existence; this is the wondrous existence of true emptiness, and the true emptiness of wondrous existence.
Those such as Kuśarī were deluded and mistook it for the obscure principle (tattva).
The commentary states: Question: If one now neither perceives the "wondrous existence" (*miao-you*) nor attains the "empty truth" (*zhen-kong*), what of such a person?
Answer: This is identical to Kauśika; he is a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) of the eternalist view (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
In Sanskrit, he is called Makkhali Gosāla. *Makkhali* is his personal name, and *Gosāla* is his mother’s name. He is named after his mother, as is the custom for the six teachers.
Among them, the second teacher holds the principle of the primordial darkness (*avyakta-tattva*) as his tenet. He maintains that the Way is fundamentally spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

This includes all six teachers of the non-Buddhist heterodox schools (*tīrthika*). The "primordial darkness" (*míngdì*) is precisely the tenet of the Sāṃkhya school. The teacher is ignorant of the "dark" (*míng*), while *tattva* means "reality.
He merely clings to the eighth [principle], the primordial darkness, and reckons this to be *nirvāṇa*, yet he does not know that it is the eight consciousnesses that arise.
The place of arising is free from the conditions of all phenomena and possesses a non-conceptual nature.

Subsequently, it is detached from the sensory objects of phenomena (*dharmālambana*) and fades away. The commentary states: "If, suddenly, there should appear the shadows of the sensory objects of phenomena—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—"
When there is an image, the sixth consciousness-mind arises; if this dharma-object image were absent, the sixth consciousness-mind would likewise not exist.

Thus, when the mental faculty (*manas*) is separated from dharma-objects, it lacks discriminative nature. It is clearly understood that this is merely the deluded mind chasing after objects until it perishes, and the mental faculty following the dust until it fades away.
Each of the eight consciousnesses has its own respective object of perception.
Thus, your mind-nature has each its own place of return.

The subsequent passage concerning the "erroneous text" is twofold; first, it points out that delusion is identical to the guest. The commentary states: "The eight returns each return to their preceding objects."
Visual consciousness returns to the realm of visible forms; the sixth consciousness returns to the realm of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*); the seventh returns to the eighth;
and the eighth returns to the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*). This is delusion; it is understood as such simultaneously upon its dissolution.
"What is meant by 'being the master'?
Later, the true substance is questioned and examined. The commentary states: "How can it be your mind? This is the true mind of another.
Since the deluded mind follows after sensory objects, each has its own place of return; for what reason, then, could it be the sovereign master of the mind?"
The fourth section, "Entrusting and the Eight Returns," refers back to the previous discussion on the finger at the inn. The commentary states:
This section addresses the question, "If your mind-nature has each its own place of return, how can it be the master? This is why Ānanda inquired about this point here.
He then requested, saying, "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, up to: how is it that there is nothing to return?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to explain eight kinds of phenomena, each of which has something to which it returns: light returns to the sun; [and so on, until:
...then finally he pointed out and said, "All those things that can return are naturally not you; they do not return to you."
"That which is not you, [you] nevertheless know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, bright, and pure. The preceding exposition on the eight returns is concluded.
Ānanda said: "If my mind-nature has various things to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, bright, original mind has nothing to which it returns?
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

Section Four: Entrusting and Bequeathing; Section Eight: Returning to the Text. Part Two: The First Request. The *jiàn* (memorandum) states: "Each has that to which it returns; this refers to the 'eight returns.
What, then, is the 'absence of returning'? This refers to the previous statement: "If it were truly your mind, then it would have nowhere to go.

This is a request regarding the absence of returning. [The petitioner says: "If this is the true nature that does not return, I have not yet realized it. I pray that the World-Honored One will proclaim it for me."
[The Buddha] spoke. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Furthermore, as for your seeing me—this is the luminous essence of seeing.

[The following] consists of four sections showing this. First, the section granting permission and instructing him to listen, which has five parts. First, pointing out delusion. The commentary states: 'Furthermore, you...'"
Ānanda, when you see me as a Buddha, this clarity of seeing is the fundamental source. This is the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

This mind of direct perception of the visual consciousness is the immediate reflection transformed by the eight consciousnesses. When confronting objects, it does not differentiate between subject and object, just as an image appears in a mirror.
This seeing, although it is not the wondrously brilliant and subtle mind, is next in comparison to the true [mind].
The commentary states: "To say that this eye-consciousness is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) means that it is a direct transformation of the eighth consciousness.
Although this seeing is not the wondrously brilliant and subtle mind, it resembles direct perception; it is not true direct perception. This refers to its abiding state.

In the causal stage, before consciousness has been transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), one is moment by moment perfumed by the objects of the sensory realm of form; therefore, it is said that this is not the mind of refined brilliance.

However, if one suddenly reaches the stage of Buddhahood, the five types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

This is indeed true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since it is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind, do not think that apart from what resembles direct perception, there exists a separate "true" one.
Is there not gold apart from the vessel? Below, he provides an analogy in response.
"It is like a second moon.
This is the third analogy. The commentary states: "The second moon is a metaphor for the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the visual consciousness.
This mind arises as a shadowy projection whenever any sentient being’s single thought-moment deviates from Suchness (*tathatā*). It is like the small vision seen when one presses upon the eye."
While there is still a second moon present, if the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) were suddenly to become wisdom (*jñāna*), this would resemble direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Upon returning to true direct perception, it is like pinching one's own hand and then releasing it: there is only a single bright full moon.
"It is not the reflection of the moon.
The commentary states: This means that the true does not depart from the delusory, and the delusory does not depart from the true; the true and the delusory are of one essence.
It is not like the moon in the water—a phenomenon consisting of images and appearances that lack substantial reality.
"You should listen attentively.
Listen well to these four instructions.
Now I shall show you the ground from which there is no returning."
"Five: Granting the Demonstration. The commentary states: This refers to Ānanda’s request to the Buddha. This "granting the demonstration" concerns the ground of non-return for others.
"Non-return" is the true mind. The World-Honored One first returns the eight kinds of phenomena of the external objects, and only then demonstrates to him that which does not return.
Ānanda, this great lecture hall opens wide toward the east; when the sun rises in the sky, there is brilliant radiance.

[The second section, "The Various Characteristics May Return to the Text," Part Four, first provides a general description of the manifold characteristics. The commentary states: "This great lecture hall..."
This refers to the hall where the World-Honored One expounded the wondrous meaning—a place of profound penetration and vast openness.

Since the eastern direction is the foremost among all directions, it symbolizes that this *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* marks the beginning of Ānanda’s path to the Way. It is like the solar disc emerging from Mount Fusang.
Surpassing the heavens and the Milky Way, he then beheld a brilliant radiance shining in the sky; such was this light.
Yet at midnight, during the dark of the moon, when clouds and mist shrouded the world in gloom, it would again become obscured by darkness.
The commentary states: After the midpoint of the month, during the third watch of the night, one may see the dark moon; clouds and mists gather, and even the new moon is dim and obscure.
Yet, through the gaps between doors and windows, one again perceives the penetration of light.
The commentary states: "Gaps" refers to pores and crevices.
Between walls and buildings, one then observes obstructions. The commentary states:
"Observing" refers to the appearance of the signs of being blocked and congested.
"In the place of discrimination, one again perceives conditions.
The commentary states: "This is that which is discriminated—namely, jars, bowls, carriages, elephants, horses, gardens, and groves. These are objective conditions appearing as forms;
they are not the subject that performs the discrimination."
Within the vast void, there is everywhere the nature of emptiness. As for the image of "swirling smoke" (*yùbó*), it refers to the winding of turbid dust.
The commentary states: when there is no rain, the dust and dark mists arise as a swirling, smoky haze; this is what is meant by being "entwined."
When the sky clears and the mists subside, one again beholds purity.
The commentary states: "Clearing" (*jì*) refers to the end of rain; "subsiding" (*liǎn*) means to withdraw or gather in; "mists" (*fēn*) refers to the turbid vapors.
When these turbid vapors are dispelled, it becomes a clear sky—the mark of purity. This is to be free from the eight marks.
"Ānanda, you have all observed these various manifested forms. I shall now each return them to their original causal source.

[The Master] twice exhorted him to examine thoroughly where they return. The commentary states: "This refers to the eight kinds of original causal sources mentioned below, which will then be investigated."
What is the fundamental cause? This refers to the three inquiries regarding the causes to which they belong.
Ānanda, these various transformations return their clarity to the solar disc. Why is this? Because there is no clarity without the sun; thus, the cause of clarity belongs to it.
Day. Therefore, brightness returns to the day.
Fourth, each [section] describes the cause for the return; there are three textual parts. First, the return of brightness. The commentary states:
"Brightness returns to the solar disc. Without the sun, one would not see brightness. Since brightness is dependent upon the sun, it therefore returns to the day."
Darkness returns to the black moon; penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and eaves; conceptualization returns to discrimination;
stubborn vacuity returns to emptiness; stifling miasma returns to dust; and clarity returns to a cloudless sky.
Next, it returns to the remaining seven. The commentary states: "It returns to the dark moon. Why is this? Without the dark moon, there would be no darkness;
since darkness is caused by the dark moon, it returns to the dark moon. The subsequent six types perform this same mode of activity (*ākāra*).
"Then all that exists in the world does not transcend these categories.
This is the final summary. The Commentary states: "Thus, all phenomena (dharmas) existing in the world do not transcend these eight kinds of characteristics;
they are entirely encompassed within them at once."
"You have seen eight kinds [of phenomena]. As for the luminous nature of seeing, to whom would you wish to return it?

This section, consisting of three parts, demonstrates that the nature has no place to which it can return. First, it generally clarifies the state of being free from all objects of negation. The commentary states: "The 'eight kinds' refers to the eight types of appearances mentioned previously.
The 'luminous nature of seeing' is the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the visual consciousness. [The text] asks the other person to whom they should return it."
What is this phenomenon? The mind, through inference based on the interval [of thought], does not return to the present object of visual consciousness.
Why is this? The subsequent inquiry describes the absence of returning; the text has three parts, the first of which is the hypothetical inquiry.
If one returns to the light, then when it is not light, one would no longer perceive darkness.
Next, he establishes the principle, with the commentary stating: If you say that upon returning to the light, the characteristic of darkness appears, then one should not see the darkness;
yet we know that the nature of seeing does not return to the light.
Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, one perceives them without distinction.

To clarify this later, the commentary states: "While the preceding objects possess differences such as aging and particularity, this single portion of the seeing-nature (dṛṣṭi-svabhāva) has no difference."
"Those things that can be returned do not inherently belong to you; as for that which cannot be returned by you, if it is not you, then who is it?
This latter passage points to the actual reality of true purity and consists of two parts. First is the removal of the returnable to point toward the actual reality.

The commentary states: "Who" means "what. Those various things that can be returned are false; this refers to the eight kinds of objects mentioned previously. That which cannot be returned by you is the true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is not...
That which returns following the preceding sensory objects is not your true mind, Ānanda. What else could it be?
This points to that ground which is without anything to return to.
Thus you should know that your own mind is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure.
"Later, the nature will manifest as eternally luminous. The commentary states: "This refers to this mind that does not regress. It is fundamentally subtle and wondrous, perfect, bright, and pure.
Yet you have become deluded and distressed by yourself, losing your original nature and undergoing the cycle of rebirth; thus, within birth and death, you are constantly drifting and drowning."
IV. On the Wounds of Being Lost and Drowning in Water (in two parts). First, the reprimand for being lost. The *Jian* states: "To be lost means not to awaken;
to be muddled means not to enter. The *Shu* states: "To be lost means to follow the current without awareness;

to be muddled means not to realize that the mind is eternal, thereby losing the original celestial mind and vainly undergoing drowning within the fullness of birth and death, constantly falling deeply into the realms of humans and devas, and sinking in the three [realms]."
Anointing.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named "The One Worthy of Compassion.
Later, he rejoiced at the injury.
"Regarding the fifth, 'the nature has no object-condition,' the commentary states: This refers to the section on the 'eight returns' (*aṣṭa-pratyāgama*) mentioned earlier.
Therein, the World-Honored One pointed to the present perceptual consciousness (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) as being the true nature. Ānanda then raised a doubt, saying:

'This body is permeated by the habitual tendencies of craving and still dwells within the state of outflows (*āsrava*); how can it be called true? He then requested, saying: 'Although I recognize this nature of seeing as having no [object-condition]...'"
[Ananda] returned. [The Buddha asked: "How can you know that this is my true nature? Thereupon, the Buddha lent his majestic spiritual power and looked upward to the first Brahma heaven.

He then directly revealed and analyzed the relationship between the mind and its objects, saying: "Take the limit of your faculty of sight as your starting point—from the palaces of the sun and moon, which are external things and not you, up to the seven golden mountains;
then gradually observe further the rising clouds, the flying birds, the blowing winds, the stirring dust, and the trees."

Mountains, rivers, grasses, shrubs, humans, and livestock—all these things are not you; thus, while all phenomena are subject to decay and possess their own distinct differences, the nature of seeing remains without distinction.
Only after this can one proceed from the insight into phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*) to the insight into principle (*tattva-dṛṣṭi*). It is then said:
"If seeing were an object, then you would also be able to see my seeing. This is the insight into phenomena. "When I do not see... What?
"Not seeing the place where there is no seeing" is the vision that penetrates principle. Furthermore, it concludes by stating:
"If one sees 'not-seeing,' it naturally is not that which is characterized as 'not-seeing. The above exposition on the nature of non-conditioned characteristics is completed.
Ānanda said: "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has no place to return, how can I know it is my true nature?

This is the first section on the five natures being without conditions and pointing [at the nature]. All [subsequent] passages recount the preceding inquiry and examination. The commentary states: The Buddha’s pointing is like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Ānanda was a bodhisattva of great expedient power; fearing that all sentient beings might cling to this as the truth, he [spoke further].
He did not practice [the teaching]. Showing signs of doubt, he came with this question. Perhaps Ānanda’s thought was:

"Although I am able to recognize this eye-consciousness through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it does not return to its former object. Previously, [the Buddha] had said: "If it returns to light..."

At that time, when there is no longer clarity, one no longer perceives the conditions of darkness; this is said to resemble direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moment by moment, it is perfumed by the reception of the objects of the sensory realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Furthermore, as it has not yet been transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), it remains in the causal stage and is thus with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Therefore, it is said: "This is my true nature.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I shall now question you.

[The following consists of] two parts: first, the secret examination of the true source; second, the text that clarifies the mind and its objects. Within the first [section], there are five parts: first, a general clarification of the contemplative measure.

The fifth section [of the text] has five parts. The first part, concerning the fruit of the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna), has three sections. First, the announcement and the counter-question. The commentary states: "To utter words to another is called a 'question.
Now, you have not yet attained the untainted purity (*anāsrava-viśuddhi*)."

Next, it clarifies that Ānanda still possesses outflows (*āsrava*). The commentary states: "Ānanda is a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer). He has only exhausted the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
therefore, the innate afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) remain unextinguished.

If one were an Arhat of the fourth fruit, they would have severed the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Since Ānanda abides in the first fruit, he [still] possesses them."
This outflow still exists.
Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, one perceives the first dhyāna without obstruction.

Later, it clarifies that the Buddha, by borrowing supernatural powers, attains the contemplation of the first Brahma realm. The commentary states: "The Buddha then borrows his majestic spiritual power."
By the power of this, he saw that within the first dhyāna of the form realm there are three heavens: the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā.
As for Aniruddha, he saw Jambudvīpa as clearly as observing an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand.
"Two Arhats. The commentary states: "Jambū is the name of a tree; this land [China] is named after it.
It is the realm of transformation for one Buddha within the Sahā world. Āmalaka fruit: this fruit is like a crabapple; it is the same as the *yúgān* (citron) of Guangzhou."
It is said that this Venerable One has attained the "half-head" divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). This refers specifically to Arhats, who see only the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
The various Bodhisattvas, however, see hundreds of thousands of worlds.
Third, the Bodhisattvas. The commentary states: A Bodhisattva of the first stage sees a hundred Buddha-worlds; a Bodhisattva of the second stage sees a thousand Buddha-worlds;
a Bodhisattva of the third stage sees ten thousand Buddha-worlds; a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage sees one hundred million Buddha-worlds;
and so on, until a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage sees unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-worlds.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively survey all pure lands as numerous as motes of dust, leaving nothing unseen.
Regarding the "Four Buddhas," the commentary states: the worlds of the various Buddhas are as numerous as the motes of dust in space; these are the Pure Lands of Dharmatā.
Regarding "the ocean of fragrant waters" and so forth: although the Buddhas have no phenomena external to their own minds, there is nothing they do not see exhaustively.

As for "sentient beings seeing through [only] inches," the sub-commentary states that "tong" (洞) means "vast. This implies that even if sentient beings were to gaze with vast vision, it would still not exceed a few inches.
This is because, perhaps due to the fact that hindrances have not yet been eliminated, one perceives external objects (*viṣaya*) as being capable of acting as obstructions.

This is the purport of this section of the sutra. Although the question concerns seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*), it is distinct from the preceding inquiry. That is to say, Ānanda had previously asked:
"Although I recognize that this seeing-nature is non-reversible, how can I know that it is my true nature? Therefore—
World-Honored One, at this time, regarding the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), the vision of an Arhat is such;
the vision of a Bodhisattva is such; the vision of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is such; and the vision of all Buddhas is such.
This intends to clarify that the vision of the Buddhas exhausts the pure lands as minute as atoms, such that there is nothing they do not see, thereby manifesting the true vision of the Buddha.
There is no limit; this very absence of limit is the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

By clarifying that cause and effect are distinct, it causes all sentient beings to realize what appears as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) so that they may return to true direct perception—realizing that delusion is itself the truth.
"Ānanda, let us first observe the palaces where the Four Heavenly Kings reside;
next, we shall raise our eyes together to behold them. The commentary states: The word "first" (*qiàn*) is a term indicating that [the matter] is not yet exhausted.

Previously, the Buddha relied on the supernatural power of another to perceive the First Dhyāna; now, he restricts this by using "first" to discuss what is proximate, and thus begins from the Desire Realm.
Question: Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings: the King of the East is Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the King of the South is Virūḍhaka; the King of the West is Virūpākṣa;
and the King of the North is Vaiśravaṇa. The palaces in which they dwell are all composed of the seven precious gems.
In the interim, he surveys everywhere across water, land, and air.
Although there is both obscurity and clarity, the commentary states: "In the interim," he observes all-pervasively.

"Obscurity" refers to the regions within the Cakravāḍa mountains—both the Great Cakravāḍa and the Lesser Cakravāḍa mountains—where the sun and moon do not reach; the hells are situated therein. "Clarity" refers to...
This refers to Mount Sumeru, which is composed of the seven treasures and possesses radiance; this radiance is precisely the range illuminated by the sun and moon.
Its various forms and appearances are nothing other than objective sensory objects (*viṣaya*). They are merely the result of conceptual discrimination and the obstruction of lingering attachments.
The commentary states: "The various forms and images of external objects are the objects of discernment (*ālambana-vikalpa*), not the discerning subject (*ālambaka-vikalpa*).
This means that among all phenomena of the external objects, there are none that do not bind and obstruct."
"You should, in this regard, distinguish between self and other.

The three instructions thus differentiate between self and other. The commentary states: "Self" refers to the perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga) which is the subjective faculty; "other" refers to the perceived aspect (nimitta-bhāga) which is the objective object.
"Now I shall lead you to select [the true nature] from among what is seen.
The Commentary states: "This is the Buddha employing the majestic power of another. This text is too concise; it should read:
"Now I shall lead you toward the external objects before you, causing you to discern between the seeing-part and the perceived-part."
"Who is my substance? What constitutes the objective image? The commentary states: "Who is my substance?
This refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). What constitutes the objective image? This refers to the perceived-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Ānanda, exhaust the source of your vision; from the palaces of the sun and moon onwards, these are objects and not you."
4. Pointing out that objects are not of the nature [of the seer]. This section has three parts. First, the measure of the two luminaries is exhausted. The commentary states:
"To exhaust the source of your visual consciousness through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one must trace it back from the palaces of the sun and moon.
The sun palace is fifty-one *yojana* wide; the moon palace is fifty *yojana* wide. Both are external objects (*viṣaya*). They are not your seeing, Ānanda."
One arrives at the Seven Golden Mountains.
Next is the Circular Mirror Golden Mountain. The commentary states: "Thereafter, one proceeds in succession to the Seven Golden Mountains, which are composed of the seven precious substances:
first, Mount Yugaṃdhara; second, Mount Īṣādhara; third, Mount Kāḷāñjara; fourth, Mount Sudarśana..."
He beheld the mountains: (5) Horse-Ear Mountain, (6) Elephant-Trunk Mountain, and (7) Mount Nimindhara. He surveyed them thoroughly and with precision.
The commentary states: "To survey means to look around exhaustively; to observe with precision means to view them with exactness."
"Though there are various kinds of light, these objects are not yours either.
The commentary states: "Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, the sun, the moon, and so forth all possess radiance; these are referred to as 'various kinds of light.'"

Gradually, one further observes the rising clouds and flying birds, the movement of the wind and the stirring of dust, the trees and mountains, the grasses and shrubs, and humans and animals—all these things are not you.
Subsequently, the clouds and animals are collectively subsumed within the preceding phenomena. The commentary states: "Gradually, one further observes from below."
The clouds rise again; the birds fly again. That which has water is called a lake; that which lacks water is called a stream.
A single blade of grass, a single speck of dust, humans, and animals—all are but things. It is not you, Ānanda, who sees them.
Ānanda, although these various natures of things, whether near or far, differ from one another, they are equally what is beheld by your own pure essence of vision.
[The five sections on the mind’s unity with the objects; the second section clarifies that while appearances differ, the mind is one. Commentary: "Far" refers to the first.

Chan: "From the nearby Four Heavenly Kings, up to the Seven Golden Mountains and so forth—all existing things and their natures, though they may be diverse and distinct, are all equally your single visual consciousness as direct perception."
Thus, while all things and categories possess their own distinctions, the nature of seeing is without difference.
[The Master] later points to the faculty of seeing and instructs him to withdraw [the mind]. The Commentary states: "Things" refers to grasses, weeds, trees, and so forth;
"categories" refers to all types of forms, such as humans, animals, and the like. These possess inherent differences, yet the nature of seeing is fundamentally without distinction.
"This subtle, wondrous, and luminous [clarity] is truly your seeing-nature.

The commentary states: "Truly" (chéng) means "actually" (shí). Furthermore, it indicates that this subtle, wondrous, and luminous [clarity] is the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of the visual consciousness;
it is actually your seeing-nature.
If one sees this object, later it is secretly examined as in the fourth section of the source text. First, there is a general inquiry regarding the manifest consciousness. The commentary states:
"Even if another's seeing is identical to the object, this is granted so that the deluded consciousness may be treated as identical to what is seen."
"Then you may also see my seeing. The Commentary says: "I am also like you;
our seeing is the same as that of objects. Since you see me as being the same as objects, you should also see my seeing, which is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that apprehends things.
Since you already see me as being the same as objects, my seeing is likewise the same as objects. Furthermore, even granting for the sake of argument that seeing is the same [as objects],"

"Object. As with an object, it is clearly manifest. The *Śū* (Commentary) says: "If you see this as an object, then even granting that the mind is identical to the characteristics of the object, since your mind already perceives the object, why do you not see my seeing?"

"If your seeing were the same [as the Buddha's]"—this is the third section, "The Two Secrets Lead One to the Ultimate Text. First, it grants the preceding point of commonality and commands that one’s perception be illuminated as the source.

The commentary states: "If your seeing were the same as the Buddha’s realization of the reality of phenomena," this refers to leading Ānanda to share with the Buddha the conditions of phenomena, and then...
To attain the wisdom that penetrates the conventional and realizes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is called "seeing me.
The commentary states: Ānanda’s seeing and the Buddha’s seeing are one; both are the seeing that penetrates phenomena. Thus, he is led into penetration.
"Seeing through principle. When I do not see, [it is because] the commentary states:
this is when the Buddha, within the fundamental wisdom that penetrates principle, does not produce the dualistic view of subject and object; thus it is the fundamental [wisdom]."
When wisdom merges in profound harmony with True Suchness (tathatā), principle and wisdom merge, and mind and spirit unite. Like a box and its lid, subject and object are not distinguished;
like salt and water, there is no differentiation at all; like the sun and space, there is no separation between this and that.
This is realized only through the internal self-verification of true sages and is not accessible to those in the stage of causal practice.
"Why do you not see the place where I do not see?
The commentary states: This means, "Why do you likewise not see the place where I, having realized the principle, see? This is the ground of realization."
This is the Buddha inviting others. It leads from the perception of phenomena (*dharma-nirvedha*) into the perception of principle (*tattva-nirvedha*). Question:

The Buddha’s wisdom is untainted (*anāsrava*), yet even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) still possess delusion. Why, then, does the Tathāgata see the same as Ānanda? Answer: The Buddha is purely untainted; how could he observe in the same manner [as one who is not]?
Nevertheless, while the stage of cause and the stage of fruition are difficult to distinguish, their nature (*dharmatā*) is not different. Therefore, the Tathāgata...
[The Buddha] granted his secret permission.
Whether [the disciple] saw it or not, next he explained that wisdom is unable to perceive the profound removal of formlessness. The commentary states: The Buddha said to Ananda: "You..."
If one perceives my fundamental wisdom—the vision that takes principle as its object and is free from all dependence—it is naturally not that state of non-seeing.
The commentary states: "If one enters the realm where I have realized the principle and seeks a mark of non-seeing, even there it is not found."
It can be attained; this eliminates the characteristic of non-seeing.
If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, you will subsequently realize the ultimate truth and attain the Buddha-mind. The commentary states: "If you do not see me..."
The stage of "seeing" occurs after one has entered the fundamental realization of the principle and transcended that mark of non-seeing.
This stage is the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*); not a single speck of dust is admitted there. How, then, could there be any mark of non-seeing?
"Spontaneity is not a thing.
The commentary states: "If you perceive this realm as non-existent, then what was previously perceived as a 'thing'—how can that not be you?"
The commentary states: This refers to the fundamental true nature. It cannot be said that it is not your Ānanda’s seeing;
this is precisely your Ānanda’s seeing-nature.
Furthermore, when you now see an object, since you see the object, the object also sees you.
Third, the realms of mind and objects are intermingled and appropriate. The commentary states: "Objects also possess seeing; you also possess seeing.
Sentient beings become insentient things; insentient things become sentient beings."
"Their essential natures are confused and intermingled.
The commentary states: "If one's own essential nature is in a state of chaotic confusion, becoming intermingled with external objects, then you and I [are no different]."
The commentary states: "Thus, you are Ānanda and I am the Buddha; these constitute the dependent, along with all the world.
The commentary further states:
"These constitute the supported."
It cannot be established as a stable order.
The commentary states: "Objects also constitute persons, and persons also constitute objects; by what means could they be established?

Only when there is a world that serves as a support does there subsequently exist the sentient beings who depend upon it, whereby the meaning of 'establishment' is realized. Yet now, sentient beings have become non-existent."
Sentient beings [arise] from the insentient; how could they be established? "Establishment" has the meaning of "enjoyment.
That which is capable of functioning is the mind, while that which is enjoyed consists of elephants, horses, gardens, groves, jars, garments, vehicles, and so forth.

Now, since the subject and object are thus conflated, the meaning of "enjoyment" cannot be established. This single passage from the sutra was intended by the former Buddha to accommodate the views of others.
This refers to the same object. Fearing that others might cling to the notion that both the object and the person possess vision, this passage was written.
Ānanda, when you see, it is you who see, not I.
4. Challenging the Reliance on Another to Sever Delusions. The Commentary states:

"If it is when you see that it is solely your seeing and not my seeing, and if outside of your seeing one cannot find my seeing, then why did you previously borrow the majestic spiritual power of another to perceive the First Dhyāna?
Fearing that others might cling to the view that this is the seeing of another person, these words were spoken."
"The nature of seeing is all-pervasive; if it is not you, who else could it be?
The commentary states: This means that the nature of seeing pervades the entire Dharma-realm; if it is not you, Ānanda, then who else could it be?
"Why do you doubt your own true nature? You consider your own nature to be unreal, yet you seek the jewel from me.
[The Commentary states: "This nature is your own nature; why do you say it is not real, and instead seek truth from me?
This was a reprimand to Ānanda for having previously said, "Although I recognize that this seeing-nature is non-reverting, how can I know for certain that it is [the true self]?"
"The true nature of my self.

The sixth essence has no expansion or contraction. The commentary states: "This means that previously the Buddha relied upon Ānanda’s majestic spiritual power to look upward as far as the first Brahma-heaven;
now, within this context, the Buddha withdraws his majestic spiritual power, so that Ānanda can only observe the eaves and rafters."
He then became doubtful, thinking: "Does this vision shrink the large into the small, or does it cause it to be severed by being squeezed between walls and buildings?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One explained this by pulling back what was difficult to shrink and drawing out what was difficult to squeeze through a crevice.
He further spoke the analogy of various vessels dividing space, saying: "For example, within a square vessel, one sees a square void. I shall ask you again: regarding this square vessel..."
The space seen within a square vessel—is it fixed as square, or is it not fixed as square? If it were fixed as square, then when a round vessel is placed there, the space should not be round.

If it were not fixed, then while inside a square vessel, there should be no "square space. This concludes the preceding exposition on the fact that the substance [of space] neither expands nor contracts.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing must be mine and not that of another, yet the six physical bodies neither expand nor contract when the finger is moved.
This section has two parts: first, stating his doubts and requesting a resolution. This part has three sections;

first, observing the expansion and contraction of objects. The commentary says: “If this is the nature pointed out by the Buddha, it is yours and none other’s. All [the disciples] were thus [convinced].
That object is not your own nature; it must certainly be my vision, and not that of any other person.
I and the Tathāgata together beheld the Victorious Treasury Jewel Palace of the Four Heavenly Kings, situated within the palaces of the sun and moon.
The commentary states: This refers to the Buddha previously borrowing the supernatural power of others to observe the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings in the Desire Realm.
Within them, he saw a particularly sublime treasure storehouse and a jeweled hall composed of the seven precious substances.
He then successively beheld the palaces inhabited by the Sun Deity and the Moon Deity.
"This vision is all-encompassing, pervading the Sahā world.
The commentary states: "It means that from within it, I see [the world] as being all-encompassing and completely filling this Sahā realm.
'Sahā' in Sanskrit means 'Endurance' (Kannin) in Chinese. Śākyamuni Buddha endures and teaches all sentient beings."
He withdrew and returned to the vihāra. He saw only the monastery; he purified his mind within the halls and chambers, gazing only upon the eaves and corridors.
The commentary states: "Thereupon he withdrew and returned to the Jetavana Vihāra. He saw only the saṃghārāma. *Saṃghārāma* is a Sanskrit term;
in the language of China, it means 'Garden of the Sangha. He cleansed his mind within the doors, windows, halls, and rooms. As for the eaves..."
The eaves of a house and the two sides of the flying corridors are called the *lǚ* (verandas).
World-Honored One, when viewed in this way, its substance is fundamentally all-pervasive throughout the entire realm.

Next, he sets forth the elimination of doubts. The commentary states: "The previous contemplation of the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings of the desire realm and so forth revealed that this nature of seeing pervades this entire Sahā world."
"Now it is within the room, filling only the room.
The commentary states: "This causes him to be within this hall, observing only the matters of the single room, such as the eaves and corridors.
Is this vision then a contraction of the large into the small?"
The commentary states: It is said that if this vision were located within the palaces of the sun and moon, would it not be vastly diminished?
Would the great vision previously experienced become a small vision within these [palaces]?
"Is it that walls and buildings cause it to be severed by being hemmed in between them?
The commentary states: "Furthermore, is this vision hemmed in and cut off by walls, partitions, and houses, such that one half is on this side and the other half is on that side?"
I do not now know where this meaning resides. I pray that you will bestow your great compassion and expound it for me, so that later I may present my doubts and seek a resolution.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Throughout all the worlds, whether great or small, internal or external..."

The subsequent section explains away objections and dispels delusions; it consists of five parts. The first part rebukes delusion regarding the characteristics of objects. The commentary states: "Large refers to Mount Sumeru;
small refers to dust and chaff. Internally, it refers to the world-system; externally, it refers to the great void. This cites examples to clarify the point.
"All undertakings. The commentary states:

that which brings honor is called "affairs" (shi); the completion of affairs is called "undertakings" (ye). These collectively describe the sensory objects (qianchen), each of which belongs to the respective sensory objects.
The commentary states: Each belongs to the objective phenomena of the external environment;
one should not say that there is expansion or contraction in what is seen.
The commentary states: While the external environment may expand or contract, what is seen is neither expanding nor contracting. When it expands, opening is great.
When contracted, it merges with the small.
It is like seeing a square void within a square vessel. I ask you again: regarding this square void seen within the square vessel—
Is it fixed in direction, or is it not fixed in direction?

Second, an analogy is presented to dispel doubt; this section has four parts. First, the analogy is presented and a question is posed. The commentary states: "The vessel is a metaphor for the preceding sensory objects."

This single passage uses the analogy of empty space to illustrate seeing. Because Ānanda stated that seeing has dimensions of large and small, the Buddha therefore spoke of the analogy of space being divided by various vessels.
If seeing were fixed in its orientation, then when a round vessel is placed separately [within it], the space [of seeing] ought not to become round.
"Second, the characteristics [of the space] are not established. The commentary states: "What fault is there in asserting that [space] is fixed?

If it is claimed that when a square vessel is placed in a corner, the space becomes square, then if a round platter were separately placed upon that square vessel, the space should not conform to the round shape.
It would be as if one were looking at a square space within a square platter, like the 'pointed space' found within the horns of a sheep."

In the past, he knew that [the sun] was not fixed in its direction; since it is not fixed in one direction when situated in a cardinal point, it is likewise not fixed as circular when situated in a circle.
Now, however, it appears circular to Dharmodgata. If it were definitively above, it would be large; yet upon returning to the Jeta Grove, it should not be small, for now it is small again.
Previously, when known to be above, it did not appear large either; now, looking down at the eaves and corridors, it is seen.
Nor is it small.
