Today, the Tathāgata has universally proclaimed for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate meaning within the ultimate meaning.

Regarding the two [truths], the *Jian* (Commentary) states: "The two truths of the conventional and the ultimate each have four [subdivisions]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 47, says: "The four conventional [truths] are:

first, the truth of nominal designation without reality (*prajñapti-satya*, e.g., a jar formed from pleasant objects); second, the truth of differentiation according to phenomena (*vastu-vibhāga-satya*)."

(Three Categories) The three skillful means establish the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). (Four Teachings) The four reliances reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). (Two Emptinesses) Furthermore, there are four kinds of the ultimate:

first, the truth of the manifestation of essence and function (Three Categories); second, the truth of the differentiation of cause and effect (Four Truths); third, the truth of the realization of the ultimate (Two Emptinesses);
and fourth, the ultimate of the ultimate (beyond words and transcending marks). "Wei" (猶) means "to accompany," and "xuan" (宣) means "to proclaim."
It is said that "victory" (vīta) means "extraordinary" (viśeṣa). This ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established in contrast to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
although it is real, it is still established in relation to the false. The nature of the true ultimate, however, is the ultimate truth itself; it is not established in contrast to conventional truth.
This is the aforementioned ultimate truth of the ultimate truth, because it is free from names and transcends all signs. The Commentary states: "It is non-conceptually established (*aprajñapti*)."
The Gate: The former, the "superior ultimate," is the gate of formal establishment. It contrasts the real with the false and the superior ultimate with the conventional.
This nature of the true superior ultimate brushes away both the real and the false; it does not stand in opposition to them.

He causes those of fixed nature among the śrāvakas in your assembly to undergo three types of transformation, making their differences accord with the truth. The commentary states: "Those of fixed nature" refers to those within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly who were of indeterminate nature and have turned [toward the Mahāyāna].
This concerns Śāriputra and the twelve hundred bhikṣus present at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly.
"All shall receive the prediction" means that those of indeterminate nature are transformed. The Commentary permits that during the Buddha's lifetime, he transformed śrāvakas of determinate nature.

If one follows the doctrine of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*), it is not permitted for those of determinate nature to attain Buddhahood. If those of determinate nature were to attain Buddhahood, they would no longer be called "determinate.
Now, this is not the case; if those of determinate nature do not attain Buddhahood, for what reason does the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [teach otherwise]?
It is said: there is no other vehicle by which one may attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Even when various teachings state that one does not become a Buddha, these are merely temporary refutations intended to cause them to turn their minds away from stagnation.

If one were to say directly that all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) simultaneously become Buddhas, then ordinary beings would falsely take their outflows (*āsrava*) to be the path and desire to return to the Truth. If one were to say directly that Śrāvakas become Buddhas, then the Śrāvakas...
Among such people, those who sink into emptiness are many; thus, there are varying praises and differing censures.
Now, reaching the forty-ninth year, he finally turns his fixed nature to achieve Buddhahood. How could ordinary minds doubt what was spoken from the Golden Mouth? As the Lotus Sūtra says:
"The rest of the assembly of śrāvakas shall also attain such [realization]. Those who were not present at this assembly, you should..."
"Expound for them, as well as for all others. The commentary states:
"This refers to speaking universally to both ordinary beings and sages."
"Those who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness.
The commentary states: "This refers to śrāvakas still in training, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and others who have turned toward the Mahāyāna, such as arhats."
The commentary states: "Thus, the great-power śrāvakas who enter the Mahāyāna, as well as those who include the pratyekabuddhas, all attain the ground of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle."
The commentary states: This is the fundamentally awakened nature, the pure and true essence. Therefore, Avalokiteśvara’s description of his realization says:
"When birth-and-death has ceased, quiescent extinction manifests; suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds. This is the realization of the true essence of quiescent extinction.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "The seat of the field of quiescent extinction. Here, "Way" (*mārga*) refers to the unsurpassed path of awakening, and "field" (*kṣetra*) refers to...
The site of quiescent extinction. As for the seat, it is the emptiness of all phenomena that serves as the seat.
This is true *araṇya*. The commentary states:
"True [practice] excludes the false. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "There may be those who dwell in *araṇya*, wearing patched robes in the open air."
Xian claimed for himself that he practiced the true Way and held those in the human world in contempt. He further said, "This man harbors an evil mind and constantly dwells on worldly affairs;
he merely borrows the name 'āraṇyaka' while delighting in exposing our faults. True *āraṇyaka* is also called a "place of tranquility," and there are two kinds:
first, being far from the sounds of chickens and dogs; second, being far from the sounds of axes and hatchets. Now...

The statement "speaking of the true to distinguish it from one part that is false" means: if it is the false, then [the practitioner] wears patched robes in empty, secluded places and other such sites of formal cultivation.
The commentary states: this distinguishes them from sites of heterodox cultivation; if one dwells among rafters or lies upon thorns, these are heterodox.
"Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
Having received the subtle intent of this fourfold injunction, Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s voice of Dharma, listened in silence.
Later, the assembly of sages all held him in high esteem.
The Buddha said to Pūrṇa, "As you have said, [the nature of reality] is fundamentally pure; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?"

The subsequent section, "Correctly Expounding and Resolving Doubts," has two parts. The first part, "Resolving the Sudden Arising of Doubts Regarding Reality," has two sections. The first section, "Resolving Previous Doubts," has four parts.

The first part, "Clarifying that Fundamental Delusion and Conditions Form the Seeds of the Three Consciousnesses," has two sub-sections. The first sub-section, "Provisionally Distinguishing Reality and Delusion," has five parts.
The first part is the statement of the previous doubt. The *Jian* (Commentary) says: "This refers to the preceding passage where the questioner asked about the purity of the ground."

It is primordial. How could it suddenly arise? As for the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena, have you not constantly heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the fundamental awakening is wondrously luminous?
The second question concerns what was previously said. The commentary states: "You have simply not heard me say, etcetera.
To conceive of the mind as arising from nature is to forcibly produce a conscious illumination; this is the origin of the initial emergence of ignorance.
As for 'wondrous clarity,' its essence does not depart from the Truth (Tathatā); yet it turns its back on that essence to follow after clarity—this is the clarity of nature."

"Fundamental enlightenment is luminous and wondrous. The commentary states: "Fundamental enlightenment" refers to the enlightened nature of the fundamental substance (*dharmatā*). This nature is "luminous" because when it gives rise to wisdom, it illuminates principle;

it is "wondrous" because it is free from subject and object. An outsider asks: "If the signs of weariness [of delusion] appear within this enlightenment, then by merely speaking of 'delusion,' one immediately grasps its essence."
For what reason is it established as the name "awakened nature" (*xingjue*)? Answer: Delusion arises from the True; thus, delusion receives the name "awakening.

The signs of weariness arise from awakening; when one censures that weariness, it is termed "delusion. The meaning is that these deluded phenomena do not arise from a separate location, just as waves arise from water;
therefore, they receive the name "awakening. Because the signs of weariness manifest for the sake of awakening others, one censures that weariness and thereby designates it as "delusion."
The outsider asks again: "If the awakened nature (*xing-jue*) is delusive and original awakening (*ben-jue*) is true, why does [the text] not begin with the true, but rather begins with the delusive?
Answer: To subsume the branches within the root, the original should properly come first; however, to reveal the delusion by tracing it back to its source, the nature is first designated.
As for "nature," it refers to the nature that brings forth illumination.
Pūrṇa said, "Indeed, World-Honored One. I have constantly heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning;
I have heard the ancient intent three times. [The] *Jian* (Commentary) says: "‘Indeed’ (*wei ran*) is a word of assent."
The Buddha said, "You call this 'awakened clarity.
It has been tested through four examinations. The commentary states: Since the Buddha had seen his answer, he spoke of the meanings of these two types of awakening—'constant' and 'hearing.'

He then caused him to discern whether this concentrated clarity was the luminosity of the nature itself, such that it was called "awakening," or whether it was an awakening that lacked luminosity, such that it was called "luminous awakening. The commentary states:
The Buddha then asked: "Is it that you take this luminosity of the nature and its deluded awakening as being 'true,' or is it that [a further state] arises?"
The wisdom of initial awakening realizes that this intrinsic luminosity is illusory; only then can it be called "luminous awakening.
Since this is truly not luminous, there is no intrinsic luminosity. Pūrṇa said: "If this is not luminous..."
5. Distinguishing the True. The commentary states: Pūrṇa is counted among the thousand Buddhas; thus, by being selected, he attains the true.
It is not that he clarifies the absence of nature (niḥsvabhāva) as clarity;
rather, he is named an Awakened One (buddha).
The commentary states: "Since there is no 'illumination of nature,' this is precisely the Real. Thus, there is nothing to be illuminated. The commentary continues:

"Since this is not an illumination [of something external], it is the illumination of the awakened nature; thus, there is nothing to be illuminated. That which is illuminated is the illumination of the nature itself."
Regarding the single dharma of self-delusion, the Buddha said: "If there is nothing that is illuminated, subsequently the deluded consciousness arises.
This consists of four parts; first, the two conditions intersect and are refuted. The commentary states: "That which is illuminated does not exist."
It is clarity.
Thus, there is no deluded awakening.
The commentary states: "Thus, there is no powerful cognition capable of being the object-condition."
"There is something that is not awakening.
The commentary states: "If there is something illuminated and something unilluminated, then it is not the truth;
there is nothing that is not illumination."
The Commentary states: "If there were no ignorance that is to be illuminated, then there would be no powerful awakening capable of illuminating it;
yet ignorance is not itself the nature of profound, lucid awareness.
This pair [of statements] distinguishes between the two [aspects of] clarity. Part Three: First, distinguishing the false from the true. The Commentary states: "Ignorance is the nature."
The mark of clarity. Furthermore, this is not the nature of true awakening, which is profoundly still, tranquil, and perfectly luminous.
The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous;
these two [phrases] reveal the true luminosity and profound stillness. The commentary states: "Nature" refers to the essential body; "awakening" is true awakening; it is necessarily perfect.
"Clarity. To falsely take this as a conscious clarity.
Third, the reprimand for the false arising of clarity. The commentary states: "It arises because the deluded minds of all sentient beings give rise to something separate from the mind."
Seeking [it], there arises the characteristic of luminous nature and forceful awakening; yet awakening is not that which is illuminated. Section Three:
On the Extinction and Arising of Identity and Difference (two parts). Part One: Establishing difference based on delusion regarding the Truth. The Commentary states: This is the true awakening...
"Nature" refers to the "awakening" in the previous phrase, "the nature-awakening must be luminous"; it is not the characteristic of the luminosity of nature.
"Based on luminosity, the object is established.
The commentary states: because there is the luminosity of nature, one immediately establishes the luminosity of nature as the object.
"Once that which is perceived has been falsely established," the commentary says, "this luminous nature of the essence gives rise to your false capacity for perception."
The commentary states: This is forced awakening; this forced awakening arises from nature and characteristics.
Within that which is neither identical nor different, the commentary states: it is at the time when the characteristic of luminous nature has not yet been divided into subject and object.
"Blazingly it becomes differentiated.
The commentary states: "Blazingly" describes the intensity of the fire. The characteristic of the luminous nature has neither sameness nor difference;

yet because of the arising of forceful awareness, there subsequently arise the three subtle consciousnesses of karma, transformation, and manifestation—this is what is meant by "blazingly it becomes differentiated. Because of the arising of forceful awareness...

It comes; because it involves activity, it is called "karma" (action). Once there is activity, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) subsequently arise. They are called "evolving" (*pravṛtti*) because they turn away [from their source].
This turning away is from the true essence; this constitutes the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the cause of the delusions of the twelve classes of sentient beings.
Once the evolving consciousnesses have arisen, there subsequently arises the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*). It is called "manifest" because it manifests;
this is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is the cause of the delusion regarding mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
"It differs from that which it differs from.

This refers to two successive differences in the source of the *tàn* (eddies). The commentary states: "The 'difference' (*yì*) is that which is capable of differentiating; this refers to the three subtle consciousnesses (*sān xì shí*).

That which it differs from is ignorance (*wú míng*). Alternatively, 'difference' may be the characteristic of the luminous nature (*xìng míng xiàng*), and that which it differs from is the three subtle consciousnesses."

Although these are equally described as being contrary to the truth, upon closer inspection they are nonetheless distinct. Now, one realizes that these three subtle consciousnesses are different from the previously mentioned nature of luminous appearance; hence the repeated explanation.
"Based on difference, one establishes sameness.
The commentary states: "Because one can differentiate from delusion, one intends to restore the sameness of ignorance; this may be acceptable.
Since these three subtle consciousnesses are established as being different, one then posits the preceding characteristic of the luminous nature as being the same."
"Elucidating Identity and Difference.
The Commentary states: "Identity refers to the luminous aspect of the nature; difference refers to the three subtle consciousnesses.
Because they give rise to clarity and understanding, one further establishes 'neither identical nor different' based upon this."

The commentary states: Since one has already become weary of the three subtle consciousnesses as being "different," one establishes the preceding nature-luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) as "identical.
Once the previously established identity of the nature-luminosity is found untenable, one further establishes the nature-luminosity as being "neither identical nor different.

Alternatively, it may be that the nature-luminosity is "different" because it turns its back on the True [Suchness]. Thus, in opposition to the three subtle consciousnesses, the nature-luminosity is established as "identical. Having been established as identical...

He then seizes away the designation of "difference. Since difference has no name, he uses the verse concerning "sameness" to create confusion; thus, he establishes the position of "neither sameness nor difference.
In this manner, he causes turmoil.

The fourth [section], "The Signs Arising from Fatigue," consists of three parts. First, it clarifies how fatigue arises through confusion. The commentary states: "Internal mental activity involves mutual dependence, which gives rise to fatigue.
The commentary further states: "Thereupon, the duality of subject and object arises, producing weariness and exhaustion."
"Exhaustion over a long duration gives rise to dust.

The Commentary states: "Once one perceives that the mind has become weary from prolonged exertion, delusory dust arises, defiling its own true essence and causing its own characteristics to become turbid."
The commentary states: "From within the luminous aspect of the nature itself, its turbidity arises. This delusion does not arise from any other place;
it arises solely in relation to the luminous aspect of the nature."
From this, worldly toil and afflictions are incited.
Second, the similarities and differences of the realm of space are clarified. The commentary states: "Because of this, one then incites the causes of dust and gives rise to toil."

Therefore, it is called "dust and toil. To be vexed is to be afflicted by resentment; to be troubled is to be disturbed by turmoil. Thus there arise the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and so forth, which give rise to the world.
The commentary states: Because there is movement within the inner mind, the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) arises;
when stillness is established, empty space appears.

The commentary further states: When there is no movement within the inner mind, the characteristic of empty space immediately manifests. All of these refer to the direct transformations of the eight consciousnesses.
"Space is the same. The commentary states: "Because space is one, it is said to be the same;
worlds are different."
The commentary states: There are horizontal worlds, vertical worlds, worlds of sentient beings, and worlds of insentient things;
because there are many such designations, they are considered distinct.
That [state] is without identity or difference; it is truly conditioned phenomena.
The three fingers are the source from which the differentiated aspects arise. The commentary states: The outsider asks, "This absence of identity and difference—is it real or false?"
The Sūtra states: "Therein, there is neither identity nor difference. It is truly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), not unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Consciousness-awareness (*bodhi-vijñāna*) and the darkness of space—these two, seven conditions and eight attachments, strike at the objective division (*nimitta-bhāga*) to produce [phenomena]. This section has two parts. First, the four wheels spread forth; this section has four parts. First: [Text continues]
"Wind. The commentary states: "Awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) arises from the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), which clings to the eighth consciousness as its object and grasps it as a self.

It is not the fundamental nature of clarity (*xing-ming*). Since it clings to the eighth consciousness as a self, the inner mind becomes weary and exhausted, and externally it carries with it a portion of stubborn emptiness (*wan-kong*) that obstructs the sensory faculty.
Therefore, it is called "empty and obscure" (*kong-wei*); "obscure" (*wei*) means dark. Because of this stubborn emptiness being dark and obscure, [it is called wind].
Mutual dependence gives rise to oscillation; thus, there is the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
The commentary states: Having perceived that the dark, dull, and stubborn void corresponds to one's own mind, one then comes to loathe this dark and obscure void.
One gives rise to the thought of wishing to restore it to its original nature of luminosity and identical essence; thereby, one begins to oscillate, which externally induces the wind-circle.
It sustains the world.
The commentary states: When the world is formed, it is likewise the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*); when the world is destroyed, it is likewise the wind-circle.
However, as the world is about to be destroyed, the Vairambha winds strike Mount Sumeru and crush it like fine powder.
"Because of emptiness, movement arises.
(Two lines of gold. The commentary states: Because of deluded attachment to empty space, one becomes weary of emptiness; intending to return to clarity, movement thus arises.
"Solidity and clarity establish obstruction.

The commentary states: "When the nature of solidity and craving further solidifies the nature of the preceding luminosity, there are then the six obstructions. 'Obstruction' means having solidity as its nature."
Regarding "those gold treasures":

the commentary states that Mount Sumeru is composed of the seven precious substances, while the seven golden mountains are composed of four precious substances; all are comprised within the earth element.
"Clear awakening establishes firmness.
The commentary states: "One clarifies the nature of deluded awakening and establishes firm love; because one returns to the clarity of the original nature, there is the Golden Wheel."
The commentary states: "Thereupon, the element of earth manifests, sustaining the land.
The commentary states: "The land is that which is encompassed by the element of earth."
The precious adamantine awakening is accomplished.
There are three fires. The commentary states: this reiterates the preceding earth element;
through the agitation of luminosity, wind emerges.
The commentary states: When the inner mind stirs and manifests, wind is produced; this cites the preceding element of wind.
"Wind and metal grind against each other.
The commentary states: Wind and metal rub and polish one another.
"Therefore, there is the fire-element.
The Commentary states: "Since [the mind] wavers and desires to return to its former nature of solidity while its luminous essence gives rise to agitation, there is the fire-element.
It arises based upon the aforementioned great element."
It is of the nature of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
The commentary states: "Transformation" refers to the maturation of what has arisen; furthermore, because fire depends upon various conditions, it is called "transformation.
Fire is the very nature of transformation.
"The jewel's brilliance produces moisture" refers to the four waters.

The commentary states: Because the inner mind is stubbornly attached and its craving further obstructs the brilliance, it is said that "moisture is produced. This cites the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
"The fire-light steams upward.
The Commentary states: "To steam is to rise and billow. The inner mind rises as agitation, evoking the vast and enduring. This refers to the fire-element;
therefore, there is a water-wheel that contains the realms of the ten directions."
The commentary states: Since he was firmly intent on restoring that nature of luminosity, his mind became agitated; thereupon, love arose within his heart, causing the water-element to manifest.
As the fire ascended and the water descended, they interacted and solidified into a firm mass.
The subsequent section on the Great Elements consists of three parts. The first part clarifies the text on mutual pervasion and consists of two sections.

In the first, the two wheels manifest their forms through surging, descending, swirling, and billowing. The commentary states: "Fire ascends toward what is dry; water moistens and flows toward what is wet.
Fire symbolizes the mind seeking within; water symbolizes love for what is within."
The moist becomes the great ocean; the dry becomes the islands and sandbanks. The Commentary states:
When the mind is weak and persistent, it increases the moisture of water; when the mind is strong, it increases the wind. When the mind is weak, [it increases] the water;
when the mind is strong, it internally evokes the earth element. As it is said: "The accumulation of sand in the river is due to human effort."
It is called a "continent" (*dvīpa*).
For this reason, within that great ocean, flames constantly arise; and within those continents and sandbanks, rivers and streams constantly flow.

Second, the drawing forth [of fire] from the ocean, the fire-island, the river, and the clarity pervading all. The commentary states: The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says, "There are always four great precious jewels;
from within these jewels, fire issues forth, burning and drying up the ocean. If these jewels did not exist, the people of the world would be submerged and swept away by it;
thus one comes to know that fire exists within water."
The power of the water is inferior to that of the fire, which solidifies into a high mountain.

This section, which clarifies their relative superiority and inferiority, is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies that the fire is powerful while the water is inferior, standing like a peak reaching into the heavens. This is further divided into two parts;
first, it clarifies the formation of the physical characteristics. The commentary states: "If the power of the water is inferior to the fire, it will be dried up by the fire. Thereafter..."
They form soil. Through successive accumulation, they become high mountains. Within the great element of water, there are also the elements of fire and earth;
therefore, when mountain rocks are struck, they produce flames, and when melted, they become water.
"Second, they are mutually pervasive. The commentary states: "Therefore, when mountain rocks are struck by objects, fire erupts; when steamed by mists, water flows.
Within the earth element of the Dharma-realm, there are likewise the fire element and the water element."
The power of the earth is inferior to that of water; it is drawn up to become grasses and trees.

In these two cases, the earth is weak while the water is dominant. The grasses spread in circles and the forests rise high, their patterns clearly manifesting as interconnected forms. The commentary states:
When the force of water is great, it draws forth grasses and trees, thereby benefiting parched and withered places so that the vegetation flourishes.
Likewise, when the mind of Dharmottara is weak and his attachment is predominant, afflictions will ultimately arise.
Therefore, regarding "forests and marshes" (*vana-khaṇḍa*):
the two [terms] are cited as being mutually pervasive. The commentary states: "That which has water is called a marsh (*saras*); that which lacks water is called a thicket (*khaṇḍa*).
When burned away, it becomes earth."
The commentary states: It is like a place of mountains, forests, marshes, or swamps that, once scorched by fire, is about to turn into ash and dust.
When the mind’s attachment to dharmas is weak while the parched mind is predominant, if one's desires are not fulfilled, the mind of anger severs that attachment and gives rise to stubborn fixation.
By wringing, it becomes water.
The commentary states: Just as by wringing grass or wringing wood, water is produced;

so too, when the mind of firm attachment is weak and the mind of affection is intense, the object follows that affection and moistens the firm attachment. Grass and wood are categorized within the earth element.
The mutual interaction of delusions gives rise [to phenomena].

Regarding the second part, which explains the external manifestations of the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), the commentary states: "The four great elements first interact and thereby give rise [to phenomena]. This first section concludes the preceding discussion on the seeds of interaction.
"They act as seeds for one another.

The commentary states: "Within a single Great Element, all other Great Elements are fully present. Taking the earth element as the seed, there likewise arise the characteristics of the water element and others.
For example, when the internal mind vibrates, it externally evokes the wind element; when the internal mind is parched and urgent, it externally evokes the fire element."
The earth element: when the internal mind is firm and persistent, it externally perceives the earth element; when the internal mind is increasingly moist, it [externally perceives] water.
By these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
"Later, it is concluded that the world flows eternally. The commentary states: "Thereby, the continuity of worlds exists.
Both the four great elements (mahābhūta) within and without the world are transformations of the mind. This refers to the world as the objective basis (*āśraya*)."
Furthermore, Pūrṇa, the delusion of clarity is not from another.

[The text] "The three and six consciousnesses grasp objects, forming heavy categories and seeds" (6) consists of six parts. First is the heading that points back to the previous error. The commentary states:
To clarify that these illusory phenomena are not produced by another, but are all created by oneself:
the fault lies in the clarity of awakening.
The Commentary states: Because of forced awakening, one awakens to the luminosity of other natures; subsequently, the four great elements arise from one another, and thus [suffering] occurs.
Fault. Once that which is falsely imagined has been established, the commentary states:
"The establishment of 'other-nature' (parabhāva) is made clear as the object-condition (ālambana-viṣaya)."
"Clarifying principle does not exceed [it].

The Commentary states: "Being able to clarify vigorous awakening, it does not deviate from the clarity of the established nature. Within the interval between the two dharmas of subject and object, one cannot transcend them;
subject and object mutually suppress one another, yet they have not been forgotten."
For these reasons, hearing does not transcend sound, and seeing does not go beyond form. Form, fragrance, taste, and touch—these six delusions are fully established.
The commentary states: "This is because of such causes and conditions. Being obstructed by the sensory object of sound, one cannot escape from sound.
If one were a sage, one would transcend sound, and likewise with respect to the six objects of the senses, including form, fragrance, taste, and touch."
From this, seeing, sensing, hearing, and knowing are distinguished.

Second, the false consciousness is analyzed. The commentary states: "Seeing" refers to the eye; "sensing" refers to the body; "hearing" refers to the nose and ears; and "knowing" refers to the tongue and mind.
The above constitutes consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since the sense organs (*indriya*) are not mentioned, they are included by implication.
"Mutually entangled by common karma; through union and separation, transformation is formed.
Regarding the three pairs of causes that trigger karma, there are three sections. First, the two causes are raised to establish the four classes of birth. The Commentary states:
Beings of similar karma entwine one another; they raise up craving and grasp at perception. These two serve as causes, whereby union and separation bring about transformation.

Although "transformation" (nirmāṇa) is mentioned, it subsumes the womb-born, egg-born, and moisture-born. In the moisture-born, perception is predominant and feeling is slight; in the womb-born, perception is slight and feeling is predominant;
in the moisture-born, feeling and perception are combined; in the transformation-born, feeling and perception are separated.
"Seeing light and the manifestation of forms.
Second, the description of the causal momentum of arising distinguishes between the two single and double [factors]. The commentary states: "They mutually induce one another;
through seeing, light, and perception, they are established."
The commentary states: "Form leads to perception;
divergent views give rise to aversion.
The commentary further states: "Perception proceeds whether it be agreeable or disagreeable."
"Similar perceptions give rise to craving.

The commentary states: "Craving arises solely from objects that are agreeable to the mind; similar perceptions include the perception of father, the perception of mother, and the perception of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)."
The father conceives love for the mother; the mother conceives love for the father. If the intermediate state being is male, it conceives love for the mother;
if the intermediate state being is female, it conceives love for the father.
The flowing of craving constitutes the seed.
The three modes of conjunction give rise to two causes, manifesting the roots of the seeds. The commentary states: "Craving is received within as the seed;
that is to say, emotional attachment serves as the moistening cause."
"Taking thought as the embryo.
The commentary states: "Thought acts as the agent of birth;
through their mutual union, life is produced."
The commentary states: "The two dharmas of emotion (*qing*) and thought (*xiang*) intersect and congregate;

therefore, they give rise to [rebirth] by attracting those of similar karma (*tongye*). The commentary further states: "'Absorb' (*xi*) means to draw forth. Both terms refer to the two dharmas of emotion and thought. "Similar karma" refers precisely to these emotions and thoughts.
This refers to the cause.
Thus, there is a causal condition that gives rise to the *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.

Regarding the four [stages] that draw forth the fruit as retribution for the cause, the commentary states: "The *kalala* is translated in the Tang language as 'impurity' (*záwèi*). (First week)" The sub-commentary says: "Translated..."
This refers to the meaning. The same applies to all subsequent terms. *Āpudamāṃsa* (遏蒲曇): in the language of Tang, "congealed. (27) *Kaśipu* (蔽尸): in the language of Tang, "thickened congealment.

(37) *Ghanas* (健南): in the language of Tang, "fetal membrane" (*kalala*). (47) *Praśākhā* (鉢羅奢佉): in the language of Tang, "limbs" (*ghana*). (57) The commentary states: "The term 'parts' (*aṅga*) is also taken by way of its meaning; thus there is a causal relationship.
This [membrane] is the cause, and the production of the *kalala* is the effect," and so on, including the three stages.
Section on the Stages.

Regarding the five types—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—the textual commentary on "mutual permeation" has two parts. First, distinguishing the types. The sub-commentary states: "Womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born" merely cites [the categories].
The fruits of the four modes of birth are simultaneously reflected and grasped by the twelve categories [of beings].
According to what is appropriate for each.
The commentary states: "Appropriate" (yìng) means "to manifest" (xiàn) and "to accord with" (hé).
Eggs are produced solely through thought.
The Commentary states: Nine parts consist of form (nimitta), while one part consists of emotion (sneha).
The womb-born arises because of emotion.
The commentary states: "Nine parts are *qing* (sentiment/emotion) and one part is *xiang* (perception/imagination).
They are moistened by their mutual resonance.
The commentary further states: "Sentiment and perception are combined; five parts are *qing* and five parts are *xiang*."
"Transform them by means of detachment.
The commentary states: "When both emotion and thought are detached, and emotion and thought alternate between union and separation, they undergo further mutual transformation."

Later, [the text] excludes *xūn* (perfuming). The commentary states: "The mention of 'conjoining' and 'separating' here serves to cite moisture-born and transformation-born beings by way of implication, while including womb-born and egg-born beings.
To undergo change is called *biàn* (transformation); to undergo alteration is called *yì* (change). To abandon one life and universally receive another is termed *biàn*;
to weary of the old and follow the new is termed *yì*."
All sentient beings, according to their karma, undergo the cycle of flying and sinking.
The six bonds form the internal and external realms. The commentary states: those with much conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and little emotion (*vedanā*) become flying birds;

those with much emotion and little conceptualization become the class of walking creatures. "Sinking" refers to the class of walking creatures. Alternatively, the character *shui* (遂) may be read as *zhu* (逐); this interpretation is also valid.
For this reason. [The] commentary states: "This cause refers to the continuity of sentient beings."
The commentary states: This refers to the fruit.

Pūrṇa, the conjunction of conceptualization and craving constitutes the root of the fruit of suffering—the three delusions within the four modes of bodily activity. The text has three parts; the first solely clarifies the three delusions, which is further divided into three sections. First: [Text follows]
"Sexual intercourse. The commentary states: "The perception of father, the perception of mother, and the perception of the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*).

If the intermediate state being is male, it gives rise to desire toward the mother's body; if the intermediate state being is female, it gives rise to desire toward the father's body. The father then conceives love for the mother."
The mother conceives love for the father; they share the same fetters.
Love cannot be parted from.
The commentary states: this refers to this single dharma of desire, which cannot be abandoned. Since it cannot be abandoned...
Thus, throughout all the worlds, fathers, mothers, sons, and grandsons are born in succession without interruption.
The commentary states: "Son" (*zi*) is synonymous with "procreation" (*zi*). One who procreates and shows compassion for those below is called a son.

The son’s son is called a grandson (*sun*). The grandson’s son is called a great-grandson (*zengsun*). The great-grandson’s son is called a distant descendant (*xuansun*). The distant descendant’s son is called a further descendant (*laisun*). The further descendant’s... [text continues].
"The descendant of this son is called the 'cloud-grandson' (yúnsūn)," which refers to the sixth generation. Thus, sons and grandsons succeed one another in birth, without interruption.
These [beings] take desire and greed as their root.
The commentary states: "To point directly to these [states] means that they take desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) as their root;
greed and craving nourish one another, and greed cannot be rectified.
Second is killing. The commentary states: "This cites the preceding single dharma of desire and introduces the following passage concerning the killing-greed. This is...
Simultaneously nourishing and benefiting one another, their minds become attached to physical forms;
as greed and craving cannot be stilled, all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, from transformation, from moisture, or from a womb—devour one another according to the strength of their power.
These acts are rooted in the greed for killing.
The commentary states: The strong covet the weak. Humans eat sheep;
when the sheep dies, it becomes a human; when the human dies, they become a sheep. This continues through ten successive births.
"Third, the stealing [of life]. The commentary states: 'The ten classes of beings' refers to the complete enumeration; these are the twelve categories.
Dying and being born, they prey upon one another in turn."
The commentary states: In this realm, one dies and dies again; one is born and is born again. In other realms as well, one is born and is born again;
one dies and dies again.
Evil karma arises together with them, persisting until the end of the future.
The commentary states: "The seeds of evil karma arise simultaneously;
these are rooted in the greed for theft. The commentary further states:
"Because one steals and kills others, it is called 'greed for theft. These three delusions are all termed 'greed' because they are all [of that nature]."
The single dharma of desire is the root. Taken collectively, it is said that within the inner mind, greed is the cause and desire is the effect;
delusion is the cause and theft is the effect; hatred is the cause and killing is the effect. If there were no lustful greed, the other two would not exist;
therefore, only greed is mentioned.
"You owe me my life.
Second, the two debts follow one another in succession. First, the mutual debt of killing and stealing. The commentary states:
"It means that in a previous life you killed me, and thus in this life you now owe me my life. This concludes the section on killing.
"I shall repay your debt. By reason of this cause and condition, may I remain constantly within birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
The commentary states: This means that in a previous life I owed you a debt, and in this life I am repaying that debt to you; this concludes the section on stealing.
"You love my heart; I cherish your form. Because of these causes and conditions, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we shall always remain bound in entanglement.
Subsequently, he raises the characteristic of defilement; the commentary states: "This is the text on the formation of desire."
Only the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—constitute the fundamental [unwholesome] roots. By these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession.

[The text] concludes these three by summarizing them through three conditions and tracing them back to their source in delusion; this constitutes the third section. First, it summarizes the preceding three afflictions. The Commentary states:
Previously, one followed the Hinayana, placing sexual misconduct first; here, when forming the bonds, one returns to the Mahayana, placing killing first.
Pūrṇa, these three types of inverted continuity are all the luminosity of awakening.
Second, tracing delusion back to its source. The commentary states: "Awakening" (jue) refers to the forceful awakening; "clarity" (ming) refers to the innate clarity of the nature.
Both arise because this forceful awakening, which is capable of illuminating, takes the innate clarity of the nature as its object. Consequently, delusive phenomena emerge through mutual suppression.
"Clearly and fully knowing the nature.
The commentary states: This is the eighth consciousness;
because it clearly perceives, it gives rise to appearances.

The commentary states: Because the eighth consciousness undergoes transformation, it becomes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). That which manifests as its object is the manifesting-consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*), serving as the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

It arises from deluded seeing. The commentary further states: These three delusions and their associated phenomena all arise from the seeing-part; this is because they take the seeing-part as their objective condition.
The twelve classes of beings have inversion as their cause. The perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the cause of the inversion that constitutes mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

These mountains, rivers, and the great earth, along with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), undergo successive transitions and flows; because they are false and illusory, they end and then begin again.

"Third, the external divisions are subject to flux and transformation. The commentary states: "In this section, he answers the previous question from the beginning of the sutra regarding how true reality suddenly gives rise to delusion.
It says that all things arise from deluded vision, whereby there is the flux and transformation of mountains, rivers, and so forth, which end and then begin again;
this is the arising and ceasing of the four phases."
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrously enlightened and luminous, [the subsequent text consists of two parts:

first, the passage on resolving new doubts; within that, first, the passage on raising difficulties based on the causal vehicle; within that, first, the manifestation of the identity of ordinary beings and sages]."
The commentary states: "If this wondrous awakening is the nature of true awakening that is inherently subtle and wondrous"—this is a doubt.
This passage cites the preceding text, referring to the Buddha-nature within the causal stage.
It is identical to the mind of the Tathāgata—neither increasing nor decreasing.
The commentary states: This nature of the one true reality does not increase within the realm of the Buddhas, nor does it decrease within the realm of ordinary beings;
this is the Buddha-nature within the state of fruition.
Without manifest cause, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise.
