The Śūnyatā-deva has no body yet possesses touch.
The commentary states: "Śūnyatā is the deity of emptiness. This deity of emptiness has no body, yet is able to experience touch."
The light of the Tathāgata reflects it so that it appears for a moment.

The commentary states: The sūtra-author asks, "Since there is no body, by what means will one experience the object of touch? The answer is as follows: This appearance is the manifestation of the body that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-kāya*).
"Since it is of the nature of wind, its substance is fundamentally non-existent.
The commentary states: "Since it is of the nature of wind, it is formless. 'Its substance is fundamentally non-existent' reiterates the text regarding the absence of a body."
"Śrāvakas who have attained the tranquility of the various meditative absorptions of cessation.

The commentary states: It is also called the "meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception. This means that while the six [consciousnesses] are ceased, it also includes the exhaustion of the seven defiled portions;
the pure portions are not ceased. "Attaining tranquility" refers to attaining the principle of empty stillness.
In this assembly, Mahākāśyapa has long since extinguished the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*).

The commentary states: "Kāśyapa" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "Drinking Light. This is a Brahmin clan name. "Drinking Light" refers to the lineage of the *ṛṣis*; he was named after his clan.
It is also said that because the light of his own body eclipsed the light of the sun and moon, he is called Kāśyapa. [The term] "faculty of mind" (*manas-indriya*)...
"Then the sixth consciousness clearly and fully knows.
The commentary states: "This is the true nature."
"It does not depend on mental cognition.

The commentary states: "This refers to the mental cognition of the sixth consciousness. 'Cognition' (nian) carries the meaning of latent recording. All of the above is discussed in terms of the absence of the physical sense organ (*bu-chen-gen*)."

"Ānanda, now as for your various faculties (*indriya*), you shall later be exhorted to melt away delusion and swiftly realize [enlightenment]. The commentary states: "The 'various faculties' refer to the six sense organs.
If they are already uprooted in their entirety..."
The commentary states: "When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are simultaneously liberated;
the inner clarity gives rise to radiance.
The commentary further states: "The pure wisdom of initial awakening initiates luminosity."
"Such floating dust.
The commentary states: "The six sense organs and the physical world."
The commentary states: "That upon which they depend.
The various manifestations of transformation.
The commentary states: "Because the aforementioned faculties, objects, and so forth are all devoid of reality, they are called 'manifestations of transformation.'"
It is like hot water dissolving ice; with a single thought, it transforms into supreme awakening. The Commentary states:
True wisdom is like the hot water, and the dissolution of others' deluded attachments is like the melting of ice. "With a single thought" means a slight thought;
a slight thought leads to non-thought; non-thought leads to non-discrimination. At the moment when wisdom accords with principle, the very substance [of reality] is immediately realized.

It accomplishes the insurpassable true suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of spiritual awareness and cognition. This nature is the principle of the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Ānanda, it is like that person in the world who gathers their vision within the eye.
The subsequent section, "The False Unifies with the True," consists of two parts. First, regarding the distinctiveness of withdrawing the sense faculties:
the commentary states, "It is like people in the world who gather various perceptions and all claim they reside in the eye."
If one causes them to close suddenly, the appearance of darkness manifests before them and the six sense organs become darkened; head and feet appear as one.

The commentary states: "If one causes another to suddenly cover both eyes so that they no longer perceive external objects, they will immediately perceive the appearance of darkness according to their own experience.
If one sense organ is thus affected, all six sense organs will likewise suddenly close, becoming pitch black."
It is confronted with its object; it is much like the relationship between the head and the feet.
When that person uses their hand to trace around the exterior of the body, although they do not see it, once the head and feet are distinguished, the cognition is identical.
The commentary states: That person who is hurriedly joined together takes a single hand and follows it along the body;
from the outside, it comes to unify and pervade across the six sense organs, such as the eyes, ears, and nose.

Although those eyes do not see, all the sense organs simultaneously become darkened, yet the head and feet are each individually discerned, and the nature of the single, numinous awareness knows them all. What further need is there for the various [organs]?
The faculty [of sight]. Because all sentient beings grasp at the eye as being definitively capable of seeing, it becomes a sovereign master.
Taking seeing as its condition, it requires light; in darkness, it constitutes non-seeing.
Later, it emits illumination that is perfectly luminous. The commentary states: "All sentient beings, in relying upon this seeing, must depend upon the object of light."
Only then can one see. Since it is said that one must have light in order to speak of seeing, when one sees darkness, one must first be not-seeing;
why, then, does one still "see" the darkness?
If it does not depend on light to manifest, then all dark forms can never obscure it.
The commentary states: This true nature of seeing does not rely on luminous objects; it manifests spontaneously and is thus vividly clear, never being clouded by afflictions.
"Since the faculties and their objects have both been extinguished"—the commentary states: "The six faculties and the six objects perish simultaneously.
How then can there be conscious clarity?"
The commentary states: The wisdom of initial enlightenment does not achieve perfect subtlety.
The commentary states: This refers to the principle of original enlightenment.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, if one wishes to seek the eternally abiding mind through the ground of practice, its name and designation must correspond with that of the fruition stage."

Section Two: The Text on Doubts Regarding the Extinction of the Manifesting Consciousness through the Six Supernatural Powers. Part One: The Text Citing the Previous Proposition to Raise an Objection (eight sections).
First, citing the previous proposition. The Commentary states: Because it was said in the preceding exhortation:

"If you merely do not follow after the dharmas of movement, stillness, penetration, or obstruction, and instead pull out one faculty, detaching from its stickiness and settling inwardly, so that it returns to the original reality," for this reason, Ānanda—

He then raised an objection, saying: "If this seeing and hearing exist apart from light and darkness, just as the mind of recollection exists apart from external objects and is fundamentally non-existent, how can you take this ultimate cessation and annihilation as the cause for cultivation?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke of striking a bell to test one who is in deep sleep, using the hearing of the sound to answer that the manifest consciousness has never been severed.
He then commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We hear it.
[The Buddha continued,] "Even you are still inverted; you mistake sound for hearing. How can you not be astonished that you are so deluded as to take the permanent to be intermittent?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha: 'As the Buddha has said, even down to the correspondence of names and designations, this is...'"
This refers back to the preceding passage. Herein, an objection is raised against the Buddha’s previous statement:

"If, during the causal stage, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for practice, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither born nor extinguished—this is impossible.

For within the causal stage, one must attain a mind that is itself neither born nor extinguished before one can correspond to the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, the opponent seizes upon these words.

An objection arises: Why does the Buddha say that the mind of awakening on the causal stage is the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*), while the desire to seek the eternally abiding is the principle of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*)?
If one wishes for the names of the cause and the fruit to correspond, it must be that the non-arising and non-ceasing mind accords with the non-arising and non-ceasing principle;
if one were to employ a mind of arising and ceasing, it would not accord. The following passage explains this:
Regarding the seven names and titles within the state of fruition, they come to pose a challenge to the World-Honored One:

"World-Honored One, if within the stage of fruition there are two [categories], then one must describe the collective names of the fruits. The commentary states: "Within the stage of the Buddha-realm, there are the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the five eyes, and the six..."
Penetration. All are fully complete.
Regarding *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*:
the commentary states that the Sanskrit term *bodhi* is translated here as "awakening" (*jue*) or as "the path" (*dao*). Among the five types of *bodhi*, this is...
Unsurpassed Bodhi. Alternatively, Bodhi is a conditioned fruit; by transforming defilement to attain purity, it is a produced virtue.
Why, then, are the two obstacles not produced now? Because the obstacles are not produced. In Sanskrit, *parinirvāṇa*; in the language of Tang, "perfect quiescence" (*yuánjì*).
Among the five [types of nirvana], it refers specifically to Great Parinirvana. Alternatively, Nirvana is an unconditioned fruit; by transforming delusion...

Realization is the manifestation of virtue. These two are the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) within the stage of Buddhahood. Regarding "True Suchness as Buddha-nature" (*tathatā-buddhadhātu*):

the commentary states that True Suchness is derived from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. In the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is universal practice; in the second stage, it is supreme; in the third stage, it is superior.
The flow [of the stages]: in the fourth stage there is no grasping; in the fifth stage there is no differentiation; in the sixth stage there is neither defilement nor purity;
in the seventh stage there is no differentiation among phenomena; in the eighth stage there is no increase or decrease; in the ninth stage there is mastery over wisdom;

and in the tenth stage there is the basis for mastery over karma. This refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) at the level of the Buddha-fruit; it is the stainless, pure *tathatā*. [This concludes] the fourfold analysis of Buddha-nature.

Regarding cause, principle, practice, and fruit: here we speak only of the Buddha-nature as the fruit, excluding the cause. Alternatively, when it resides in sentient beings it is called Buddha-nature, and when it resides in insentient things it is called Dharma-nature.
The *amala-vijñāna*. The commentary states:
this is called the "stainless consciousness" (*vimala-vijñāna*); it is the pure portion of the eighth consciousness, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

The commentary states: "Furthermore, this refers only to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*). 'Emptiness' (*śūnyatā*) refers to the principle of the two kinds of emptiness; 'Tathāgata' refers to the manifestation of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*);
and 'Treasury' (*garbha*) encompasses the cessation of both mundane and supramundane phenomena."
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

The commentary states: This belongs to the stage of Buddhahood. By transforming the eight consciousnesses, one achieves the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; it is a transformation of the name, not a transformation of the essence.
Regarding these seven names: although their designations differ, the commentary states that while these seven names are distinct in their verbal expression, their essence is one.
It is pure and perfect; its nature is firm and solid, like a diamond king, eternally abiding and indestructible.
The commentary states: "Pure" means free from defilement and stain. "Perfect" (yuan) means perfect illumination; "complete" (man) means fulfillment.
Its essence is True Suchness (*tathatā*), and its nature is the essential nature. This nature is firm, solid, and lucid, like a vajra jewel that cannot be destroyed or impaired.
Thus, these seven names for the stage of fruition are eternally abiding, unchanging, and indestructible.
If this seeing and hearing were to exist apart from light and darkness, motion and stillness, or penetration and obstruction, they would ultimately have no substance.

This thoroughly clarifies that the substance of delusion is false. The commentary states: "If this seeing and hearing were merely the two faculties of eye and ear, they would encompass [the functions of] nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Light and darkness belong to the eye faculty; motion and stillness belong to the ear faculty; hunger and satiety change the tongue; penetration..."

Block the nose; separate from the body; extinguish the arising and ceasing of the mind. The intent of the sutra here is that when seeing, hearing, and so forth are separated from their preceding objects, the mind then has no substance.
It is just as when the thinking mind is separated from its preceding sensory fields—it fundamentally has nothing at all.
"Four lead to six, which is the fifth. The commentary states: *Mingji* says "recollection. This refers to the sixth mind of recollection, which is distinct from the preceding five sensory objects;
it is fundamentally non-existent. As for being the sixth, if one were separated from the five, there would be nothing upon which to rely or establish itself.
How can one take this ultimate cessation as the cause for cultivation, desiring to obtain the sevenfold eternally abiding fruits of a Tathāgata?
[The text] states that the five manifest causes do not correspond to the fruit. The commentary says: How can one take this mind—which is free from dust and lacks substantiality—as the cause?
Taking this as the fundamental cause for cultivation, one desires to obtain the fruit described below—that of the Tathāgata. "Desires" refers to aspiration.
World-Honored One, if one is separated from light and darkness and perceives ultimate emptiness, then, as there are no external objects before one, the nature of thought itself ceases.

Whether advancing or retreating in this cyclical investigation, when one minutely examines it, there is fundamentally no self-mind nor any mental factors associated with a self. With whom, then, could one establish a cause? How could one seek that which is non-existent?
"Supreme Awakening. (6) "Re-examining the emptiness of causes. The commentary states: "If one advances, the preceding five [consciousnesses] lack substance; if one retreats, the sixth lacks a basis.
"My mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses. "Mental factors" refer to the fifty-one dharmas. It says: "If there were no objective dharmas..."
The six consciousnesses would likewise be non-existent.
Since the Tathāgata previously taught that they are profoundly pure, perfect, and eternally constant, to contradict these sincere words would ultimately result in mere frivolous discourse.
How, then, could the Tathāgata be considered one who speaks the truth?
Seventh, the reproach for contradicting one's own previous statements. The commentary states:

"The Tathāgata previously stated"—referring to the preceding passage which says, "If, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes the mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause of cultivation," and so forth—[whereas here it speaks of] profound stillness, brilliant clarity, perfect fullness, and eternal abiding.
This is the true mind. If one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood, one must employ this non-arising, non-ceasing mind.
Otherwise, the World-Honored One’s previous statements would contradict his own words of truth, resulting ultimately in mere frivolous discourse that expresses nothing of substance.
The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth.
I pray that you will bestow great compassion and dispel my ignorance and stinginess.

Regarding the phrase "the eight assemblies and the two paths," the commentary states: "Ignorance" refers to being muddled and deluded; "stinginess" refers to being parsimonious regarding the Dharma. This mind does not relinquish [its attachments].
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).

In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you truly cannot recognize it. Fearing that your sincere heart may still not be fully convinced, I shall now test you with various mundane matters to remove your doubts."
The subsequent section on resolving doubts regarding specific matters consists of two parts. The first part, "Striking the Bell to Test the Inversion," consists of two sections.

The first section, "The Proper Presentation of Questions and Answers," consists of three parts. The first part reproves those who possess much learning yet harbor strong delusions, granting them the opportunity to resolve their doubts.
The *Jian* (Commentary) states: "In vain" means empty. They take inverted words and present them as the Way; how can they take this ultimate annihilation as the cause for cultivation?

If you wish to attain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding, yet the reality of the inverted [delusions] manifests before you and you fail to recognize it—this "reality" (cheng) means truly so, and this "faith" (xin) means understanding.
"Subduing" (fu) means to suppress. This is said because I fear that you may truly not yet be able to believe, understand, and subdue this deluded mind;
or perhaps you have not yet been able to believe in the true mind and subdue the deluded mind.
Immediately, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now?
He then commanded Rāhula to strike the bell again and asked about the absence of sound; [this consists of six sections]. First is the question. The commentary states:
*Rāhu* in Sanskrit means "Seizer of the Sun" in the language of Tang (Chinese); it is also called "Obstructor," but that is incorrect. He is the son of the Buddha. This question is esoteric.
This refers to the five types of direct perceptual consciousness (pratyakṣa-vijñāna) acting as the immediate hearing;
Ānanda and the great assembly all say, "I have heard," which is the subsequent response.
When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
He asked this three times,
and Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "We do not hear it."
The fourth response:
At that time, Rāhula struck once more. The Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
This was the fifth question.
"Ānanda and the great assembly," it is further said, "all heard together.
This is the sixth response. The commentary states: "The question and answer consist of three layers. The intent of the sutra concerns the nature of hearing.
The Buddha asks Ānanda: 'How do you hear? How do you not hear?'"
The subsequent double inquiry regarding existence and non-existence consists of two parts. First is the question:
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying, "If the bell is struck, I am able to hear it; once the striking has ceased and the sound has faded away..."
When both sound and resonance are utterly transcended, it is called "no-hearing.
Regarding the subsequent answer, the commentary states: "Sound" refers to the sound of a bell; "resonance" refers to the echoing sounds produced by the mountain valleys.
The Tathāgata again commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear the sound now?

The subsequent section on establishing delusion to reveal confusion consists of two parts. The first part, responding to the sound through question and answer, contains six sections. First is the question. The commentary states:
He questioned [Ānanda] regarding the dust (the sensory object), wishing to shatter false attachments. For now, let us examine the nature of the delusion regarding the dust.
Can you distinguish between these two phenomena—the nature and the dust?
Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "There is sound."
Next, the answer was given.
After a short while, the sound faded away. The Buddha asked again, "Do you have a voice now?
He asked this three times. The commentary states: "Selection (xuan) means to withdraw."
Ānanda and the great assembly replied, "There is no sound.
This was answered four times.
After a short while, Rāhula came again and struck the bell. The Buddha asked once more, "Is there a sound now?"
The fifth question. The commentary states: This is a question regarding the immediate moment.
Ānanda and the great assembly all say that there is sound.
The sixth answer.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "What is sound? What is the absence of sound?
Later, he restated the two passages concerning existence and non-existence. First, the question:
Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha, saying, "If a bell is struck, it is called 'having sound. After striking for a long time, the sound fades away."
When both sound and resonance are utterly transcended, it is called "soundlessness.
The Buddha later replied,
"Ānanda and the great assembly, why do you now speak with such self-contradictory confusion?"

The subsequent section, which clarifies that all minds regarding objects are eternal, consists of three parts. The first part, which specifically refutes [the view of] annihilationism and eternalism, consists of two sections. The first section criticizes the afflictions that follow the mind;
it contains three sub-sections. The first is the formal critique. The commentary states: "Jiǎoquáng (矯誑) means to act with deceit and confusion.
This criticizes the opponent who takes sound as the object of hearing, asserting that while the sound-object perishes, the hearing of sound remains eternal.
The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha, "How is it that we are now called evasive and confused?
They then sought to shift the blame.
The Buddha said, "I asked you whether you heard, and you said you heard; I further asked you about the sound, and you said it was a sound. It was simply hearing."
Regarding "responding with sound": the response is not fixed. How, then, is this not called evasive equivocation (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*)?

The subsequent explanation states: the commentary notes that "the response is not fixed" means that when asked whether "nature is permanent," one responds by mentioning the auditory object (*śabda-dhātu*).
To hear various sounds and objects is due to the instability of one's own mind, which follows whether those objects exist or not;
this is precisely equivocation. How can you say it is not equivocation?

Ānanda, when the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say that there is no hearing. If, in reality, there were no hearing, then the nature of hearing would have already ceased, becoming like a withered tree.
If the bell were struck again, how could you know it?

The subsequent section, "Correctly Simplifying the Mind," consists of six constant passages. Regarding the line, "When similar kinds are extinguished, they wither together; one reproaches hearing for its double resonance," the commentary states:
When sound has vanished, there is no resonance; thus, one speaks of "no hearing. Since the nature of hearing has already ceased, it is metaphorically likened to a withered tree, an insentient object.
"Knowing existence and knowing non-existence.

This second section clarifies that while objects arise and perish, the nature remains eternally present; it consists of three parts. First, it clarifies that the nature possesses dual knowledge. The Commentary states:
"The nature of hearing knows both when there is sound and when there is no sound."
From this point on, the auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) may be absent or present;
this subsequently indicates the arising and ceasing of the object. The commentary states: "Since the auditory object may be present or absent, it is insufficient [to define the nature];
how could that nature of hearing be subject to your presence or absence?"
"Later, he points out that the substance [of hearing] is eternally as-it-is. The commentary states: "The nature of hearing does not follow existence or non-existence.
If one says the nature of hearing is actually non-existent, who is it that knows it is non-existent?

This is the third time he reprimands him for claiming it is non-existent. The commentary states: "If you say the nature of hearing is actually non-existent, then who is it that knows it is non-existent?"

Who, then, is this? Therefore, Ānanda, within the act of hearing, sound itself has its own arising and ceasing; it is not your hearing that arises and ceases with the sound, such that your nature of hearing would thereby become either existent or non-existent.

"Fourth, it reveals that [the nature of hearing] does not follow non-existence. The Commentary states: "It is not the case that your faculty of hearing arises and ceases in accordance with other sound-objects.
Now, as for your faculty of hearing—is it existent or non-existent? When hearing a sound, it is neither fixedly existent nor non-existent; yet the faculty of hearing is eternally constant.
For what reason do you allow yourself to be deluded by this and claim that the faculty of hearing is the same as the sound-object?"
"You yourself are still inverted; you mistake sound for hearing. Why then do you marvel at the confusion of taking the eternal to be the intermittent?
This fifth point reiterates the previous delusion regarding echoes to reprimand the dull mind that mistakes the eternal for the intermittent. The commentary states:
"What kind of demonic anomaly is this, so dark and murky, such a state of delusive error—to take the nature of the eternal as the sound of the intermittent?"
Ultimately, one should not say that it is apart from all movement and stillness, or closure and openness, while asserting that hearing has no intrinsic nature.
One should constantly cause the six heavy fetters of the mind to dispel dust-like delusions. The commentary states: "Closure" refers to the objects perceived by the nose.

It opens up the objective sphere (ālambana-viṣaya) of the eye-faculty. At the conclusion of this statement, one must not say that it lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) simply because it is separated from the external objects (viṣaya).
It is like a person in deep sleep, resting soundly on his bed and pillow; while he sleeps, someone in the house pounds silk or husks rice.
While dreaming, that person hears the sound of pounding and mortaring, yet perceives it as something else—either as the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell.
At that moment in the dream, they wonder to themselves how the bell can be making the sound of wood or stone.
Next, the text reiterates the analogy of stillness in three parts. First, regarding "repeatedly listening to sounds," the commentary states:

"The time of waking is when the sixth consciousness functions in conjunction with the five [sensory] consciousnesses; this nature of singular spirituality is clear and distinct. This is the clearly aware manovijñāna (mental consciousness).
When one falls back into deep sleep, the sixth consciousness returns to its seeds, yet this portion of true nature likewise does not [perish]."

At dusk, there was the sound of pounding rice; this "pounding" (dǎo) refers to the pounding of silk. Because one is grasping objects incorrectly within a dream, one perceives them as something else entirely.
Suddenly waking up, one immediately recognizes the sound of the pestle and tells the family members: "While I was dreaming, I was deluded by this sound of pounding."
It will serve as a drum’s resonance.
Next, it awakens Chen Wen-huo. The commentary states: *chuán* means "swift"; *huò* means "doubt. Both pounding rice and beating silk for refinement involve the pestle.

Ānanda, while this person is in a dream, how could they recall whether things were still or moving, open or closed, or permeable or obstructed? Although their body is asleep, the nature of hearing is not obscured.
Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of your life-force were to pass away, how could this nature be extinguished within you?
This subsequently reveals that the nature is without transition. The Commentary states: "Opening and closing are functions of the eyes, not only during sleep;
even when this body perishes—were you to dissolve in form and pass away—this portion of true nature remains. "Life-light" refers to the vitality of the physical body.

Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds and drifted with every thought, they have never awakened to the nature that is quiescent, wondrous, and eternally constant.
Failing to follow that which is eternal, they pursue all that arises and perishes; thus, life after life, they wander through the flow of defilement.

The subsequent exhortation to leave behind the dust and realize perfect enlightenment consists of two parts. First, the compassionate description of how the mind pursues objects. The commentary states:

"Following forms" refers to the eye seeing the dust of form and the ear hearing the dust of sound; this pertains to the mental consciousness within a dream. Under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is called "flowing" (*pravāha*);

under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), it is called "turning" (*parivarta*). "Recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to the sixth consciousness. "Flowing" means migrating or shifting; "turning" means changing or revolving.
You have never attained even the slightest opening of understanding or realization. "Nature" (xing) refers to the essential nature; "purity of nature" (xingjing) refers to clarity and purity;
"subtle" (miao) means wondrously subtle; and "constant" (chang) refers to true permanence.

Furthermore, you are unable to accord with this ever-constant truth, as your deluded consciousness follows after external objects, arising and ceasing moment by moment. Because of this, one realm gives rise to another realm, or perhaps it arises and perishes.
Furthermore, birth and defilement are but illusory phenomena that follow after delusion, shifting and transforming.

If one abandons arising and ceasing to maintain the true and eternal, the light of constancy will manifest before one; the sense objects, faculties, consciousness, and mind will, at that moment, dissolve away.

Conceptualization and its signs constitute the dust; the consciousness and its emotions constitute the defilement. When you distance yourself from both, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright.
How could it then fail to become unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

Later, it is exhorted that one should wipe away defilements to perfect the True. The commentary states: "To 'maintain' (shou) means to attain. Alternatively, "maintaining" refers to the meaning of firm contemplation; it is the light of constant wisdom (*jñāna*).

When the light of wisdom manifests, conceptualizations arise based on causes and signs; these are termed "characteristics of conceptualization" (*xiangxiang*). These are the three transforming consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
One simultaneously abandons both the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*), awakening to phenomena as if seeing objects with the eyes, or with the Dharma-eye.
Contemplating reality is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Being clear and bright in accordance with the occasion is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Supreme cognitive awakening is the principle of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Question: In the preceding text, [the Buddha] taught others these five [aspects of] mind;

for what reason does he now further instruct them to abandon this deluded consciousness? Answer: It is because he previously observed that others were clinging to this manifesting consciousness as being subject to annihilation. Therefore...

The Buddha, for his part, sets aside the dust [of conceptualization] because the nature of constant direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is without cessation; this refers to the mind of true direct perception (*tattva-pratyakṣa-citta*).
He points to this [mind] so that one may leave behind false consciousness, which is the phenomenal aspect (*nimitta*); this is the mind of true direct perception.
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Four, Part Two;
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Five (Part One).
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra;
the Śramaṇa Migaśrī from Uddiyāna provided the oral interpretation;
and the Bodhisattva-śīla disciple Fang Rong transcribed it in writing.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Weiqu of Daxingfu Monastery in the Western Capital;

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning, as I now observe the world..."
Regarding the person who has formed a knot: if one does not know the origin from which that knot was tied, I believe such a person will ultimately be unable to untie it.
Part Three: A Discussion on the Identity of Knotting and Untying (in two sections). Section One: Presenting Delusion and Requesting Instruction (in five parts).
First: Restating the Previous Delusion Regarding Knotting. The Commentary states: Although the Tathāgata has explained this second gate of meaning, it is the fourth sutra for definitive discernment.
The "Dual Source" refers to the section on the secret cause within the *Two Decisive Meanings*. In the second section, which provides a definitive resolution regarding afflictions, it says:
"Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots; if they do not see what was knotted, how can they know they are untying it?
Nor have you ever heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Ānanda now follows upon the preceding passage to pose a question herein, his intention being to resolve this doubt.
The Buddha’s previous statement was intended to resolve the doubt regarding the identity of the knower and the known. Having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda now requests within this context:
"World-Honored One, I and the śrāvakas in this assembly are likewise so; from time immemorial, we have been with all..."
Ignorance (*avidyā*). It perishes and arises simultaneously with [the mind].
Regarding the phrase "two cases of malaria," the commentary states: "The various ignorances are precisely the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
If, according to other teachings, this is said to be a single dharma of delusion (*moha*), here it is simply the aspect of the luminous nature; that is, co-nascent affliction."
Affliction. Since beginningless time, it has arisen simultaneously with body and mind;
thus, although one may have attained such roots of merit from extensive learning and is called a renunciant, it is still like a quotidian malaria.
The commentary states: The roots of goodness of extensive learning consist in upholding the untainted teachings of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
this is called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*). It is a "leaving home" characterized by attachment, like a tertian malaria.

A *śrāvaka* such as Dharmodgata, although having severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), has not yet severed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This is like a person suffering from malaria who remains well for one day and then relapses for one day.
I pray that you will bestow great compassion and take pity on those submerged in suffering. Regarding my body and mind today, what constitutes a knot, and from what is it called "untying"?
Having made this request three times, he pointed to the knot and straightened it out.
He also caused sentient beings suffering in the future to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence. Having spoken these words,
which encompassed the karmic effects of the past, present, and future,
he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly, raining down tears with uplifted sincerity as he waited for the Buddha, the Tathāgata.
This is the unsurpassed revelation.
It is the compassionate intent of the Five Paramitas.
At that time, the World-Honored One felt pity for Ānanda.

The second part, the extensive explanation for dispelling doubts, has two sections. The first, the prose section, has two parts. The first, the passage on the simultaneous manifestation by others, has two parts.
The first, the passage on Śākyamuni’s touching [the crown] with his hand and the Buddhas of the dust-motes emitting light, has four parts. The first, the opening inquiry of lamentation.
Furthermore, among those present in the assembly, there are those still in training;
out of compassion for them and for all future sentient beings as well, he acts as the cause for their transcendence from the world and serves as their eye for the future.

"Third, preparing for the future. The commentary states: "Acting as the eye for what is to come. If this refers distantly, it concerns these five secret causes and the three texts on cultivation and realization.
If it refers proximately, the passage below regarding the "common source of the faculties and objects" is precisely the present moment.
Now, all sentient beings give rise to wisdom through their practice and illuminate the principle, just as the eye illuminates objects without delusion.
With his hand of Jambūnada purple-gold light, he rubbed the crown of Ānanda’s head.
He extended his golden hands four times. The commentary states: "Rubbing the crown of the head symbolizes the teaching of this *uṣṇīṣa-samādhi*."
Immediately, the worlds of all Buddhas in the ten directions shook in six ways.

[The subsequent passage on the emission of light consists of three parts. First, the universal shaking of all lands. The Commentary states: The *Dīrgha Āgama* explains that there are six occasions for such movement:
first, entering the womb; second, emerging from the womb; third, leaving home; fourth, attaining enlightenment; fifth, turning the wheel of the Dharma; and sixth, entering [parinirvāṇa].
Nirvāṇa. Now, regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, it is said that six types of movement occur. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, these are:

moving, surging, shaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. To move restlessly is called "moving. To be rugged, uneven, and undulating is called "surging," or alternatively, to surge in the six directions.
A deep, rumbling sound is called "shaking. To be struck or tapped is called "striking. To produce a sound through clashing and friction is called... [bursting].

"Roar. To emit a sound that is startling and extraordinary is called "explosion" (*bhaṭ*). Each of these has three stages, which together are known as the eighteen signs. These are: trembling, equal trembling, and extreme trembling;
up to explosion, equal explosion, and extreme explosion. A sudden, slight movement is called "trembling. Movement that pervades all parts is called "equal trembling.

Movement that causes the eight directions to tilt and shake is called "extreme trembling. Following the same principle, these are collectively termed the six tremblings among the eighteen transformations.
There was a great trembling. Thus did the teaching of the *Uṣṇīṣa-samādhi* manifest, awakening the entire great assembly.
From the crowns of the heads of all the Tathāgatas dwelling in the worlds, rays of jewel-light issued forth.
Simultaneously, those lights came from their respective worlds to the Jeta Grove and descended upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
Next, the assembly of Buddhas radiates light. The commentary states: "Dust-like Tathāgatas" refers to the great number of Buddhas.
"Those dwelling in worlds" means each resides in their own native land. Each possesses a precious light that issues from their crown, signifying the transcendence of views regarding self and other.
This light is poured upon the crown of the Tathāgata—specifically, the crown of Śākyamuni Buddha—signifying the dharma of this *uṣṇīṣa-samādhi*. The text signifies...
The Way of all Buddhas is the same; the essence of their births is one. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can know this.
This great assembly has attained what they have never experienced before.
Thereafter, those present in the assembly attained benefit.
Then, Ānanda and the great multitude together heard the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, speaking with one voice:
"Excellent, Ānanda! You wish to recognize and know co-nascent ignorance, which causes you to revolve in saṃsāra."
The root of the bonds of birth and death is none other than your six sense faculties; there is no other thing.

Hereafter, the external manifestation and the true sound are explained, through which this assembly hears [the teaching]. Part Two. First, the presentation of the root of the bonds. The commentary states:

Because the sounds are distinct, the mouths are different; because the speech is identical, the voices are the same. Question: What is the intent behind the Buddhas of the ten directions speaking together?
Answer: It signifies this Dharma-gate of perfect interfusion. "Simultaneous arising" refers to the simultaneous arising of afflictions; the nature of ignorance is itself clarity.

Furthermore, if you wish to know unsurpassed Bodhi—which enables you to swiftly realize peace, liberation, quiescence, and wondrous permanence—it is none other than your own six sense faculties; it is not some other thing.
The following explains the true source (*zhényuán*). The commentary states: As it is said in the *Verse on the Unlearned* (*wúxué sòng*) of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:

"This is the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), inconceivable, virtuous, and eternal; it is the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*), which the Great Muni calls the Dharma. "Peaceful bliss" (*ānle*) refers to the principle of cessation (*śānti*).
"Liberation" (*jiětuō*) means being free from the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). "Quiescent, wondrous, and eternal" all refer to the Dharmakāya.
Thus it was.
Although Ārāḍa had heard such sounds of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet enlightened. He prostrated himself before the Buddha and said:
"How is it that my cycle of birth and death and the blissful, wondrous, and eternal state are both these same six sense faculties, and nothing else?"
Subsequently, this Buddha again proclaimed two passages of text. First, regarding the confusion [of Ānanda], he requested instruction once more.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The faculties and their objects share a common source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky."

Later, out of compassion for those who are deluded, he further expounded the fourfold text. First, the metaphor of flowers in the sky compares consciousness, the sense organs (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*) as sharing a single source.
The commentary states: the "organs" are the six sense organs; the "objects" are the six sense fields. These share the same true source, which is the *tathāgatagarbha*.

"Bondage" refers to the fetters of birth and death; "liberation" refers to the liberation of *tathatā*. "Non-duality" means that the true and the false are of the same substance, just as waves and water are one.
Moisture. Since consciousness and the flower arise together, their characteristics cannot be separately grasped.
Ānanda, knowledge is triggered by objects;

these two are further illustrated by the metaphor of twin reeds, which mutually support one another. The commentary states: "By means of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) that is perceived, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is induced."
"Conditioned by the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga), there arises the appearance (nimitta) due to the sense-faculty (indriya).
The commentary states: "Due to the sense-faculty as the supporting basis (āśraya), the appearing object (nimitta) that is seen is produced."
The perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving faculty (*darśana-bhāga*) lack inherent nature;

they are like two reeds leaning against one another. The commentary states: The perceived object and the perceiving faculty are like two reeds supporting each other. Alternatively, consciousness may arise due to external objects;
its nature is the faculty of cognition, namely the six sense-faculties. Both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) lack any substantial essence. II.
Both are without reality; they are like two bundles of reeds standing in mutual dependence, both being empty.
Therefore, when you now establish "knowing" within seeing and hearing, this is the very root of ignorance.
(The third section marks the unification of the pair. The commentary states: Knowing is originally true knowing; seeing is originally true seeing. If...
Turning toward this [state] above, one establishes the capacity to know and the capacity to see; this is precisely the root of ignorance.
When knowing and seeing are themselves non-seeing, this is nirvana—taintless, truly pure. How could any other thing be admitted within this?
The Commentary states: "If one can truly know and see that which lies above [conceptualization], such that neither seeing nor knowing is established, this is itself *nirvāṇa*.
This is here termed 'perfect stillness' (*yuánjì*). Master Sengzhao said: 'As for the Way of *nirvāṇa*, it is silent, desolate, empty, and vast; it cannot be attained through form or name.'"

Subtle and wondrous, it is without marks; it cannot be known by a mind possessed of thought. It transcends all existence and ascends into the profound; its magnitude is as vast as space and it endures forever.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Fourth, the recitation and exposition of the *gāthā*. The commentary states: "To conclude the preceding prose (*prose-verse*), it is rendered as a verse (*gāthā*);
or, for those who delight in verses, it is concluded as five-syllable lines; or, for the sake of those who come later, it is repeated. The Sanskrit term is *gāthā*, also called *gātha*.
In the language of Tang, this is called *geya* (repeated verse). It is so named because it repeats the preceding prose (*gadya*).

"The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty" constitutes the second part, the repeated verse, which has two sections. The first is the section on abandoning doubt by simultaneously brushing away [extremes], which has three parts. The first of these is the simultaneous refutation of existence and non-existence. [Commentary:]
It is said: Within the essential nature of true thusness (tathatā), all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are entirely empty and quiescent, for they lack substantial reality;
because they arise dependently, they are like illusions.
The commentary states: All permitted phenomena arise by relying on causes and depending on conditions. Since conditions lack intrinsic nature, their very substance is emptiness;
therefore, they are like illusions and transformations, possessing no substantial reality. As the Sūtra says: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be empty."
"Unconditioned, it is without arising or ceasing.
The commentary states: "Arising" means birth. The principle of the unconditioned is fundamentally without birth; now it is likewise without cessation.
It is unreal, like flowers in the sky.
The commentary states: Conditioned phenomena are unreal, like flowers in the sky; they fundamentally do not exist.
By speaking of the false, the various truths are revealed.
Next, both truth and falsity are discarded. The commentary states: An outsider asks, "If false phenomena are already unreal, then as for the present cause..."
What? Furthermore, there are all manner of delusive dharmas. The commentator answers: "By speaking of the delusive, one reveals the various truths.
This means that the mention of the delusive is spoken solely for the purpose of revealing the truth.
"The false and the true are equally both false.
The commentary states: Again, he asked, "If one now abandons the false to pursue the true, how is that? He replied, "The false and the true are equally both false."
If there were one delusion that could be discarded and one truth that could be grasped, even that truth would be a delusion; therefore, it is said that both are delusions.
"Yet neither true nor untrue" (猶非真非真).
The commentary states: "Yet" (猶) means "still. The preceding "not true" (非真) refers to the truth that is a counterpart to delusion; yet now, this [truth] itself is still...

No. Furthermore, there is no "true" that exists in opposition to the "false. The phrase "not true" refers to the "false" that stands in opposition to the "true," yet there is also no "false" that exists in opposition to the "true.
Thus, "not true" is itself the "false. This sentence reiterates the previous statement that both are equally false. Alternatively, the subsequent "not true" may also mean "not so."
"What is meant by 'seeing' and 'the seen'?
The commentary states: Since there are already no dharmas of either truth or falsehood, how could there further be a seer and that which is seen?
Between them, there is no real nature."
The subsequent exhortation to realize the common source consists of three parts. First, citing the "one" to clarify that the "two" manifest as non-dual suchness.
The Commentary states: "The 'intermediate' refers to consciousness; this consciousness has no reality and is, in its very essence, delusion."
Therefore, regarding the phrase "like two reeds":

the commentary states that root and object depend upon one another. This restates the preceding discussion on the two divisions of seeing and seen, asserting that the nature of both the seen and the seeing is non-existent, being identical to the analogy of the two reeds.
"The cause for both bondage and liberation is the same.
The commentary states: "Birth-and-death is also your six sense faculties; liberation is also your six sense faculties. This reiterates the preceding text:
"The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual."
"There are no two paths for the sage and the ordinary person. The commentary states: "All sentient beings are also thus; all worthy sages are also thus.
You should observe the nature within their interaction."
Next, the identity of delusion and awakening is emphasized to further eliminate both extremes. The Commentary states: "He again exhorts one to contemplate the false consciousness:
that which is internal is the sense organ (*indriya*), that which is external is the sense object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness intersects between them."
"It is neither emptiness nor existence.
The commentary states: "If one says it is empty, then since the Buddhas transform consciousness into wisdom, the substance of consciousness is not empty.
If one says it exists, then the characteristics of consciousness are absent. Therefore, it is said to be neither of the two."
"Deluded obscurity is ignorance.
The commentary states: "Delusive confusion and dark obscuration are precisely ignorance. All sentient beings, after becoming deluded, lack the clarity of true awakening;
their essence is dark and murky—this very state is ignorance."
"Upon realization, there is liberation.
The commentary states: "To awaken to delusion as being identical to the True is to explain their common source.
"The cause for untying the knots follows a sequence."
Later, he exhorted [Aniruddha] to select [the knots] and enter the stream, thereby preemptively resolving the sequence of one and six. The commentary states:
"If one understands this knot, there is a sequential order for its resolution. It is like a person untangling a knot: once one knot is untied, another is untied."
"The six are liberated and the one also perishes.
The commentary states: "Once the six sense organs are liberated, ignorance is also eliminated. 'The one' refers to ignorance. These two preceding lines give rise to the doubt:
"the six are liberated and the one perishes."
"Selecting a faculty for perfect penetration, one enters the stream and achieves true enlightenment.

The commentary states: These two lines introduce the section on "Perfect Penetration. One selects whichever single faculty provides perfect penetration to enter the Path, such as Avalokiteśvara’s realization through the faculty of hearing.
The subtle consciousness of *ādāna* (appropriation).

This subsequently points again to the third section of the "Transcending the Gates" (*chao men wen*). First, it sets forth the ancient exposition. The commentary states: "Ālaya" is an alternative name for the eighth [consciousness].
In the language of Tang, it is called the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), because it is able to contain and store the seeds of all phenomena. If one speaks of it simply as "ālaya,"...
It is thus translated as *ālayavijñāna*. This name, *ālaya*, is broad in scope because it encompasses the meaning of all three types of "store" (*ālaya*).

If one were to use the term *ālaya* alone, it would be translated as "that which is clung to and stored," and this designation would be narrow in application, as it would only capture the sense of being "clung to and stored" among the three meanings of store.
Now, speaking according to the broader sense, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. From the stage of cause to the stage of fruition, there are three positions. First:

First, regarding its status as that which is "loved and grasped as a self" (*ātma-grāha-ālaya*): this exists in all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), as well as in those from the first through the seventh bhūmi, and in those who have attained the first three fruits of the path;
for they give rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) by taking these sentient beings as their object and clinging to the eighth consciousness.

Second, regarding its nature as the fruit of good and evil karma: it is called the maturation consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). It takes the performance of good and evil in previous lives as its cause.
In this present life, the eighth consciousness, which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), is the fruit; its causes may be either wholesome or unwholesome, while its fruit is exclusively indeterminate.
Because the fruit differs from its cause, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*). The name "maturational consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*) applies universally to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one refers to its manifest location, it becomes evident at the moment one relinquishes the designation "ālayavijñāna. This refers to the stage of grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is stated that the stage of Buddhahood is itself non-existent. Third is the stage of continuous apprehension and maintenance, which is called the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
This name applies to all stages; however, if one speaks according to its manifest location, it becomes manifest only at the stage of the Buddha-fruit.

Because it is able to maintain the sense organs (*indriya*), the body, and the seeds (*bīja*) so that they do not disintegrate or scatter, it is named *ādāna*. In the language of Tang (Chinese), this means "apprehension and maintenance. — Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang].

Regarding these [three aspects]: the capacity to store (*āśraya*), that which is stored (*āśrita*), and being clung to as a store (*ālīna*). First, as for the capacity to store: it refers to the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying portion) of the eight consciousnesses in their active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).
Because it can maintain all prior seeds, it is called the "capacity to store. It is like a treasury or a storehouse;

just as a treasury or storehouse can contain external wealth, silks, and so forth—where the treasury or storehouse is called the "capacity to store" and the wealth and silks are called "that which is stored"—so too, within the dharmas, all originally existing seeds [are contained].
Child, because they have not been lost or dispersed since beginningless time, they are all contained within the eighth consciousness’s self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
As for what is said to be "contained," it is so called because the self-verifying portion is the locus of perfuming (*bhāvyasthāna*); thus, it is termed the "container.
That is to say, the seeds of all dharmas perfumed by the preceding seven consciousnesses fall, moment by moment, into the self-verifying portion of the eighth consciousness.
[The *ālayavijñāna*] has four parts. Within the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), it is the place where the newly perfumed seeds of the other seven consciousnesses return and are stored;
because it receives the perfuming of those other seven, it is what is stored within the self-verifying part. These two types of "storage" belong exclusively to the self-verifying part.

As for the term "appropriated storage" (*ādāna*), this refers to the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness], which is the locus of appropriation by the sixth [consciousness]. This is called...
It is called "clinging" (ālaya) because, although it was originally not an object of clinging or storage, it is now clung to as a self by the seventh consciousness;
thus it is named the "storehouse of clinging.
Its habitual tendencies form a violent torrent.
The commentary states: *Vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) possesses three meanings. First, "seed" (*bīja*) is called *vāsanā*; "tendency" (*vāsa*) refers to the "portion of tendency" (*vāsa-bhāga*).
"Habitual" (*vāsa*) means "perfuming" (*vāsana*). Because this portion of tendency is acquired through perfuming by those manifest activities (*pravṛtti*), the seed is termed *vāsanā*.
Second, manifest activity (*samudācāra*), which is also called *vāsanā*. This means that by means of the seeds themselves, manifest activity can arise;
thus, manifest activity is the *vāsanā* of the seeds. Third, habitual tendency (*vāsanā*), which is named *vāsanā* because it is like a scented paper that possesses a fragrant residue.
Of these, two types of *vāsanā* are explained solely in terms of seeds. As the seven-syllable verse of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "A..."
The *ādāna-vijñāna* is extremely subtle; all seeds form a violent torrent. I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, for fear that they would conceptually grasp it as a self.
It is said that these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are as fierce and violent as the rapid flow of water at the head of a mountain stream, surging in succession and streaming downward.
"If it were truly real, there would be fear of delusion; therefore, I have never openly expounded it.
The commentary states: "If one says that the eighth consciousness is truly real, all sentient beings would again cling to the false as being real.
If one says it is not truly real, they would further simultaneously negate the pure portion [of the mind], equating it with total annihilation. This is because I fear all sentient beings..."
Delusion has departed; I am now ordinary. I have not yet opened up or expounded upon this. This was forty-five years ago, when I did not speak of this eighth consciousness.

This section is a standalone passage; the intent of the Sūtra is fully contained within its brevity. Within the eighth consciousness, there are both the true and the delusory, the defiled and the pure.
Below, I wish to explain the "six dissolutions and the single disappearance," yet fearing that others might mistake the "True" for [the first of the six], I have hesitated.
At that time, because [the practitioner] refutes [them] as being identical to annihilation, or perhaps merely encourages others to sever delusion and return to the Real, it is said:

"If even the non-illusory does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established? It is further stated: "The non-illusory constitutes illusory phenomena. This refers to the moment of the arising of delusion, intended to cause others to know the Real and recognize the delusory.
Alternatively, this is directed toward the subsequent desire to shatter the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate); herein, one first makes a distinction to cause others to understand.
"True knowledge realizes the delusion. Herein, the defiled portion is refuted, but the pure portion is not.
"The self-mind grasps the self-mind.
Next, the fourth section of the text, "Investigating Delusion to Reveal Suddenness," first investigates the arising of delusion. The commentary states: "The true mind of the self... [text continues].
Furthermore, one gives rise to a mind capable of awakening and takes that very mind as its object; thus, the self-mind grasps the self-mind.

"That which is not illusion produces illusory phenomena"—the two sons are the essence of delusion. The commentary states: "The truth that is not illusion becomes the delusion that is produced by illusion."
"Not grasping is non-non-illusion.
[The Master] suddenly realized this with three fingers. The commentary states: "If one simply does not give rise to the mind that grasps, then even the name 'the Real' cannot be attained;
hence it is said, 'non-non-illusion. 'Non-illusion' refers to the True Dharma, wherein attachment to dharmas has perished."
If even that which is not illusion does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established?
(4) This reveals the simultaneous removal [of both extremes]. The commentary states: This restates that even the Real itself does not arise;
since this Dharma is about to perish, how could illusory and delusive phenomena possibly be established further?
This is called the "Wondrous Lotus.

Regarding the subsequent section on the manifestation of the Dharma through the eyes, which transcends the four [categories] of text: first, the metaphor manifests three excellences. The commentary states:

Since there are neither the two dharmas of truth nor falsehood, it is like a lotus flower that emerges from the mud of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), leaves the turbid water of the *śrāvakas*, and rises from the clear [water] of the *bodhisattvas*.
Water: A single *dou* suddenly becomes fragrant; it is not defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening" (*vajrarāja-ratna-bodhi*), the commentary states: "Vajra" has the meaning of indestructibility; "King" has the meaning of sovereignty; and "Jewel" means that which is precious and worthy of honor.
Awakening is the wisdom of true awakening.

Regarding "the samādhi that is like an illusion," the commentary states: "All dharmas are like an illusion; this is precisely samāpatti. In the language of Tang, it is called *dengzhi* (equilibrium-attainment). Dharma.
The Great Samādhi of the Realms.
With a snap of the fingers, one transcends to the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Next, in a single thought-moment, one leaps far beyond. The commentary states: "A snap of the fingers" signifies extreme speed; "transcend" means to arrive at. "No-More-Learning" refers to [the stage of] *aśaikṣa*.
To cite its realized stage, it is precisely the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*).
Regarding this *Abhidharma*, the *Jian* (Commentary) states:
"The Sanskrit term *Abhidharma* translates in the Tang language as 'Dharma in Conjunction' (*duìfǎ*). It subsumes..."
The Mahāyāna-śāstra states: There are four pairs. First, "pairing" (*pratipakṣa*): this dharma is paired with and directed toward non-abiding nirvāṇa;
it is called "pairing" because it can explain the truths, the factors of enlightenment, and the gates of liberation. Second, "enumeration" (*saṃkhyā*):

for each individual dharma, one enumerates its explanations and etymological definitions, both in their specific and common distinctions; this is called "enumeration. Third, "subduing" (*vinaya*): this refers to the application of the treatise to the proper locations and so forth.

To be able to overcome the arguments of others is called "subduing" (*vāda*). To be proficient in the four [types of] reasoning is called "resolution" (*vyākaraṇa*), for by means of this one can explain the meaning of the *Sūtras*.
Furthermore, the Sanskrit term *Abhidharma* is translated in Chinese as "Treatise on the Dharma" (*Lun Zang*). "A" signifies "without"; "bi" is equivalent to "comparison" (*upamā*);
and *dharma* is translated as "Dharma. This refers to the incomparable Dharma.
"The Bhagavāns of the ten directions"—the four directions are indicated in the same way. The commentary states: A verse in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Sovereignty, brilliance, and magnificence;
renown, auspicious speech, and nobility—possessing these six qualities, one should be given the general title [of Bhagavān]."

"Bhagavān. Regarding "Bhaga," the term *bhaga* signifies the possession of virtues. If one is designated by the title "Bhagavān," they must possess six qualities in order to have conquered the four māras:
first, sovereignty, because they are forever unbound by any afflictions;
second, brilliance, because they have been refined by the fiercely blazing fire of wisdom; third, majesty, because they are adorned with the thirty-two marks.
1. Because he is majestic; 2. because his fame is renowned, for there is no one who does not know the Buddha’s supreme name; 3.

because he is auspicious, for he constantly gives rise to skillful means to benefit sentient beings; 4. because he is noble, for he is revered by all those above and below, both in heaven and on earth; 5.
if one speaks of the "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*), it encompasses fewer than these five meanings. This is a praise of the Buddha’s virtues.
"The Single Path to the Gate of Nirvana. The commentary states: "The single path means there is no second path. 'Path' refers to the place traversed by the sages of the Three Vehicles.

'Nirvana' refers to the principle of quiescent extinction. 'Gate' carries the meaning of entering and exiting. The Buddhas of the three periods of time give rise to wisdom that accords with this principle."

One enters through this gate. Alternatively, the Buddhas of the three periods of time arise from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and, through subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), reach the conventional world;
they emerge through this gate. All sentient beings, who create the general and specific karmic retributions of saṃsāra, likewise emerge through this gate.
[They] take birth within the three realms.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata, [are divided into] four sections for explanation and six sections for resolution, with the first section being the disappearance of doubt.
Part One: The Text on Requesting a Decision Based on the Initial Title, which has five sub-sections. First: Receiving the Explanatory Terms.
Wuyi’s Commentary states: Following the preceding verse which says, "The six are liberated and the one is also extinguished," Ānanda therefore makes this request therein, saying:
"I have now heard the Buddha’s unobstructed great compassion... even to the point of washing away deep-seated defilements.
Having made this request, the World-Honored One then took the flowers offered by the Kāpālika deva.
Before the great assembly, he tied a single knot in his headcloth. Even if one wishes to untie the knot, it must be done at its very center.
This symbolizes that for a follower of the Mahāyāna, all phenomena are cultivated within the mind.

As for the "unsurpassed compassionate instruction," from the previous passage titled "The Wondrous Lotus" up to "the Single Path to the Gate of Nirvāṇa," these constitute the parable of the unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
*Geya* and *Gāthā*. The commentary states:
*Geya* in Sanskrit is translated in the Tang language as "recited verse" (*fèngsòng*). This refers to verses that do not follow a prose narrative (*chángxíng*) but arise independently.

The passage "the subtle consciousness of *dhātu*" (*tuó nà wēixì shí*) below in the sutra is an example. *Gāthā* in Sanskrit is translated in the Tang language as "repeated verse" (*chóngsòng*). Repeated...
This verse summarizes the preceding prose. It refers to the passage below concerning "the emptiness of conditioned phenomena within true nature.
