First, as for "counting," one counts the breath-wind from one to ten, and when finished, begins again. Regarding this, there are three errors: first, the error of under-counting; second, [the error of over-counting]; third...
First, the error of increasing the count: taking one as two. Second, the error of confusion: taking what is inhalation as exhalation.

Regarding the second [point], "following" means that the bound mind follows the breath as it enters and exits. Third, "stopping" means stabilizing the mind wherever it finds pleasure, not allowing it to become distracted.
Fourth, "contemplating" means contemplating the wind of the breath within the body, like a thread passing through a pearl.
The five transformations refer to the shifting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), continuing up until the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

The six purifications refer to the superior progress entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), continuing up until the stage of Non-arising (*anutpāda*). Furthermore, four conditions must be present: first, the basis for the breath;
second, the passage of the wind-channels being open; third, the pores being opened; and fourth, the coarse mind manifesting in the stage of inhalation and exhalation.
At that time, I contemplated the breath, [observing] its subtle exhaustion and the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) moment by moment.

Through these four reliances, one becomes a noble one (*ārya*). The Commentary states: Question: Are not arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing the subtle four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna?
"How can those of the Hīnayāna know this? The answer is that there are two meanings. First, within the sixth consciousness, there are also coarse [forms of] arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Alternatively, this Venerable One may be a great-power Śrāvaka manifesting as a follower of the Hīnayāna.
He understood the four subtle characteristics.
His mind became suddenly expansive and clear.
The commentary states: He comprehended the arising and ceasing of the inhalation and exhalation of breath, and awakened to the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing.

He attained great non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*). Eventually, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), he became an Arhat. Abiding beneath the Buddha’s seat, he was sealed as one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The commentary states: "True emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not obstructed; thus it is able to manifest and function according to conditions (*pratyaya*) to achieve realization, or it is unobstructed."
The wisdom of emptiness manifests before one; there is no obstruction.
When the Buddha inquires regarding the perfect penetration of the Way, that which I have realized—reversing the breath to follow emptiness—is the foremost.

The fifth is the cause for awakening through the fetters. The commentary states: "Return" means to turn back. It refers to turning back the breath and returning in accordance with the principle of true emptiness;
this is realized through the faculty of the nose.
Kauṇḍinya immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have committed verbal karma;
during past kalpas, I used to mock and ridicule śramaṇas. Consequently, in life after life and birth after birth, I have suffered from the ailment of rumination like an ox."
Section Three: The Case of Kāvaṇavaṭṭa (Kauṇḍinya), Part Four. First, regarding the inheritance of past karma.
The commentary states: Kāvaṇavaṭṭa is also called Kauṇḍinya; [the term] *vaṭṭa* means "round" or "swirling. In the present sutra, he is said to have "mocked the śramaṇas";
in the *Hetupratyaya-sūtra*, it says that due to a past cause, he stole several grains of rice that fell to the ground, and for five hundred lifetimes... [text fragment].
I was born as an ox and gave my life for others. Although I have now obtained a human body, I constantly manifest the characteristics of an ox’s hooves and an ox’s rumination.
Tathāgata, please show me the Dharma-gate of the single-flavor, pure mind-ground.
Next, he was shown the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*). The commentary states: "One contemplates that the nature of all flavors is entirely empty and quiescent;
only a single flavor manifests before one, with no other flavors remaining. It is pure and free from the obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

"Mind" (*xin*) refers to the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). "Ground" (*di*) refers to the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi-tattva-bhūmi*). "Dharma" (*fa*) refers to that which serves as a track for generating understanding. "Gate" (*men*) refers to the means of entering and exiting.
The meaning of mastery (*vaśitā*). This refers exclusively to the ultimate truth; it is the Buddha’s demonstration to others of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
I have attained the cessation of the mind and entered into *samādhi*.
The commentary states: "The cessation of the mind" refers to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). "Entering" is the act of entering; "samādhi" is that which is entered.
This is based on direct realization. Prior to this concentration, the names differ while the essence remains the same.
The cognition that contemplates flavors is neither the essence nor a substance. By recollecting this, one attains transcendence over all worldly outflows (*āsrava*).
"The third dhyāna contemplation transcends the mundane. The commentary states: "Not the essence" means that [the flavor] is a deluded consciousness and not the True [Mind]. "Not a substance" means...
It is neither tongue nor food; yet the food does not know itself, and the tongue does not perceive itself. It is only the deluded sixth consciousness that discriminates them.

Internally, it is liberated from body and mind; externally, it casts off the world. It distances itself from the three realms of existence, like a bird escaping its cage. Thus, it is freed from defilement and its dust is extinguished.
The commentary states: "To transcend the body is to be free from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); to transcend the mind is to be free from the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

This 'mind' refers either to the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*) or, according to some, the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). However, this is incorrect. While it may be appropriate for the six consciousnesses to correspond to the six sense organs, here, internally transcending both body and mind means there is no *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) as that which depends;
externally relinquishing the world means there is no *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) as that upon which it depends. Thus, one speaks of the absence of both the dependent and the depended."
Relying on this, both the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) are empty.
With the purification of the Dharma-eye, one becomes an Arhat; the Tathāgata personally confirms this attainment, establishing one in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
The commentary states: "Dharma-eye" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), and "purity" refers to principle (*tattva*). This means that wisdom arises to illuminate principle.
Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, that which I have realized—reversing the flavors and returning to the faculty of cognition—is the foremost.
"4. Manifesting the Realization of the Cause. The commentary states: "The six sense faculties turned toward the tongue faculty to bear witness.
Piṅgala-bhāradvāja immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I followed the Buddha to enter the Path.'"

IV. Piṅgala-avadāna (The Story of Piṅgala), Part Five. First, he repeatedly received the Buddha’s teachings. The commentary states: "In the language of Tang, this means 'dissolving residual habits' (*vāsanā*).
The correct Sanskrit is *Piṅgalavatsa*; in the language of Tang, it means 'residual habit. For five hundred lifetimes he was a Brahmin; his disposition was harsh and his speech coarse.
Although he has now attained the fruit [of Arhatship], his residual habits still remain, as when he cursed the goddess of the Ganges, calling her a slave."
It is so. I have frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the various things in the world that are not to be enjoyed.

The commentary states: regarding internal bodies, external environments, and other such phenomena—within a single body, there are the large intestine, small intestine, stomach (the raw receptacle), and the matured [receptacle]...
He contemplated the various impurities within his body.
While begging for alms in the city, he focused his mind on the Dharma-gate of contemplation; unaware, a thorn pierced his foot on the road.

Because of this single thorn piercing his foot, he reflected [on the teaching]. The commentary states: "Because he contemplated with his mind this Dharma-gate of the practice of the contemplation of impurity."
"My entire body aches. I am mindful and aware.
He contemplates the mind through the three causes of pain. The commentary states: "This awareness that knows the pain is the awareness that knows this profound suffering."
The commentary states: "To know this is the [nature of] pain.

Although there is the awareness that perceives pain, the commentary states: "Although 'awareness' is the subject that perceives, the 'awareness that perceives pain' is the object perceived; it is the mind that experiences pain."
Awakening the pure mind.
The commentary states: "Arising wisdom to illumine principle, there is no sensation of pain within the sensation."
The commentary states: "There was neither a mind that felt pain, nor a cognition that perceived the pain.
I then reflected further: how could this single body possibly possess two cognitions? Before long, as I focused my mindfulness, both body and mind suddenly became empty."

Within thirty-seven days, all outflows were completely exhausted; he became an Arhat, received the seal of personal certification, attained the realization of the stage of No-more-learning, and entered the realization of the four pairs of noble ones.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties. According to what I have realized, the pure awakening that leaves the body behind is the foremost.
Regarding the statement "the five manifestations mark the cause-principle," the commentary says: the six sense-faculties take the body-faculty as their point of realization.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas of the past, my mind has been free from obstruction;
I recall my own births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

"Five: Subhūti exhausted the texts on emptiness; Six: From his first existence, he inherited supernormal wisdom. The commentary states: "He attained the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
From the very beginning while in his mother’s womb, he immediately realized emptiness and stillness."
Second, dwelling in the realization that the abdomen is empty. The commentary states: "One thereby awakens to the principle of true emptiness.
In this manner, it extends until the ten directions become empty and the three realms are transformed into nothingness."
Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to realize emptiness;
fourth, they enable others to obtain benefit by being inspired by the Tathāgata to awaken to the true emptiness of their own nature.
"Five: Wondrous Awakening Penetrates the True. The commentary states: "Innate awakening is wisdom; true emptiness is principle.
Emptiness and nature are perfectly luminous.
The commentary states: "Wisdom and principle are darkly unified."
Having attained arhatship, they suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s ocean of jewel-like luminous emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Thus sealed as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they realize that liberation is the nature of emptiness; for them, "I" am supreme.
The commentary states: "Treasured Radiance" refers to wisdom; "the Ocean of Emptiness" refers to principle.
The Buddha inquired about perfect penetration; [Aniruddha] spoke thus according to his own realization.
These six headings manifest the causes for awakening.
"All characteristics enter into non-existence.
The commentary states: "Non-existence" means absence. One shatters all existent characteristics and enters into the characteristicless.
When that which is negated is exhausted, one turns back from phenomena to return to non-being; this is the foremost.
The commentary states: "The 'one' that is negated is the mind capable of emptying; that which is negated is the object to be emptied.
Since both are equally empty and quiescent, it is said to be 'exhausted. Alternatively, 'negation' refers to the absence of an object of cognition;

'exhaustion' refers to the absence of the cognizing mind. As for the cognizing mind, why is it called 'not exhausted'? This means that the previously arisen cognizing mind does not negate the object."
The objects of perception are now exhausted, just as the mind that was not their locus has been exhausted. Among these six sense faculties, it is the mental faculty (*manas*) that bears witness.
Śāriputra then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Throughout kalpas past, my mind..."
The purity of vision.

Third, the proof of the text through the three breaths being clear and flowing. First, Śāriputra’s realization and penetration; this section has five parts. First, the statement that his mind has long been pure.
The commentary states: "When the mind's vision is pure, the eye-consciousness is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and the mind takes it as its object of contemplation."
The eight consciousnesses are collectively termed "mind" (citta); when the mind-vision is pure, it does not confront external objects.
Such modes of rebirth are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Second, the remote insight of prior wisdom.

Regarding the mundane and supramundane, the three types of wondrous wisdom penetrate both. The commentary states: "Mundane" refers to the internal body, the external vessel-world, and the dharmas such as the three aggregates and the seven elements;
"supramundane" refers to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, true thusness, nirvāṇa, and unconditioned dharmas.
"Various transformations.
The commentary states: "This concludes the worldly dharmas; by means of their reflection, the supramundane dharmas are brought forth. These are not [mere] transformations.
Upon a single vision, one attains penetration and achieves non-obstruction."
The commentary states: "The first set [of encounters] universally applies to all [the five bhikṣus], as there is no distinction in their realization.
While on the road, I encountered the brothers Kāśyapa pursuing one another;
through these four encounters, they attained awakening and realization. The commentary further states: "While various sūtras speak of encountering Aśvajit, here it says encountering Kāśyapa."
The brothers Pūraṇa and the others pursued one another; namely, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa.
Through the proclamation of the causes and conditions, they awakened to the boundless mind and left the household life to follow the Buddha.
The commentary states: A verse says: "All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease, their nature is extinguished.
My teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly speaks thus."
When the clarity of seeing and awareness becomes perfectly full, one attains great fearlessness and becomes an Arhat.
The commentary states: "Seeing and awareness" refers to the transformation of the visual consciousness into the perfection of the light of wisdom.
He is the eldest son of the Buddha; born from the Buddha’s mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma.

The commentary states: All Buddhas take wisdom as their primary faculty. Because Śāriputra possesses great wisdom, he was born into the family of the Buddha, having been proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Buddha and transformed by the Dharma he taught.
The Buddha asked about perfect penetration. According to what I have realized, the five manifestations mark the emergence of knowledge and vision;
from the mind and vision, light is emitted.
The commentary states: The eye-consciousness is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind; it emits the light of wisdom.
When this light reaches its ultimate limit, it constitutes the foremost vision.

The commentary further states: When the light of wisdom reaches its ultimate depth, the *dharmadhātu* becomes true knowledge and vision. Among the six consciousnesses, this refers to the eye-consciousness.
Upon entering into realization,
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have previously served as a Dharma prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Next, the sixth section: "The Universal Worthy Mind Listens to the Text. First, the extensive assistance to the Dharma King. The commentary states:

"Universal Worthy" (Puxian) was formerly called "Pien-chi" (Universally Auspicious). "Universal" (pu) means pervasive. He pervasively enters the lands within every mote of dust to teach and transform sentient beings;

he possesses great worthiness and goodness. Furthermore, the Sanskrit name is Maṇjuśrī (Man-lï-lo); in the Tang language, it is "Universal Worthy" (Puxian). "Universal" refers to the Dharma; "Worthy" refers to the person. Thus, it is the person and the Dharma.
This is a dual designation. Furthermore, "all" being "one" is called "Universal" (Samantabhadra); "one" being "all" is called "Worthy" (Bhadra).
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions instruct their disciples whose faculties are those of Bodhisattvas to cultivate the practices of Samantabhadra; they establish this name based upon me.
Second, the completion of the names of others. The commentary states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all take practice as their initial aspiration.
World-Honored One, I employ the faculty of mental hearing to discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings."

"Third, the mind-hearing penetrates and perceives. The commentary states: "Mind-hearing" refers to the manifestation of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereby the mind illuminates and discerns all the cognitions and views of sentient beings.
If there should be a single sentient being in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions who brings forth within their mind the realization of Samantabhadra’s practice,
at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant, manifesting hundreds of thousands of emanations, and arrive at that very place.
"Reaching the four quarters, he responds to the minds of the multitudes. The commentary states: "The six tusks symbolize the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Their pure whiteness symbolizes the brilliance and purity of the gate of practice (*caryā-mukha*). Question: "The gate of practice of this Bodhisattva is so all-pervasive;

why then is it singled out as not being the 'perfect penetration' (*yuan-tong*)? Answer: "This is merely because it concerns the arousal of the conduct of Samantabhadra (*Samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna*). It is singled out because it pertains to those of great resolve."

Even if their obstacles are profound such that they have not yet been able to see me, I shall, in the darkness, place my hand upon the crown of their heads, protecting and comforting them so that they may achieve success.
"Five Hidden Aspects Consoling the Ordinary. The commentary states: An outsider asks, "What should one do if there are those whose karmic obstructions are profound and heavy?
The Sūtra answers at length.

Regarding the inquiry into perfect penetration, I declare its fundamental cause: when the hearing-faculty of the mind is illuminated and awakened, and discernment becomes sovereign, this is the foremost.
"The six knots arise from the mind's perceptions. The commentary states: This is verified by means of the ear-consciousness.
Sūndarananda then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When I first left the household life and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I was fully endowed with the precepts, my mind was constantly distracted and agitated regarding *samādhi*, and I had not yet attained [liberation]."

[The section on] the outflows (*āsrava*). Regarding the subsequent [section], Nanda transformed the breathing exercise into three parts. It is said that at the initial stage, the mind is mostly distracted and agitated.
The commentary states: There are three [Nandas]: first, Nanda, whose name means "Joy," who was a cowherd; second, Sundarananda, which in the language of Tang means "Exquisite Joy"; third...
Ānanda: This is the question of Ānanda. *Yan* is the name of his wife; *Xi* is his own name. Why does he cause [himself] to be called by his own name instead of using his wife’s name?
Answer: This is to distinguish him from those who are not two people [but one]. He was the Buddha’s own younger brother, one zhang, five chi, and two cun tall.
He was the son of Mahānāman. His transformative activities are recorded in the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. Pure.
King Ikṣvāku had three consorts: first, Gopī; second, Māyā, also called Māyāvatī;
she gave birth to Nanda. Third, Queen Māyā, who gave birth to the World-Honored One.

"The World-Honored One taught me and my teacher, Kūṭadanta, to contemplate the white at the tip of the nose. When I first applied myself to this contemplation, after twenty-one days had passed, I saw the breath within the nostrils entering and exiting like smoke."
Next, observe the breath transcending the dust. The commentary states: Observe a single white point at the tip of the nose, causing the mental factors (*caitta*) to be gathered into one mass;
because the mind is thus not distracted.
The body and mind are internally luminous; the world becomes a perfect void, universally pure and clear, like lapis lazuli.
The commentary states: "The body and mind are internally luminous" means that they universally become the light of wisdom; this is the wisdom that is void, clear, and pure.
The appearance of smoke gradually fades away, and the nasal breath becomes white.
The commentary states: "This is the luminosity of the essence of wisdom. Alternatively, white is the source of all colors, symbolizing wisdom."
The mind opened and the outflows were exhausted. All inhalations and exhalations were transformed into radiant light, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions, and he became an Arhat.
The commentary states: "To be transformed into radiant light refers to the functioning of the illumination of wisdom."
The World-Honored One has prophesied that I shall attain Bodhi;
later, I obtained the prophecy that marked the cause. The commentary states: The *Lotus Sūtra* says, "Five hundred arhats and two thousand śrāvakas."
All have received their predictions of enlightenment; I fear I may be among their number.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration (*yuantong*), I replied that I attained it through the cessation of breath.
The commentary states: "Cessation" (*xiaoxi*) refers to the stopping of the inhalation and exhalation within the nostrils.
"Breathing ceases for a long duration and luminosity becomes manifest.
The Commentary states: "When the practice of contemplation is about to reach perfection, transformation gives rise to wisdom, initiating luminosity.
When this luminosity is perfected, outflows are extinguished; this is the foremost [stage]."
The commentary states: This was directed toward the olfactory consciousness as a witness.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Since the beginningless kalpas, my eloquence has been unimpeded as I proclaim suffering and emptiness.
[This consists of three parts: the fourfold mastery of eloquence, the subduing of heterodoxy, and the realization of the text. First, regarding eloquence and fearlessness:
the commentary states that the proclamation of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness constitutes the *niṣyanda* (outflow) teaching; this is the expressive text.
Profoundly penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*).
The Commentary states: "This refers to the principle that is elucidated.
Thus, even regarding the secret Dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have revealed them with subtle and wondrous clarity amidst the assembly."
He attained fearlessness. The commentary states:
"The secret dharma-gate refers to the teachings of equal outflow (*niṣyanda-dharma*). That the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know it is called 'secret' (*bī*);
that ordinary beings cannot fathom it is called 'mysterious' (*mi*). [This applies to] Pūrṇa of today; why then does he alone know that this is truly great?
I am a provisional śrāvaka, secretly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva within.
Knowing that I possess great eloquence, the World-Honored One has used the wheel of his voice to instruct me to proclaim it forth. Before the Buddha, I—
Assisting the Buddha in turning the wheel [of Dharma], he attained arhatship through the lion’s roar. The World-Honored One certified him, saying, "Your preaching of the Dharma is unsurpassed.
Next, he assisted in the transcendence of the mundane. The commentary states: "The sound is like a wheel, capable of crushing all malevolent spirits, heterodox paths, and externalists;
or, it is like a wheel that can revolve as one person transmits it to many. Furthermore, the Buddha is the True [Dharma]."
"Turning. Pūrṇa is one who assists in turning. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?
I have always praised him as being foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
I have also constantly extolled his various merits: his diligent application in protecting and upholding [the teaching], and his assistance in proclaiming my Dharma."
He is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly, fully explaining and interpreting the Buddha’s true teachings to provide great benefit;
apart from the Tathāgata himself, no one is capable of exhausting the eloquence of his discourse.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied that by means of the Dharma-sound, I subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows (*āsrava*); this is the foremost.
Later, in the "Manifestation of the Cause," it is distinguished; the commentary states: "Among the six consciousnesses, one takes the tongue-consciousness as the point of realization."
Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Threefold Text on the Divine Realization of the Five Reins, the Bridle, and the Tongs. First, 'Holding Firmly to Transcend the Dust. The commentary states: 'Reins' refers to saddle-reins;
'bridle' means to restrain; 'tongs' means to seize; and 'divine' refers to the divine consciousness (*vijñāna*). It speaks of all sentient beings’ delusions..."
The body is the deluded mind; it is clamorous, restless, and agitated, like an unbroken horse.

If it is not restrained by the bonds of the precepts, it will ultimately give rise to delusion and create karma, just as a horse is held steady with a bit and bridle so that it does not scatter or move about.
In Sanskrit he is called Upāli, also known as Upali; in the language of Tang, it means "Close Attendant. When the Buddha was a prince, he served as his personal attendant.
Approaching the Crown Prince, [he was] among those attending to his affairs.
I personally followed the Buddha as he left the city to renounce the world.
The commentary states: When the Buddha was a crown prince, having reached the age of nineteen, at the third watch of the night, a deity in the air announced [the news].
It is said: When the time for the Prince’s renunciation arrived, the Buddha went toward the northwest corner of the city;
the Four Heavenly Kings supported the hooves of his horse as he leaped over the city walls and departed, eventually dwelling among the Snow Mountains.
He personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity.
The commentary states: regarding the six years of ascetic practice, he subsisted on one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat; this was intended to subdue the non-Buddhist practitioners of asceticism.

For five years he cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and in the eleventh year he completely severed all fetters (*saṃyojana*). Then, beneath the Bodhi tree, through the three watches and four minds, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Perfectly Awakened.
He personally beheld the Tathāgata subduing all Māras and restraining all non-Buddhists, attaining liberation from the worldly outflows of greed and desire.
The commentary states: After the Buddha attained the Way, there were various Demon Kings atop the summit of the Desire Realm who created adverse and favorable conditions [within his sphere].
The ordinary realms were agitated and disturbed. The World-Honored One entered the samādhi of loving-kindness and emitted the moon-like light of compassion to illuminate them;
all the māra kings and their hosts were completely dispersed and retreated.
"I have received the Buddha’s teaching on the precepts; thus it extends even to the three thousand modes of dignified conduct.
The commentary states: "A śramaṇa has two hundred and fifty precepts. Each precept possesses twelve aspects, totaling three thousand."
Alternatively, one may proceed from the three roots; each root possesses one thousand roots, totaling three thousand, with eighty thousand subtle variations. The commentary states:

"Take the aforementioned three thousand modes of deportment and apply them to the seven branches, assigning them to the three bodily transgressions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and [the corresponding verbal ones]."
The four [types of unwholesome speech]—false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech—each branch possesses three thousand [subdivisions].
Seven times three is twenty-one; thus, they total twenty-one thousand. These are further assigned to the three fundamental roots of greed, anger, and delusion.
Each root contains twenty-one thousand precepts. Four sets of twenty-one thousand constitute eighty-four thousand. As the Sūtra says:
The eighty thousand [precepts] are summarized thus:
both natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*) are entirely purified; body and mind are stilled, and one becomes an Arhat.
The commentary states: Natural offenses are fundamental and cannot be expiated; they are like cutting down a *tāla* tree, from which no further growth can arise.

Just as when a person's head is severed, they do not live again, so too are the remaining [precepts] all considered *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibitory offenses), intended to prevent the censure and suspicion of non-Buddhists and laypeople.
Among the two hundred and fifty rules, those concerning killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and great falsehood are *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offenses);
the rest are all prohibitory precepts. The Mahāyāna precepts are likewise called *prakṛti-sāvadya*, and these four grave offenses are also termed *prakṛti*.

For example, when the Buddha was on the bodhisattva path, he once was a brahmin traveling together with five hundred people on a single boat. At that time, there was a thief..."

Within that ship, they intended to kill these five hundred people. The World-Honored One, knowing the thieves' intent, immediately slew those thieves, for he valued the preservation of the many lives.

Thus it is accomplished. Once one realizes that the four great elements (mahābhūta) of both the internal and external are entirely false and illusory, one no longer clings to either the internal or the external;

The intrinsic nature of atoms does not touch one another.

The commentary states: "To realize that both the internal and external are transformations of the four sense-objects (dhātus) and possess no substantial reality, [one understands that] even weapons such as swords do not come into contact."
The commentary states: "The body is composed of minute particles, and its great nature is entirely empty. By not grasping at the body as a self, how could weapons possibly cause harm?

"Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I have realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attained arhatship.

It is neither emptiness nor form; this is the entrance. As for the "ground of earth," it is the ground of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), which does not admit even a single speck of dust.

"Fourth, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The commentary states:

Body and mind emit light, penetrating all things without obstruction.

The Commentary states: "Above the forty thousand [yojanas] of the eastern direction, at the initial point where the myriad things manifest their brilliance, and at the place where the solar disc first rises—all these symbolize the commencement of the pure wisdom of *ādi-bodhi* (initial awakening) as it enters the principle of the Dharma-realm. *Fan*: [This refers to the realm of Brahmā].

It says "Akṣobhya," which in the language of Tang means "Immovable. This signifies the quiescence of the Dharma; because it is quiescent, there is nothing that can be turned. Thus, one beholds the land of Akṣobhya Buddha in the eastern direction.

That the body and mind emit light signifies the arousal of [the bodhicitta].

This clear and lucid illumination and examination is wisdom (*prajñā*). Having generated wisdom from concentration, one then contemplates that both the internal body and the external world are equally the One True Reality (*ekasatya*).
Emptiness.

Wisdom. Internally, it emits ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-light. The commentary states:

This is the light of wisdom, flowing and permeating the ten directions to the very limits of empty space. The Commentary states:

"The three bodies encompass the Buddha-lands. The commentary states: the various *dhvajarāja* lands are the dependent *āśraya* (retributive support);

They interpenetrate one another; their bodies are identical to empty space, sharing the principle of emptiness. They do not obstruct one another, but rather interpenetrate, attaining complete mastery.
The body is able to skillfully enter lands as numerous as motes of dust and extensively perform the Buddha-activities, thereby attaining great accordance.

Regarding the phrase "the four substances entering the square of the dust," the commentary states: "That the body is able to skillfully enter lands as numerous as motes of dust refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

thus, in my third account, I testify to the realization of non-arising.

"Regarding 'manifesting within the same' (*tongming*)," the commentary states: "This means that, with respect to the principle of original sameness (*bentong*), one gives rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*houdezhi*), which is precisely the recognition of the aforementioned principle of original sameness."

I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The commentary states: "Non-arising" refers to the principle that [phenomena] are fundamentally identical to the unconditioned; "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the act of sealing and affirming this truth.

Section Eight: Text on the Realization of Mind-Only Consciousness. Regarding the phrase "The initial mind is repeatedly named 'floating'":
the commentary states that the Sanskrit name is Maitreya, or alternatively Maitreyīna; this is translated as "Maitreya" (The Compassionate One). His mother’s nature was not compassionate;
it was only after she conceived him that her nature became compassionate. A skilled physiognomist therefore gave him the name "Maitreya. As for "compassion," it refers to a compassionate nature.
"Lineage" refers to family clans.
I recall that in the past, after the passage of atoms of kalpas, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.
From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness; yet, my mind held family reputation in high regard, and I delighted in frequenting noble lineages."

The commentary states: The *Lotus Sūtra* says that the Dharma Master Wonderful Light had at that time a younger brother who constantly harbored a two-fold mind of indolence and was greedily attached to fame and profit.

Insatiable in his pursuit of fame and profit, he frequented the houses of the noble families; he was called "Seeker of Fame" (*Qiú-míng*), who was none other than Maitreya during his stage of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to cultivate the samādhi of mind-only consciousness and enter into samādhi.
Throughout kalpas past, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges by means of this samādhi.
"Resting while roaming through the gates of the two concentrations. The commentary states: "This merely excludes external objects; 'consciousness' (vijñāna) distinguishes it from the mind (citta).

As the Sūtra says: 'Because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. This samādhi is the concentration of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)."
The mind that seeks worldly fame has ceased and no longer exists.
The commentary states: "Thus, the *parikalpita* (imagined) mind perishes. This refers to the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
It was only when Dīpaṃkara Buddha appeared in the world that I attained the supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind.
Third, the realization through kindling the lamp. The commentary states: "These are the Buddhas encountered by Śākyamuni.

The four transformation lands are coarse and subtle.
World-Honored One, because I have realized that such things are solely mind and consciousness, the five [realms] flow from the mind of the many Buddhas.
The commentary states: this "consciousness-mind" refers to the Dharmakāya, which is able to manifest both the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya.
From the body, the nature of consciousness flows forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas.

"Body" (*kāya*) carries the meaning of "giving birth. Just as a mother can give birth to her child, [this one] has now received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that he shall next succeed to the Buddha’s position.
Sixth, the present record of succession. The commentary states: The *Sūtra on the Birth Above* says: "World-Honored One, in the past, at Vaiśālī..."
In the *Madhyama Āgama* and various other sūtra collections, it is said that Ajita shall in the future become a Buddha.

Regarding the inquiry into perfect penetration, I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). This conscious mind is perfectly luminous; through it, I have entered the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

To remain far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), thereby attaining the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), is the foremost [attainment].

Seventh, the description of the realization that indicates the cause. The commentary states: When the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Being far removed from the dependent nature, one does not cling to the deluded body composed of the four great elements, nor does one cling to the imagined nature; the mind that seeks worldly fame has already perished, leaving only...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "By means of that pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), one conceptualizes various objects. This nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist at all.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the differentiation produced by conditions. The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is eternally devoid of the former natures and so forth.

The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Section Three:
Establishing the Text on the Nine Wondrous Lands. First, describing the encounter with the Buddha's teaching. The commentary states:
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta" should be read as "one who has attained great power. It means that wherever he goes, the worlds tremble; [he possesses] great majesty...
When sentient beings encounter this deity, their suffering naturally ceases and they attain great, supreme bliss. The *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states:
"Next, he shall succeed Avalokiteśvara and become a Buddha named Suvihita-guṇaratna."
Together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his own rank, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light."

The commentary states: "Regarding those fifty-two bodhisattvas of the same class, it is likely that these are the fifty-two bodhisattvas from the beginning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, starting with Samantadarśin and ending with Mañjuśrī."
Twelve Tathāgatas appeared in succession over the course of one kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū.
The commentary states: "The twelve Tathāgatas are also names of Buddhas found within the sūtras; however, these twelve Tathāgatas are not fixed [in number]."
That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddhas.
The commentary states: From the point of reaching non-thought (*amanasikāra*), non-thought is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
When non-conceptual wisdom accords with the principle (*tattva*), one perceives all Buddhas as ever manifest before one.
It is like two people: one is single-mindedly intent on remembering, while the other is single-mindedly prone to forgetting. Such two people may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see.
Next, the analogy illustrating the teaching has two parts. First, the analogy of the mother and son meeting, which has two sections. First, the formal presentation, which has two parts.
First, demonstrating that meeting is not certain due to memory and forgetfulness. The commentary states: "It is like a person named Zhang remembering a person named Wang."
Furthermore, the king’s man forgot the man from Zhang. When these two met, it was as if they had not met; though they met, it was as if they did not meet.

Dharma-upariṣṭa, it is like this: just as the Buddhas keep sentient beings in mind, yet sentient beings do not keep the Buddhas in mind, so from birth to birth, meeting a Buddha is as if they had not met him, and seeing a Buddha is as if they had not seen him.
The two remember each other; their mutual remembrance is profound. Thus it continues from birth to birth, like a form and its shadow, never diverging.
Later, it is revealed that the two shared the same thoughts and followed one another through successive kalpas. The commentary states: "It is like when Zhang remembers Wang."
People remember kings, and kings also remember people; these two do not part from one another from birth to birth.
Likewise, the Buddhas of the Dharmāgrya lineage mindfully regard sentient beings, and sentient beings also mindfully regard the Buddhas; thus, they will certainly behold the Buddhas in the future.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings like a mother remembers her child. If the child has fled and wandered away, what can be done by such remembrance?

This consists of two parts: first, the general analogy, and second, the specific application of the analogy. First, it reveals that while the Buddha’s compassionate mind is ever-present, sentient beings forget and turn their backs on him.
The commentary states: This corresponds to the first point above. One person focuses exclusively on remembering, while the other focuses exclusively on forgetting. It is like a son who has run away;
even if [the father] remembers him, what is the use? This means that if sentient beings do not recollect the Buddha, then even if the Buddha remembers sentient beings, what is the use?
If the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers [the child], then throughout successive births, mother and child shall not be separated or distant from one another.

Later, when the child, like the mother, remembers [the Buddha], they will presently receive the illumination. The commentary states: "Fashang: When sentient beings practice the mindfulness of the Buddha..."
Just as the Buddha thinks of sentient beings, so too the Buddha and sentient beings have not been far apart throughout successive kalpas. This corresponds to the second [case]:
when two people remember each other simultaneously, they are like a form and its shadow, never failing to coincide.
If sentient beings, with their minds, recollect the Buddha and think of the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or the future. They will not be far from the Buddha;
without relying on expedient means, their own minds will spontaneously open.
The subsequent exhortation is like a person who has been stained by incense; their body possesses a fragrant scent. This is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.
This is the analogy for the subsequent proof through the permeation of being stained by incense.
In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Subsequently, I shall describe the realization and indicate the cause. This section has three parts; first, pointing to the cause:
"Now, in this world, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land."
Next is the common cause of present activity.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, I made no selection; I simply gathered all six sense organs together, maintaining a continuous stream of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining samādhi.
This is the first [section].

The Sixth Fascicle (Part One) of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
