The Imperial Song Dynasty’s Shouleng Master Kedu, Commentary:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named...”
Avalokiteśvara. Second, the commentary on the text of the testimony by Avalokiteśvara, in two parts. First, the testimony of realization based on cultivation, in three sections.
First, the description of the name of the Original Teacher. The sub-commentary states: In Sanskrit, *avalokiteśvara*; in the language of Tang, "One who Observes Oneself."
It is abbreviated as Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara). Master Zhiyi of Tiantai said: "Guān" (Contemplation) is the wisdom that contemplates; "shì" (World) is the object contemplated;
"yīn" (Sound/Voice) refers to the sentient beings to be saved. Because one responds to their needs and goes forth to rescue them when they invoke his name and take refuge, he is called Guanshiyin.
As for the title Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara), the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang said: "He contemplates existence without dwelling [in it]."
Regarding existence, one contemplates emptiness without clinging to emptiness; hearing names, one is not deluded by names; seeing marks, one does not sink into marks.

One should not destroy existence while in the midst of existence. When all things are non-existent, one does not undermine that non-existence; though there are various kinds of existences, they are all such.
Therefore, the mind cannot be moved, and external objects cannot cause it to shift; though there is movement, the truth remains undisturbed. This may truly be called unimpeded wisdom.
Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who undergo various sufferings and afflictions..."
Upon hearing of this Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly invoking his name, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately perceives their cries, and they all attain liberation.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that in the past he was named Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa.
The *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states that in the future he will succeed Maitreya as Amitābha, named Samantaprabhā-guṇa-parvata.

There was a Tathāgata named King (Rāja). Furthermore, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteśvara; he was given his name from the perspective of the fruit resulting from the cause, and he received the title of Master (Ācārya) to represent the mutual illumination between teacher and disciple, wherein cause and effect intersect in their subtlest essence.
I, before that Buddha, gave rise to the bodhicitta. That Buddha instructed me to enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Subsequently, having given rise to the mind and received his instruction—[the] commentary states: "Giving rise to the bodhicitta" refers to the *cittotpāda-bodhi* among the five types of bodhi.
"Hearing" means listening attentively to the authentic teaching; "reflection" means making definitive discernment within the mind; "cultivation" means practicing according to the principle.
Regarding practice: the teaching is the expressive text, and the meaning is the expressed principle. By relying on the expressive text, one awakens to the expressed principle;
thereafter, one practices in accordance with that principle and proceeds toward Buddhahood.
First, regarding the section on "Entering the Stream within Hearing": one enters the stream and loses the objects of perception.

Second, regarding the section on "Relying on Cultivation to Realize the Text," there are two parts. First, regarding the sub-section on "Cultivation according to the Text," there are two parts. First, "Reversing the Stream to Extinguish the Six [Sense-Objects].
The Commentary states: The ear-faculty gives rise to the ear-consciousness; therefore, it is called "hearing. All sentient beings follow the current and cannot flow against it.
To speak of "entering the stream" means not following the current. Thus, the perceiving mind does not follow its perceived objects.
When the object is lost, there is neither the perceiving mind nor the perceived object. Alternatively, "entering the stream" refers to entering the stream of the sages.
"Lost" means non-existent; it means there is no sound-dust to be heard. Having entered the stream of the sages, one is no longer affected by time.
Regarding the "transcending of what is shifted": among the five turbidities, this transcends the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Regarding the "loss of the locus":

when the sensory object of sound does not arise, one has transcended the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) within the five aggregates. Since sound is one of the eleven types of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), the absence of sound means that the aggregate of form is transcended;
for "form" refers to substantial obstruction, and by saying "the locus is lost," one removes this substantial obstruction.
Since that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise.
The Commentary states: These three phrases provide a reverse explanation of the aforementioned "entering the stream and losing the object. "That which is entered" refers to the sensory objects;
"entering" refers to the mind that enters. Both the object entered and the subject entering—the sound-object and the contemplating mind—are equally tranquil.
Then there can be no arising of movement or stillness. If there were the sensory object of sound, then there would be movement and stillness. The above constitutes the sixth extinction.
Thus, by gradually increasing [this practice], both hearing and that which is heard are exhausted.
"Subsequently, both the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are eliminated. The commentary states: "In 'gradual,' it proceeds by degrees; in 'increasing,' it adds incrementally.

Since the six [consciousnesses] have already been extinguished, there still remain the two consciousnesses—the seventh and eighth. Now, as those seventh and eighth are gradually increased, the one that hears is the sixth consciousness, and what is heard is the objective realm of sound;
these two are both extinguished. Furthermore, one does not abide in the extinction of the six."
As for the mind: if one dwells in the cessation of the six [senses], there is the view of the cessation of the six;

now, you do not dwell in the view of the cessation of the six, and thus among the five turbidities, you transcend the turbidity of views. If there were a mind that ceases the six, there would be the sense of reception;
now, since you do not dwell in the mind that ceases the six, among the five aggregates, you transcend the aggregate of sensation.
"Exhaustively hearing yet not abiding.

The commentary states: When both the object heard and the subject that hears are extinguished, one does not even form the notion of extinction. Because there is no abiding in either subject or object, it is called "not abiding.

This refers to not abiding in the understanding that the subject and object of hearing have already ceased; if one were to abide in this non-abiding or in the cessation itself, it would not be true non-abiding.
If one dwells within the six abodes, there is that which can be grasped and that in which one can dwell; this constitutes affliction (*kleśa*).

Now, since one does not dwell in the cessation of the six abodes, one transcends the affliction-turbidity (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) among the five turbidities. If there were a cessation of the six abodes, it would constitute the formation of mental images (*nimitta*).
Now, since one does not even dwell in the cessation of the six abodes, there is no activity of grasping at images. Among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), [this is so].
One emerges from the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). One realizes that the perceiver is empty of what is perceived.
The commentary states: "The 'upper' perceiver refers to the eighth consciousness; the 'lower' perceived object refers to the seventh consciousness. This gives rise to the eight types of awareness.
7. The eighth is the subject (the grasper), and the seventh is the object (the grasped). This seventh consciousness, which is the object of awakening, is empty.
Although the seventh has ceased, the eighth, which is the subject capable of awakening, still remains. Alternatively, that which awakens is the subject—the seventh consciousness;

that which is awakened is the sixth [consciousness], which has already ceased. If the seventh were present, it would grasp the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth, and being accompanied by the four afflictions, it would [function as such].
Wandering through the various realms of existence, there are sentient beings; that which is now awakened is the sixth consciousness. It does not abide in the mind that seeks cessation.
The seventh consciousness is able to awaken to its own emptiness as well. Among the five turbidities, it transcends the turbidity of sentient beings.

If the seventh consciousness were present, it would be accompanied by the eighth consciousness to form defilement, possessing the characteristics of shifting flow and conditioned activity. Now that the seventh has ceased, the five...
Within the aggregates (*skandha*), one transcends the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

When emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are perfectly perfected, the Commentary states: "Emptiness gives rise to the wisdom that can empty; awakening refers to the eighth [consciousness]. When this wisdom arises, it empties this eighth [consciousness]."

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the mind capable of awakening; therefore, it reaches the ultimate perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). Alternatively, that which is capable of awakening is the eighth consciousness.
When awakening extinguishes those seven, now that the seven have been extinguished, the eighth serves as the awakener and [the seventh] becomes the object of emptiness.

Since both are utterly extinguished, it is called "ultimate perfection. If the eighth were still present, there would remain the functional capacity for grasping and maintaining [existence], and thus [attachment] would persist.
Sentient beings. Therefore, now that the eighth *nirmāṇacitta* (the "capable of awakening") has ceased, its function of continuous maintenance is lost.

Among the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it transcends the turbidity of lifespan. If there were an eighth [consciousness], then the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) would abide throughout the three realms;

consciousness would be dominant and wisdom weak, and strong cognition would perform the act of discernment. Now, since the capable-of-awakening is empty, wisdom is dominant and consciousness is inferior. Among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)...

Transcending the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), that which is empty and that by which it is emptied are both extinguished. The commentary states: "The 'emptiness above' refers to the wisdom that performs the emptying; the 'that which is emptied' refers to the eighth consciousness. [When] this wisdom arises, [the consciousness] is emptied.
That which is empty—the wisdom that is capable of emptying it—likewise does not exist. This wisdom capable of emptying corresponds to the eight consciousnesses;

the eight consciousnesses are also the object. This, then, eliminates the wisdom of the three [aspects] that act as the subject. Alternatively, the wisdom that is capable of emptying is the subject, while the eight consciousnesses are the object.
Now, although both the wisdom capable of emptying and the consciousnesses that are the objects of emptiness have departed, there is still neither the subject capable of emptying nor the object.
The realization of emptiness:

when arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one. Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, the ten directions become perfectly luminous, and one attains two kinds of excellence.

The subsequent section on the textual proof has two parts. First is the general indication of arising and ceasing. The commentary states: "Arising" refers to the three transformative capacities; "ceasing" refers to the arising of wisdom.
Now, when this wisdom arises, that [deluded] arising and ceasing is extinguished; once that is extinguished, this wisdom also ceases. Therefore, it says, "having already ceased."
The extraordinary is distinguished from the ordinary, and the superior is distinguished from the inferior.
First, it harmonizes upward with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas.
The subsequent separate listing of the text has two parts. First, "superiorly harmonizing with the Buddha-mind. The commentary states:

"Superiorly harmonizing" refers to the arising of *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (discriminating wisdom), which harmonizes with the *mūlabodhicitta* (fundamental awakened mind); this is the principle of *mūlajñāna* (fundamental awakening).
It means that one’s own mind is no different from the Buddha-mind, and one’s own wisdom is no distinct from Buddha-wisdom; for compassion is able to bestow happiness.
Second, [the practitioner] merges downward with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same compassion and longing as all those beings.
Later, [this state] penetrates the nature of ordinary beings. The commentary states: "This means that just as the Suchness is non-dual, so too is the Suchness of sentient beings.
Because the Buddha possesses great compassion of the same essence."

World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the transmission of the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation, which is like an illusion.

[The subsequent section on] the wondrous response to the minds of the multitudes has two parts. The first, on the universal compassion and broad response, has three parts. The first is the deduction of the teacher’s bestowal of realization.
The commentary states: It is said that the Tathāgata has instructed me that [all things] are like illusions—appearing to exist yet not existing—and like space—not empty yet not non-empty.
"Hearing and perfuming" refers to the perfuming of the faculty of hearing. Hearing, reflecting, and cultivating constitute the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Reflecting by way of shadows" means that through hearing one hears the external teachings, through reflection one contemplates their internal meaning, and through cultivation both the internal and external are encompassed. "Vajra" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).

Arising wisdom to sever one's own afflictions is samādhi. "Samādhi" is translated into Chinese as *zhèngshòu* (Right Reception); because it does not receive any [defiled] sensations, it is called "Right Reception.
Because I share the power of compassion with the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, my body manifests thirty-two transformations to enter all lands.
The commentary states: The Buddha possesses great compassion of identical essence (*sahaja-karuṇā*).

As for the thirty-two manifestations, these are the manifestation of bodies within the bodiless and the manifestation of forms within the formless. Regarding "entering," he is able to enter all lands; these are the objects entered.
World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas enter samādhi and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*), their resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) becomes fully manifest.

Next follows the extensive listing of the text for seeking [enlightenment] in two parts. First, the text for seeking supramundane [realization] in four sections. First, the Buddha-body. Commentary states:

"Entering" means being able to enter. Samādhi is that which is entered. "Advancing in practice" means increasing one's cultivation of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), whereby initial enlightenment-wisdom (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*) arises and unites with the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Alternatively, "resolute conviction" has the nature of confirming and maintaining a determined object, and its function is to be unshakable by others. "Manifesting perfection" refers to this bodhisattva’s desire to attain such resolute conviction.
The manifestation is perfected.
I manifest in the body of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

The commentary states: if these are Bodhisattvas at the stages of accumulation (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), they manifest as small transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) by means of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Using grass as a seat, he manifests a sixteen-foot form and preaches the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing. If it is for Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi), he manifests a great transformation body with a thousand-fathom form.
Once they have entered the stages, at the first stage he appears one hundred *yojanas* tall, sitting upon a lotus flower of a hundred petals and preaching a hundred gates of dharma names.
At the third stage he appears ten thousand [yojanas], and at the fourth stage he appears one billion [yojanas], continuing up to the [Dharmameghā] Stage.
Regarding the stage of the body: manifesting bodies of unspeakably unspeakable *yojanas* in height;
if there are those in training (*śaikṣa*) whose tranquil, wondrous, and luminous state is supremely marvelous and fully manifested, before them I manifest the body of a Pratyekabuddha.
And he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
Second, the bodies of the Pratyekabuddhas. The commentary states: "Quiescent, wondrous, and luminous"—this refers to the *khadgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha).

This serves as a metaphor for the pratyekabuddha being one of sharp faculties who appears in an age without a Buddha, acting as the final flame of the Buddha’s lamp; their body is solely virtuous and tranquil, and their mind...

Delighting in the pure and void, when one experiences stillness, wondrous clarity, and the wisdom of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), then the supreme and wondrous [state] manifests perfectly, giving rise to the *nirvāṇa* of the emptiness of sentient beings.
If those in training (*śaikṣa*) sever the twelve links of dependent origination...

Third is the body of the Pratyekabuddha. The commentary states: [The Pratyekabuddha] severs the twelve links of dependent origination: the two causes of the past—ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);

the five fruits of the present—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*); the three causes of the present—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*);
and the two fruits of the future—birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

When the conditions for existence were severed and their supreme nature was realized, and as that sublime state became fully manifest, I appeared before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preached the Dharma to them,
causing them to attain liberation.

The commentary states: "The severance of conditions and the supreme nature is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*). The supreme, wondrous, and manifest perfection is the nirvāṇa of the emptiness of persons.
This belongs solely to the category [of teachings] practiced when there is no Buddha in the world; it is the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination taught for those of dull faculties."
If there are those in training who have attained the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, enter cessation through the cultivation of the path, and manifest the perfection of the supreme nature,
I appear before them in the form of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

Fourth, the body of a śrāvaka. The commentary states: Because one cultivates the wisdom of the Truth of the Path and realizes the principle of the Truth of Cessation, it is called "entering cessation.
When the supreme nature manifests perfectly, this is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā). One then preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

If all sentient beings desire to awaken their minds clearly regarding desire and do not transgress the dust of desire, so that their bodies may be pure, they shall subsequently aspire for the threefold excellence of the world.
First is the text on the supreme bliss of the heavens in seven sections; first, the section on the multitude who transcend worldly karma.

The commentary states: "One who clearly awakens to the mind of desire" means that although one does not physically engage with the objects of desire, one clearly awakens to and understands the experience of pleasure when mindfulness is lost.
One perceives the lower desire realm as suffering and takes delight in the higher realms as purity and bliss.
Before him, I manifested in the form of a Brahmā King and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to attain liberation.

The commentary states: "Brahmā" means pure; "King" means one who goes toward. He is the one toward whom the various devas of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu) turn; he is the ruler of the three heavens of the First Dhyāna.

The three heavens of the second dhyāna, the three heavens of the third dhyāna, and the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna—these two groups of nine make eighteen heavens, which are governed by the Brahmā King.
They mostly teach dharmas such as generosity and the observance of precepts.

As for "liberation," it means departing from the suffering of the desire realm and seeking the bliss of the higher form realm. In the sūtras, all three vehicles are said to lead to liberation; now the Brahmā King also speaks [of this].
Liberation (vimukti) refers simply to being free from the dust of non-desire; it is called liberation because it is not the same as the liberation from suffering of the Three Vehicles.
Below this, it is stated that [this] is accomplished.
If there are sentient beings who wish to become lords of heaven and exercise sovereignty over the devas,
I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
Next is "Delighting in Dwelling as Honored. The commentary states: "Wishing to be the Lord of Heaven" means wishing to be the lord of the six heavens of the Desire Realm.
As for Śakra, in Sanskrit it is correctly *Śakradevendra*. In full, it is called "Indra of the Gods of Śakra.
*Śakra* is the clan name; *deva* is "heaven"; and *indra* is "emperor. Thus, he is called "Emperor Śakra. This is the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit.
Both are mentioned together; the text is abbreviated. The manner of preaching the Dharma below is as described previously.

If there are sentient beings who wish to travel freely throughout the ten directions with their bodies, I appear before them in the form of a Śakra-devendra and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
"Trinetra follows the mind. The commentary states: "This refers to Maheśvara (the Lord of Freedom).

However, the primary intent of this sub-commentary is to identify him as the Nirmāṇarati Heaven (the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations), which is the fifth heaven of the Desire Realm. There, one experiences sensual pleasure by transforming objects within the sensory fields. Ci'en says..."
The two heavens of Yāma and Tuṣita obtain the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) with mastery; according to their thoughts, they surpass the two lower heavens.
Just as the two higher heavens obtain [their enjoyments] by relying on trees, here they obtain them according to their desire, and are thus called the Heaven of Mastery (Vaśavartin).
"Mastery" (vaśa) has the meaning of being free from bondage.
If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to fly through the void,
I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.

"Fourth, 'others honor and play with oneself. The commentary states: The intent of the *Shu* (sub-commentary) is that this refers to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
It means that within the sensory objects (*bhautika-rūpa*) of others, one emanates [objects] for enjoyment. Cien (Ci'en) says:

The Heaven of Delight in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*) and the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations are called Mahāmaheśvara. They do not delight in the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), but rather delight in transforming both self and others into pleasure.
He possesses these qualities and receives them; he is named Mahādeva.

If there are sentient beings who love to govern spirits and deities and to protect their lands, I appear before them in the form of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
Regarding the five camps that govern thought:
if there are sentient beings who love to govern the world and protect its inhabitants,
I manifest before them in the body of a Caturmahārāja and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

"Sixth, the Peaks and Ridges of Majestic Power. The commentary states: These are the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, Virūḍhaka of the South, Virūpākṣa of the West, and Vaiśravaṇa of the North; they dwell upon the fourth tier of Mount Sumeru.
If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and to command spirits and deities,
I manifest before them in the form of a prince of the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.
"Seventh, he gallops forth, commanding a hundred spirits. The commentary states: "The Prince governs the ghosts and spirits of the four continents under heaven.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being lords of men, I manifest before them in the body of a human king and preach the Dharma for them."
May they achieve fulfillment.
Next is the vow concerning human prosperity, eight characters in length. The first vow is to "hang down robes to transform the people. The commentary states:
"Yao and Shun hung down their upper and lower garments, and the world was governed. The upper garment and lower skirt were modeled after Heaven and Earth."
If there are sentient beings who cherish their status as heads of clans and are esteemed by the world,
I appear before them in the form of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
Part Two: Seeking to Harmonize with the World and Delight the Spirit. Section One: The Elder. The Commentary states: One who causes others to grow is called an "Elder" (zhǎngzhě).
[This refers to] their clan, lineage, and personal name.
If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and phrases and dwell in self-purification, I manifest before them in the body of a layperson and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve fulfillment.
"Later, the layperson (gṛhapati). The commentary states: "One who delights in discussing refined and elegant speech; a gentleman who governs his household with internal order.
Though dwelling within the three realms, he does not mingle with the dust of desire and constantly cultivates the pure conduct (brahmacarya)."
If there are sentient beings who love to govern territories and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts,
I appear before them in the form of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

Third, "cutting brocade and drawing back the curtain. The commentary states: regarding "cutting brocade," Confucius said, "One has not yet mastered the use of the knife, yet one is made to cut brocade.
If there is fine brocade, why not have someone learn how to cut it? This is a metaphor for a county magistrate administering government.

To lift up is called *qiān* (raising). That which is at the side is called a *wéi* (curtain), which also serves to screen oneself. During the Later Han dynasty, Jia Zong served as the Inspector of Jizhou.

His official carriage was equipped with curtains and skirts. As he ascended the carriage, he rolled up the curtains and said: "An Inspector ought to look far and hear wide, investigating and scrutinizing both good and evil.
Why, then, do you instead hang down the curtain-skirts to obstruct and conceal yourself? When the people of the hundred cities heard this, they were struck with awe and trembling.

Regarding "states," this refers to states ruled by feudal lords; regarding "districts," this refers to those governed by magistrates. "To divide" means to partition; "to sever" means to judge and decide.
If there are sentient beings who cherish various arts and sciences to protect themselves and maintain their station, I manifest before them as a Brahmin.
He manifests in bodily form and preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve perfection.
Fourth, he possesses profound penetration of extraordinary arts. The commentary states: "Numerical arts" refers to the methods of calculation and numerical techniques;
"guarding and maintaining" refers to employing the arts of collection and protection. The term *brahman* (梵婆羅門) is translated in the Tang language as "Pure Lineage."
He was of the second caste in the Western Heaven (India). At the age of seven, had he pursued the study of the four Vedas, he would have become a national preceptor.
As for the four Vedas: first, medicine; second, sacrificial rites; third, divination, physiognomy, music, and the arts of war;
and fourth, the secret arts.

If there is a man who delights in learning and leaves the household life, upholding the various precepts and regulations, I will manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him,
causing him to achieve fulfillment.
Section Two: The Vinaya Text on the Three Śramaṇas. First, the Monk. The commentary states: *Śramana* is also called *śramaṇa*;
in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "diligent cessation. It refers to one who diligently seeks the path of practice and quiets all evil thoughts.
If there are women who delight in learning and leave the household life, upholding the various prohibitive precepts,
I shall manifest before them in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
Regarding "Later Nuns" (*hòu ní*). The commentary states: "The prohibitions are the five and the eight. The five precepts are:

not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, and not drinking alcohol or eating meat. The eight precepts add the sixth: one must not wear necklaces or pendants."
7. One must not apply fragrant oils to the body, wear incense as clothing, or intentionally engage in singing, dancing, or performing music, nor watch or listen to them.
8. One must not ascend high or large beds. Furthermore, there are three hundred and forty-eight precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*.
If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I shall manifest before him in the form of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him,
enabling him to achieve fulfillment.
Six: Observing Rites at Home, Part Two. First: Upāsaka. The commentary states: "Upāsaka" is the Tang-language term for "near-attendant pure one.
If there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I manifest before her in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for her, causing her to achieve accomplishment.
"Later, the *upāsikā*. The commentary states: 'In the language of Tang, this means "female lay follower.
Regarding those who abide by the five precepts themselves, it means that they merely reside at home while observing those five precepts, as explained previously.'"
If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves as pillars of their households and nations, I will appear before them in the form of a queen,
a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
Section Seven: The Gate of Refining Form through Elegant Instruction. The commentary states: "Cultivating family and state" refers to refining the household and governing the nation.
"Female ruler" refers to the Empress (the female Son of Heaven), or as some say, the Princesses or the Ladies of the State; these are the royal consorts (*wáng hòu*).

"Appointed ladies" (*mìng fù*) are those women who have received an official appointment, such as the Nine Consorts (*jiǔ pín*) and below. "Great ladies" (*dà jiā*) are women of preserved virtue, such as Cáo Dàjiā.
At the age of nineteen, he composed eight chapters as an admonition concerning the affairs of women.
"If there are sentient beings whose male organs are not impaired, I shall manifest before them in the form of a young man and preach the Dharma for them."
To cause them to achieve accomplishment.
Section Two: The Eight Chaste Maidens in the Inner Chambers. First, regarding the young boys:
if there is a maiden who delights in remaining chaste and does not seek to be violated, I shall manifest before her in the form of a young girl.
And he preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

Regarding the term "later maiden" (hòu tóngnǚ): the commentary states that one who dwells within the chamber is called a "maiden" (chǔnǚ); if she is "invaded," it means she is invaded by the realm of desire.
As for violence, the violent mind that desires to flourish as it does today has now vanished.
If there are devas who wish to emerge from their celestial ranks, I manifest a celestial body to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve realization.

The subsequent section on "the mind’s liberation from deviant categories" consists of nine passages. The first, "the initial resolve transcends the intoxication of emotions," includes a commentary stating:

"As for those who are gods, their pleasure is like that of a person intoxicated by wine. Question: Previously, you spoke of Brahmā, Maheśvara, and others; why then do you here speak of "all the gods"? Answer:

This statement refers to the joy of emerging from the ranks of the gods, which gives rise to world-weariness (*saṃvega*). That previous statement referred to the joy of being a lord of the gods. This is the distinction.
They give rise to joy.
If there are dragons who wish to leave their dragon status, I manifest in a dragon body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve perfection.
Second, when they feel weary of their dwelling, I raise clouds.
If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own kind, I shall manifest in the form of a yakṣa before them and preach the Dharma for them,
enabling them to achieve success.
"Third, the joy of being free from flying spirits. The commentary states: *Yakṣas* (in the language of Tang, meaning "valiant and robust," or "fierce and evil") fly through the air;
they also include those who roam upon the earth as their prey.
If there are gandharvas who desire to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve success.
"Four Intentions Exclude Music and Performance. The commentary states: "The new [translation] calls them *gandharva*. In the Tang language, this means 'Fragrance-Seeking' (*xūnxiāng xíng*).
Among the various deities who perform music, there are such classes as these. For this reason, in the Western Regions, all itinerant musicians are called *gandharva*.
They do not engage in productive labor, but merely seek out fragrances and play music to beg for alms."
If there are asuras who wish to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve success.
"Five times Kausika fought in battle. The commentary states: "Kausika is translated in the Tang language as 'Cocoon Child' (*jiǎnré*); this is an alternative name for Śakra.
He constantly fights with the Asuras. Formerly they were called *Āsura*; according to the new [translation], they are called *Asura*. *Ā* means 'not,' and *sura* means 'deva.
Because they frequently practice flattery and deception and lack the conduct of those devas, they are called 'Non-devas' (*fei-tian*)."
If there is a kiṃnara who desires liberation from his kind, I manifest before him in the form of a kiṃnara and preach the Dharma for him,
enabling him to achieve success.
"Six people harmonized with the dust motes on the beams. The commentary states: Regarding "harmonizing," there was a song by Song Yu;

among those who could harmonize in Ying, there were no more than a few individuals. The higher the singing rose, the fewer those who could harmonize—this refers to the melodies of the "Yangchun" and "Bai xue."
Regarding "dust on the beams": it is said that when one sings well the songs of Shun, the sound causes the dust on the beams to stir.

*Kinnara* (alternatively *Kiṃnara*; newly transliterated as *Kiṃnara*) means "Deity of Song" in the language of Tang. First they sing the Four Noble Truths; next they sing the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
next they sing the Six Perfections and the myriad practices; and finally they sing the One Vehicle. Just like worldly musical tones, they sing of Your Majesty.
Virtuous One,
if there are mahoragas who desire to be liberated from their own kind, I manifest before them in the body of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve success.

"Seven types of those who practiced heterodox arts. The commentary states: "To 'practice' (cāo) means to maintain or employ. This class of beings were fond of practicing heterodox arts in their previous lives;
therefore, they have incurred this retribution. Formerly called *mahura*, and in the sutras called *mahura*;
the correct transliteration is *mahoraga*. In the language of Tang, it means 'large-bellied. These are the kinds of creatures such as frogs, pythons, and snakes found in fields."

If there are sentient beings who delight in being human or in cultivating the human state, I manifest in a human form and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment and bringing joy to their minds throughout the eight directions.
If there are non-humans— whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception— who wish to transcend their own kind,
I shall manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
"Nine: Generally Dispelling the Burdens of Form. The commentary states: "Non-human" refers to thought. "Having form" refers to those with physical substance;
"formless" refers to the heavens of formlessness. "With perception" refers to the heavens of perception; "without perception" refers to the heavens without perception.

This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies for entering lands, all of which are accomplished with mastery through the effortless, wondrous power of cultivation based on hearing and the permeation of hearing via samādhi.
"Later, the wondrous power is manifested. The commentary states: "Samādhi is principle (li); the permeation of hearing is wisdom (hui).
The wondrous power of non-action is a subtle and marvelous power that is unconditioned and without contrivance. As for 'power' (li), it carries the meaning of being difficult to subdue."
World-Honored One, by means of this power of the effortless wondrous samādhi of the vajra— perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—
and because I share in the same compassionate longing as all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and three periods of time across the six realms, [I vow...]

The subsequent section on "Compassion Saving the Multitude from Wounds" has two parts. The first part, "Dispelling Delusion and Rescuing Those Submerged," has three sections. The first is a general manifestation of fearlessness. The commentary states:

"Hearing-perfuming" (*śruta-vāsanā*) refers to the perfuming of the faculty of hearing. "Hearing-cultivation" refers to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), which implicitly include "reflection" (*cintā*).

"Vajra" refers to gnosis (*jñāna*); "samādhi" refers to principle (*tattva*). "Compassion" (*karuṇā*) means to feel sorrow for one's own suffering and thereby extract others from their suffering. "Looking up" (*ālokana*) means to bear [the burden].
With holy virtue, we reverently look up to Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata as our teacher,
who causes all sentient beings to attain fourteen kinds of fearless merit within our own bodies and minds.

The commentary states: All sentient beings, by merely entering the stream at the gateway of the ear-organ and losing the perceived object, can believe that their own bodies are no different from the Buddha’s body and their own minds are no distinct from the Buddha’s mind.

Because they are identical to Avalokiteśvara, they obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious virtues of fearlessness within my own body and mind. "Gong" (功) refers to functional power; "De" (德) refers to virtue.
Karma: it is the body that manifests as a thousand heads and ten thousand heads, or a thousand arms and ten thousand arms. Mind: it is the mind of great compassion.
First: because I do not contemplate [the sound of] Avalokiteśvara for myself.

Next, the section on extensively protecting against the various calamities consists of four parts. First, the manifestation of rescue and protection, which has two sub-sections. First, observing sound to provide universal rescue. The commentary states:
"All sentient beings observe Avalokiteśvara by following the sensory object of sound; they do not [observe him] by not following the sensory object of sound."

"Using contemplation to contemplate the contemplator. The commentary states: "The upper [term] refers to the wisdom that is able to contemplate; the lower [term] refers to the principle that is the object of contemplation. This is because one turns back the hearing to hear one's own nature.

Alternatively, "contemplation" refers to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) which is able to contemplate, while "the contemplator" is the object of contemplation. By means of this ability to contemplate, one contemplates.
That which is observed—the auditory object—has no intrinsic nature; this is self-benefit.
It causes those suffering sentient beings throughout the ten directions who observe its sounds to immediately attain liberation.
The commentary states: This refers to benefiting others. The former [section] concerns the fundamental [wisdom], while the latter concerns the subsequently attained [wisdom].
As for "observing their sounds," whether one hears the name of Avalokiteśvara or hears the Dharma taught by Avalokiteśvara, one immediately attains liberation;
that is, one becomes free from the three sufferings and the five sufferings that afflict all sentient beings.
Second, knowing and seeing the revolving restoration.

The subsequent section on the "Supporting the Imperiled" (扶危) consists of seven texts. First, "The Blazing Gale Does Not Burn. The commentary states: "This refers to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*)."
The mind of false cognition and false vision turns back and returns to the true source, causing all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.
The commentary states: All sentient beings give rise to anger toward objects that oppose their feelings and give rise to greed toward objects that accord with their feelings.
This is the mind of attachment. Now that it has been exhausted, one will no longer be tormented by the fire of desire.
