Regarding the function of illumination: when there is that which is produced, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), and there arises a powerful awakening wisdom that illuminates that which is illuminated, ignorance then ceases to arise, and one attains a state where the object corresponds to the mind.
"The nature of that which establishes [the object] perishes.
The Commentary states: "Once there is the appearance of that which is illuminated, ignorance accords with one's sentiment; then there arises the mind that acts as the subject-perceiver.
Once both subject and object are established, the wisdom that previously acted as the illuminator also becomes obscured. Originally, the nature of the ocean of awakening was tranquil and perfect."
It is also hidden. That the deceased have nothing means that delusion gives rise to empty space. The commentary states:

that which deludes is the false awakening, while that which is deluded is the true nature. Since there is both the subject (the deluder) and the object (that which is deluded), there then arise the seven [elements].
The consciousnesses and the manas carry along those dull and empty appearances as their objective field; thus, they form the commonality of sentient beings (*sabhāgatā*) and empty space.
Relying upon this space, the world-systems are established. The Commentary states:

When the appearance of weariness arises within awakening, it obscures the fundamental perfect luminosity. Turning one's back on the original mind and becoming muddled, one perceives the appearance of the great void. This is...
When the four great elements flourish and arise, they form a world; space is that upon which it relies, and the world is that which is transformed.
"Thoughts coagulate to form a land. The commentary states:
"Thought" (*xiang*) means to grasp an image; "coagulation" (*cheng*) means to congeal. This means that when the mind of thought congeals, it forms a land.
The receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and so forth constitute the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
Sentient cognition is the sentient being;
the commentary states that this refers to the sentient beings who are the supported (*āśrita*), which is the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*).
"Empty space arises within the Great Awakening.
The commentary states: "How does inert emptiness arise from the True? The following line provides a metaphor:
'Like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.'"
The commentary states: The ocean of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is like water, while insentient emptiness (wankong) is like a bubble.

This is because one forcibly generates conscious illumination upon the true substance, thereby giving rise to this "emptiness that serves as the basis for the homogeneous" (sabhāga-āśraya). It is like a single bubble emerging upon the sea.

Yet, insentient emptiness does not depart from True Suchness, just as a bubble does not depart from water. The two preceding lines express the meaning of origination; [the following line] proceeds from the bubble...
"Extinction and emptiness are fundamentally non-existent" below refers to the meaning of remedial severance.
"The lands of subtle atoms with outflows all arise from emptiness.
The commentary states: "Outflows" (sāsrava) excludes that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences?
The commentary states: these are the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of formlessness.
Returning to the source, their nature is non-dual.
Next is the section on returning to the realization of the multitude. The commentary states: "The twenty-five [groups] return to the nature of the source, which is without distinction;
all have awakened to perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). While the expedient means (*upāya*) have many gates..."

The commentary states: According to the various capacities of others, there are many different approaches. The preceding sentence concludes the response regarding the realization of perfect penetration;

these are the twenty-five individuals. Since there are many gates of skillful means, this initiates the section on the single gate of Avalokiteśvara, which accords with the capacities of those in this region.
The nature of the sages is such that there is nothing they do not penetrate.
Later, it is revealed that this nature penetrates all provisional means. The commentary states: "The twenty-five [patriarchs] have all attained the dharma-gate of perfect, universal penetration."
"Both following and reversing are skillful means.
The commentary states: "If it is 'following,' this refers to the gate of Avalokiteśvara accords with the mind; if it is 'reversing,' this refers to the other twenty-four sages."
"The beginner enters samādhi. The commentary states:

"Enters" (ru) is that which enters; "samādhi" is that which is entered. In the language of Tang, it is called "correct reception" (zhèngshòu), which is another name for meditative concentration (dìng).
"Slowness and speed do not belong to the same category.
The commentary states: "As for slowness, it is like that of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, who said, 'Throughout beginningless kalpas, I have been a skilled physician for the world.
It is also like Dharaṇīdhara, who maintained the earth-practice during the era of the Buddha Viśvabhū, yet did not realize perfect penetration until the time of the Buddha Śikhin."
Furthermore, it was like the youth Candraprabha, who first encountered the Buddha Varuṇadeva and was taught the contemplation of water; yet he had not yet attained the dissolution of the self.
Only after passing through the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas, up until the Buddha Sāgaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña, did he finally awaken to true emptiness.

As for swiftness, it is like Avalokiteśvara, who suddenly transcended both the mundane and supramundane worlds, attaining perfect clarity throughout the ten directions and obtaining two kinds of excellence.

The section on "Form-perception forming dust" consists of nine texts, the latter of which specifically excludes the non-spherical. The first section, "Wiping away dust to prove the spherical," consists of six texts; the first addresses the fault of adding dust while still loathing form.
The commentary states: "The internal mental activity binds together from the great dust, analyzing it into 'neighboring atoms' (*paramāṇu*). 'Neighbor' (*lin*) means 'proximate'."
"Empty" refers to empty space. However, when the twenty-five individuals recount their realization of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), Dignāga (*Cen-na*) appears first;

as he was the senior elder (*sthavira*) among the assembly, it is appropriate that his account be given first. When distinguishing the temporal sequence, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is placed first, for among the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), form is the primary one.
"Though refined, it cannot penetrate thoroughly.
The Commentary states: "If this were a refined and true discernment, then this contemplation would not be clear and penetrating;
for [in this view], form itself is emptiness, without needing to analyze form to return to emptiness."
"How is it that one does not attain clear penetration?
The commentary states: This question arises as to how one may thereby obtain perfect penetration.

The commentary states: This is the answer. Regarding this point of non-penetration, it is because one seeks to attain perfect penetration by analyzing form for the sake of others that one fails to attain perfect penetration.
One must instead cultivate contemplation upon the white bones and subtle particles.
"Phonemes (śabda) and mixed speech (vākya).
Regarding the fault that "the two—phoneme and speech—are not universal," the commentary states: "Phonemes refer to the five tones: gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu. Speech refers to the four tones.
A single utterance is called 'speech' (yan), while a string of characters is called 'language' (yu). This is the Venerable Kauṇḍinya."
"However, these names, phrases, and flavors...
The commentary states: "These names and phrases refer to the meanings and flavors of the phonetic body (*vyañjana-kāya*). The tongue takes the phonetic body as its flavor."
"First, one does not contain all.

The commentary states: This Venerable One realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths; he distinguished between suffering and its origin as the causes and effects of the mundane world, and cessation and the path as the causes and effects of the supramundane.
"How does one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "If the faculty of perfect penetration were [identical to] all [objects], this would not constitute perfect penetration.
Fragrance is known through contact."

Third, the fragrance of incense has the fault of being devoid of cognition. The commentary states: Regarding Fragrance-Veneration (Gandha-vyūha), because he entered meditative observation when his neighbor’s room was burning aloeswood incense, [he found that] when separated from it, there was originally nothing there;
since its perceived object was not constant, how could he have attained perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "If it were universal penetration (yuantong), there would be no lack of awakening and illumination; it has never been interrupted or extinguished.
It is not the case that one is aware when in union [with the object] and unaware when separated from it."
The nature of flavor is not original;

the nature of the four flavors is not permanent. The commentary states: Thus, the two Bodhisattvas, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, through their tongue-faculties, tasted the grasses, trees, minerals, and metals of this Sahā world and thereby entered the Perfect Penetration.
"It exists only when there is flavor.
The commentary states: "It is only by depending on flavor that its nature exists; without flavor, there is no discrimination.
Thus, its cognition is not constant or uniform."
The commentary states: "When there is flavor, there is perception; when there is no flavor, there is no discrimination. Therefore, it is not constantly one.
How, then, can it attain perfect penetration?
The commentary further states: "The nature of the dharma-gate of perfect penetration is eternally one."
Contact is clarified by that which is contacted.
There is the fault of the five tactile objects being indeterminate. The commentary states: "The subject that contacts is the body; the object contacted is water.
Without the object contacted, the subject that contacts cannot be clarified. A subject exists only in relation to an object. This is Bhadrapāla.
"There is no contact that is not clearly manifest.

The commentary states: "Only through the conjunction of the three can contact be established—namely, the conjunction of the faculty (*indriya*), the conjunction of the object (*viṣaya*), and the conjunction of consciousness (*vijñāna*). If any one of these is lacking, contact cannot be formed."
The nature of conjunction and separation is not fixed.
The commentary states: "Conjunction is known at the time of contact; when there is no contact, there is again no discernment. Since this nature is not fixed, how can one attain perfect penetration?"
The commentary states: "If it were universal penetration (yuantong), its nature would be eternally one.
The dharmas are termed 'internal objects' (neichen);
the six dharmas divide into subject and object. The commentary further states: "Thus, [it applies to] Kāśyapa and the Bhikṣuṇī Śailā."
He then applied contemplation to the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*), saying: "I observe that the six objects of the world undergo transformation and decay; they are nothing but empty and quiescent.
These images of the mental object are the objects perceived by the sixth internal consciousness."

"Relying on the sensory objects (dusts), there must necessarily be [the object of] mental phenomena (dharmas). The Commentary states: "Relying on the five sensory objects, there must necessarily be the dharmas as objects. These dharmas as objects are the mental concomitants (caitta) of the sixth consciousness.
The subject and object do not pervade all [consciousnesses]."
The commentary states: Because the perceiving mind and the perceived object are each distinct, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary further states:
If the faculties are perfectly penetrating, then subject and object are of one suchness, and the faculty and the object are non-dual.

Although the seeing-nature is transparently clear, the two [aspects] leave no trace; this is the fifth section on the text concerning the verification of the returning of the faculties. First, regarding the deficiency of merit when viewing objects:
the Commentary states, "This refers to the five sages practicing contemplation upon the five faculties. Thus, Master Yìrúì practices contemplation upon the eye-faculty. The world...
The Venerable One showed me the Samādhi of the Illuminating Vajra that I Delight to Behold.
It was clear before but not clear behind.
The commentary states: "Clear" means "to see. This means that one sees only what is in front, but does not see what is behind.
"The four intermediate directions are diminished by half. The Commentary states: "The four intermediate directions" refers to the four corners: southeast, southwest, northeast, and northwest.

When two corners are not visible and only two corners remain, this is based on the allocation of merit. This treatise discusses the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*); the previous description, however, was...
The celestial eye.
How does one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: this refers to the lack of correspondence between cause and effect.
The inhalation and exhalation of the breath are unimpeded;
secondly, there is no fault of the two gases intermingling. The commentary states: "If it were the case of exhalation and inhalation, they would be unimpeded.
This refers to the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka."
"Manifestly there is no intersecting breath.

The commentary states: "If there were an intersection between inhalation and exhalation, then the interval between them would lack this non-intersecting breath, because the breath would be subject to interruption.
If it is perfectly pervasive (yuan-tong), then there is no interruption."
"Fragmented and disjointed, it does not involve entry. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "Exhalation is not inhalation; inhalation is not [exhalation]. 'Zhi' (支) carries the meaning of division."
The divisions of entry and exit are each separate from one another; because they cannot interpenetrate, the tongue is not an entrance into the boundless.
Only when the three [elements] are purely flavor does the transgression arise. The Commentary states: For this reason, the tongue-root is not an entrance into the boundless.
The location of the tongue can be discerned; it can only be discerned when there is flavor.
This Venerable Kauṇḍinya, because he gave rise to cognition through flavor, found that when flavor was absent, his cognition vanished. How, then, did he attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "If it were universal penetration (*pariṣvaṅga*), it would be constant and uninterrupted;

the body and its objects of touch would be identical, resulting in the error of the four elements exceeding their respective boundaries. The commentary further states: "This refers to the practice of pride (*māna*) directed toward the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*)."

While practicing contemplation, he entered the city to beg for food; a poisonous thorn wounded his foot as he was absorbed in contemplation. The body is that which performs the touching, and the poisonous thorn is that which is touched.
Since both of these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are said to be the same.
"Each is not the contemplation of perfect enlightenment.
The commentary states: "The subject that touches and the object that is touched are both indeterminate; each lacks the true enlightenment of contemplation and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*).
If it were a faculty of perfect penetration, there would be true enlightenment, and one would arise to observe and illuminate."
If their respective limits do not meet in harmony, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: This is because the body and the thorn each occupy their own distinct boundaries and measurements, such that they do not merge or coincide with one another.
"Knowing the roots of the senses, thoughts are disordered;
the fivefold mixed perceptions provide the basis for transgression. The commentary states: Thus, the Venerable Subhūti contemplates the faculty of mind (*manas*), saying:
"Throughout kalpas as vast as the sands of the Ganges, my mind has attained non-obstruction. I recall my successive births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The seventh basis is the faculty of cognition (*jñendriya*). When mixed with and conjoined with the sixth, it becomes distracted and discursive;
thus, despite its profound clarity, it ultimately lacks vision.
The commentary states: "If one attempts to discern through profound stillness, one will not be able to attain the true nature."
"Thoughts and perceptions cannot be escaped; how then can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "If it is perfect penetration, one must sever such chaotic thoughts and perceptions.
Consciousness and views are a mixture of the three harmonies."
Section Three: Testifying to the Flow of Stillness through the Three Breaths; Part One: The Essence Contains Three Muddled Faults. The Commentary states:
Thus Śāriputra, upon the mind of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of visual consciousness, testified, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mind and vision have been pure."

Up to various transformations, such as "seeing through a single glance" and so forth—these are distinguished by the term "cognition" (*vijñāna*). The eight consciousnesses are collectively termed "consciousness.
This visual consciousness must rely upon the eye-faculty and the object of form; only through the conjunction of these three factors can it perceive.
The original text states that the fundamental nature is called "non-characteristic.
The commentary says: Now, since the consciousness which depends [upon the sense organs] has no substance, what further characteristics could the sense organs and their objects possess?
Since its own essence was originally non-existent and indeterminate, how could it attain perfect penetration?

The commentary states: If it were the Perfect Penetration (*yuantong*), its essence would be eternally constant and unchanging, unlike the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness which lack a fundamental basis.
Its mental hearing penetrates the ten directions.

Next, it says: "The initial mind does not exceed [the present]. The commentary states: Samantabhadra performs contemplation upon the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), saying:
"World-Honored One, I use my mind to hear and discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings. As for "mind" (*citta*), it refers to the mind that cognizes through objective conditions;
the eight consciousnesses are collectively termed "mind. This mind is said to penetrate and perceive throughout the ten directions, as follows:

As stated previously: "If there is a single sentient being beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions who brings forth the realization of Samantabhadra’s conduct within their mind, at that time I shall mount my six-tusked elephant, manifesting hundreds of thousands of bodies, and arrive at that place."
"Born from the power of the great cause.
The commentary states: "The practices of Samantabhadra are the great cause. Because they possess the sense of being invincible, they are termed 'power.
In contrast to the Mahāyāna of other bodhisattvas, these are given the name 'the power of the great cause.'"
Those with a beginner's mind cannot enter it; how, then, can they attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "The threshold of this gate is so lofty that it transforms only those of superior faculties; those of inferior faculties cannot enter it.
If it were a method for perfect penetration, it would accommodate both the middle and lower faculties."
"Contemplation on the nose is fundamentally a provisional expedient;
later, becoming stuck in that provisional method increases the fault of attachment. The commentary states:

Venerable Yaṣṭika performed contemplation upon the nose-consciousness, saying, "The World-Honored One taught me and Kūṭadanta to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose. Upon reaching the twenty-first day, within his body and mind...
Regarding [the methods of] clarity and so forth: when the Buddha saw that others possessed much greed and desire, he caused them to collect their minds; this was merely a provisional expedient.
It only causes the mind to abide in collection, and once abiding is established, it becomes a mental factor (*caitta*). How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: If one takes "that which dwells" to be the mind and "that which is dwelt upon" to be the nose, this still does not accord with perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
If it were perfect penetration, there would be neither subject nor object.
"Expounding the Dharma by playing with sounds and texts.
(Section Four: Refuting the Deviant through Eloquence; Proof of the Text, Part One). "The taints [are] the true fault. The commentary states:
"Sound refers to vocal sound, and text refers to written characters. This is the Venerable Pūrṇa.

Regarding "those who first achieve awakening through opening [the mind]," the commentary states: This refers only to those who have been shown and awakened to the truth, but whose prior practice has not yet reached fulfillment.
Since names and phrases are not themselves untainted (*anāsrava*), how can one attain perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-saṃbodhi*) through them?

The commentary states: The bodies of names, phrases, and syllables are included within the "non-active" (asaṃskṛta) category; they cannot be untainted (anāsrava). Upholding or violating [the precepts] merely restrains the body.

The five [senses] are like shackles that bind the spirit. The scriptural proof for this is found in one passage: "The form lacks universal pervasiveness. The commentary further states: "[He] closely grasps the Honored One."

This refers to performing contemplation regarding the body-consciousness. The Sūtra says: "I am the leader among the assembly of Tathāgatas," and so forth, up to "the assembly recognizes me as unsurpassed.
To stop [the mind] is to maintain [the precept]; to act [upon it] is to transgress it; it merely involves restraining the body.
"Without a body, there is nothing to bind.
The commentary states: "If one has a body, there is that which can be grasped; that which has nothing to grasp is the absence of a body, such as those in the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu)."
Having no body, what could possibly bind it?
Fundamentally, it does not pervade all things.
The commentary states: "It pertains only to the two realms of desire and form; it does not pervade the formless realm."
"How does one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "If it is perfect penetration, there is nothing it does not pervade.
Spiritual powers are fundamentally due to past causes."
Six: Surging and Submerging in the Void; Textual Evidence, Part One. "Past thoughts and conditions have passed. The commentary states:

"The Master of the Bean-Gathering (the Buddha) performed contemplation upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). For the sake of the three Kāśyapas, he proclaimed the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions.
I suddenly gave rise to the resolve for enlightenment and attained great penetration; thus it is called a supernormal power (*abhijñā*). This must have been cultivated in previous lives."
How could this have anything to do with the discrimination of dharmas?
The commentary states: "Thus, the true discrimination of the dharma-nature is to discriminate all day long, yet never to discriminate at all."
"Mindfulness takes objects as its conditions and is not separate from them;
how, then, can one attain perfect penetration? The commentary states: When first practicing supernatural powers, one visualizes this body as being like flying flowers or willow catkins.
This mind that performs the visualization does not depart from the objective phenomena it contemplates.

If one contemplates by way of the nature of earth, there are seven points regarding the realization of characteristics, the doubt concerning emptiness, and the scriptural evidence for the five [stages]. First, regarding the obstruction that contradicts penetration:

the commentary states that "characteristics" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), while "congealed emptiness" refers to the element of space (*ākāśa*). The "realization" refers to the five sages, who are called the five [emptinesses].
When one practices contemplation upon the marks, one becomes a Bodhisattva who maintains [the precepts]. In the past, I encountered the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa;
at all major thoroughfares and crossroads, I leveled the ground or constructed bridges. Later, I met the Buddha Viśvabhū, whose instruction was:
"You must level the mind-ground. Only then did I realize perfect penetration.
Solidity and obstruction are not penetration; that which is conditioned is not the nature of the sage.
How, then, can one attain perfect penetration? The commentary states: The path of conditioned effort is not the nature of the sage.
It exists within the cause but is absent within the fruit; thus, cause and effect do not correspond.

"If one contemplates through the nature of water, the two types of mental constructions will give rise to faults. The commentary states: "The youth Candraprabha contemplates upon the element of water;
he perceives that the internal fluids of his own body and the external Floating Banner King Land (Uṣṇīṣarāja-vyūha) are equal and without distinction."
Conceptualization is not real; suchness is free from vitarka and vicāra. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

The commentary states: "When principle is suchness and wisdom is suchness—within this single essence of suchness—one is detached from the mind that performs the functions of awakening and observation.
Awakening (vitarka) and observation (vicāra) are mental factors belonging to the six consciousnesses."
If one contemplates through the nature of fire, the threefold arising of aversion is not a true fault. The Commentary states: This is the Vajra of Fire-Head.

It says that when a Buddha appeared in the world named King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*), he taught that those who indulge excessively in lust become a mass of fierce flames. Consequently, the divine light of this deity coagulates within and undergoes transformation.
The mind of excessive lust becomes like the fire of wisdom and so forth.
"Weariness with existence is not true detachment.
The commentary states: "If one is weary of the existence of desire, yet this is true detachment, then there is neither longing nor weariness."
This is not a skillful means for beginners. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "The gate of the Fire Element is high and remote;
if one contemplates through the nature of Wind..."
4. The error of defining movement and stillness by way of mutual form. The Commentary states: Thus, the Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha contemplated the element of wind (*vāyu-dhātu*) and said:

"I have surpassed the Tathāgata Anantaghoṣa, who instructed me to contemplate this world and the bodies of sentient beings as all being turned by the power of delusive conditions of wind. Thereupon, when observing the movement of the world, [he observed] even unto all movements."
"Non-duality, etc. [The text continues:
"Movement and stillness are not without opposition.
The commentary states: "This is because movement opposes stillness."
Regarding that which is not the unsurpassed awakening, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: Because there is duality, it is not the truth.
If one contemplates through the nature of emptiness, [one attains it].
Fifth is the fault of being clouded and dull like empty space. The commentary states: "Thus, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha said:
'At the place of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I attained the boundless body. The various kings of banners and lands enter into my body;
my body is identical to empty space, and there is no mutual obstruction.'"
"Obscured and dull, it was not originally awakening.
The commentary states: "Because this is a mark of emptiness, it is not the nature of true emptiness.
Being devoid of awakening, it differs from bodhi; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
The commentary states: *Bodhi* has the meaning of awakening. Now, the essence of emptiness is devoid of awakening and is thus different from *bodhi*.

If one contemplates by means of the nature of consciousness, one enters the "One Mind" and realizes the text of "Consciousness-Only" (Section 1). To abide in consciousness while maintaining a sense of emptiness is an error. The commentary states: Thus, Maitreya...
Bodhisattva, when I encountered the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, the World-Honored One at that time instructed me to practice the samādhi of mind-only consciousness and enter into samāpatti.
Reaching the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the world, I then attained the unsurpassed, wondrous,
and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind.
"Observe that consciousness is not permanent.
The commentary states: This is to give rise to the observing mind capable of discernment; one observes this entry into consciousness as being non-permanent.
Since maintaining the mind is itself illusory, how can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "If one maintains a mind that perceives through contemplation, this too is a delusion.

First, regarding the passage on seeking peace within the nine wondrous lands: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; because birth does not accord with [the truth], it is a fault. The commentary states: "Thus, [it is] the Great Power..."
When it comes to the Bodhisattva’s statement, "In my original stage of practice, by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, I entered the patience of non-arising;
now, in this world-realm, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land," such actions constitute conditioned activity and flux.
"The nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing.

The commentary states: "That which constitutes this mindfulness is also subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and is associated with the sixth consciousness; its arising and ceasing do not pause for even a moment."
Cause and effect now yield different results; how can one attain perfect penetration?
The commentary states: "The cause is characterized by arising and ceasing, while the fruit is pure.
I now address the World-Honored One: when the Buddha appeared in the Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this land was that purity resides in hearing.
Regarding the desire to attain samādhi, it is in fact entered through hearing.

Later, the text is divided into three parts to select and demonstrate the true perfection. First, the description of how Avalokiteśvara uniquely accords with [the truth], which consists of six sections. First, the teaching-body (dharmakāya) of this Sahā world.
They leave suffering behind and attain liberation.

Second, a broad eulogy of Avalokiteśvara. The commentary states: they leave behind the three sufferings, the five sufferings, and the two types of birth-and-death—namely, the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) and the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa*).
"How excellent is Avalokiteśvara!
The commentary states: "Excellent" (liáng) means "good. It is an expression of praise.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as minute as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings.
The commentary states: What has preceded [describes] bestowing the fourteen kinds of fearlessness upon sentient beings.
Regarding "Wondrous Sound" (Miaoyin) and "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanshiyin):

the commentary states that "wondrous sound" is so called because it is free from subject and object, and thus does not conform to the sensory dust of sound. "Observation" (guan) refers to the capacity for exhortation.
Wisdom (*jñāna*). "The World" is the object of contemplation; "Voice" refers to those beings to be delivered.
Regarding "Brahma-voice" and "Ocean-tide voice," the commentary states:
"Brahma" means tranquility; thus it is the sound of profound stillness, its nature free from clamor. As for the "Ocean-tide voice," it is...
The warning cry of the male [voice] signifies that the response through transformation does not miss its proper time.
"The world is saved and all are at peace.
The commentary states: "If one seeks a son, one obtains a son; if one seeks a daughter, one obtains a daughter."
"Transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding.
The commentary states: "Seeking great nirvāṇa, one obtains great nirvāṇa.
I now address the Tathāgata."
The third section describes the realization of perfect penetration as spoken by Avalokiteśvara. The commentary states:
"It may be said according to what Avalokiteśvara spoke."
It is like a person dwelling in stillness; when drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they hear them all at once from those ten locations.
The commentary states: "This is a metaphor established by Mañjuśrī.
This represents the perfect reality."
The commentary states: "This metaphor illustrates perfect penetration.
The eye does not observe what lies beyond its immediate obstruction;
the four [other senses] are compared as being secondary rather than primary. The commentary further states: "Thus, the eye cannot perceive things that exist outside of itself."
The mouth and nose are likewise so.
The commentary states: The mouth, nose, and tongue perceive through contact;
the body perceives only through contact.
The commentary states: "It is only through contact with sensory objects that one comes to know [this state];
mental thoughts are chaotic and without order.
The commentary states: "The sixth consciousness is characterized by a profusion of discursive thoughts, utterly lacking any coherent sequence."
"Listening to sounds across a wall.
The commentary states: "Wall" refers to a fence or barrier. "Sounds" (*yin*) refers to various types of sounds; "echoes" (*xiang*) refer to the resonance of voices in mountains and valleys.
These can be heard both from afar and nearby.

The commentary states: This is a comparative evaluation based on the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), specifically taking the ear organ (*śrotrendriya*) as the point of reference to manifest its perfect penetration (*pariṇata-samudāgama*).
It is not uniform across the other five organs.
The commentary further states: The remaining five are not equal to the ear organ.
"This, then, penetrates the ultimate reality.
The commentary states: "The meaning of 'penetrating transformation' refers to the nature of sound as movement and stillness."
"Five: Manifesting Sound to Reveal the Holy. The commentary states: "If it were of the nature of sound, then there would be movement and stillness.
For example, a tree moves because of the wind and is still when there is no wind. Alternatively, the presence of sound is called movement, and the absence of sound is called stillness."
"Regarding 'existence or non-existence within hearing,' the commentary states:
This 'hearing' refers to the true nature of hearing. Within this, the auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) may either exist or not exist.
It is because all sentient beings cling to sound that they claim there is hearing when sound is present, and claim there is no hearing when sound is absent."
"When there is no sound, there is no hearing.
The commentary states: "This refers merely to the object of sound (śabdaviṣaya) being sometimes present and sometimes absent;
it does not mean that the nature of hearing itself is non-existent."
The commentary states: "The nature of hearing does not cease when the object of sound is absent;

since the sound is absent, there is no cessation. The commentary further states: "The absence of sound refers to the absence of the objective dust of sound; this would indeed mean the cessation of hearing. However, the nature of hearing itself is without cessation."
"Even when sound exists, it is not born.
The commentary states: "When sound exists" refers to the time of the auditory object; even then, it is not born. This means that the nature of hearing has never been born.
"Arising and ceasing are both perfectly transcended.
The commentary states: "Arising and ceasing" refers to the auditory object; "both perfectly transcended" means the absence of arising and ceasing.
This, then, is the eternal reality.

The commentary states: This refers to the manifestation of the nature’s perfect penetration. The preceding two cases concern the state of being awake; "even if" and what follows concern the state of sleep and mental dullness—the latter being deeper.
Even if one is in the midst of dreams, it does not become non-existent due to the absence of thought.
The sixth section, "Expounding the Teaching," should clarify this. The Commentary states: Even when one is in a state of sleep, this nature remains constant;
since it does not even give rise to the thought of non-existence, how could it give rise to the conceptual understanding of existence?
"Awakening and contemplation transcend discursive thought.

The commentary states: "This refers to the commencement of the observation and penetration of pure wisdom of initial awakening, which transcends and casts aside the prior deluded consciousness's conceptualizations regarding the existence or non-existence of thought."
Body and mind cannot reach it.
The Commentary states: The deluded body and deluded mind cannot reach the Truth.

Now, in this Sahā world, the treatises on sound and discourse can proclaim and clarify [the Way]. Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow sounds, they wander through saṃsāra.
The commentary states: "Original hearing" refers to the nature of true hearing. "To follow" means to accord with;
because it accords with the sensory object of sound, even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts.

Next is the fourth section, "The Text on Admonishing and Rebuking the Multitude. First is the lament for others and the admonition and rebuke. The commentary states: "Though one possesses much learning, it cannot cleanse karmic obstructions;
though one possesses dry wisdom, one cannot yet escape the wheel of suffering."
"Is it not that he followed what he was submerged in?
The commentary states: "Is it not that Ānanda, following the preceding sensory object of sound, suffered his own submersion?
By turning back the flow [of consciousness], he attained the state of non-delusion."
The commentary states: "Simply by turning the hearing back to hear its own nature, one naturally attains freedom from delusion.
Ānanda, listen attentively! Upholding the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra King."
The second part, the specific reprimand of Ānanda, consists of two sections. First is the account of how he received [the Buddha’s] majestic power to expound the wondrous.
The commentary states: "Vajra" refers to wisdom; it is capable of destroying all illusory phenomena. This insight-observation is perfectly penetrating.
"Like an illusion, inconceivable.
The commentary states: "It appears to exist yet does not exist; it is like arising yet not arising.
This is the true samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas."
The commentary states: "Mother" signifies the meaning of giving birth. It is a metaphor for the Dharma-body’s ability to give birth to the two bodies of reward and transformation.
In terms of this gate of perfect penetration, it is the true principle of the Dharma-body.
Though you have heard from as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust,
you subsequently rebuke external practices and fail to trace the source of delusion.
Regarding all the gates of secrecy, if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, your accumulation of learning will become a fault and an error.
The commentary states: "To accumulate much learning results in faults and calamities; it is a deception.
Regarding "using what is heard to uphold the Buddhas," the commentary states: "Using the nature of extensive learning to sustain the untainted teachings of the Buddhas of the past and the future."
"Why not listen to that which hears itself?
The commentary states: "Why not turn back to the mind that is capable of hearing and unite it with the nature of true hearing?
Hearing does not arise spontaneously."
The commentary states: This mind that is capable of hearing does not arise spontaneously; it must rely upon the sense-object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) to arise.
It is because of sound that names exist.
The commentary further states: "Because of the objective realm of sound" refers to such sounds as those of oxen, sheep, men, and women.
"Upon turning back hearing, sound is liberated.
[The commentary on] "Observing with three fingers to transcend the three words" states: First, "turning back hearing to universally liberate. The sub-commentary says:
"Simply by turning back deluded consciousness to return to true hearing, the sense-object of sound is naturally liberated."
"Who can be named 'one who is able to escape desire'?
The commentary states: "If there is not even an object of perception—the sound-dust—how can there be the name 'one who is able to escape'?
Once a single faculty returns to its source, the six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts."
The commentary states: "Seeing and hearing are consciousness; they are merely like illusions and like visual distortions, both lacking any reality.
The three realms are like flowers in the sky.
The commentary further states: "The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are like flowers in the midst of space."
"By hearing, the obscuring faculty is removed.
The commentary states: "The 'obscuring faculty' refers to the seeing-portion; by merely returning to the hearing of one's own nature, the deluded mind of the seeing-portion ceases to exist.
When the sensory objects are eliminated, awareness becomes perfect, pure, and clear."
The commentary states: "The dissipation of dust" refers to the aspect of formlessness; true awakening is spontaneous, perfect, luminous, and pure.
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through to all things;
this subsequently clarifies the metaphor for transcending the dust. The commentary states: "This refers to wisdom."
"Quiescent illumination contains the void.

The commentary states: This is the wisdom of the essence itself; it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, containing the substance of true emptiness. This is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "One should know that space is manifested by awakening."
Returning to observe the world, it is like the events of a dream.
The Commentary states: "It is like awakening from sleep;
Mātaṅgī is within the dream."
The commentary states: First, the Brahma-mantra says that things are like dreams and illusions and lack reality;
who can retain your form? The commentary states:
Who can retain your form, Ānanda? It is simply because you do not understand that the objects before you are like dreams. Thus...
Bound, like a skillful worldly illusionist who conjures various men and women through illusion, they are later dissolved back into their original state.
The text has two parts; first, the analogy. The commentary states: "This is the reality. If these were sentient beings..."
This is provisional.
Although one sees the movement of the various sense faculties, the commentary states:
"It is like all sentient beings who engage in activity at the gateway of the six sense organs."
"One must draw [the mind] back with a single mechanism.
The commentary states: "This is entirely due to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
"When the mechanism ceases, one returns to stillness."
The commentary states: Merely by ceasing fundamental ignorance and turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature, one returns to the tranquil principle-body;
thus, all illusions become devoid of inherent nature.
The commentary states: The six faculties of cognition lack intrinsic nature;
the six sense organs are likewise. [This] is combined with what follows.
"Originally based on a single, pure brilliance.
The commentary states: "Thus, the characteristic of the luminous nature is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which divides into the sixfold combination."
The commentary states: The six sense-faculties have ignorance as the transforming agent, while the six faculties and the six objects are that which is transformed.
When a single locus achieves "restoring to renewal" (*xiūfù*), the functions of all six faculties fail to be established.
The commentary states: "One place" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). Were it not for fundamental ignorance, the six functions would not arise at all.
Alternatively, "one place" may refer to the ear faculty as the gateway for entering perfect penetration; therein, the other six faculties lack inherent self-nature.
"Dust and defilements dissolve as soon as they are thought of.
The commentary states: "To think of them as they arise is to have few thoughts; to have few thoughts is to be without thought.
Thus one achieves perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity."
The commentary states: "This is the essence of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
'The remaining dust still pertains to those in training'—the commentary states:
this refers to the aforementioned twenty-four individuals."
"The ultimate limit of clarity is the Tathāgata.
The commentary states: "The ultimate limit of clarity refers to wisdom. To say that true wisdom has reached its ultimate limit is precisely to be the Tathāgata.
This applies to the great assembly as well as Ānanda."
4. Encouraging the Return to Realization.
"Return your inverted hearing-faculty.

The Commentary states: To turn one's back on the essence and take conditions for sound is inversion; now, simply to reverse the hearing and return to self-nature is "returning" (*xuán*). You are deluded...
Hearing outwardly is the fundamental ignorance;
hearing inwardly toward one's own nature brings that nature to the realization of the Unsurpassed Way.
The Commentary states: "To turn back and repeatedly listen with the mind that hears is to hear the other, true hearing."
"Perfect penetration is truly thus.
The commentary states: This concludes the response to Ānanda’s request regarding the attainment of Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and *dhyāna* as the primary expedient means.
Furthermore, it concludes with the response: "I am now like a traveler staying overnight; I must rely on the essential cause."
Entering through the gate:
these are the gates to nirvāṇa along a single path for countless buddhas.

Hereafter follows the text clarifying the sudden teaching and its circulation, in three parts. First, penetrating the three periods of time to clarify and point directly to the sublime reality. The commentary states:
Mañjuśrī, furthermore, fearing that Ānanda might take this as his own personal testimony, [the Buddha] then said: "This is the single path to nirvāṇa for all Buddhas;
there is no second path. There is only this one gate. "Path" (mārga) refers to the place traversed by the noble ones of the three vehicles.
"Nirvāṇa" refers to the stage of Buddhahood, consisting of the two fruits of transformation—both conditioned and unconditioned. "Gate" (dvāra) refers to the point of entry and exit.
This is the meaning. The sages of the Three Vehicles all enter through this gate.
The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; the Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter its perfect clarity.
Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon such a Dharma; I too have realized it through this, not merely through Avalokiteśvara.
It is truly as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has asked me regarding these various skillful means.
The commentary states: This follows from what the Buddha previously taught, wherein he was made to discern who possesses the capacity [for the path].

It also intends for sentient beings in the future Dharma to cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle. Xuan asked: "In teaching me, which expedient door do you discern as being easy to bring to accomplishment?"
This is for the sake of rescuing all beings in the final age.
The commentary states: This is also an answer intended to cause all sentient beings of the final era to seek the Bodhisattva Vehicle and to seek those who transcend the world.
The commentary states: "Those who seek the Bodhisattva vehicle, or those who seek the two vehicles of the Śrāvaka, achieve the mind of nirvāṇa.
The commentary further states: "This refers to unsurpassed bodhi."
"Avalokiteśvara is supreme. The commentary states:
"It would have been more appropriate to say that there is nothing superior to this one gate;
all other various skillful means are entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power."
Second, the "Pitying and Praising" section shares the same source as the previous one to distinguish it from what is not the orthodox teaching. The commentary states:
"The gateways of contemplation of the twenty-four sages are all received through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas of the past."
"Immediately through affairs one abandons worldly toil.

The commentary states: "Because of residual habits, one encounters the thorns of poison; thus, when Bhadrapāla enters the secular world, he employs the phenomena of worldly affairs to cast off worldly toil and afflictions."
"It is not that one must practice for a long time; those at shallow or deep levels alike may preach the Dharma.
The commentary states: This means it is not the case that one must have practiced the gates of contemplation for a long duration; even a beginner may seek to approach the steps [of the teaching].

To be wounded by a poisonous thorn is to seek entry into the Way; it is not as good as Avalokiteśvara’s entry into samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, whereby one attains two kinds of excellence, both mundane and supramundane.
Homage to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is untainted and inconceivable.
The commentary states: "Homage" carries the meanings of taking refuge and clearly perceiving. As for the "Tathāgatagarbha," it is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
I pray that you will bestow your grace upon the future.

Later, having clearly indicated the perfect diameter, I request that it be circulated so that there may be no confusion regarding this gateway; its skillful means are easily accomplished, making it fit to be taught to Ānanda.

The commentary states: This concludes the answer to the previous question regarding who possesses this faculty, as well as the response to the point that even those submerged in the final kalpa can, by cultivating through this faculty alone, attain a perfect penetration that transcends others; such is the nature of the true mind.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly were clear in both body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.

This concludes the third section, "The Benefits Gained by Hearing the Sutra. Part One: The Metaphor Illustrating Shared Enlightenment. This section has two parts; first, the narrative. The Commentary states:
By means of the body of the five aggregates, one accomplishes the Dharma-nature body; by means of the deluded mind of the eight consciousnesses, one realizes the true mind of *prajñā*.
Thus, it is perfectly clear.
To contemplate the Buddha, Bodhi, and Great Nirvana is like a person who has traveled far away on business and has not yet returned home.
He clearly understands the path leading back to his home.
This is the latter analogy. The commentary states: "I now dwell on the stage of one still in training (śaikṣa) and have not yet realized the Dharma-body;

this is much like being on a long journey and not yet having returned home. Today, by means of explaining Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong), I clearly know how to practice and attain the fruit of realization."
On this path of the essence,
there was a vast assembly gathered together: the eight classes of devas and nāgas, those of the two vehicles still in training,
and all the bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands.
Next, the attainment of purity that transcends the mundane consists of two parts. First, attaining the same great stage as Mahāsthāmaprāpta. The commentary states:
"Heaven is one; dragons are two; this includes the six classes of yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth."
All attained their original mind.
The commentary states: they attained the Great Samādhi of the Dharma-realm;
far removed from dust and free from defilement, they obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The commentary states: This means to be separated from the defilements of affliction. To give rise to wisdom that illuminates principle is no different from the eye seeing an object.
Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrī became an arhat.
Later, she alone realized the Lesser Vehicle stage. The commentary states: "In the past, she was named the Maiden of Innate Nature (*prakṛti*).
Immeasurable sentient beings all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is peerless."

Subsequently, he gives rise to the supreme mind. The commentary states: Regarding the initial phrase "without equal," it means that when comparing all Buddhas with all sentient beings, there is no one who is their equal.
Regarding the subsequent phrase "equal," it means that these Buddhas and those Buddhas are mutually equal.
*A* means "non-"; *nuttara* means "supreme"; *saṃ* means "correctly"; *yak* means "equal"; *saṃ* means "correctly"; *bodhi* means "awakening."
This is the Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Complete Enlightenment.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and prostrated with his head at their feet.

Next follows the section on the cultivation and realization empowered by the two powers, which is divided into three parts. First, the preliminary inquiry for distant preparation, which is further divided into three sections; first, compassion.
Xinshu’s *Wu* (Awakening) states in its commentary: "It is said that the empowerment of these two powers primarily benefits those of inferior capacity.
The preceding section on the 'Complete Penetration of Wisdom-Contemplation and Cultivation and Realization' addressed only those of superior faculties.

Ānanda, fearing that all sentient beings of the future age would have inferior conditions and feeble minds, unable to achieve realization, he therefore requested: 'I wish to gather and control their minds.'"
Entering samādhi, how does one establish the *maṇḍala* and remain far removed from all demonic activities?

Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to explain the ritual procedures for the *maṇḍala* over a period of twenty-one days: during the first seven days, one practices the path and performs prostrations;
during the second seven days, one makes the vow for *bodhicitta*; and during the third seven days, one recites only the *Uṣṇīṣa-śītavana-mantra*.

This unsurpassed divine mantra: by the twenty-first day, the Buddhas of the ten directions emerge from the place where the mirrors reflect one another’s light and stroke the practitioner’s head in consolation.
This is because the practitioner and Avalokiteśvara together realize the principle of the Dharma-realm.
"The mind and its traces are perfectly luminous.
The commentary states: "Mind" refers to the true mind; "traces" refers to the traces trodden by all throughout the ten directions.
"A mixture of sorrow and joy" arises because he desires to benefit all sentient beings of the future.
The commentary states: "Sorrow" refers to sorrowing over the false teachers of the final age; "joy" refers to rejoicing at encountering the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Intersecting and gathering" means they intersect and assemble together.
[The Bodhisattva] bowed his head and addressed the Buddha: "O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood. Within this, I shall practice."
One attains freedom from doubt and confusion.

The commentary states: The preceding sections discussed the Bodhi of the Buddha and Great Nirvana, up to the point of clearly understanding the path by which one’s home is reached; therefore, this section follows upon the previous text.
I have often heard the Tathāgata speak these words: "He who has not yet crossed over himself first seeks to cross others over.
Next, he sets forth the Great Mind. The commentary states that setting forth the Great Mind refers to the Four Great Vows.
When a bodhisattva resolves their mind, they awaken to their own perfection.
The commentary states: this is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
That which can awaken others—
The commentary states: "This is the wisdom subsequently attained (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
When the Tathāgata appears in the world," the commentary states: "Question: Who is it that, having personally realized their own perfection, is able to awaken others? Answer: [As follows]."
"Although I have not yet attained liberation, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final age.
The commentary states: Ānanda is a person of great transformative power; it is not that he has not attained liberation, but he merely speaks thus out of humility.
“World-Honored One, these sentient beings have become increasingly distant from the Buddha. Teachers of false dharma are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

Later, those who establish true fields and provide remote guidance during the final age—[the commentary] states that the Age of True Dharma lasts for one thousand years, the Age of Semblance Dharma for one thousand years, and the Final Age for ten thousand years; this is precisely our present time. These teachers of false dharma harbor their own false thoughts.”
He expounds the teachings of the heterodox paths,
desiring to gather their minds and lead them into samādhi. How may he cause them to be established in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far from all demonic activities,
and attain non-retrogression regarding the bodhicitta?
The commentary states: "Dōjō" (道場) refers to the field of attaining the Way of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). "Teki-kutsu" (退屈) means to regress and be suppressed or cowed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, praised Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent! It is just as you have asked."
Establishing the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age.
Next, the praise for the mandate to uphold and explain the text, in three parts. First, the praise for generating the mind of compassion. The commentary states: "To extol and praise."
"Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
Having thus granted permission to proclaim the formal instruction, Ānanda and the great assembly replied, "So be it; we respectfully accept your teaching."
Later, the assembly raised the question regarding the true meaning. The commentary states that "weiyuanye" (唯然吔諾) is a term of assent.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three principles of certainty for the practice of cultivation."
Part Four: Texts on the Far-reaching Propagation and Assistance to the Dharma. First, two texts exhorting the purification of *śīla* (precepts).

First, a general exposition of the three trainings. The Commentary states: *Vinaya* is the Chinese term for "Discipline" (*tiáofú*); it refers to the *Vinaya Piṭaka*, which primarily elucidates the training in ethical conduct (*śīla*). The *Śāstra Piṭaka*... [text continues]

The Abhidharma-piṭaka primarily elucidates the training in wisdom; the Sūtra-piṭaka primarily elucidates the training in concentration. "Discipline" (vinaya) refers to the refinement of the three karmas;

"subduing" (viniyama) refers to the suppression of faults and transgressions. Refinement pertains to both cessation and action, whereas subduing clarifies only the cessation of evil. Thus, the rules of conduct remain unshakable.
Therefore, it is called "definitive.

That is to say: collecting the mind constitutes the precepts; from the precepts, concentration arises; and from concentration, wisdom is developed. These are known as the three trainings in the outflow-free (anāsrava).
The commentary states: "What is called the precepts is the root of Bodhi; one should fully maintain the pure precepts. It further says: "The precepts are like a boundless ocean;
as with jewels, one seeks them without satiety. Thus, the Mahāyāna maintains the precepts of the mind, while the Hīnayāna maintains the precepts of the body.
From the precepts arises concentration (*samādhi*); from concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is developed. These three trainings are termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Outflow-free...
Setting aside that which is with outflows, Ānanda, what is the gathering of the mind? I call this "precept" (*śīla*).
Hereafter, the section on the gate of precepts is elaborated in two parts: first, a general inquiry followed by the bestowal of the precepts.

Regarding the various worlds, there are four sections for the initial exposition of the first chapter. First, the text on the precept against sexual misconduct has two parts. First, the section clarifying ascent and descent has seven parts.
First, "Transcending Birth by Upholding the Precepts. The Commentary states: This is that upon which one relies.
"The sentient beings of the six realms.
The commentary states: "These are the sentient beings who are the supported;
their minds are free from lust."
The commentary states: For a Mahayana Bodhisattva, who maintains the precepts of the mind, every arising thought or movement of intention constitutes a transgression.
For a Hinayana practitioner, who maintains the precepts of the body, it is sufficient not to engage with sensory objects; this is what constitutes maintaining the precepts.
Then one will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
The Commentary states: The preceding text says that fathers and sons, generation after generation, produce one another in succession; all of this has lustful craving as its root.
If, as now, there were no sexual desire, one would naturally not follow along with the continuity of birth and death. However, regarding the Mahāyāna...
First, taking the precept against killing as primary: for those of the Mahāyāna, compassion is their power; if they were to kill, they would lose the seed of great compassion.

For those of the Mahāyāna, the precept against defilement is primary, as it serves to produce successive generations—father and son, father and daughter—all of which have craving and desire as their root.
For those of the Hīnayāna, who fear birth and death, [the precept against killing] is therefore placed first.
"Severing defilement": this teaching belongs to the Mahāyāna. Why is defilement mentioned first? The answer is: because Ānanda had previously fallen into a chamber of lust;
this was done to accord with the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and thus defilement was raised first. Nevertheless, even so...
This is also the Mahāyāna. Because you maintain the precept of the mind, you cultivate samādhi;
yet, since your practice originally aims to transcend worldly toil (*saṃsāra*), if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot transcend the world.
Second, failing in observance leads to stagnation and bondage.
Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever lust, they will inevitably fall into the path of demons (*māra*).
Third, they will surely wander upon deviant paths. The commentary states: *Māra* is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "the slayer. This refers to that which is capable of killing.

They are the life-force of wisdom for sentient beings. Because the Demon King frequently indulges in desire, the subsequent text states: "He takes all manner of vulgar and lewd acts as the transmission of the Dharma;
such is the Demon King of the Superior Grade."
"Fourth, ascending according to the three grades. The commentary states: "Those to whom various māras resort are called 'māra'; those whose blessings are superior are the middle-grade māra subjects.
The commentary states: "That is, those whose blessings are middling."
"Low-grade māras. The commentary states: "This refers to those of inferior merit.
These various māras also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way."
Fifth, they describe the heterodox as orthodox.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such demonic followers will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust.
Acting as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), you cause sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and views, losing the path to Bodhi.
