Ānanda, this *Śvetā-bhūtārtha-pradīpa* (The White Essence of Reality) from the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa is the fourth section on the miraculous power of the mantra-deity.
Part One: Establishing the Realization through Compassion, consisting of three sections. Part One: Clarifying the Establishment of Realization, consisting of six sections.
Section One: A General Praise of its Capacity to Give Birth. The Commentary states: *Śvetā* means "white"; white is the source of all colors.
This indicates that this mantra is the most honored among *dhāraṇīs*. *Parivāra* means "canopy" (*chattra*).
A canopy has the sense of providing shade and protection; it signifies that this mantra provides shelter and protection for all sentient beings.
The secret gāthās, these subtle and wondrous verses.
The commentary states: *gāthā* is the Chinese term for "repeated verse.
They give birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
The commentary states: This mantra elucidates the principle of the *dharmakāya*. The *dharmakāya* is able to give rise to the two bodies of *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.
Furthermore, this mantra refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). As the Sūtra says: "Wisdom is the mother of all Buddhas, and it is also the mother of Bodhisattvas.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* likewise elucidates wisdom, stating that "all Buddhas emerge from this sūtra."
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of this mantra-heart, have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Regarding the two vehicles, they attain the fruit through the cause. The commentary states: "Perfect knowledge" (*samyak-jñāna*) is fundamental wisdom; "complete knowledge" (*sarva-jñāna*) is subsequently attained wisdom.
Possessing both these forms of knowledge—perfect and complete—is termed "unexcelled enlightenment."
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold this mantra-heart; they subdue all māras and restrain all heterodox paths.
"Three times they crush the māras and control the heterodox. The commentary states: "To 'hold' means to observe with firm concentration through meditative power. The Sanskrit term is *māra*."
In the language of China, "to kill" means to kill the life-force of wisdom of all practitioners.
As for "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika), they turn away from the teachings of the Three Vehicles and practice the five heats that scorch the body; their diligent austerities yield no benefit.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, riding upon this mantra-heart, sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust;
they respond in the four [directions] throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust. The commentary states: "Riding" means to transport. The mantra is the Dharma; the "heart" is a metaphor.
Regarding "sitting upon a precious lotus flower," the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "I, now as Vairocana, am currently seated upon the lotus pedestal. This refers to oneself.
The Sambhogakāya Buddha enjoys [the fruits of] retribution; the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha should appear in lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions contain this dhāraṇī-heart within them, turning the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.
He correctly turns the Great Dharma Wheel.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions hold this mantra-heart; they are able to touch his head with their hands and bestow predictions of enlightenment throughout the ten directions, even before his own fruition has been fully realized.
Furthermore, they receive the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha throughout the ten directions.

Sixth, regarding the prediction received by both oneself and others: the commentary states that "receiving the prediction by stroking the head" refers to bestowing the prediction upon disciples whom one has transformed.
Alternatively, it refers to when one, though not yet having realized [enlightenment] oneself, receives the prediction for oneself from another Buddha.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, relying upon this mantra-heart, are able to rescue and deliver all beings from suffering throughout the ten directions.
Next, the passage on the mobilization of compassion begins: first, compassion removes the hardships of suffering.
What is called "hell" (dīyù).
The commentary states: there are prisons beneath the earth, which are named "earth-hells" (dīyù).
[There are also] hungry ghosts and animals.
The commentary states: "Those with large bellies and small throats are born from the nourishment provided by human households; they are called 'beasts' (chusheng).
Those who are blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired—the commentary states: these are those without roots."
The suffering of encountering those one hates and loathes.
The commentary states: Because they have killed my parents, or my brothers and friends, and now that we have met once more, the extent of this suffering can be known.
The suffering of separation from what one loves.
The commentary states: "Just when one is fit to rejoice together, there is yet further separation.
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
The commentary states: Whether seeking wealth or seeking sensual beauty, failure to obtain them is suffering.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are in a state of intense combustion; this is even more painful. The commentary states: Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—when these five aggregates are in a state of intense combustion, it is even more painful. This is called the eight sufferings.
All great and small calamities shall be simultaneously liberated from.
The commentary states: "Great calamities" refer even to death;

"small calamities" include falling upon public roads, the perils of bandits and armies, the perils of kings and prisons, the perils of wind, fire, and water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty—all shall dissolve and vanish the moment one thinks of them.
The commentary states: "To 'accord with thought' means that whenever one thinks, it should be so.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, following this mantra-mind, are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions during the four modes of deportment."
"Offering according to one's wishes.
Second, "serving all affairs according to the mind. The commentary states: "The four modes of deportment" refer to food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine.

"Offering" refers to these four requisites, while "nurturing" refers to attending and caring for [the Buddha]. Because he serves as the Buddha’s attendant, it is called "according to one's wishes" (yìrú).
Within the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he is promoted to the rank of a Great Dharma Prince.
He assists in the transformation of beings for three kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The commentary states: "This refers to the practitioner who upholds the mantra."

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this mantra-heart; they are able, throughout the ten directions, to gather in and sustain their close causes, and to hold and observe their retinues through the four means of integration.
The commentary states: "Gathering in and sustaining" has the meaning of delivering and liberating, as when the Buddha delivered Ānanda.
Just as Ānanda and Devadatta saw the Buddha simultaneously, [the teaching] causes those of the Hīnayāna to hear the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*) without giving rise to alarm or fear.
"Five [aspects] of the small containing the large": the commentary states that the "secret" refers to the Mahāyāna teachings; that is to say, for those of the Hīnayāna...
If one hears of the Mahāyāna and feels fear or trepidation, one should cause them to hold this mantra; then they will no longer feel fear or trepidation regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart and thereby attain unexcelled enlightenment.
Sixth, reciting [the scriptures] leads to the realization of Bodhi;
sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, one enters Great Nirvana.
Seventh, realizing tranquility and possessing capability. The commentary states: This refers to the *svasaṃbhogakāya* Buddha proceeding toward the Bodhi tree to become a Buddha.
When his time to depart had come and his work of transforming beings was nearly finished, he returned to the state of perfect stillness; all of this was due to the recitation of this mantra-heart.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart so that, after their parinirvāṇa, the affairs of the Buddha-dharma may be entrusted to it for its ultimate maintenance and upholding.
The precepts are strictly purified, attaining complete clarity. Regarding the "entrustment of the legacy" (*bā-fù chí-yí-huà*):
the commentary states that this refers to transmission and reception. Following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was entrusted to the Buddha’s disciples to transmit this mantra-heart (*dhāraṇī-citta*).
"Ultimate" (*jiū-jìng*) means reaching the final goal; "abiding" (*zhù*) refers to dwelling in practice, and "maintaining" (*chí*) refers to sustaining and upholding. It signifies strict purity.
Purity is this Dharma. As for precepts (*śīla*), they prevent what is wrong and cease evil; it is also said that "to adorn and purify" is called *śīla*.

If I were to recite this Buddha’s Crown-Radiance *Sītātapatrā* mantra from dawn until dusk, with sounds linked in succession and syllables and phrases never overlapping, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one would still not reach its end.
The concluding exhortation to uphold [the mantra] consists of three parts. First, the praise for its inexhaustible proclamation. The commentary states:
The Buddha further extols the efficacy of this mantra, intending to express that the principle of the Dharmakāya is inexhaustible even when discussed.
This mantra is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the true name of this mantra:
you who are still in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship, you must not fail to uphold this mantra.
And to sit at the site of enlightenment while allowing their body and mind to remain distant from all demonic activities—this is impossible.

Later, he exhorted them to maintain [the practice] so that they might realize it. The commentary states: "Those who have not exhausted saṃsāra" refers to those whose innate afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been eliminated.
This refers to transmigrating through the three realms. The Return Gate states: "You who are still in training have not yet exhausted saṃsāra;

if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship and maintain this dhāraṇī while seated in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), causing your body and mind to remain far removed from all demonic activities—this is indeed possible.
As for the term "arhat," according to the Mahāyāna, it designates a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage.
If one were to discuss the Hīnayāna, it would not be so designated.
Ānanda, if in any world, in whatever land, among all sentient beings born in that country, one were to write this dhāraṇī on birch bark,
palm leaves, paper, silk, or white cotton cloth, and store it within a fragrant pouch.
Section Four: Text on the Threefold Extinction of Faults and Removal of Poison. First, the six sections on the excellent removal of all poisons.

First, the removal of all poisons by wearing [amulets]. The commentary states: *Huāpí* (birch bark) refers to the bark of the birch tree. *Bèiyè* (palmyra leaf) refers to the *pattra* leaves of India.
"Writing horizontally upward" refers to paper, which was invented by Cai Lun. *Sù* refers to plain silk. *Dié* refers to white cotton cloth (*kārpāsa*).
If this person’s mind is dull and they are unable to recite it from memory, whether they carry it upon their person or write it within their home,
one should know that throughout their entire life, they cannot be harmed by any poisons whatsoever.
The commentary states: "One whose mind is clouded" refers to one who is dull-witted and lacks the capacity for memory. To "recite against the text" means to recite it in reverse.
"Throughout the span of one's life" refers to a period of perhaps eighty, ninety, or even a hundred years.
Ānanda, I shall now further explain this mantra for you, which protects and delivers the world, grants great fearlessness,
and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.
"Second, regarding the recitation that wards off all calamities. The commentary states:

"Supramundane wisdom, such as Bodhi and Nirvana—if after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings of the final age are able to recite this themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that for such sentient beings who maintain this through recitation, fire cannot burn them, water cannot drown them, and neither great nor small poisons can cause them harm."
The commentary states: "Fire" refers to the fire of form; "water" refers to the water of craving.

Whether great, such as poisonous insects, or small, such as the poisons of plants and trees—even extending to all evil spells of dragons, devas, ghosts, spirits, terrestrial deities, and malevolent demons—none can take hold [of the person].

"Samyadharma is not as it should be. The commentary states: "That which the demonic essence returns to is called a ghost (*gui*). That which the Yin and Yang cannot fathom is called a spirit (*shen*).
A celestial spirit is called a *ji*. A human spirit is called a ghost. As for 'refined spirits, deities, and demons' (*jingji momei*), these refer to refined souls, spirits, and deities."
"Malignant spirits" refers to *chimei* (goblins and specters). "Evil incantations" refers to the spells of the *tianmo* (heavenly darkness) and *heimo* (black darkness), etc.

"The mind attains *zhengshou*" (right reception) means that the four minds roam within right concentration (*samādhi*). The commentary states: the Sanskrit term is *samādhi*; the Chinese term is *zhengshou*. This is a synonym for concentration.
All curses, malevolent spells, poisons from insects, gold poisons, silver poisons, plants, trees, insects, snakes, and the poisonous vapors of all things—

"The five transformations become ambrosia. The commentary states: "Curses (*zhòuzǔ*) refer to the practice of *yànwù* (suppression/incantation). Gold and silver also both possess poison;
sometimes poison takes on the appearance of gold and silver, which is called 'the poison of gold and silver.'"
All malevolent stars, as well as ghosts and spirits with cruel hearts who poison people, cannot give rise to evil toward such a person.

The Vināyakas and all the malevolent kings of ghosts, together with their retinues, shall all receive this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.

He attended [the Buddha] day and night.

Furthermore,

the commentary states this means "from birth unto birth."
Yakṣa. The commentary states: in the language of China, this means "Valiant Builder. Rākṣasa.

Together with all the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Such evil places, O son of good family— if one reads or recites it, writes or copies it, wears it or conceals it,

The three blessings and virtues follow in sequence, forming three sections. The first concerns eternally transcending poverty and low status. The commentary states:

Even if these sentient beings do not personally perform meritorious deeds themselves, all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon them.
By this means, for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—indeed, for unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas.

Cultivation: there is never any dispersion.
Second, sharing merit to be born together. The commentary states: it is like the *akṣa* cluster, which grows from a single stem and does not separate.
This serves as a metaphor for the person who upholds the mantra. The first sutra states: "The seeds of karma arise spontaneously, like a cluster of akṣa fruits. The commentary (*śū*) says:

Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify the root of their discipline; it enables those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them;

Ānanda, when this son of good family holds this mantra, even if he has transgressed the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, by holding the mantra—
Thereafter, all offenses of violating the precepts, regardless of their gravity, are extinguished at once. (Section Four:
Text on the Exhaustion and Elimination of Faulty Karmas; Section Five: Initial Complete Extinguishing of All Offenses). Commentary: This occurs before one has received the full precepts.

This refers to the period before one has received the mantra. "Various offenses against the precepts" refers to many kinds of transgressions: minor ones are *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibitory offenses), while serious ones are the four *mūlāpatti* (root offenses).
Even if one has consumed alcohol, eaten the five pungent roots, or engaged in various forms of impurity, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras,
celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will not regard this as a transgression.
"Second, 'forgiving faults and following in the darkness. The commentary states: 'Various impurities' refers to various impure practices.
Even if one wears impure, tattered clothing, every movement and every stay are entirely identical to the pure."
"Third, purity and impurity are equal in efficacy. The commentary states: Previously it was said that one should wear new, clean robes;
however, as when reciting mantras now, even if one wears unclean robes, they are still equivalent to being pure.

Even if one does not construct an altar, does not enter a dharma-hall, and does not practice the Way, yet recites and upholds this mantra, it is identical in merit to entering the altar and practicing the Way; there is no difference between them.

The commentary states: As previously mentioned regarding the construction of octagonal stupas and so forth, if one has committed the grave offenses of the five heinous acts (*ānantarya*) or the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* transgressions of monks and nuns, upon reciting this mantra, such heavy karma will be entirely eliminated—just as a fierce wind scatters a heap of sand. Furthermore...
There is not even a hair’s breadth [of fault].

Fourth, it can eliminate grave offenses. The commentary states: the five heinous crimes include killing one's mother, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and so forth. Regarding the "eight abandonments" (*pārājika*):
the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that *pārājika* in Sanskrit means "abandonment" (*qi*) in Chinese. If one commits such an offense, they are expelled.
Outside the assembly, it is like the great ocean which does not harbor the dead or the putrid. There are four [offenses] for monks:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. For nuns, there are eight: first, not to allow physical contact with a man who has lustful intent;
second, a bhikṣuṇī who knows a man has a defiled mind must not walk, sit, or converse with him; third, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense, [not to conceal it].

He addressed the great assembly: "For one who has concealed a grave offense, the community of monks—having four things known—performs the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension) after three admonitions;
because he does not relinquish the transgression, he is suspended according to the rule.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, have committed all manner of light or heavy offenses..."
Obstructions inherited from previous lives that have not yet been repented— if one can read, recite, copy, or wear this mantra upon one's person,
or place it within one's dwelling, house, garden, or villa— then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in hot water; before long,
all shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"May the five distant karmas be long dissolved. The commentary states: "Repentance (*chàn-huì*) is an expression that combines both the Indic and the Chinese. *Chàn* (懺) is an Indic term;
it should be called *kṣamā*, which carries the meaning of 'cleansing' or 'purifying. *Huì* (悔) is a Chinese term, meaning 'to retreat,' 'to regret,' or 'to repent.'"
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet borne children and desires to conceive,
if she can mindfully recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or if she can wear this Śītātapatrā on her person,
she will give birth to a son or daughter endowed with merit and wisdom.

Section Three: The Mantra for the Universal Protection of the World. Part One: The Text on Attaining Rebirth through the *Sampuṭa* (Universal Protection). Subsection One: Rebirth as a Result in the Present Life.
Commentary states: "If a son is born, he shall possess wisdom; if a daughter is born, she shall possess merit."
Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who wish to achieve the swift fulfillment of karmic rewards shall swiftly attain fulfillment.
It is likewise so for their physical life, complexion, and strength.
The commentary states: "Some seek retribution in the present life; others seek the natural accomplishment of the pure land as their reward in a future existence.
Worldly rewards refer to kings, ministers, and officials, while supramundane rewards refer to the Buddha. 'Color' refers to physical appearance, and 'strength' refers to vital energy."

After the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows; they will certainly not be born in border regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.
Thereafter, they will be born in accordance with the wondrous lands. The commentary states: "Mixed forms" refers to eunuchs, those with dual sexual organs, or beings of different species.
Ānanda, if in any kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages there should be famine, pestilence, or the calamities of war, bandits, strife,
or any other such places of misfortune, one should transcribe this divine mantra and install it at the four gates of the city,
as well as at various caityas or atop gate-towers. Thereby, all sentient beings within that kingdom shall welcome this mantra with reverence and prostrate before it.
With reverence and single-minded devotion, one should make offerings so that the people may each wear it upon their bodies or place it within their respective dwellings;
thereby, all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished.
Next, the fourth section contains the text for the rite of offering to avert calamities. Regarding the first three types of calamities, they are fundamentally distinct.
The *Jian* (annotation) states: according to the *Guangya*, that which people inhabit is called a *ju* (settlement), while that which a multitude inhabits is called a *luo* (village).
An epidemic is a calamity of pestilence. As for *caitya*, it means a stupa. *Tuoshe* (pronounced *dú*)—the *Erya* calls it a *tai* (terrace); here, it refers to a stupa.
Ānanda, wherever there may be lands and sentient beings, as long as this dhāraṇī exists, the devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will fall in their proper seasons;
the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will live in peace and happiness.
"Second, the five grains are abundant. The Commentary says: "When wind and rain follow their proper seasons, there are 'the ten winds and five rains.

As for the five grains, they are millet, wheat, rice, panicled millet, and beans. 'Grain' (穀, *gǔ*) means 'continuity' (*xù*); it is said thus because the seeds succeed one another without interruption.
'Dùn' (敦) means 'many' or 'multitude' (*shù zhòng*)."
Furthermore, it can also suppress all malevolent stars and their transformations in various directions, so that calamities and obstacles do not arise, and no one suffers untimely death.
Shackles, fetters, stocks, and manacles shall not touch their bodies; they shall sleep peacefully day and night, never having evil dreams.

The three calamities do not arise as untimely misfortunes. The commentary states: "Malevolent stars" refers to comets, portents, and the like; "untimely" (*heng*) means falling prematurely upon the public way;

"premature death" (*yao*) means dying in one's youth. That which is on the hands is called *niu* (handcuffs); that on the feet is called *xie* (shackles); that on the neck is called *jia* (a wooden collar);
and that on the body is called *suo* (fetters). One will constantly have no evil dreams. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "One always has such auspicious dreams," and so forth.
Ānanda, in this Sahā world-system, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars,
with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders, and furthermore, eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns.
"The four malevolent stars depart from their spheres. The commentary states:

"The eight great malevolent stars are the sun, the moon, Mars (Hénghuò), Jupiter (Chén), Saturn (Suì), Venus (Tàibái), Rāhu (Zhèn), and Ketu (Luóméi). These are all termed *graha* (seizing luminaries); the sun and moon are counted as one."
They manifest in various forms when appearing in the world.
The commentary states: they may appear in the form of śramaṇas, or as boys, women, and so forth, capable of producing various calamities and anomalies for sentient beings.

The commentary states: All manner of calamities, auspicious omens, and strange anomalies within this consecrated ground are entirely extinguished; for twelve *yojanas* around, it becomes a consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*), wherein all evil calamities and omens [are likewise eliminated].
They can never enter.
The Commentary states: One yojana is sixteen *li*; thus, one hundred and ninety-two *li* constitute a single boundary division.
For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaimed this mantra to protect all beginners and practitioners in future ages.
He enters samādhi; his body and mind are serene, attaining great peace and stability.
Following this, there are two sections concluding with an exhortation to practice. First is "Securing the Practice of Samādhi. The commentary states:
because the body is not invaded by calamities or epidemics, and the mind is not disturbed by demons or malevolent spirits, it is therefore serene.
Furthermore, there are no devas, māras, or spirits whatsoever, nor any karmic calamities or transgressions from beginningless time. [The commentary states:
"Karmic enemies (*yuánjiā*), calamitous transgressions (*zāihèng*), and misfortunes from former days (*sùxī zhī yāng*)."
"Past karma and old debts come to cause affliction and harm.
The commentary states: "The karmic deeds of previous lives—enemies seeking to collect their debts—do not come again now."
You, as well as all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, shall rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma.
Having received the precepts from a master and encountered pure monks, you shall harbor no doubt or regret regarding this dhāraṇī-heart-mantra.
If this good man does not attain mental mastery over this body born of his parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsely.
Therefore, I later urge you to rely upon and uphold [this teaching].

When these words had been spoken, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Vajrapāṇis in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall restrain our minds and protect those who thus cultivate bodhi."
The Fourfold Assembly and the Spirits Secretly Guarding [the Buddha], Section Six. First, the Malla Warriors Rise in Succession. The Commentary states: Question:
For what reason does Vajrapāṇi first rise and address the Buddha? Answer: Because Vajrapāṇi protects the Dharma and is constantly by the Buddha’s side, he is the first to rise.
At that time, Brahmā-rāja, together with Śakra-devendra and the Four Great Heavenly Kings, also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with all our hearts and with utmost sincerity."
May all that they have done throughout their lives be fulfilled according to their wishes.
Next, the Heavenly King shall protect these vows. The commentary states:
"Shen" (審) means sincerity. Furthermore, there are immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, and kumbhāṇḍa kings.
The King of Piśācas, Vināyakas, the great kings of ghosts, and the various ghost generals likewise joined their palms and prostrated before the Buddha.
I, too, vow to protect and sustain these persons, causing their bodhicitta to be swiftly and fully perfected.
The protection of the Trichakra realm was completed.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sun and moon deva-kings, as well as the masters of wind, rain, clouds, and thunder, along with the lord of lightning and others.
The Annual Age-Inspecting Officer and the retinues of all the stars likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, shall protect these practitioners of the path, establishing them in the site of practice so that they may attain fearlessness."

The four luminaries and the lunar mansions lie hidden therein. The commentary states: "Year" refers to the *lán-suí* (orchid year); "Circuit Official" (*xúnguān*) refers to the stationing of officials throughout the year.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable mountain deities and ocean deities, as well as all spirits of the land, and the quintessential energies of all things moving through water, on land, and in the air.
Together with the Wind Deity King and the gods of the Formless Realm, they simultaneously prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi, forever free from the works of Māra."

"Five spirit-essences uphold [it]. The commentary states: "Including the Wind King (Vāyu-rāja). Since there was previously mention of the Wind Master (Vāyu-pati), this 'Wind Spirit' should likely be the Space Spirit (Ākāśa-deva).

The preceding text states: 'Since it is of the nature of wind, its substance is fundamentally non-existent. In the Heaven of No Form (Ārūpyadhātu), the body is formed from the four aggregates (skandhas);

thus it is called the 'formless aggregate' (ārūpya-skandha). It manifests only the body of the fruit of meditative concentration (samādhi-phala-rūpa), and lacks the body of karmic fruition (vipāka-rūpa)."
[It is] the body.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*-koṭis of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, within the great assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as I..."

O equals, the meritorious deeds you have cultivated have long since brought enlightenment to fruition; yet you do not enter nirvana, but constantly follow this mantra to rescue and protect those who practice samādhi and engage in correct cultivation during the final age.
The Great Sixfold Majestic Protection Text, Part Four. First, the Exposition of Vows. The commentary states:
"Not taking [final] nirvāṇa" means arising from the realm of nirvāṇa to rescue and protect sentient beings.
World-Honored One, whenever such a person who cultivates the mind to seek right concentration is at a place of practice, or while walking for meditation,
or even when their mind is distracted as they wander through villages, we and our followers shall always follow and attend upon this person.
Second, the concentration of scattering is constantly present;
even if Māra or Maheśvara were to seek an opportunity for it, they would ultimately never find one, let alone minor spirits and ghosts.
"Beyond ten *yojanas* from this place of virtuous people, the demonic spirits are driven far away.
The commentary states: "The Demon King resides at the summit of the Desire Realm, in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Even though he seeks the methods and skillful means of the practitioner, he can ultimately never find them."
"Except for those who have resolved their minds [on awakening] and delight in practicing dhyāna.
The commentary states: An outsider asks, "If there are those who delight in practicing dhyāna, are they permitted to approach you? The answer is:
"Only by excluding those who delight in practicing dhyāna can one draw near to this practitioner."
World-Honored One, if such evil Māras or their retinues should come to harass these virtuous people,
I shall shatter their heads with my precious vajra until they are like fine dust, and I shall always ensure that these people’s undertakings are fulfilled according to their wishes.
"Fourth, 'Eliminating Enmity and Granting Vows. The commentary states: Question: Bodhisattvas possess a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
how can it be said that they crush the heads [of enemies] with a precious vajra? Answer: To destroy Māra and manifest the True Dharma is itself great compassion."
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We were dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;
regarding our minds still subject to outflows, we had not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation.
Our bodies and minds are refreshed and delighted, and we have gained great benefit."

The subsequent section on the "Perfection of Myriad Practices and the Division of Cultivation and Realization" consists of three parts. First, the introduction, enumeration, and request, which itself has three sub-sections.
First, expressing humility regarding one's ignorance while acknowledging the reception of the Dharma. The commentary states: "The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma does not exceed two gates:

first, the Sudden Gate; second, the Gradual Gate. Within this Sudden [Gate], the Gradual is clarified; that is to say, the World-Honored One has, within a single thought-moment, arrayed the sixty sagely positions."
The sixty stages of the sages do not depart from a single thought-moment. Those who seek sudden enlightenment must not obscure the gradual gate;

those who tread the gradual path must clearly understand the principle of the sudden. This is the "Sudden and Gradual Harmonized into a Single Unity" within the three cycles [of the *Avatamsaka Sūtra*].

If these sixty stages of the noble ones are the sequential dharma-gate (*pratipatti-dvāra*), then sudden realization in a single thought-moment is the perfectly integrated dharma-gate (*pariniṣpanna-dvāra*).
The World-Honored One maintains that this perfect integration is not separate from the sequential; thus, they are subtly interpenetrated.

The sequential is likewise not separate from the perfect integration; therefore, they enter into one another in layers upon layers. What has preceded is the complete provision of the myriad practices. What has preceded...

There are three parts: first, the section on the cultivation and realization of the perfect penetration through the observation of wisdom; second, the section on the cultivation and realization through the empowerment of a single power;

and third, the section on the cultivation and realization through the perfect provision of myriad practices. Although these three sections differ, they all collectively manifest the cultivation and realization of the universally perfect essence of the fruit.

Above, there have been two parts: first, the explanation of the secret cause; and second, the clarification of cultivation and realization. Although these two segments differ, they are all collectively...
The exposition of the section on the Correct Teaching is hereby completed.
"World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization.
Next follows the listing of the stages for inquiry. The commentary states: "Cultivation" refers to that which is capable of cultivating; "realization" refers to the fruit of realization.
"Buddha-samādhi. The commentary states:
"This refers to the Great Samādhi of the Dharma-realm;
it has not yet reached Nirvāṇa."
The commentary states: This refers to the two fruits of the twofold transformation of the basis—conditioned and unconditioned—within the stage of Buddhahood.
Why, then, is it called the "ground of dry wisdom"?
The commentary states: This dry wisdom is the first of the three gradual stages; the preceding mention of "dry wisdom" referred to the arising of wisdom, which was parched and withered.
These are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are forty-four minds.

The commentary states: these are the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
"To what gradual sequence does one attain the eye of practice? The commentary states:
"Gradual" (*jian*) refers to proceeding by stages; "sequence" (*ci*) refers to the proper order; and "eye" (*mu*) refers to the name of the eye.
To which destination does one arrive to be called "entering the stages" (*di*)?
The commentary states: "To go" (yì) means "to arrive. It refers to arriving at the various stages of the path, which is called "entering the grounds" (rù dì zhōng).
These range from the first ground (Prathamā-bhūmi) up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
"What is meant by 'Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva'?
The commentary states: "Equal" means "equally matched," referring to the equalization of principle and phenomena.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. The great assembly, with one mind, awaited the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with fixed and wide-eyed devotion.
Regarding the subsequent ritual for the Buddha, one awaits the imperial decree. The commentary states: "Staring vacantly" means that with eyes fixed and unblinking, one gazes upon the Buddha;
this is because one requests this portion of the scripture concerning the perfect cultivation and realization of the myriad practices.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You have been able to universally cause the great assembly and all sentient beings of the final age to cultivate samādhi."
Next, there are three sections concerning the response to inquiries. First, praising the ability to hang open the gate:
for those who seek the Mahāyāna, [the text] suspends and displays the path of supreme, correct practice, from the stage of an ordinary person up to Great Nirvāṇa.

The commentary states: Beginning from the ground of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one gives rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikarmika-jñāna*) and culminates in Great Nirvāṇa, thereby uniting with the principle of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
This is presented as a distant yet clear path for all sentient beings of the present age to follow in their correct practice.

It constitutes a portion of these myriad practices; it is the gradual within the sudden. It identifies a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) and arranges the sixty stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*). Six...
The ten stages of the sages do not depart from a single thought-moment. It is like painting images in the sky: by opening one gate, all gates are simultaneously opened;
by discussing one chapter, all chapters shine forth together. It is like the Indra’s net, where they interpenetrate one another.
If one were to discuss the sequential stages of these various Hinayana treatises, that would not yet constitute correct cultivation. Within this [Mahayana], one...

"Stages. To be fully endowed with all stages is what is correct. Furthermore, 'correct cultivation' excludes 'deviant cultivation,' such as the five types of ascetic mortification practiced by non-Buddhists.
Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
Next, the Emperor issued an edict granting permission for questions and answers.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, emptied their hearts, and silently received the instruction.
Later, Píyí waited for the imperial decree; his commentary states: "Kū means 'to open'."
The Buddha said: "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous.
[This section] subsequently explains the sequence of cultivation in two parts. First, searching for the root of delusion (1).
Second, the text on the initial realization of delusion and the certification of the True (3). First, the source of nature is without marks. The commentary states: "Wondrous" means...

The essence is free from subject and object; its nature is the essential nature (*tathatā*). When the perfect nature is universally concentrated and luminous, it is the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

It is free from all names and marks. The commentary states: "Name" refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined), which is the sixth consciousness that universally produces conceptualization. "Mark" refers to the *paratantra* (dependent). Thus...
Regarding the characteristics of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—from the very beginning there have been neither worlds nor sentient beings.
The commentary states: "Worlds" refers to the lands that serve as the objective support; "sentient beings" refers to the conscious beings who depend upon them.
"Because of delusion, there is birth.
This next section describes the cause of deluded birth. The Commentary states: An outsider asks, "If fundamentally there were no sentient beings or worlds, why do they now exist?
The answer is: "Because of delusion, there is birth. Delusion is the characteristic of the luminous nature; it is the root.
Ignorance. Because there is ignorance, the arising of worldlings in the world occurs;
because there is birth, there is cessation.
The Commentary states: "As soon as there is birth, there is cessation; this refers to the arising and ceasing of deluded consciousness."

Arising and ceasing are termed delusion; the extinction of delusion is termed truth. This is designated as the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi and great nirvāṇa—the two names for the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
It is subsequently realized through the perfection of the factor of understanding. The Commentary states: "Bodhi transforms defilement; nirvāṇa transforms delusion."
Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate true samādhi and proceed directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
you must first recognize these two causes of delusion regarding sentient beings and the world.
Later, he exhorted [them] to eliminate the two types of inversion. The commentary states: "To 'yi' (詣) means 'to arrive.

The karma that transforms the two consciousnesses is the cause of inversion for the twelve classes of beings; the manifesting consciousness (*xiànshí*) is the cause of inversion for the vessel-world. The cause of inversion is ignorance (*avidyā*)."
When inversion does not arise, this is the Tathāgata’s true samādhi.
The commentary states: Where the deluded mind has no place, that is bodhi.
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversions of sentient beings?
The subsequent explanation of the passage on the dual causes consists of two parts. First, the description of the delusion of sentient beings, which itself has two parts.
The first is the inquiry: "Ānanda, from the luminous mind of nature...

The subsequent explanation of this text also has two parts. First, the description of the source of delusion, which has three parts. The first is pointing out that delusion has no cause. The commentary states:

The arising of the mind is called "nature" (*xing*). Clarity (*ming*) involves carrying along marks (*xiang*); to turn one's back on the essence and seek outwardly is the functional operation of the intellect.

Because the nature is clear and perfect (*yuan*), the commentary states: "This reiterates the preceding 'nature-clarity. 'Perfect' means that subject and object have not yet been differentiated; this is the perfection that carries along marks."
"Because of this, nature manifests clarity.
The commentary states: "Because nature clarifies, the karmic consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is immediately activated. Because its nature is active, it is called 'karma' (action).
Its nature gives rise to deluded perception."
The commentary states: "This refers to the transformation of consciousness. It is called 'transformation' (turning) because it turns away [from its objects].
It is ultimately non-existent.
The commentary further states: "This ignorance is ultimately without substance."
It constitutes ultimate existence.
The commentary states: Because sentient beings in delusion produce actual karma, ignorance arises;
thus, this existence possesses [the nature of] being.
Next, one realizes that delusion has no substance. The commentary states: "This 'existence' refers to ignorance; 'that which belongs to it' refers to karma, its fruits, and afflictions.
It is not a cause for a cause."
The commentary states: "Cause" means reliance. Since ignorance has no reliance, it is without cause; since ignorance has no substance, it has nothing upon which to rely.
This refers to the characteristic of that which abides and that in which it abides.
The commentary states: "If ignorance has no basis, then there is no abiding; if ignorance has no substance, then there is nothing in which it dwells;
it is utterly without root.
The commentary further states: "This means that ignorance has no fundamental source."
Based on this "abiding nowhere," the worlds and all sentient beings are established.
Subsequently, the establishment of dharmas is described. The commentary states: Ignorance is the root of abiding nowhere; it establishes all dharmas.
What are called establishment and enjoyment both arise from the eight consciousnesses.

Being deluded regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity, one subsequently becomes deluded regarding all phenomena. This constitutes the sixth section on the manifestation of phenomena. First, it describes how delusion has no basis. The commentary states: "Deluded regarding the single true perfection..."
It is ignorance (*avidyā*).
This gives rise to delusion.
The Commentary states: "That is, it is ignorance."
"The nature of delusion has no substance.
The commentary states: This means that this ignorance has no self-nature; its very essence is emptiness, and it does not have anything upon which it depends.
The commentary states: "If there is no substance, what is there to rely upon?
One wishes to return to the True, yet once one desires the True, one has already departed from it.

Next, "delusion arises and one abandons the direction [toward the True]. The commentary states: "One gives rise to a mind capable of returning, yet in returning, one is again covered by the true substance; one desires the True..."
This is already not so. Why? It is because there is that which is truly worth adopting and that which is falsely worth abandoning; this, however, is not the true mind.
The true nature of *tathatā* does not require seeking or returning to.
"The Three Truths have no further principle to be restored. The commentary states: "The upper truth is true wisdom; the lower truth is true principle.
Since these are the single nature of True Suchness (tathatā), there is nothing of the 'true' that needs to be sought after or restored."
It thus becomes the non-characteristic. It is neither arising nor abiding.

Regarding the phrase "the four causes subsequently arise as non-existent," the commentary states: If one gives rise to a mind that seeks to restore, desiring to restore the True that was to be restored, then by seeing the delusion as having characteristics, one clings to the Truth as being non-characteristic; by seeing the delusion as having arising, one clings to the Truth as being non-arising.
One perceives that the delusory has abiding, and consequently clings to the truth as being non-abiding;
it is neither mind nor dharma.

The commentary states: "To perceive that the delusory exists refers to the eight consciousnesses of the deluded mind; to cling to the truth as being without mind; to perceive that the delusory exists refers to the tracks [of phenomena] that give rise to things."
Explanation: Clinging to the truth does not serve as a basis for generating sentient beings' understanding;
rather, they arise through mutual succession.
"Five [factors] arise through mutual perfuming. The commentary states: "They come forth and turn about, thus arising."
"Generating power through illumination.
The commentary states: "Deluded consciousness conditions sensory objects, and through this perfuming, karma is formed."

The commentary states: When the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) mutually perfuse one another, they constitute the retributive karma—both collective and individual—of the three realms and nine stages.
Through the mutual resonance of similar karma, there arises the karma of perception (*saṃvedana-karma*).

The commentary states: This refers to "feeling" (qíng) and "conception" (xiǎng). These are the two dharmas of feeling and conception. Thus, birth from an egg arises solely from conception; birth from a womb is due to feeling;
moisture-born beings result from a response through union; and transformation-born beings result from a response through separation.
"Mutually extinguishing and mutually producing.
The commentary states: Because there is lust, there is craving; thus they mutually produce one another. Because there is killing, there is hatred;
thus they mutually extinguish one another. Theft resides between these two realms.
For this reason, there are sentient beings who are subject to inversion.
"The six knots constitute the analogy for birth" [the commentary states]: although the four modes of birth are mentioned, they implicitly encompass the twelve categories of sentient beings.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion of the world"?

The subsequent explanation of the causes for the arising of the world consists of two parts. The first part provides a general explanation of the three transformations. This section has two sub-parts. First is the inquiry. The commentary states:
"First, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the agent of transformation (*pariṇāmin*), and the world is that which is transformed (*pariṇāmya*). Second, the world is the agent..."

Transformation. The sense organs and objects are that which is transformed. Third, the sense organs and objects are the transformers, while the twelve classes of living beings are that which is transformed.
The world’s inversion is the manifesting consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
This is the existence of that which exists; it arises as fragmented and delusively produced.

The subsequent explanation of the text has two parts. First, the provisional establishment based on delusion. The commentary states: "It means that there is a portion or a segment, wherein the characteristics of the four great elements arise."
Because this realm is established, it is not a cause for a cause, nor a dwelling place for a dwelling place; it flows on without abiding, and thus the world is formed.
The commentary states: "World" (*loka*) has the meaning of flux. The past flows into the present, and the present flows into the future.
The three periods of time and the four directions harmonize and interpenetrate.

Regarding the subsequent transformation where the phases successively multiply, there are two parts. First, citing the directions to clarify the categories. The Commentary states: "This refers to the first transformation."

The subject that undergoes transformation is ignorance (*avidyā*); the object that is transformed is the world (*loka-dhātu*). As stated in the fourth sutra: "The world (*loka*) refers to temporal flux;
the realm (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation. From one up to ten, hundred, and thousand, now by applying space to time, twelve are formed;
by applying time to space, twelve are likewise formed. Within this, the second transformation—the world—is subsumed.

The capacity for transformation consists of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), which are that which is transformed. These six organs and six objects constitute twelve. Now, excluding the mental organ (*manas*), it remains hidden and unknown;
furthermore, the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) is subtle and difficult to perceive. Thus, only the five organs and five objects are taken as belonging to the past.
In the eastern direction, there are likewise five organs and five objects; the same applies to the south, west, and north. This is also true for the future and the present.
Thus, three times four makes twelve, totaling one thousand two hundred.
These transform sentient beings into twelve categories.

The Commentary states: "In the third transformation, the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) act as the transformers, while the twelve classes of living beings are the transformed. [The category of] the womb-born...
Among the twelve [modes of birth], such as egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born, excluding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is emptiness, dispersal, dissolution, and sinking.

As for the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñin*), it is like earth, wood, metal, or stone. Taking only these ten, they constitute the ten categories of beings within the past world: the five sense organs and the five sense objects.
Upon each single atom, ten categories are formed, totaling one hundred. In the future, there are likewise one hundred in the eastern direction;
in the present, there are likewise one hundred in the eastern direction. The same applies to the south, west, and north—three times four makes twelve, totaling one thousand two hundred.
When the three periods of time and the four directions are harmonized and interpenetrate, this is the first transformation. Transformation.
The transformation of sentient beings into twelve categories is the third transformation. By mentioning the first and the third, the second transformation is included by implication.
Therefore, in this world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form; and touch arises from fragrance.
"Because of contact there is flavor; because of flavor one knows phenomena.
Later, the faculties and objects are explained individually. The commentary states: "When the inner mind vibrates, the wind-element arises and light manifests;
thus there is sound, and so on, up to 'because of flavor one knows phenomena'—these are the six faculties and their objects."
"Because the six disordered delusions constitute the nature of karma.

The commentary states: "These are the six consciousnesses. As for 'karma' (karman), its meaning is that which summons and evokes [retribution]. Since the six consciousnesses already grasp sensory objects, they thereby form the general and specific retributive karmas of the three realms and nine stages."
The twelve divisions. By means of these, one revolves.
The commentary states: "By means of" refers to the causes. The six sense organs and the six consciousnesses constitute the twelve divisions.
Since the consciousnesses and their objects are each distinct, the six consciousnesses revolve according to those objects.
Therefore, the sounds, smells, tastes, and touches of the world, exhausting twelve transformations, constitute a single cycle of rotation.
The commentary states: "The world" refers to that which is supported; this collectively enumerates the six faculties and the six objects.
It says that these six faculties and six objects all arise through a single transformation. Here, the world serves as the transformer, while the six faculties and six objects are [the transformed].
Regarding these transformations: based on the second transformation, it induces the third transformation;
because one rides upon this wheel-turning of inverted characteristics, there are beings in this world born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation.

There is that which has form; that which is formless; that which has perception; that which is without perception; and that which is neither with form nor without form, neither with perception nor without perception.
Later, the nature of sentient beings is further elucidated. The Commentary states:
"When the spirit is clarified and the will is stilled, the vital energy (*qi*) becomes quiescent and the mind coalesces. A single thought that deviates from Suchness is truly a deluded movement.
The Sub-commentary states: "This refers to the function of the differentiation and agitation of the vital energy. Originally quiescent, the 'coalescence of the mind' is the True Mind."

The Commentary (*Shu*) says: "Movement and exertion cause the spirit to become obscured; form and appearance take over as the master. The Sub-commentary (*Jian*) says: "This means that movement and shifting turn one’s back upon the essence;

through the toil of life, awakening and illumination [are lost] and consciousness becomes dark and obscure. Consequently, form and appearance manifest before the mind, completely covering the perfect luminosity. One rides upon this..."
[Beings] are born; thus there are those born from eggs. "Eggs arise solely from thought. The Commentary says:
"Furthermore, when encountering various sensory objects (*viṣaya*), one subsequently gives rise to emotional desire (*rāga*). The Sub-commentary says:
"Because there are sensory objects to encounter that correspond to one's feelings, emotional desire then arises. The womb-born [are so called] because they exist due to emotion."
The Commentary states: "When emotion arises and craving intensifies, they meet and coalesce immediately. The Sub-commentary explains:
"If this single dharma of emotion arises, and the mind of craving becomes fervent and intense, they meet and coalesce immediately. This is because moisture combines with emotional ideation;
it is like dust settling upon a moist ground."

The Commentary states: "Delight must be followed by revulsion before one can transform and guide sentient beings. The Sub-commentary explains: "When one perceives sentient beings as objects of delight, after prolonged delight, revulsion arises.
Revulsion then follows delight. For those whose perceptions of sentient beings have been detached, transformation is applied through detachment."
The Commentary states: "Confronting sensory objects, one reflects and discerns; this manifests and develops the spiritual mind. The Sub-commentary explains:
"When there are material sensory objects (*rūpa-dhātu*) to confront, reflective discernment arises, which incites craving; thus, the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is established."
The Commentary says: "When form (rūpa) ceases, one falls into confusion regarding emptiness; this leads to the renewed arising of the obscured aggregates. The Sub-commentary says:

"This means that although there is a mind capable of craving, there is no corresponding objective realm of form; it is merely the dark arising of disordered thoughts, which constitutes the category of the formless (ārūpya)."
The Commentary states: "The mind takes a hollow reflection as its object; thought may be harbored in secret. The Sub-commentary explains:

This means that although the appearance of form accords with one's feelings, there is still a conceptualizing mind that takes a hollow reflection as its object, harboring it secretly within the heart; therefore, there is the category of those with perception (*saṃjñin*).

The Commentary states: "If that which is confronted were non-existent, the principle would become withered and parched. The Sub-commentary states: "Non-existence is like the *luán* tree of a desolate man, and so forth. The Commentary states:

"Although the objective realm awaits its convergence, it depends upon the records and documents [of consciousness]. The Sub-commentary states: "This is because the images of the preceding sensory objects exist."
Thus, its existence is difficult to determine. It must rely upon causes, conditions, and objects before it can be said to accord with reality and become defiled.
This is not a case of having form; rather, it belongs to the category of being without form, such as the water mother (*siphonota*) and similar creatures.
The Commentary states: "Because there are matters that do not accord [with one's wishes], one thus gives rise to summoning. The Sub-commentary states:

"Because the objects before one are pleasing yet cannot be obtained to fulfill the heart's desire, one resorts to incantations and curses as a causal condition for summoning. Therefore, there exist those that are 'not non-material' categories.
'Not' (fei) means 'no' (bu); it does not mean there are no material objects."
The Commentary states: "The primary cause is difficult to encounter; they mutually rely upon one another for support. The Sub-commentary explains:
"When acting as causes and conditions, it is difficult for them to be directly paired. One must rely on a process of indirect, reciprocal formation to finally bring their minds into union.
Once they are united, there arises a class of beings who 'do not have thoughts' (fei you xiang). "Not having thoughts" means the absence of thought.
The Commentary states: "Deception arises even in small matters, leading to the invitation of resentment and harm. The Sub-commentary says:

"Because one seeks the objects of prior forms and fails to obtain them, it instead results in resentment and harm; thus there arise things resembling 'non-existence,' yet this is not that their mental conceptions do not exist."
The Commentary states: "Although there are twelve causes. The Sub-commentary says: "That is, the twelve categories. The Commentary states:
"When investigating the root, there are only two. The Sub-commentary says: "This means that conceptualization acts as the agent of birth, while emotional attachment serves as the moistening cause."
The Commentary states: "Investigating these two, the arising [of the world] originates from perception (*saṃjñā*). The Sub-commentary says:

"This means that regarding these two causes—sentiment (*ch’ing*) and perception—the arising [of the world] is said to possess perception in both cases. This perception pervades all objects, whether they be agreeable or disagreeable."

The Commentary states: "Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the root of birth; the third and fourth [categories] are designated as such collectively. The Sub-commentary says: "Indeed, perception acts as the seed;
when one subsequently proceeds toward rebirth, it likewise relies upon that perception, which is thus the root of birth. Furthermore, among the twelve classes of beings, all possess perception."

The Commentary states: "Sentiment (*qing*) acts as the cause for moistening; it is restricted in its scope yet encompasses the principle of delight. The Sub-commentary states: "Affection (*ai*) follows only from objects that are agreeable to the mind. The Commentary states:

"If one were to divide them equally and synthesize them, speaking in terms of the middle way," the Sub-commentary states: "This refers to the inclusion of cases where sentiment is predominant and [affection] is slight."
Perception follows feeling. If feeling is slight and perception is abundant, one subsumes feeling under perception; this is a case of dual inclusion.
When balanced, it is a case where feeling is more abundant and perception is less so, or where perception is more abundant and feeling is less so.

The Commentary states: "The integration of the substance and its mutual formation is truly difficult to investigate and analyze. The Sub-commentary says: "Thus, when emotion and thought combine, they constitute moisture-born birth;
when they separate, they constitute transformation-born birth. Therefore, it is said that they 'mutually form' one another.
Because of these emotions and thoughts, although the twelve classes of beings are permeated in this way, they encompass everything; it is indeed difficult to investigate and analyze them."
The Commentary says: "The first two indicate the categories. The Sub-commentary says: "The egg-born are produced solely through thought;

the womb-born arise because of emotional attachment. The Commentary says: "The next two clarify them together. The Sub-commentary says: "The moisture-born are induced by conjunction; the transformation-born respond to separation."
The Commentary says: "Others may arise intermittently as divergent branches. The Sub-commentary says: "This refers to the latter eight categories;
these are the 'remnants' of the preceding four triads, arising in an intermingled fashion like the forks of a road or the branches of a tree. Thus, they possess both form and perception."
It is neither with form nor with perception; it is neither formless nor without perception; it is neither non-form nor non-perception. The Commentary states:

"Alternatively, this refers to the repeated classification of the egg-born. The Sub-commentary explains: "This refers to [the categories of] having form and being formless, neither having form nor being formless;
having perception and being without perception, neither having perception nor being without perception, and so forth."

The Commentary states: “The latter passage generally cites instances that contradict the text. Furthermore, although these five stages are within the womb, for what reason are they listed exhaustively?

The Sub-commentary says: “The meaning of the question is this: These five stages—the kalala and so forth during the first seven days—are taught in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the *Womb Treasury Assembly* (*Garbha-kosa-parivarta*), as existing only within the womb.
Why, then, are they present throughout all twelve classes of beings in the subsequent sutra?”
The Commentary states: "The term 'restricted' refers to the single [category of] rebirth; 'universal' refers to the discussion of the various seeds. The Sub-commentary says: "The answer is this:

while the *Ratnakūṭa* Sūtra is restricted solely to the stage of gestation, the fact that all twelve classes of beings are listed universally in this present sūtra is because it discusses them in terms of the perfuming of seeds.
It concerns how, in a single thought-moment, one deviates from Suchness and undergoes transformation. Generally, the intent of this sūtra is to address Ānanda’s encounter with Māra..."

Driven by the defilements of desire, he showed himself entering a brothel and preached this single sutra; what was taught therein as the perfuming of seeds was for the most part formed through the perfuming of defiled dharmas.
The Commentary says: "Although the categories have been increased, why is it that they still cannot encompass all [beings]? The Sub-commentary says: "It asks again:

'If the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of ten categories—namely, those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation; those with form, and those without form;
those with perception, those without perception, and those who are neither with nor without perception—why does this present sūtra add [to these]? "

Second. The Commentary (*Sū*) states: "That treatise [the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra*] explains the stages of cultivation, whereas this [text] concerns delusion regarding sensory objects; their intended meanings differ, so why trouble oneself with reconciling them? The Sub-commentary (*Jian*) states:
"This is the answer, referring to the *Vajracchedikā* and the Separate Teaching (*Bie-jiao*), which speak in terms of the arrangement of the path of cultivation. This refers to the present sutra.
This is explained according to the sense of arising based on the delusion regarding objects; therefore, they are not the same. Thus it is said: "Why trouble oneself with reconciling them?
This answer will be clarified below. Furthermore, there is an answer by way of both advancing and retreating.
The Commentary states: "Alternatively, there are radiant essences of form that can be comprehensively included above. The Sub-commentary says:

"As in the following scripture, the eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of radiant essence, the brilliant spirits of good and ill fortune, and those that become the stars and constellations, are also comprehensively included within the Desire Realm."
The Commentary states: "Formless dissolution and subsidence encompass all four dhyānas. The Sub-commentary says:

"As in the following sutra, eighty-four thousand subtle, hidden, and chaotic thoughts flow through the realms, becoming dispersed, scattered, dissolved, and subsided; this may also comprehensively include the station of infinite space."
The sphere of consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The commentary states: However, this sutra was initially translated with its text not yet complete; it awaits the later extensive version, which will provide its own definitive analysis.
The commentary states: Furthermore, in response: as within the Tripitaka, there are both retranslations and single translations; this present version is a single translation.
The preceding text is incomplete; the subsequent text must certainly follow. However, based on these six sense organs and six sense objects, the twelve categories of living beings arise.

Ānanda, because the world’s false transmigration arises from movement and inversion, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
