Next, the explanation of the text has three parts. First, clarifying the auxiliary causes, which consists of four sections. First, birth depends on the sustenance of food.

This refers to what is called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Second, the names of foods are listed in detail. The commentary states: Formerly it was called "lump-food" (*piṇḍa-āhāra*), because it can be gathered into a lump.

Its substance consists of the three—odor, flavor, and tangibility; its characteristic is transformation and decay. When these three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—first enter the stomach, they have not yet undergone transformation.
That which cannot provide nourishment to the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) lacks the meaning of "food.

Once it has entered the stomach and been digested, transformed, and broken down, it possesses the quality of providing nourishment and thus receives the name "food. "Edible" (*kavaḍīkāra*) refers to that which consists of distinct portions; its substance is the three objects of the senses.
Regarding this essence, it possesses the sense of benefiting the faculties and the function of encompassing nutriment; it is subsumed within the category of "morsel-food" (*kavaḍīkāra*).

Thus far has been the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analysis. Within the three realms, it exists exclusively within the four modes of birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), where it is fully present.
Question: Since there is also the sense-object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) in the higher realms, why is there no edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) there? Answer:

Because the two types—visible form (*rūpa*) and odor (*gandha*)—are known by way of dissociation from their respective faculties (*svendriya-viprakṛṣṭa-jñāna*), they are too remote to provide immediate nourishment; therefore, they do not constitute the essence of food. Question:

Regarding odors, tastes, and so forth, whether in relation to their own faculties or other faculties, how can they be designated as the essence of food? Answer: They are so designated because they undergo transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma*).

At that time, it first benefits its own faculty (*indriya*), and subsequently is also able to benefit all other faculties, causing consciousness (*vijñāna*) to arise with clarity and sharpness, thereby serving as the substance of nutriment (*āhāra*).

Question: Among the three types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) within the matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), can they also function as nutriment? Answer: They also possess the meaning of nutriment.

Just as in the kalpa of famine, there are fish and rice produced as the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), since the higher realms possess color, odor, flavor, and tangibility produced as the fruit of concentration, must there not also be edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) there?
Answer: Although the three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—exist, they lack the quality of entering the stomach, undergoing transformation, and nourishing the sense faculties.

The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). The commentary states: Its essence is the mental factor of contact (*sparśa*). That is, when contacting an object, it constitutes tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*).
When encountering an agreeable object, it can produce the two feelings of joy and pleasure, as well as a beneficial feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*); all of these provide nourishment and benefit.
The meaning [of "nutriment"] is that which can function as nutriment; this applies to all three realms. Regarding "contact" (*sparśa*): its essence is contact within the mind.

Upon this essence, it functions to benefit the sense faculties by confronting their respective objects. Thus, the function of taking food is subsumed within the essence of contact. The above has been explained using the *dharmadhāraṇa-karma-svabhāva* (identity of substance and function) definition. Question:
Since the two sensations of joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*) can benefit the body and mind, why are they not designated as having the meaning of "nutriment"? Answer:

Because the apprehension of objects is remote, through the aforementioned agreeable contact (*manāpa-sparśa*), one first grasps the fundamental object and gives rise to the nutriment of joy and pleasure (*prīti-sukha*).
Question: In which consciousness does this contact function as the meaning of "nutriment"? Answer:

Although this contact is associated with all consciousnesses, its status as nutriment is particularly predominant in the first five consciousnesses. By contacting coarse and manifest objects, it is able to produce joy and pleasure. And...

The feeling of equanimity that is conducive and beneficial is superior; because it is superior, the eighth and seventh consciousnesses contact [their objects] frequently, and their apprehension of objects is subtle, such that they cannot produce the two feelings of joy and pleasure, as these do not serve as the substance of nutriment.

The nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*). The commentary states: This has as its essence the single dharma of volition (*cetanā*) among the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). Therefore, its characteristic is aspiration.

That is to say, when it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and desire (*kāma*), and one aspires toward an object of attachment, it possesses the sense of providing sustenance and is thus able to function as nutriment.

As for its objective referent (*ālambana*), it also extends throughout the three realms (*dhātu*) and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The single dharma of volition (*cetanā*) is the volition among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*);

this is its substance (*svabhāva*). Upon this substance, when there is an aspiration toward an object that can be experienced, it possesses the function of providing benefit and sustenance, thereby acting as nutriment (*āhāra*).

This is like pointing at a plum with a grain of sand; while the root and the function differ, they both return to the substance of volition. The above has been explained by means of a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Question: Which consciousness is this?

[Question: What is volition (*cetanā*)? [Answer: It is the volition of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because the mental consciousness possesses discrimination and its objects are superior in terms of aspiration.

[Question: Why is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) volition not taken as the substance of nutriment? [Answer: Because the uncontaminated cannot provide nourishment or benefit to that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*).

The nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). The commentary states: Its substance consists of the eight consciousnesses, and its characteristic is grasping and maintaining (*dhṛti*). This refers to contaminated consciousness;

because it is benefited by the power of the preceding three nutriments, the nutriment of consciousness is then able to increase. It is particularly capable of grasping and maintaining the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

That which functions to provide sustenance and benefit is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*). The single term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the eighth consciousness; this is its substance (*svabhāva*).

Upon this substance, there exists the function of maintaining continuity and providing sustenance, which constitutes its nature as nutriment. Since nutriment is a function, the function of nutriment is subsumed within the substance of consciousness.

Thus far, this has been explained by way of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Question: Why are the other consciousnesses not taken [as the subject]? Answer: Because the first six consciousnesses are intermittent.

Therefore, because the seventh consciousness is not appropriated (*anupātta*), whereas the eighth consciousness possesses three characteristics, it is the true consciousness that serves as nutriment (*āhāra*).
First, it is of a single type of neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature; second, it is constant and uninterrupted; third, it pervades all three realms. Thus, the treatise says:

"From this it is known that there exists a distinct consciousness, different from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which is of a single type, constant, and pervasive, and which sustains the body and life."
To ensure that [the food] is not interrupted or destroyed, the World-Honored One has made this statement: "All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.

Regarding the two sensations of joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*), it is said that they are "distant" in their engagement with objects because joy and pleasure only arise when there is something conducive and beneficial; thus, they are "distant.
Now, if one merely takes up what is conducive and beneficial, but it has not yet entered the stomach and does not yet have the sense of providing sustenance, how can it be called "nutriment"?
Answer: This is a case of referring to the effect by means of its cause.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that all sentient beings subsist upon nutriment;
this has been constantly proclaimed throughout the three [periods].
Ānanda, all sentient beings are born because they consume what is sweet.

"The four parts of sweet poison" (sì fēn gān dú)—the commentary states: "consuming what is sweet" refers, for example, to eating rice, millet, and the like, or to abstaining from the five pungent roots.
"Because they consumed poison, they died.
The commentary states: "Consuming poison refers to eating things such as *gǔ* (poisonous fungi), wild *gé* (aconite), or the like; or it is like eating the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-kaṭuka*).
All these sentient beings who seek *samādhi* ought to sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world."
Next, Xin was instructed to cease [the practice]. The commentary states: "The five kinds are leek, garlic-leek, chives, garlic, and hing (hiṅgu).
Regarding the phonetics and meanings: *hing* refers to asafoetida (*ārdraka*). It is also said to be a type of vegetable.
Regarding these five kinds of pungent roots: eating them cooked arouses lust; eating them raw increases anger.

The subsequent section on the faults of consuming raw meat is divided into two parts. The first part, concerning the teaching of the Dharma, is further divided into three sections. The first clarifies how they give rise to anger and desire.

In this way, those in the world who consume pungent roots, even if they can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, will be loathed for their foul stench by the celestial immortals of the ten directions,
who will all distance themselves from them.
Next, the celestial beings abandon them from afar.
The various hungry ghosts (preta), following the sequence of that food, lick their lips and mouths; dwelling constantly with such ghosts, their merit and virtue daily diminish.
It brings no long-term benefit;
later, one dwells together with ghosts. The commentary states: "Ghosts" refers to those who lack food and drink. [This occurs when] one has created superior grades of greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Superior" refers to the upper lip, and "lower" refers to the mouth. "It brings no long-term benefit" means that it does not result in lasting benefit.
Furthermore,
when those who consume pungent roots practice *samādhi*, Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals (*deva-rṣi*), and virtuous deities from the ten directions will not come to protect them.
Regarding the subsequent four passages on the cultivation of concentration, the first concerns protection by worthies and sages.
The Great Power Mara King, seizing an opportunity, manifested in the form of a Buddha and came to preach the Dharma for them.

The two Mara Kings were deluded by his discourse. The commentary states: "The celestial Mara of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) obtained the skillful means of the practitioner's method."
He disparaged the precepts and praised lust, anger, and ignorance.
The commentary states: "As for those who maintain the precepts, they follow the path of the Hīnayāna; what 'observance' or 'violation' could there be for a Bodhisattva?"
They take various heterodox teachings as their means of propagation and transformation;
at the end of their lives, they become part of the retinue of the Demon King.
Through three deaths, they become members of the heterodox host. The commentary states: "Retinue" refers to the demonic subjects and demonic women.
When their demonic blessings are exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
It is further evident that those who possess the four blessings likewise fall into hell;
this can be known. Ānanda, one who cultivates Bodhi must forever renounce the five pungent roots. This is called the first advancement in cultivation.
Gradually. The concluding exhortation at the end is as follows:
What is right nature?
Next, the exhortation to eliminate the three karmas consists of three parts.
First, the inquiry: "Ānanda, such sentient beings who enter samādhi must first strictly maintain pure precepts."
Next, the explanation consists of six parts. First is the exhortation to eliminate delusion regarding karma. The commentary states: "Entering" (*praveśa*) is the act of entering;
"samāpatti" is that which is entered. Regarding "strict purity and non-transgression": "precept" (*śīla*) has the meaning of preventing what is improper and warding off evil.
Forever sever the mind of lust; do not consume wine or meat; purify food with fire; do not eat raw, living things. The Commentary states:
The Vinaya says that the "mark" is purified by the knife and the "seed" is purified by fire. This means that piercing it with a knife is to purify its mark.
Steaming them over a fire purifies the seeds. It is further said: "No one who observes the precepts may eat raw food.
Ānanda, for a practitioner of the Way, it is impossible to transcend the triple world without severing lust and killing."
Second, it clarifies the non-cessation of killing. The commentary states: "If one were to sever both lust and killing, there would indeed be such a way to transcend the three realms.
One should contemplate lustful desire as being like a venomous snake, or as seeing an enemy thief."
Third is the exhortation to cultivate revulsion toward desire as an antidote. The commentary states: Yongjia said, "It is like grasping the stem of a flower without realizing it is a venomous snake;
one craves only female beauty without knowing the suffering of death. A venomous snake kills once, whereas female beauty binds one for a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas."
First, one upholds the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of the Śrāvaka.
Regarding the "fourfold exhortation to uphold the two sets of discipline," the commentary states: the four [offenses] are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and great falsehood;
when these are combined with the aforementioned four [preliminary offenses], along with touching and the eight [offenses of] concealing and following, they constitute the eight.

He maintains his body without movement. Subsequently, he practices the pure discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva. He maintains his mind without arising [distractions]. His prohibitory precepts are perfected. The commentary states:

"Maintaining the body" means not engaging with sensory objects. "Maintaining the mind" means that if one hears the sound of hairpins or bracelets from across a wall and discriminates whether it is a man or a woman, one immediately commits a root offense.
"Prohibitory precepts" refers to the perfection of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna codes of discipline.
Then, in all the worlds, there would forever be no karma of mutual procreation or mutual slaughter;
the five [karmas] would forever lack the karma of cyclic existence. The commentary states: "Mutual procreation" refers to fathers and sons, and such things take greed and desire as their root.
"Mutual slaughter" refers to saying, "You owe me my life," or "I shall repay your debt"; such things take theft as their root.
With greed as the root, theft and robbery do not occur; there are no burdens of mutual indebtedness.
The commentary states: because there is no killing, there is no debt of life; because there is no defilement, there is no burden of karma.
Furthermore, in this world, he does not return old debts.
The commentary states: Because he does not steal, he does not owe debts;
he is a person of purity who cultivates samādhi. His parents’ physical bodies need no divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); they naturally perceive him.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma; personally receiving the holy instructions, they attain great supernormal powers and travel through the realms of the ten directions.
Their past lives are purified, and they encounter no hardships or perils.

Sixth is the supernormal power of direct realization (*abhijñā*). The commentary states: "To travel through the worlds of the ten directions" refers to attaining the supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*).
This is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
The subsequent conclusion.
What is present karma?
The subsequent section on the cessation of conditions, the lineage, and the purity of the text consists of three parts. First is the inquiry.
Ānanda, for such a person who purely maintains the prohibitive precepts, there are two subsequent sections concerning the delusion of words.
First, the three sections on the text regarding the purity of gold through the cessation of conditions. First, the clarity of the mind through upholding the precepts. The commentary states:
This reiterates the previous point regarding those who have eradicated their inherent nature:
their minds are free from lustful desire, and they do not allow themselves to flow excessively toward the six external sense objects.
The commentary states: "The sixth consciousness does not share the same objects as the [first] five; it does not race and flow toward the realms of the six sense objects."

□□. Because it does not flow out or disperse, the subsequent sense-faculties have no corresponding objects. The Commentary states: This follows from the preceding passage on "entering the stream and losing the object."

"Returning to the source, one reverts to the fundamental. The commentary states: "To 'return' means to turn back the deluded consciousness; to 'revert' means to return to the original source of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
When sensory objects are no longer conditioned, the sense faculties have nothing with which to pair."
The commentary states: "This refers to 'pairing with objects. It means that the six sense faculties have no external objects to pair with;
they flow back to their source and become entirely one.

Regarding the phrase "the subsequent mind is pure and receives," the commentary states: "Flowing against the current to return to the source, it becomes entirely the nature of the single True Reality."
"The six faculties do not function.
The Commentary states: "The eyes and so forth, which receive and utilize the objects of the sensory realms such as form, no longer engage at the gates of the six sense organs.
This is because deluded consciousness does not arise; it is the transformation of consciousness into wisdom."
The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure. The commentary states:
"The non-functioning of the six faculties is the primary retribution (zhengbao), while the lands of the ten directions are the secondary retribution (yibao).
These two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—interpenetrate within body and land; both the internal body and the external vessel-world are entirely pure."
It is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.

The subsequent passage on the realization of non-arising consists of five sections. The first presents a metaphor to clarify both aspects simultaneously. The commentary states: "The essence of True Suchness..."

Primordial and manifest purity are without flaw, like a precious moon suspended within lapis lazuli; thus, one gives rise to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādikarmika-jñāna*) and realizes the truth of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
Since both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms] are entirely without marks (*animitta*), they are thus.
Body and mind are blissful.
Second, "tranquil amidst the dust. The commentary states: "Body" refers to the *dharmakāya*; "mind" refers to the firm and solid mind; they are joyful and at ease.
"Wondrous, perfect, and equal; one attains great peace and security.

The commentary states: This refers to the practitioner who awakens to this subtle, wondrous, and perfectly luminous true mind, which is equal and non-dual; this is the realization of the true principle of the *dharmakāya*.
The secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas are all manifested therein.
The three Buddha-bodies are contained and manifested within it. The commentary states: "The Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas is manifested within the mind of the practitioner.
The practitioner’s mind is like a mirror; the bodies of the Buddhas are like reflections. The Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas enter into me."
Nature. My nature likewise merges with that of the Tathāgata;
such a person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Fourth, the stage of realizing and cultivating [the fruit].
From this point, one gradually cultivates.
There are five stages of gradual ascent in cultivation; these stages are as described in the text.
According to the practices one initiates:
The commentary states: "To give rise to the practices of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, and even up to the ten stages, etc., and thereby establish the positions of the sages.

The commentary states: "To establish the sixty positions of the sages; or, according to the practices initiated, this is the commencement of *shiqi* (initial enlightenment) wisdom. To establish [these]...

Establishing the stages of the sages (ārya-bhūmi) is to accord with the principle of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti). By passing through these three gradual stages, one attains the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

However, while this sutra establishes sixty sage-stages upon the principle of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) within a single thought-moment, it clarifies the patience of the non-arising dharma specifically within this gradual mental process;
it is only upon reaching the seventh stage that one attains the patience of non-arising. This is explained according to the gradual approach.
Treatise:
This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.
Herein ends the conclusion.
Ānanda, these sons of good family have the craving of desire dried up.

Hereafter, the text on the stages of cultivation is arranged in six parts. First, the opening foundation that reveals the principle, which is divided into two sections. First, the explanation of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), which is divided into three parts.
First, it is said that "pure wisdom" excludes and exhausts all other mental states. The commentary states: this reiterates the previous three gradual steps, which were contrary to...
Manifest karma: when the mind does not crave lust, this is the non-arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Root and object do not encounter one another.
The Commentary states: "To 'encounter' means to have expectations. Since consciousness does not arise, what can the sense-faculties expect?
The remaining physical substance present before one no longer continues to arise.
The commentary states: "That is to say, this very body born of parents—the remaining physical substance—does not give rise to further moments of existence hereafter."
The grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.
The commentary states: When this false grasping ceases, it naturally becomes empty, penetrating, and clear; within its very substance, the evolving consciousness is transformed into wisdom.
The nature of wisdom is perfectly luminous, illuminating the ten directions. When this wisdom is dry and devoid of moisture, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*kandha-bhūmi*).
Next, as the habit-energies of desire are about to dry up, the attachments of affection are extinguished.
The habit-energies of desire are first dried up;

subsequently, because the subsequent [stages] have not yet been reached, it is revealed that one has not yet attained penetration into the Truth. The Commentary states: "This explains 'Dry Wisdom' (śuṣka-vipaśyanā).
One has not yet connected with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata."

The commentary states: Because one has not yet entered the initial stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), where "entering the stream causes the objects of perception to vanish," the fifty stages described below are arranged for this sutra solely as entry into the holy path upon the single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*). These fifty stages are not separate from that single thought-moment;
the mind does not depart from the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-svabhāva*). It is like drawing fifty lines in empty space. One must not interpret it otherwise.

This is spoken in terms of the sequence of temporal divisions. Thus, the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states: "Therefore, the ten bodies are clearly distinct yet mutually interpenetrate;
the six stages are not disordered yet encompass one another. The vast and great enter and emerge within the infinitesimal; the dust mote contains the entirety without exception.
They manifest simultaneously and in perfect clarity, like a mustard seed and a jar being fully contained at once, or compared to a drop of water in the ocean."
It is further said: "The dawn of enlightenment in the Eastern Temple is no different from the initial aspiration;
abiding in the Southern Quest, the perfection of causes does not exceed a single pore. Such is the meaning of this sutra. Thus it is.

Using this very mind, the subsequent section clarifies the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). The text consists of ten parts; first, it clarifies that the function of the mind of faith is represented by the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*), wherein one flows into the central center.

The "upper-middle" refers to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). The "lower-middle" refers to entering the truth of the Middle Way; the mind realizes the single reality and departs from the characteristics of the middle.
Since there are no characteristics of the middle, one internally realizes and witnesses perfect centrality, flowing moment by moment into the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Perfectly wondrous and fully blossomed;
awakening like the opening of a lotus,
proceeding from the true, wondrous, and perfect.
The commentary states: "True" means originally true and wondrous; "originally wondrous" refers to the fundamental principle-body (*dharmadhātu-tattva*).

"Repeatedly manifesting the true and wondrous" means that wisdom reveals the profound suchness (*tathatā*). The commentary further states: "Repeatedly manifesting" refers to the true, essential, subtle, and wondrous outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
"Sublime faith abides eternally.
The commentary states: "The mind trusts in itself; without giving rise to discursive thoughts, it dwells in faith.
All delusive imaginings are extinguished without remainder."
The commentary states: "Delusion is exhausted.
It is the pure truth of the Middle Way.
The commentary states: "This clarifies the principle of the Middle Way, for it transcends the two extremes."
This is called the "Abiding in Faith.
The commentary states: "To abide in reliance upon faith is called 'abiding in faith.
True faith is clear and lucid."
Second is the mind of mindfulness. The commentary states: "This follows upon the preceding mind of faith;
all things are perfectly interfused.
The commentary further states: "One attains the principle of perfect, pervasive penetration."

"The three— sense bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and [consciousness]— the commentary states: this clarifies that the three— faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—
cannot act as obstructions."
The commentary states: To realize that the aggregates, bases, and elements, and so forth, are empty;
and likewise, throughout the countless eons of the past and future, during the process of discarding one body and receiving another, [to realize that] all habitual tendencies are empty.
All [phenomena] appear before one.

The commentary states: Having attained the nature of perfect penetration, it appears before one; one clearly understands that the habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time manifest with distinct clarity.
These sons of good family are all able to recollect and attain freedom from forgetfulness; this is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness (*smṛti*).
The commentary states: "Mindfulness" has the nature of darkly recording [objects]; because one dwells in reliance upon mindfulness, it is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness.
"Wondrous, perfect, and purely true" refers to the three types of the mind of vigor. The commentary states: "When the true body manifests before one, the true essence gives rise to transformation."
The commentary states: "From the essence, wisdom arises;
beginningless habitual tendencies permeate the single luminous spirit.
The commentary states: "Realizing that habitual tendencies have no substantial reality, the nature of wisdom attains thorough penetration."
To advance toward true purity solely through clarity and vigor is called the mind of diligence (*vīrya*).
The Commentary states: "The nameless and non-conceptual mind is the principle (*tattva*); advancing toward true purity is the application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, this mind advances toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The essence of mind manifests before one.
This is the fourth, the Mind of Wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). The commentary states: this follows upon the substance of the true mark (*dharmatā*) mentioned previously;
because it consists purely of wisdom, it is called the Abiding in the Mind of Wisdom.
The commentary states: It is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Abiding in reliance upon wisdom is called "abiding in the mind of wisdom" (*prajñā-citta-vihāra*).
It maintains the illumination of knowledge through the five meditative minds (*pañca-samādhi-citta*). The commentary states: This refers to the definitive contemplation of true wisdom.
"Universally pervasive, quiescent, and profound.
The commentary states: "In accordance with the essence of reality (*dharmatā*), it is quiescent, wondrous, and eternally concentrated; this is called the abiding of the settled mind."
The commentary states: When the realization of the settled nature is manifest, it is called "the mind abiding in concentration.
When the light of concentration illuminates and clarifies, there are the six non-regressions. The commentary states: It is quiescent yet constantly active.
The nature of clarity penetrates deeply.
The commentary states: "As his wisdom becomes increasingly profound, advancing only without retreating, it is called the 'non-retrogressive mind' (avaivartika-citta)."
The commentary states: "Advancing toward unsurpassed bodhi, there is no further regression;
the mind advances with tranquility.
This refers to the seventh mind that protects the Dharma. The commentary states: "The mind that advances toward unsurpassed bodhi is tranquil and immovable."
Maintain it without loss.
The commentary states: Constantly preserve its illumination so that it does not dissipate.
The interfacing of the vital energies (*qi-fen*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is called the "mind that protects the Dharma" (*hu-fa xin*).
"Because the essence of the cause penetrates the essence of the fruit. The commentary states: "The wisdom and principle of the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are no different.
Enlightened clarity maintains the eight minds of dedication, guarding and illuminating the true stage."
Able to use wondrous power to unmovingly illuminate the mind and turn back the compassionate light of the Buddha.
Secretly guiding to the source of origin,
one abides facing the Buddha,
constantly returning to fundamental suchness.
It is like two mirrors with radiant surfaces facing each other;
the fundamental and the initial illuminate one another,
and within them, wondrous reflections enter into one another in successive layers.

The wondrous principle of the fundamental substance manifests in the initial mind. Initial awakening illuminates the truth; wisdom penetrates the true substance. Within the substance, wisdom is contained; wisdom abides in the source of truth.
The principle manifests in the initial mind; the principle arises from the initial [awakening]. The principle that arises from the initial [awakening] reflects back to reveal the original truth.
The wisdom of the original truth contains the principle of arising. Principle is the foundation; it reflects back to manifest the foundation. Wisdom is...
"Beginning: Turning back and manifesting the initial mind is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).
The commentary states: "Turning the mind toward unexcelled bodhi; turning merit toward the principle."
The light of the mind secretly returns.
Ninth, the precept of the mind. The commentary states: "The nature of true illumination attains the Buddha’s eternal stillness."
The commentary states: "The wisdom of initial awakening (ādikṣānti-jñāna) gives rise to the principle of original awakening (mūla-bodhi-tattva), which is unsurpassed, wondrous, and pure.
The commentary further states: "The wisdom of initial awakening..."
"Abiding securely in the untainted.
The commentary states: "The principle of original enlightenment is attained without any loss."
The commentary states: Having attained this principle, there is no longer any forgetting or loss; this is called "abiding in the mind of precept" (*śīla-citta-vihāra*).
The commentary states: Within the essence of this principle, there is the meaning of preventing what is improper and ceasing evil; this refers to the precepts of nature (*prakṛti-śīla*).
Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline,
with the tenfold mind of aspiration, his natural precepts are spontaneous,
enabling him to travel throughout the ten directions.
The Dharma-realm is unobstructed;

wherever one goes follows one's vows, manifesting the fulfillment of one's heart. The commentary states: for the sake of all sentient beings, if they hear these ten levels of faith but do not fully awaken...

"World-Honored One, it would be well to further explain the lower ten abodes (*daśavihāra*). The preceding scriptural text states that those of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) all enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) instantaneously.
As the commentary says: 'They look down upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) from the first thought-moment; they condense the three great eons (*tri-kalpa-asamkhyeya*) into a single instant.'"
This is called the dwelling of the mind of aspiration.
Ānanda, these sons of good family, through true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds.

Second, "Refining and Seeking its Text. First, the dwelling of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*). The commentary states: this refers back to the preceding ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).
The true method is skillful means. As the Sūtra says: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two different things;
therefore, I prostrate first to the initial mind. This refers to the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Regarding "melting and refining to seek the True":

this refers to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), which are like taking gold ore and placing it within a furnace to melt and refine it. When the ore is exhausted, the gold appears; this serves as a metaphor for these ten abodes, wherein delusion is exhausted and the True is revealed.
Manifestation.
The essence of mind radiates brilliance, and its ten functions interpenetrate.
The commentary states: "The essence of mind is principle; radiating brilliance is wisdom. The following citation from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* shows that even a single stage is fully complete.
All abide in the perfect realization of the one mind; this is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind.
The commentary states: "This refers to the initial resolve of the Ten Stages."
The illumination within the mind is like pure lapis lazuli;
in the second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground, it becomes manifest, radiant, perfect, and pure,
with refined gold appearing within.
Transforming and realizing lucid clarity,
one treads upon the previously mentioned wondrous mind to establish it as the ground;
treading upon that previously perfected and pure mind constitutes the ground of universal contemplation.
This is called the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (bhūmi-karman). The commentary states: "To level and cultivate the ground of the mind is termed the Stage of Cultivating the Ground.
The ground of the mind involves cognitive engagement.

Third, the stage of abiding in cultivation. The commentary states: "The mind refers to the aforementioned wondrous mind; this is wisdom (*prajñā*). The ground refers to the ground of the principle of actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
this is principle (*tattva*). When speech involves knowledge, wisdom and principle merge in dark harmony, being neither two nor distinct."
Both are attained with clarity.
The commentary states: "All are attained with perfect, manifest clarity.
Wandering through the ten directions, one encounters no obstruction."
The commentary states: Since principle and wisdom are one, the worlds of the ten directions are all entirely suchness. Therefore, there is no obstruction or hindrance;
this is called the "Abiding in Cultivation."

The commentary states: "Cultivation" (xiū) refers to that which is capable of cultivating; "practice" (xíng) refers to that which is practiced. To abide in the state of both the cultivator and the practice is called "abiding in cultivation and practice.
When one's practice is identical to that of the Buddha, one receives the Buddha’s spiritual influence.
The fourth is the "Dwelling of Noble Birth. The commentary states: This means that the practice performed by the practitioner is equal to that of the Buddha.
The practitioner is the cause, while the Buddhas are the fruit; thus, cause and fruit are of the same essence.
"Just as the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) seeks its own parents.

The commentary states: "Among the two types of existence, this is called the intermediate aggregate (*antarāskandha*); thus, this body has already perished, yet another physical form has not yet been received."
In the interval between the two states of birth and death, one awaits the convergence of conditions with the parents; consciousness enters to proceed toward rebirth,
where the subtle influence of the aggregates communicates in darkness, silently attaining the profound principle.
Entering the lineage of the Tathāgata,
with essence and wisdom in mutual correspondence,
this is called the Dwelling of Noble Birth.
The commentary states: Being born into a noble family as a son serves as a metaphor for the practitioner’s mind aspiring toward the Way.
One must first rely on the profound union of wisdom and principle before entering the Dharma-body of all Buddhas; thus, one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata and becomes a seed of the Buddha.
Having already entered the womb of the Way,
one fully abides in the five skillful means; thus manifesting a seal of accord with the true essence,
one personally serves the lineage of the Awakened One.
O Son of the Buddha, Yisheng,
it is as when the fetus has already been formed;
the original merit is established and recorded.
The human marks are complete; this is called "abiding in the fulfillment of skillful means.

Regarding the phrase "partial realization as identical to the perfect," the commentary states: "Partial realization" refers to these sixty-two stages, which are realized gradually with distinct portions.
Although they are gradual, they do not depart from the perfect; therefore, it is said to be "identical to the perfect."
Their appearance is like that of a Buddha.
They abide in the six right states of mind; their tranquility is identical, and their mental characteristics are likewise identical.
When principle is equalized within the One, it is called the Abode of Rectifying the Mind.
The commentary states: "The *dharmakāya*s of self and other are mutually equal and identical."
Body and mind merge into a single unity;

this is the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression. The commentary states: "The body merges to form a countenance identical to that of a Buddha, while the mind merges to form a mental state whose essence is identical [to his]."
As [virtuous qualities] increase day by day and one practices spontaneously,
this is called the stage of non-retrogression.
The commentary states: "In the study of the Way, one increases daily and never regresses; this is called the Dwelling of Non-retrogression.
The spiritual marks of the ten bodies are simultaneously perfected; this is called the Dwelling of Youthful Truth."

The eighth is the stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta). The commentary states: There are two aspects to the "ten bodies. One is as previously described. Furthermore, the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"Equal, pure, and inexhaustible; skillfully cultivating the dharma-nature; free from discursive thought and investigation; inconceivable and tranquil;
the wondrous wisdom of space"—this is explained in reference to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The formation [of the body] emerges from the womb; being a true son of the Buddha, this is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince.
Ninth is the Stage of the Dharma Prince: the formation emerges from the womb, manifesting its sovereign function, and one becomes a true son of the Buddha.
Shao continues the meaning; through the manifestation [of the stages], he becomes a full person.
At the tenth stage, Abhiṣeka-vihāra, he is capable of performing the Buddha-activities.
Just as a great king of a country entrusts all state affairs to his crown prince, when that Kṣatriya king’s heir has reached maturity and the consecration ceremony is performed for him,
it is called "abiding in the consecration."
How much more so regarding the entrustment [of authority]. For instance, when a Kṣatriya prince is about to succeed to the kingship, he sits upright in the main hall;
first, the consecration (abhiṣeka) is performed. Taking the horn of a white ox, one places various seeds within it, and with a great-named elephant, one takes the waters of the four oceans.
First, spread the auspicious *kuśa* grass; next, place the bull’s horn. Then, using seawater, irrigate the seed within the horn so that it moistens and flows through the body.
The court ministers prostrate and offer congratulations. Furthermore, as the Bodhisattva is a Prince of the Dharma, how much more so is this the case?
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of the four great oceans of compassion, wisdom, practice, and vows, stir the practitioner and purify their original enlightenment.
The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) arises all at once. The auspicious grass (*kuśa*) symbolizes pure conduct.

When the court officials offer their greetings, there are none among the humans, devas, or those of the two vehicles who do not express their admiration. Since the practitioner’s merit has been established, it is appropriate that they follow the Buddha’s compassion;
furthermore, what is realized and what is taught should likewise manifest his sublime practices. The commentary states: "Kṣa-kṣa" is the Tang-language term for...
The field-owner represents the noble clans of the western lands; being of royal lineage, he signifies that the crown prince is the most honored among men.
The seeds of the hundred grains represent the king as the sovereign of the hundred grains. The great name symbolizes that the king possesses great power and strength.
The waters of the four seas represent the arrival of the four seas to pay court. The consecration (abhiṣeka) represents the king.
It is most supreme. Empowerment (abhiṣeka) is the practice of the Dharma-heaven that is able to moisten all births.
As for the term "heir" (śeṣin), it refers to the son of a single lifetime.
Ānanda, once these sons of good family have become the children of the Buddha, [they are called heirs].
The third, the perfection of the three types of sublime conduct, consists of ten sections. First, in the Stage of Joyful Conduct (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the stage is about to be completed.

It is fully endowed with the immeasurable sublime virtues of the Tathāgatas, manifesting the accomplishment of these virtues. The Commentary states: "The sublime virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all perfectly fulfilled."
Accordance with the ten directions;
the Buddha permitting the conditions for transformation—
this is called the Practice of Joy.
The commentary states: "In the worlds of the ten directions where one travels, one transforms all sentient beings in accordance with their needs.

Question: Since the gates of practice are manifold, why is joy established as the initial practice? Answer: Indeed, when first opening the way for deluded multitudes, it is appropriate to skillfully accommodate the capacities of people.
Desiring to entice them back to the truth, one should first practice joy. When joy arises, reverence follows.
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called the practice of benefiting others (*anugraha-caryā*).
Second, regarding the practice of benefiting others: as for "being well able to benefit," when one seeks to transform people and civilize beings, one must necessarily act with skillful conduct.

If the preceding mind habituates itself to benefiting others such that nothing cannot be bestowed, then the Bodhisattva’s four means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*) will encompass all ordinary beings according to their needs.
Because it provides what is required, it is said that one is "skillfully able to benefit others. The commentary states:

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*)—generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—bring about self-awakening and the awakening of others, such that no opposition or rejection occurs; this is called the practice of non-ill will (*avyāpāda*).
Third is the practice of non-aversion. The commentary states: Awakening oneself is the fundamental [wisdom]; awakening others is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding the practitioner of non-aversion: since one is oneself free from anger, one causes others likewise to be free from resentment.
The categories of birth;
the four inexhaustible practices; the exposition of the causes and effects of birth, extending to the furthest reaches of the future.
By means of present cognition, one understands the past;
the three periods of time are equal.
By examining the cause, one knows the fruit.
Pervading the ten directions and taking one category to represent the rest is called inexhaustible practice.

Question: Why is it called "inexhaustible practice"? Answer: Because sentient beings are inexhaustible and each possesses distinct mentalities, how could the Bodhisattva’s benefit for others ever come to an end, given that it follows their minds? Therefore, it is called "inexhaustible practice."
All things are unified within the various Dharma-gates, attaining freedom from error.
Fifth, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion is excellent; though diverse, they all return to the same principle.
This is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.

The commentary states: "Delusion consists in clinging to difference and failing to penetrate [the truth]. Since one has realized that all various dharma-gates are of a single principle, there is no longer delusive confusion.
Thus, within the midst of sameness..."
Sixth, the manifestation of goodness. The commentary states: this refers to principle (*li*).
The manifestation of various differences.
The commentary states: this refers to phenomena (*shi*).
Each distinct characteristic manifests as identical; this is called "skillfully manifesting practice.
The commentary states: "Arising practice from manifestation and returning practice to its source differs in meaning from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which manifests difference within identity."
In this manner, it continues until the empty space of the ten directions is filled with atoms as numerous as dust motes; within each and every atom, the worlds of the ten directions are manifested.

This is the seventh practice of non-attachment: within the small, the large is manifested. The commentary states: "The small lacks the characteristics of the small; the large lacks the characteristics of the large."
Manifesting the objects of the senses and the realms of existence without mutual obstruction or hindrance is called the practice of non-attachment.
The commentary states: "This is the realization of principle; yet the large and small remain distinct and clear—this is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena."
Various [practices] manifest before one.
The eight practices of respect (*gurukāra*)— the distinctions among these gateways of practice—
are all the foremost *pāramitā*, and are thus called the "practices of respect."
Taking wisdom as the fundamental principle and being of one mind with all Buddhas is called the practice of respect.
Such perfect integration, which can establish the norms for all Buddhas of the ten directions, is called the practice of wholesome dharmas.
The nine practices of wholesome dharmas are the wondrous function of *prajñā*. Skillfully responding to the Buddha-mind, they establish all activities as the path of the sages.

Each and every one is pure and without outflows (*anāsrava*), for they are the single truth of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because their nature is thus from the beginning, they are called "true and real practices."

The Ten Practices of Reality (*daśa-tattva-caryā*). First, the wondrous function of true, perfect wisdom is quiescent; when practice accords with the true source, it is called the "Practice of Reality.
The ten practices mentioned above share a common principle throughout all three stages: the first three correspond to objects and proceed in accordance with them;

the next three open up the provisional to allow the wondrous to manifest freely; and the final three reveal its essence and function. Only the seventh clearly manifests the gate of spiritual and penetrating practice; although it has already been mastered...

Chong [comments]: It is logically appropriate to attribute this merit to the realization of the essence (*tǐ*). The *Jiàn* (Sub-commentary) states: "The preceding section provides a further detailed analysis.
The first three [practices] correspond to objects and proceed in accordance with them: 1. the Practice of Joy; 2. the Practice of Benefiting Others; 3. the Practice of Freedom from Anger.

The next three open up the provisional (*quán*) to allow for the full exercise of the wondrous (*miào*): 4. the Practice of the Inexhaustible; 5. the Practice of Freedom from Delusion and Confusion; 6. the Practice of Skillful Manifestation. The final three...
These clarify its essence and function: the eight practices of respect, the nine practices of wholesome dharmas, and the practice of seeking reality;
the seventh alone is the practice of non-attachment, which is supernormal power.
Ānanda, these good sons fulfill their supernormal powers. The fourfold turning completes the function;
the body-text consists of ten sections. First is the departure from the mark of sentient beings, which concludes the preceding universal practice.
Having completed the task of attaining Buddhahood,
he brings forth the merit of delivering sentient beings;
he is pure, pristine, and true.
Abiding in the ultimate truth,
far removed from all lingering afflictions,
one establishes neither self nor other.
