When someone comes to question him, he answers with only a single word, speaking merely of "non-existence. Apart from this non-existence, there is nothing further to be said.
The later response. The commentary states: It means that when someone comes and asks what dharma one takes as one's primary teaching, one simply says that "all is non-existent.
Beyond this non-existence, there is no further speech or description.
Third: This person minutely observes their mind.

There are three reckonings regarding the existence of [substantial] characteristics; two of these are as follows. First is the reckoning: the commentary states that this is also the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Each has its own location, and through them, realization is attained.
The commentary states: This refers to the locus where the skandha of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) arises moment by moment.
When someone comes to question him, he answers with only a single word, merely saying "it is so. Apart from this, there is nothing further he can say.
The subsequent answer. The commentary states: When someone comes to inquire, they all say "it is.
There are four such instances where one perceives both existence and non-existence;

these constitute two sections of the text concerning the dualistic calculations of existence and non-existence. First is the calculation [of existence]. The commentary states: Existence is birth; non-existence is...
When they cease, one then perceives within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) both the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Because their objects are manifold, the mind is likewise distracted. The Commentary states:
"The arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations is like the branches and twigs of a tree; now, upon this aggregate of formations, there is arising and ceasing."
This is based on the complete formulation.
If someone comes and asks, one answers: "That which is 'also existent' is precisely 'also non-existent'; within that which is 'also non-existent,' it is not 'also existent.'"
All such evasive confusion cannot be subjected to rigorous interrogation.
Regarding the subsequent answer, the commentary states: "Even within non-existence, it is not the case that there is existence. One does not realize this after the cessation of this thought.
To further contemplate where [the mind] arises and yet fail to attain the supernormal power of knowing others' minds—
thereby engaging in speculative reckoning, evasive confusion, and nihilism, falling into the ranks of the heterodox and deluding the nature of Bodhi—
is called the fifth type of heterodox practitioner: those of the four inverted natures who practice "evasive death-denial" and engage in pervasive, empty theorizing.
The subsequent section concludes with a pair of verses.
Furthermore, among the good sons within *samādhi*, their upright minds are firm and concentrated.
Regarding the three sections of the sixty-sixth fascicle on "Characteristics" (*sanimitta*), the first provides a general heading. The commentary states: "Thus, they are firm, solid, and luminous."
Rectify the mind;
then Māra will find no opportunity. Examine the fundamental source of all living beings—that which is profoundly still yet constantly agitated.
The commentary states: "Examine" is the act of observing; "that which is profoundly still" is the object of observation.
Regarding the "inexhaustible flow," the commentary states:
The incessant transition of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is called the "inexhaustible flow"; one then gives rise to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) upon this very basis.
This person falls into the inverted resolve that after death there is perception.
The commentary states: This person falls into the view that after death this body certainly exists, and that by generating such a resolve one will find peace and happiness;
they then seek peace and happiness therein. Both of these are inverted, deluded views.
Alternatively, one may firmly grasp the body, thinking, "Form is the self.
Next, the text is explained in three parts. First, form is cited to clarify its characteristics. The commentary states: "Alternatively, one may firmly grasp one's own body."
They grasp at the path. They hold that the five faculties, the five objects of form, and the forms subsumed within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are all the self.
Just as my ornaments always follow me, or as they see me perfectly encompassing the entire realm of lands, they say, "I possess form."

The commentary states: "Or, one may perceive my perfect, harmonious, and all-pervading realm, and calculate that 'I possess the matter of the five sense organs, the matter of the five sensory objects, and the matter subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), just as my wife and children are mine.'"
"Or that former object follows me in my movements; thus one says, 'Form belongs to me.
The commentary states: Or one calculates that the former object is merely form, which follows one's coming and going;
thus one says, 'Form belongs to me,' like a servant belonging to me."
Alternatively, one may rely on the continuity within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and think, "I am in form.
The commentary states: Alternatively, one perceives the nature of the self and, relying upon and clinging to the aggregate of formations, it arises and ceases in continuous succession.
They say, "I am always within form; form is my dwelling place," and they all engage in conceptual speculation, saying, "After death, there is perception.
The commentary states: They all engage in conceptual speculation, saying that after death, this bodily form definitely exists.
In this manner, they circulate, comprising sixteen perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
The subsequent three aggregates follow the same pattern as above. The commentary states: "In this way, they circulate back and forth, consisting of sixteen perceptions.

Each aggregate possesses four; four times four makes sixteen. As it says in the section on the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*): 'Sensation is me,' 'I possess sensation,' and 'Sensation [is mine]...'"
"It belongs to me; I am in sensation. The remaining aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) are likewise.
From this delusion, one calculates ultimate affliction and ultimate enlightenment;
subsequently, one calculates both the real and the false. The commentary states: "One clings to the false and the real as being distinct from one another; affliction is simply affliction."
Bodhi is bodhi. The two natures proceed side by side, yet each does not touch the other.
The commentary states: "The two natures are both left behind; each is entirely unrelated to the other."
Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of mind which posits that within the five aggregates there is the perception of existence after death.
The following is the double conclusion. The commentary states: "Among the five aggregates, this refers to the calculation of four aggregates.

Furthermore, within the state of *samādhi*, sons of good family who maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind will not be given an opportunity by demons; they exhaustively investigate the fundamental nature of all living beings.
Contemplating that profound clarity, one observes its ever-disturbed source. Within the prior elimination of form, sensation, and perception, [there are] three sections on the signless text.
First is the general heading. The Commentary states: "The past has already transcended the three aggregates."
Regarding "reckoning with livelihood": this person falls into the inverted resolve of aspiring for non-conceptuality after death.
The commentary states: "One then gives rise to such reckonings upon this very basis, generating a mind of aspiration for peace and happiness."
One perceives that as form ceases, its physical manifestation has no further basis.
Next, the explanation of the text is divided into three parts; the first provides a single clarification. The commentary states:

"One perceives that the forms of the five sense organs, the forms of the five sensory objects, and the forms subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) have already ceased. This physical substance no longer has any further cause or support."
Observe the cessation of these perceptions; the mind is then unattached. The commentary states:
"The past has already emerged from the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and is devoid of grasped images. If there were grasped images, there would be something to which one is bound by form.
This passage on perception should logically follow the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha); its placement here is likely due to a scribal error.
He knows that feeling has ceased and there is no further succession.
The commentary states: Having emerged from the aggregate of feeling, there is no longer any reception; therefore, there is no succession.
The nature of the aggregates has dissolved and dispersed.
The commentary states: "This means that the mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) now dissipate in succession;
even if there is the principle of arising, there is no sensation (*vedanā*) or perception (*saṃjñā*), and one is the same as grass and trees.
The commentary further states: "Even if there were the principle of arising and ceasing, how would it differ from grass and trees? It is just as [the past] has already ceased to exist."

The three aggregates of form, feeling, and perception—these are entirely absent in this [state of] the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It is the same as grass and trees; there is no experiencing and no grasping of objects.
How does this differ from the insentience of grass and trees? This is a misconception regarding the aggregate of formations.
If this physical form cannot be apprehended even while it is present before one, how could there be any further characteristics after death?
The commentary states: "If this shape and substance do not exist even when manifest before one, how could they exist after death?"
Based on this, he investigated and examined [the matter]. After death, there is no form (*nimitta*).
The commentary states: "Because of this, through exhaustive investigation and critical examination, it is determined that after death there is no body.
Thus it cycles; there are eight such states of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Next is the "reversal-binding. The commentary states: "Circulation" refers to the sense of coming and going. Regarding the eight types of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*):

in the case of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the past is non-existent, while the present and future are existent; yet in the future, it is again non-perceptive, the past is existent, and the present and future are non-existent.
The same applies to the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*). In all cases, one calculates that the past is existent while the present and future are non-existent.
There is no coming. One aggregate has two absences; four aggregates constitute eight absences. This is a solitary reckoning of non-existence.
From this delusion, one reckons that the causes and effects of nirvana are all empty, existing only as mere names, ultimately subject to total annihilation.

This is a separate calculation made later. To say that *nirvāṇa* is real while cause and effect are false means that when one realizes the mind and does not perceive the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), then both the real and the false are entirely absent;
if even the Buddha-body does not exist, how can one speak of the existence of karma? The Commentary states:

"From this point on, those who deludedly calculate *nirvāṇa* and so forth" refers to those who deny [the truth] and fall into nihilism, descending into the void of the evil realms. The Sub-commentary states: "Realizing the mind and not seeing..."
Regarding the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): this is because one realizes that the mind perceives neither the signless (*animitta*) nor the non-sign (*animittatā*), for this is the true mark.

To negate it as being identical to annihilation would mean that even the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*) does not exist; how then can karma be said to exist? To say this is a false attachment (*mithyā-abhiniveśa*). If one negates the Buddha-body as being the same as nothingness, what could possibly exist in such a delusion?
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the heterodox and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox school’s inverted doctrine of non-perception after death established within the five aggregates.
The following is the double conclusion.
Furthermore, O good sons among the practitioners of samādhi, when you stabilize and concentrate your correct mind, Māras will find no opportunity.
You exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, observing that source of profound purity which is constantly subject to agitation. Amidst this state of active practice:

Regarding the "eight eights" and the "neither-nor," there are three textual sections. First is the general heading. The commentary states: "Within the persistence of formations (*saṃskāra*), death has already occurred within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), while simultaneously involving the cessation of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)."

The commentary states: In the past, one has already emerged from the perceptions of the *skandha* of form (*rūpa*) and the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā*), yet still dualistically reckons in terms of existence and non-existence.

The commentary states: One reckons that the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra*) exists in the present but was non-existent in the past; as for form, sensation, perception, and so forth, in the past...

Some perceive this as existent, while others perceive it as non-existent. They calculate that the present aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is existent, whereas sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, are non-existent;
thus, their own essential natures contradict one another.
The commentary states: "If one says they are existent, existence again negates non-existence; if one says they are non-existent, non-existence again negates existence."
This person falls into the nihilistic doctrine that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, giving rise to inverted views.
The commentary states: "Neither existence nor non-existence after death" means that both existence and non-existence are simultaneously refuted;
within form, sensation, and perception, one perceives both existence and non-existence.
Next, the detailed explanation of the text has three parts. First is the general clarification. The commentary states: "Regarding these three aggregates (*skandhas*):
in the past, they existed within these three aggregates; now that one has emerged from those three aggregates, they no longer exist in the present or the future."
Within the flux of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one contemplates that they are not non-existent.

The commentary states: Because we are currently within the gate of practice (*caryāmukha*), when contemplating the past, [formations] are non-existent; hence it is said, "contemplating them as non-existent.
However, in the present and future, they arise moment by moment; hence it is said, "not non-existent."
Thus they circulate in this manner, exhausting the aggregates (*skandha*) and the realms (*dhātu*).

[The text] states: "Resolutely calculating, [one finds that] among the five aggregates and eighteen realms, eight are neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The commentary (*jìan*) says: "That is to say, within the five aggregates and eighteen realms, eight are neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

The commentary states: Regarding form, sensation, and perception, they existed in the past but do not exist in the present. Regarding formations, they were non-existent in the past but exist in the present.
Since they were non-existent in the past, how could they exist in the present? As for form, sensation, and perception, they existed in the past but do not exist in the present.
Since they do not exist in the present, how could they have existed in the past? Thus, one aggregate possesses two "non-existences," and the four aggregates together constitute eight.

Neither [of these two]. This view differs from the previous one. The former eight [views] were characterized by the absence of marks (*animitta*); they merely held that the past and future do not exist, while the present exists.

Regarding form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*), they likewise held that these existed in the past but do not exist in the present or future. In this [present case], however, all [four aggregates] are simultaneously neither [existent nor non-existent].
"Whichever single condition one encounters.
The commentary states: "This merely cites one aggregate as being neither [existent nor non-existent]; the others are likewise so.
All are said to be 'with perception' or 'without perception' after death."
The commentary states: "To calculate both existence and non-existence simultaneously, and to refute them both simultaneously, results in neither being the case.
Furthermore, it calculates all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*);

this will be explained separately later. The commentary states: "This refers to calculating the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) alone, whereas the previous [calculation] encompassed all four aggregates."
"Because the nature undergoes transformation and corruption. The commentary states: "Transformation means change; corruption means alteration.
The mind gives rise to penetrating awakening."
The commentary states: "In this preceding realization within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations), both existence and non-existence are negated.

The commentary further states: "Even though one is calculating the path of formations alone, there too both existence and non-existence are negated; for instance, the past of the *saṃskāra-skandha* is [negated]."
There is no [existence]. That which is present is existence; thus, both non-existence and existence are simultaneously refuted, and the distinction between the void and the real is lost.
The commentary states: "The void is non-existence; the real is existence. Since now both are negated, one loses the proper course of action."
Based on this, they speculate that after death there is "neither [perception] nor non-perception.

Regarding the subsequent double conclusion, there are two parts: first, concluding the preceding false speculations. The commentary states: "All say that after death there is neither [perception] nor non-perception."
There is no further existence;
the future limit is shrouded in darkness.

The commentary states: "The 'future limit' refers to subsequent moments of thought. Furthermore, one is unable to give rise to wisdom or penetrate the principle, remaining obscured, dim, and ignorant.
Because there is nothing that can be spoken of, one falls into the ways of the external paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
The commentary states: there is no Bodhi upon which one can rely; or, it may be understood as the Principle (*li*). This means that at the limit of Principle, there is nothing upon which to rely.

One must not dogmatically cling to the idea that emptiness is not non-existence but is wondrous existence (*miaoyou*), for this reveals an ignorance of the fact that wondrous existence is true emptiness (*zhengkong*) and true emptiness is wondrous existence.
There is. This is called the eighth heterodox doctrine among those established within the five aggregates: the deluded theory that after death one neither exists nor does not exist.
Hereafter, it will be revealed as falling into a false school.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, such that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.
If, subsequently, they harbor speculative calculations regarding its non-existence, [they fall into error].
Section Nine: Seven Annihilationist Views, Part Three. First, the general heading. The Commentary states:
"To say that after death in this body there is no further body—that person falls into the seven annihilationist views."

The commentary states: To regard the cessation of these seven types as *nirvāṇa* and to seek peace and bliss therein is to negate cause and effect, thereby falling into the void of the evil destinies.
Or one calculates that the body is annihilated.

Next, the text is explained in two parts: first, it is clarified according to the sequence [of the five aggregates], and then individually. The commentary states: "One calculates that after this body composed of the five aggregates is severed and extinguished, it will not be born again."
"Or [desiring] the extinction of desire.
The commentary states: This refers to the Desire Realm; one no longer takes birth in the Desire Realm. Below this, there is a missing passage:
"or the extinction of sorrow. This refers to the First Dhyāna. Various teachings state that the First Dhyāna is free from sorrow.
"Or the suffering is exhausted and extinguished.
The commentary states: "This refers to the second dhyāna; one emerges from the suffering of the second dhyāna.
Or it is extinguished in ultimate bliss."
The commentary states: In the third dhyāna, one is free from suffering and experiences pure bliss, or there is the extinction of [feeling] through ultimate equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The commentary states: The fourth dhyāna is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness; it is devoid of the two sensations of suffering and pleasure. Below this, the text is missing.
Form ceases. Question: The sutra speaks only of five; why are two added? The commentary answers: By searching according to principle, there is no contradiction in the logic.
Thus, through this cycle, one exhausts the seven limits until they are extinguished before one’s eyes; once extinguished, they do not exist again.
The commentary states: To say that after this body perishes it will not be born again is to engage in the speculative calculation that death results in annihilation.
By doing so, one falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
The subsequent passage collectively summarizes the total number.
This is called the ninth heterodox doctrine: the inverted view that the five aggregates cease and perish after death.
The final section provides a double conclusion.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized and concentrated their correct minds so that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
Observing that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, they subsequently give rise to speculative calculations regarding future existence.

Section Fifteen: The Text on Nirvāṇa, Part Three. First, the general heading. The Commentary states: "If, after this present body, one believes there is yet another body, such a person has fallen into the doctrine of the five nirvāṇas."

The commentary states: "To falsely reckon the five places as being peaceful and blissful. Regarding the meaning of *nirvāṇa* as quiescent extinction, some take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the true basis of transformation (*parāvṛtti*).
Next, the text is explained in two parts; first, the single clarification of the desire and form realms. The commentary states: "This refers to after one has cast off this present body..."
Furthermore, when taking birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one relies upon that desire realm and perceives it as perfectly luminous;
because of this, one gives rise to attachment and longing. The Commentary states:
"Either through the intrinsic luminosity of nature, or by calculating a self-soul (*ātman*); 'perfectly luminous' takes the latter meaning."
Or it is because the nature of the first dhyāna is free from sorrow;
the commentary states that the first dhyāna is without sorrow.
Or it is because the mind of the second dhyāna is free from suffering.
The commentary states: "In the second dhyāna there is no suffering;
this is because the third dhyāna follows upon extreme joy.

The commentary states: "Joy" means *prīti*. This refers to the fact that the third dhyāna is pure bliss (*sukha*); alternatively, when there is extreme joy, there is no longer the [distinction of] joyful elation (*prīti*).
"Or, in the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure are extinguished.

The commentary states: "This means that the fourth dhyāna is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness; therein, the suffering of the first dhyāna and the pleasure of the second dhyāna are extinguished."
"Not subject to saṃsāra.
The commentary states: "Calculating these five bases of reliance as being non-saṃsāric, because their nature is that of arising and ceasing."
The commentary states: "When viewed from the perspective of the Buddha-ground, these are all of the nature of arising and ceasing.
To be deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (āsrava) and to interpret them as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is the point.
The commentary further states: "This refers to being deluded regarding the heavens of outflows and forming views and interpretations of them as unconditioned."
The five locations are secure and provide a supreme, pure basis.
The commentary states: they serve as the support for that which is particularly excellent and pure.
Thus, through this cycle, the five locations reach their ultimate consummation.

The subsequent passage summarizes the total number. The commentary states: "Taking these five locations as the ultimate refuge, one thereby speculates that there is nirvana in these five present states.
Thus falling into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi, this is called the tenth heterodox doctrine:
the inverted theory of establishing nirvana in the five present states within the five aggregates."

The subsequent conclusion is as follows. The intent is as previously stated: to comprehensively search through the various views, to grasp the stem and exhaust the sprouts, and to establish the true standard for the path of awakening.

One should accordingly provide exhortations for study. The commentary states: "The *shu* (sub-commentary) says 'comprehensively searching through the various views' connects what precedes with what follows; 'grasping the stem and exhausting the sprouts' [refers to this]."
This encompasses the deluded views from beginning to end.
Ānanda, regarding these ten kinds of deranged understandings within *dhyāna*, there are two sections in the concluding exhortation.
First, the initial concluding section has two parts; the first summarizes the preceding deranged understandings. The commentary states: "Deranged understanding."
Thus, these deluded and chaotic views are all the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations). "The mind and its objects interact" (*yòngxīn jiāohù*).
The commentary states: "The mind and its objects interact and exchange. This means that one is seized by the power of Māra, who uses his demonic mind to replace one's own mental formations.
The mind of man;
therefore, this awakening manifests.
The commentary states: "This illusory understanding and awakening manifests."

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering this manifestation before them, they mistake delusion for understanding and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Later, those who falsely claim realization will invite a downfall into the depths.
You must take the heart of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit it during the Final Dharma, causing it to reach all sentient beings everywhere.

Having realized this meaning, the subsequent exhortation consists of two parts. First, regarding the far-reaching proclamation at the end of the Semblance Dharma age, which comprehensively clarifies the true teaching. The commentary states:
"The preceding sections all spoke of the Tathāgata’s words; why, in this section, does it speak of the Tathāgata’s mind? It is because [the teaching] flows forth from the fundamental wisdom."
It is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). From this subsequently attained wisdom flows forth the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*);
from the mind of great compassion flow forth the Three Vehicles and the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). Therefore, it is called "mind."
Do not allow the demon of the mind to give rise to its own pure afflictions;

later, having distinguished errors and returned to the source, one realizes the true and manifests the wondrous. The commentary states: This refers to the *xing-yin* (skandha of formations), where deluded calculations lie hidden and submerged.
All these are demonic aberrations.
Protect and shield them; cause their false views to subside; instruct their bodies and minds so that they may awaken to the true meaning within the Unsurpassed Way.
"One does not encounter branches or forks.
The commentary states: "The division of a tree is called a branch; the division of a road is called a fork. This is a metaphor for these deluded attachments and the realms of demonic interference;
do not allow the mind to seek them out, nor be satisfied with having attained only a little."
The commentary states: "To pray for.
It means to act as the pure pointer of the Great Awakened King.
The commentary states: "To speak thus" means to act as the pointer and guide of the Great Awakened King.

Ānanda, regarding that son of good family: Section Five, "The Aggregate of Consciousness," Part Two. First, the clarification of the ten differences in the source of delusion, Part Three. First, the general heading, Part Three.

First, encompassing the preceding practices to their end, Part Two. First, the heading on exhausting the nature of karma. [The] Commentary states: This refers to the preceding [discussion of] movement and stillness... not...
Shift. Recollection and forgetfulness are as one; you should rely on the person within this state to cultivate samādhi.
Regarding "the extinction of the saṃskāra-skandha," the commentary states:
those who have already exhausted the saṃskāra-skandha in the past are [realized to be] the provisional nature of the five aggregates.
"The nature of all worlds. Commentary:
Thus, the migration, flow, and activity of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) constitute the nature of the world.
Subtle clarity and turbulent movement are the generative impulses of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The commentary states: Thus, the twelve classes of sentient beings, relying on the subtle mechanism of the arising and ceasing of this *xing-yin* (formative aggregate),
simultaneously undergo a sudden disintegration within their respective stages.

The commentary states: "To 'shatter' (huī) is also to tear, like the ripping of a garment. This refers to having already emerged from the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), which is a deep and subtle net and cord.
The commentary further states: "Thus, the aggregate of formations is profound and subtle. A 'cord' (gāng) is a large rope within a net; 'subtle' (xì) refers to that which sustains all [phenomena]."
"Afflictions (*kleśa*). This is a general designation for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "Breaking through these afflictions" refers to the *pudgala*.

The commentary states: the Chinese term is "one who repeatedly takes up [existence]" (*shùqǔqù*). This means that within the aggregate of formations, one repeatedly takes up and repeatedly undergoes birth.
"Recompense for karma is the deep pulse. The commentary states:
This refers to the twelve classes of beings, who establish their "pulse" by recompensing causes and responding to effects. It is likened to the human pulse:
if the pulse exists, the body remains; if the pulse ceases, the body perishes. The pulse is like the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
"The resonance between cause and effect has been severed.

The commentary states: "This means that the faculty of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which is now already severed, is the agent of resonance; the twelve classes of sentient beings are the objects of that resonance."
Regarding "the heaven of nirvāṇa":
the commentary states that "heaven" is a metaphor for luminous purity and sovereign mastery; "nirvāṇa," on the other hand, refers to the principle (li).
It signifies that one is about to achieve great enlightenment and awakening.

The commentary states: "Enlightenment is also awakening; this is wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, when practice reaches its consummation and one awakens to the principle, initial awakening-wisdom (*ādikṣa-bodhi-jñāna*) unites with fundamental awakening-principle (*mūla-bodhi-tattva*).
It is like waiting for the cock to crow and looking toward the east: there is already a lustrous radiance."
The subsequent metaphor illustrates perceiving the true luminosity. The commentary states: It is like waiting for the cock to crow to signal a traveler;

having already departed from the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and reached the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), if the substance of consciousness is itself the truth, then its phenomenal characteristics are delusion. The East is the foremost among all directions.
The six sense organs are empty and still.

The subsequent sequence regarding consciousness remains as the text in three parts. First, it clarifies emptiness and stillness. The commentary states: "The six sense organs are empty, penetrating, and tranquil.
The six sense organs are all transformations of the eight consciousnesses.
"There is no further racing or wandering.

The Commentary says: "There is no longer any rushing flow or dissipation; one is precisely within the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate), where both internally and externally there is profound clarity."
The commentary states: "The internal refers to consciousness; the external refers to the receptacle world and so forth.

'Entering that which has nothing to enter'—the commentary states: 'Entering' is the act of entering; 'that which has nothing to enter' is consciousness. However, both establishment and enjoyment proceed from [consciousness]."
The eight consciousnesses arise. Now, by subsuming the derivative into the fundamental and subsuming the phenomenal into the noumenal, one enters that which has nothing to enter.
One profoundly penetrates the twelve types of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the ultimate source from which their lives originate.

Next, the manifestation of penetrating the truth reveals that conditioned activities are the fundamental cause. The Commentary states: "Conditioned activities" refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which serves as the fundamental cause for the twelve classes of sentient beings.
One contemplates this cause by grasping its fundamental source.

"Comprehending birth, abiding, and stillness. The commentary states: "This is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The sub-commentary says: 'To comprehend birth, abide, and be still' means that once one comprehends the birth of the aggregate of formations, its stillness cannot be summoned by any category [of conceptualization]."
"The seeds of birth do not assemble. The commentary states: "There are no further causal origins for the twelve classes of beings that can be summoned. The sub-commentary says:
"The statement that 'the seeds of birth do not assemble' means that there is no seed-nature for the twelve classes of beings within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)."
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they have already attained their commonality;
the manifested forms are identical with the substance. The commentary states: "Thus, they all return to the essence of consciousness;
the refined colors do not sink."

"The mind manifests stillness. The commentary states: "Thus, when the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is absent, the formation aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) reveals its profound mysteries;

one perceives the fundamental source of birth as the manifest self-characteristic of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The commentary further states: "This refers to the primordial source of the twelve classes of sentient beings."

This practice returns to the fundamental storehouse, which is the *vijñāna-skandha*. This means that the eight consciousnesses are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the self-characteristic of the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, these eight consciousnesses are pure and stainless; alternatively, simply realizing the nature of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is itself the Dharmakāya.
This is what is called the realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The following is the concluding summary. The commentary states: Within the first three categories, the concluding summary identifies the characteristics of consciousness.
If, among the various summonings, one has already attained identity within them...

The subsequent section, "Revealing the Exhaustion of the Aggregates," consists of three parts. First is the clarification of the characteristics of exhaustion. The Commentary states: "If, within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one brings forth the nature of that aggregate of formations so that it is identical to the essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)."
"The six gates are worn away; their simultaneous closing and opening is accomplished. The commentary states:
"There are no longer any obstructions closing off the gates of the six sense organs. The eye was obstructed by the dust of forms; the ear was obstructed by the dust of sounds.
Now that one has emerged from the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate), the six organs attain mutual correspondence, such that they close and open all at once."
A single faculty gives rise to consciousness, which universally conditions all objects;
seeing and hearing thus reach their respective neighbors.
The commentary states: "Seeing" refers to the eye; "hearing" refers to the ear. Each specifically reaches its immediate neighbor.
Mutual application is pure.
The commentary states: "If one attains this mutual application, there is purity; if one does not apply them mutually, there is turbidity throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
The commentary states: "This refers to the vessel-world as the basis, as well as the body and mind.
The commentary further states: "The body is that which is supported."
"Like pure lapis lazuli.
The commentary states: "When the substance is pure and both inside and outside are transparently clear, it is called the exhaustion of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate)."
The commentary states: "When the internal and external are transparently clear, this person is able to transcend the turbidity of life.

Next, it describes transcending the mundane. The commentary states: "Life is the functional capacity of the eight consciousnesses to maintain continuity without interruption; now that [this has been severed]..."
When it emerges, there is no turbidity of destiny.
Observing its origin, one finds that the formless, the void-primordial, and inverted false imaginings constitute its root.
Later, this reveals the fundamental source. The commentary states: "After emerging, one turns back to contemplate the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). "Wang" (罔) means "non-existent."

This is a pictograph. Delusion originally has no form; when one attains the truth, it appears like delusion. By tracing back to the source, it is fundamentally delusory; therefore, it is called "empty and primal" (*xūyuán*).
This refers to the original source of empty delusion.
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Ten, Part One;
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Ten (Part Two).
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Prajñāmitra;
the Śramaṇa of Udyāna, Meghaśikṣa, provided the oral interpretation;
and the Bodhisattva-śīla disciple Fang Rong transcribed the text.
Śramaṇa Weiqu of Daxingfu Monastery in the Western Capital, with a structural outline by Kaodu,
the Great Master of Śūraṅgama during the Song Dynasty, annotates:
"Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness."
The commentary states: "Within the present aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), the arising and ceasing has already been extinguished.
The commentary further states: "The arising and ceasing of the preceding aggregates has already been extinguished."
Yet regarding quiescence, his refined excellence has not yet reached perfection.
The commentary states: he has not yet attained the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), which enables him to cause the sense organs of his own body to either join together or separate.

Later, the mutual interpenetration is revealed. The commentary states: "The six sense objects are severed and opened; the six sense faculties are no longer obstructed by the gates of the six sense objects, thereby attaining their mutual functioning.
This is also identical to the pervasive awakening of all categories throughout the ten directions."
The commentary states: "The twelve classes of beings share equally in awakened illumination;
this awakened cognition universally permeates and is able to enter the perfect and primal source.
The commentary further states: "This awakened cognition and consciousness universally permeate and equally extinguish [delusion], being able to enter the essence of consciousness."

Regarding the refuge, the following section describes the original formulation of the thesis in three parts. First is the presentation of the thesis itself. The commentary states: "This refers to consciousness;
it establishes the cause of true permanence."
The commentary states: "Establishing this consciousness serves as the causal basis for the essence of true permanence.

Regarding "giving rise to resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*), the commentary states: "It gives rise to a distinguished understanding; its nature consists of maintaining a seal of certainty regarding the determined object, such that it cannot be led astray."
It transforms into karma.
This person then falls into the attachment to causes and what is caused by those causes.

Next, it reveals their falling into error. Regarding "causes and what is caused by those causes": the causes are the various phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), while that which is caused by them is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the cause of arising: because they do not understand that the nature [of things] is fundamentally without arising, they do not regard arising as the cause of arising.

Seeing the source of arising within their own minds, they consequently give rise to the fundamental attachment to a "cause. The commentary states: An outsider asks, "For what reason does this non-Buddhist (tīrthika) formulate such a calculation?
The answer is: "Because they see the source of arising within their own minds."
Śvika (Sobhikara). Later, he raised up those of his own kind. The commentary states: "In the language of Tang, this means the Yellow-Red-Colored Immortal.

He was a follower of the Samkhya and Vaiśeṣika masters who had returned to the Tattvas (Principles) to become their companion. He was deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and lost his true knowledge and vision."
The commentary states: Regarding the "Ultimate Truth of Obscurity" (míng dì), it is calculated that from the Ultimate Truth of Obscurity arises the Ultimate Truth of Awakened Nature (jué xìng dì).

From Awakened Nature arises the ego-sense (wǒ xīn); from the ego-sense arise the five subtle atoms (wǔ wēi chén); from the five subtle atoms arise the five gross elements (wǔ dà); from the five gross elements arise the five organs of cognition (wǔ zhī gēn);

and from the five organs of cognition arise the five organs of action (wǔ zuò yè gēn). Only thereafter does the organ of the mind (xīn píng děng gēn) arise. The divine self (shén wǒ) abides in the center, [remaining] inactive.
It decays but does not perish;

this is called the first established mind of attainment. It constitutes a fruit to which one has returned, yet it is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.
Later, they conclude by returning to deviant paths. Furthermore, the source of the mind is profoundly still and tranquil; this is the fundamental state of rest.

One does not grasp at permanence, for the original nature is inherently eternal. To forcibly establish a "cause of permanence" is to give rise to delusion; once such a cause is established, one must not allow it to arise falsely again.
When the deluded mind stirs once more, false habits are reborn. Failing to comprehend the true teaching, one falls into these deviant paths.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are good sons who have exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to the point of emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), their subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

This constitutes the second section on the attachment to "ability" and "inability. First, it clarifies that while they accord with quiescence, they are not yet perfected. The commentary states: "Although they have awakened to consciousness..."
[The section on] Characteristics. [This concerns those who] have not yet awakened to the nature of consciousness.

Regarding the destination they take refuge in, the following describes the threefold text concerning the fundamental establishment of their calculations. First, the heading for the establishment of their calculations. The commentary states: "This refers to consciousness."
"Taking it as one's own substance.

The commentary states: "To 'take' (lǎn) means to grasp. This refers to grasping this consciousness as the fundamental substance of one's own self, extending throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space."
The commentary states: "The space upon which they depend is included within the twelve categories.
The commentary states: "The sentient beings who depend [upon it] are the 'able-to-depend'."
"All sentient beings are of one kind flowing forth from within my own body.
The commentary states: "All flow forth from within my body as a single category of the nature of the *puruṣa* (spiritual self); this refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)."

Regarding "one who gives rise to resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*): the commentary states that one subsequently gives rise to resolute conviction toward this [object]. Its nature consists of confirming and maintaining a determinate object.
Such a person falls into the attachment of grasping at "the capacity to produce" and "that which lacks the capacity to produce.

Next, the text clarifies that they fall into error. The commentary states: They reckon the self to be the producer of the twelve classes of beings, asserting that these beings flow forth from within their own bodies, while those beings themselves lack the capacity to produce.

Maheśvara. Later, a similar term is cited. The commentary states: "In Sanskrit, it is Maheśvara; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means 'Great Sovereign' (Dà Zìzài). This [current form] is a corruption and abbreviation of that Sanskrit term."
He manifests as the Boundless Body (Anantatanu) to become his companion; thus they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.
The Commentary states: This deva clings to the "divine self" (*puruṣa*) as his nature, which pervades the lands and the twelve classes of beings.
From within his own body, it flows forth to serve as his illuminating companion and fellow traveler on the path.
This is called the second establishment of that which is capable of being the mind.
It subsequently concludes by returning to the deviant path. The commentary states: "It is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It accomplishes the fruit of capable activity."
The commentary states: "To grasp this consciousness as the fruit realized through the performance of karma is to distance oneself from perfect penetration and turn one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa.
The commentary further states: "To distance oneself from the wisdom of perfect penetration and turn one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is, in principle, [to err]."
Born into the Heaven of Great Arrogance (Mahāmāna).
The commentary states: This refers to the Mahāśvara Heaven (Maheśvara). The beings of this heaven have haughtiness as their nature; therefore, it is called "Great Arrogance.
It is the seed of my pervasive perfection.
The commentary states: It refers to the nature of the divine self (*puruṣa*), which is all-pervasive and perfect; this is the category [of beings] described here.

Furthermore, O son of good family, one who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state within quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected—this is the second stage.
The third section on "the permanent and the impermanent" consists of three parts. The first clarifies that while one follows the path toward tranquility, it is not yet perfected;
if, regarding that which is sought as a refuge, there is something upon which to rely.

The second describes the original establishment of conceptual constructs, consisting of three parts: the first marks the establishment of the construct. The commentary states: within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Having no refuge, one now arrives at this consciousness and immediately grasps this aggregate of consciousness as the locus of reliance,
suspecting that one's own body and mind flow forth from it.

The commentary states: "One suspects that this body and mind of one's own arise from within that *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate), and that the empty space of the ten directions all emerge from it.
The commentary further states: "The empty space upon which [all things] depend arises entirely within this *vijñāna-skandha*."
"Then, regarding the ground from which all that is proclaimed and issued forth arises.

The commentary states: This refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the place where both the internal body and the external vessel-world universally arise, and the ground from which they are proclaimed and issued forth.
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) here refers to the foundational basis.
"Forming the understanding that the true, eternal body is without arising or ceasing.
The commentary states: "True and eternal" refers to the *dharmakāya*. This means that one takes this mind of arising and ceasing and forms the understanding that it is non-arising and non-ceasing.
"Amidst arising and ceasing, one prematurely calculates it to be eternally abiding.
The commentary states: The World-Honored One refuted this by saying that, amidst arising and ceasing, one recklessly calculates this consciousness to be the nature of eternal abiding.
"Since delusion does not arise.
The commentary states: "Delusion arises and ceases; it is taken as the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing, yet one is likewise deluded regarding arising and ceasing."
The commentary states: "Since they are deluded regarding the True, they likewise do not recognize the False;
they dwell securely in their deep-seated confusion. Regarding the phrase "giving rise to resolute conviction," the commentary states:
"This refers to recognizing that which is submerged, hidden, deluded, and false."
Such a person falls into the attachment to permanence and impermanence.
Next, it reveals their falling into error. The commentary states: "They reckon consciousness to be permanent; they hold that the empty space of the ten directions flows forth from the self."
Thus, it is impermanent.
To reckon Īśvara as his companion is to be deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and to lose one's true knowledge and vision.
Subsequently, he cites similar cases.

This is called the third establishment of causes based on the mind: it accomplishes the fruits of false discrimination, distances one from perfect penetration, turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana,
gives rise to the seeds of inverted perfection,
and ultimately leads one back to deviant paths.

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to find them empty and having already extinguished birth and death, one may yet not have perfected the subtle and wondrous state within quiescent extinction.
Regarding the three sections on the four kinds of knowledge and non-knowledge: the first clarifies that while following toward quiescence, one has not yet reached perfection.

Regarding what is to be known, the following section describes the original formulation of the thesis in three parts. First is the presentation of the thesis itself. The commentary states: "This refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it is pervasive and complete."
The commentary states: It says that this nature of consciousness, which is the object of cognition, is all-pervasive and perfectly luminous;

based on this cognition, an interpretation is established. The commentary further states: Because this cognition is consciousness, it is immediately established as the "capable interpreter" (the subject).

The grasses and trees of the ten directions all possess sentience and are no different from humans. When grasses and trees become humans, and humans die, they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions.
The Commentary states: "For this practitioner, both the sentient and the non-sentient are seen to be transformations of the eighth consciousness; thus [one understands them as such]."
Thus they reckon: taking sentient beings to be non-sentient, and non-sentient things to be sentient beings.
This is merely a fabrication regarding cause and effect.
Those who harbor such views lack discerning universal knowledge and give rise to false convictions.
The commentary states: "Furthermore, there is no discrimination between the sentient and the insentient;
to calculate that there is a single conscious awareness, such a person falls into the attachment of 'knowing non-knowing.
Next, this reveals their fall into error."
Bhaṭṭācārya and Śākya.
Later, he raised up those of similar kind. The commentary states: "In the language of Tang, these are the 'Universal Awakeners' (Sarvabuddhins) among the non-Buddhists.
Clinging to the notion that all things are awakened, they became his companions; they were deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their true knowledge and vision."
The commentary states: "To maintain that both sentient and insentient beings alike possess consciousness is called the fourth view:
the calculation of the all-encompassing, cognizant mind.
It concludes by returning this to the path of heterodoxy. The commentary states: "This refers to calculating a mind that possesses all-pervasive, cognizant awareness."
It produces false and erroneous results.
The Commentary states: "To be deluded and mistaken; to grasp sentient beings as non-sentient;
to cast far away perfect penetration; to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana; and to give rise to the seeds of inverted cognition."
The commentary states: This is the seed-nature of inverted understanding.

Furthermore, O good man, although you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death, your subtle and wondrous realization within that state of cessation has not yet reached full perfection.

The passage on "five births and non-birth" consists of three parts. The first clarifies that while one accords with quiescence, it is not yet perfected. The commentary states: "One has not yet realized the substance of consciousness;
one only realizes the characteristics of consciousness.
This refers to the state of circular fusion.
Next, the exposition of the three sections on the text concerning the establishment of provisional views. First, the heading for the establishment of the views. The commentary states:
"This refers to having already attained conformity within the mutual functioning of the faculties, as described in the section on penetrating the *ālayavijñāna*."
The commentary states: This is because they reside within the *vijñāna-skandha*. One realizes that consciousness is singular; although the sense organs differ, consciousness does not differ.
Therefore, they function interchangeably, which facilitates the perfect transformation of all things and the generation of all phenomena.
The commentary states: Consider the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) as perfect and pervasive; it is capable of generating all dharma-realms and serves as the support for all dharmas.
One seeks the radiance of fire, delights in the purity of water, craves the circulation of wind, and contemplates the formation of dust—each of these being venerated and served respectively.
Taking these various sensory objects as the primary cause for their manifestation, they establish a view of permanence.
The commentary states: "The 'various sensory objects' refer to the four great elements and the external objects before one.
Such a person falls into the attachment to birth and non-birth."
Next, he mentions those who fell into error.
O Kāśyapas, later he mentions those of similar class. The commentary states: these were the fire-worshipping nāgas of Uruvilvā, Gayā, and Nadī.
The three Kāśyapas, together with the brahmins,
diligently applied their minds and exerted their bodies, serving fire and venerating water in their quest for liberation from birth and death, thus becoming his companions.
They have lost the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeited their true knowledge and vision.
The commentary states: "Brahman" (婆羅門) means "Pure Lineage" (淨胤) in the language of Tang;
some worship water and other such things—this is called the fifth type of attachment to veneration.
"Later, they bind themselves to deviant paths. The commentary states: This refers to the deluded generation of attachments, venerating and esteeming such things as the element of water;
with a deluded mind following external objects, they establish the causes for false seeking.
The commentary states: "To establish this delusion as the fundamental cause of what is sought;
to seek after delusion in the hope of attaining its fruit.
The commentary states: "To seek this delusion in the hope of relying upon it as the fruit."
They are far removed from perfect penetration and turn their backs on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the lineage of inverted transformations.
The commentary states: "They give rise to the species of inverted transformations.

Furthermore, O son of good family, you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction, your subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.
The sixth section, "Returning to the Non-returning," consists of three parts. First, it clarifies that while one may accord with quiescence, it is not yet perfected;
if, within perfect luminosity, one calculates the voidness within that luminosity.

Second, it describes the establishment of calculations based on what is shown, which has three parts. First, it sets forth the established calculation. The commentary states: "One calculates the substance of consciousness."
"Perfectly luminous. Within it is voidness, yet it does not extinguish the manifold transformations. The commentary states:
"This means that it is not by rejecting this consciousness [that one attains such a state]; rather, consciousness is that upon which the manifold transformations depend."
"By means of the eternal cessation of the basis.
The commentary states: "To take this consciousness as the basis for its eternal cessation and annihilation, so that it is eliminated without remainder, would mean that the evil realms are empty.
[Yet,] those who develop resolute conviction [in the Buddha] as their refuge..."
The commentary states: To take this eternal extinction as the place of refuge is for that person to fall into the attachment of "taking what is no refuge as a refuge.
Next, it clarifies falling into error. The commentary states: To reckon the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the place of refuge while being attached to emptiness is "no refuge."

In the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), subsequently citing those of the same class: beings in this heaven remain in meditative absorption for five hundred *kalpas*, during which the mental activity of perception (*saṃjñā*) does not function.

Within this context, by way of analogy, it is taken that in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) there are twenty thousand *kalpas*, in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) forty thousand *kalpas*, in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) sixty thousand *kalpas*, and in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)... [eighty thousand *kalpas*].

For eighty thousand kalpas in the realm of perception (*saṃjñā-āyatana*), they become companions to the *śūnyatā-rudras*. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their knowledge and vision. The Commentary states:
*Śūnyatā-rudra* refers to the spirit of emptiness; being bodiless, it subdues the sixth consciousness so that its active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) do not arise. As it is said:
The friend covers the fire;
this is called the sixth "Perfect Voidness of Mindlessness.
It concludes by returning to the deviant path. The commentary states: "Perfect voidness" refers to consciousness, and "mindlessness" refers to the emptiness of consciousness.
One achieves the fruit of empty extinction, straying far from perfect penetration and turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, thereby giving rise to the seed of annihilationism.
The commentary states: "To negate [existence] is equivalent to annihilationism; thus one achieves the fruit of empty extinction, being single-mindedly attached to emptiness."

Furthermore, son of good family: having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to reveal their emptiness, one has already extinguished arising and ceasing; yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), the subtle and wondrous [realization] is not yet perfected.
(The three sections on the seven types of craving and non-craving: first, clarifying that while conforming to quiescence, it is not yet perfected.)

Regarding the section on the "Perfect and Eternal," the following passage describes the formulation of a speculative theory based on the primordial source; this section consists of three parts. First is the presentation of the formulated theory. The commentary states: "Thus, consciousness is firmly established as the permanent abiding of the body."

The commentary states: To regard this precarious, illusory body as firm and constant, treating it as if it were the refined and perfect [essence], never to fall or pass away—this is what is meant by "giving rise to resolute conviction."
The commentary states: "To regard the pure, perfect, constant, and eternal as the Dharma-body, and to desire longevity by equating delusion with truth—
such a person falls into the attachment of craving for what is not craving."
Next, the falling into error is revealed. The commentary states: "Greed" refers to the arising of a greedy mind.
It means that one should not take what is inherently empty as being solid; it says that this body is not something to be craved.
The various Asitas;
later, those of his own kind were raised up. The commentary states: "In the language of Tang, this means 'Unconquerable' (Asita).
Those who sought long life became his companions; they were deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their true knowledge and vision."
The commentary states: Furthermore, these non-Buddhists seek the way of longevity and eternal vision.

Having heard that the Buddhas possess a true body and an eternal body that proceeds toward the Akaniṣṭha Heaven to manifest the Body of Self-Enjoyment—wherein every sense faculty and every object pervades the entirety of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu* and, throughout the limits of the future, constantly experiences the vast joy of the Dharma—they consequently form this attachment.
This is called the seventh attachment to the source of life. It establishes a cause of solid delusion, leading to the fruit of long-term toil;
it distances one from perfect penetration, turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of delusory extension.
Later, they conclude by returning to deviant paths. The commentary states: "This is solely a tendency toward the fruit of long-term toil and suffering.

Furthermore, O son of good family, though you have exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and have already extinguished birth and death, your subtle and wondrous state within quiescent extinction has not yet reached full perfection.
Section Eight: The True is Truly Non-existent, Part Three. First, it clarifies that while one accords with quiescence, it is not yet perfected;
one contemplates that life-force and destiny are mutually pervasive.

Next, it describes the establishment of conceptual calculations at the origin, in three parts. First, the heading for the establishment of these calculations. The Commentary states: "Contemplate this source of life-force."
This is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Its mutual interpenetration constitutes the opening and closing of the six gates.
Yet one leaves behind the dust of worldly toil, fearing that it might be entirely extinguished.
The commentary states: "If, having reached the aggregate of consciousness, it were to be exhausted, this consciousness would then become wisdom. Now, since you wish for it to be exhausted..."
He gave rise to this thought: "I shall instead leave behind these defilements, fearing that if they were entirely exhausted, there would be no basis for support.
Thereupon, at this juncture, he sat within a lotus palace.
The commentary states: "At this juncture, he manifested a precious lotus flower; within the flower, palaces and other structures appeared."

He extensively transformed the seven treasures and greatly increased the number of precious courtesans; those who gave rise to resolute conviction allowed their minds to run wild and indulged in the methods of defilement.
The commentary states: "Precious courtesans" refers to beautiful women adorned with exquisite jewels; they allowed their minds to run wild and practiced the methods of passion.
Such a person falls into the attachment that what is truly non-existent is real.

Next, the text reveals their fall into error. The commentary states: These non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as being real, failing to realize that its fundamental nature is the cause of birth and extinction; thus, it is not real.
Takṣaka became his companion; they were deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their wisdom and insight.

Later, another of the same kind was mentioned: Takṣaka, which in the language of Tang means "wood-seer" (or "tree-viewer"), referring to a category of beings, or perhaps an alternative name for Pāpīyān.
I have not yet dared to determine this in detail.
This is called the eighth cause for giving rise to perverse thoughts;
it subsequently leads one back to deviant paths. The commentary states: "This is the cause for giving rise to the conceptualization of perverse views."
Establishing the fruit of blazing afflictions, one becomes remote from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of Nirvana.
The commentary states: "To establish the fruit of such blazing afflictions is to adhere to the single dharma of defilement."
They give rise to the species of celestial Māras.
The commentary states: This is the same as the aforementioned category of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); they belong to the lineage of celestial Māras.

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet whose subtle and wondrous state within quiescent extinction is not yet perfected—

The subsequent section on the inferior vehicle consists of two parts. First, the section on the Śrāvakas has three parts. First, it clarifies that while they accord with quiescence, they have not yet reached perfection regarding the clarity of life.

Next, it describes the establishment of their fundamental calculations, which has three parts. First, it demonstrates that their realization of extinction stagnates in the provisional. The commentary states: "Life is the eighth..."
Consciousness maintains continuity without interruption; when clarified, its essence is perfectly luminous.
It discriminates between the refined and the coarse.
The commentary states: "The refined refers to the essence of consciousness; the coarse refers to the characteristics of consciousness."
The commentary clarifies the true from the false.

The sub-commentary states: "To 'clarify' means to discern thoroughly. The true is the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*); the false refers to the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Thus, upon the eight consciousnesses, there arise transformations such as the sense organs, the personal body, and the vessel-world."
"Causes and effects recompense one another.
The commentary states: "Citing one or two types of sentient beings, one recognizes the places where karmic fruits recompense their responses;
one seeks only for such resonance and response."
The commentary states: "The twelve categories are that which can respond; consciousness is that which is responded to.
They turn their backs on the path of purity.
The commentary further states: "In the stage of Buddhahood of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the three bodies and four wisdoms are entirely perfected."
The principle of purity is that which the noble ones of the Three Vehicles traverse; it is called the Way (*mārga*).
This refers to "seeing suffering and abandoning the origin" (*duḥkha-darśana-samudaya-prahāṇa*).
The commentary states: if this is the fruit of the world, then the origin is the cause of the world; thus, it is the fruit of seeing suffering, and [the origin] is abandoned.
This is the cause for their accumulation.

To realize cessation and cultivate the path—*jian* (commentary) states: the principle of cessation is the supramundane fruit; the wisdom of the path is the supramundane cause. This cites the supramundane.
The intermediate fruit causes one to enter by means of supramundane causes;
having abided in cessation, one rests.
The commentary states: One abides in the nirvāṇa of the emptiness of birth, taking it as the place of rest.
"He does not proceed further" means that one who has produced this resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) no longer advances toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Such a person falls into the category of a śrāvaka of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).
Next, the determination of their fixed nature is revealed. The commentary states: "Those of fixed nature" refers to those who do not turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the "monks who have heard nothing," the subsequent mention of those with increased pride is of the same category. The commentary states: this clarifies those who have not heard the Mahāyāna teachings.
Those with overweening pride become their companions; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

The Commentary states: "Overweening pride" refers to those five thousand who withdrew from their seats during the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as they gave rise to pride toward those of superior virtue.
This is called the ninth: "perfect purity responding to the mind.

It subsequently concludes by returning to the deviant path. The commentary states: "Perfect and pure" refers to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), which accomplishes the fruit of quiescent entry.
The commentary states: To take the emptiness of birth as the goal and nirvana as the fruit is the state that is realized;
yet this is far removed from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
The commentary states: Regarding the principle of the emptiness of arising, it refers to being exclusively attached to emptiness.

Furthermore, O son of good family, although you have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena and already extinguished birth and death, your subtle and wondrous realization within this state of quiescent extinction has not yet reached full perfection.
The subsequent section on the Pratyekabuddha has three parts. First, it clarifies that while they accord with quiescence, they have not yet reached perfection;

if one considers their state of perfect fusion, [the following applies]. Second, it describes how they establish conceptual calculations from the outset, which is divided into three parts. First, it demonstrates that their cessation of suffering remains stuck in the provisional. The Commentary states: "All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are fully..."
"Complete" means "round. When both substance and function have vanished, it is called "fusion.
"Pure, clear, and luminous awareness"—the commentary states:
this refers to the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
"Delving into the profound and subtle.

The commentary states: "That is, the wisdom of the emptiness of arising produced through preparatory application establishes *nirvāṇa* and does not proceed further. This refers to those who produce resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)."
The commentary states: "Thus, regarding the emptiness of persons and nirvana—if such a person exists, they fall into the category of a pratyekabuddha of fixed nature.
This next section clarifies the return to the state of fixed nature.

Those who follow various conditions and those who act alone, without turning their minds [toward awakening], become each other’s companions; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

Later, he cites those of the same class who harbor increased arrogance. The commentary states: "Various conditions" refers to those who travel in groups (*vargacārin*), while "acting alone" refers to those who are like the rhinoceros (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*).
This is called the tenth, the mind of the perfect awakening [yǒng-huì].

It concludes by returning to the deviant path. The commentary states: "Perfectly complete awakening and illumination extinguish that mind; this is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*)."
He achieves the fruit of profound clarity.

The commentary states: He realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), yet he remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns his back on the city of *nirvāṇa*. His awakening is perfectly luminous, yet it does not transform into the seeds of perfect [enlightenment].

The commentary states: Because these solitary realizers (pratyekabuddhas) do not delight in transforming sentient beings, Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* result in madness midway through their practice.

The concluding exhortation consists of three parts. First, the general explanation of the concluding exhortation has two parts. First, the concluding text itself has three parts. First, the presentation of what precedes.

"Establishing calculations. The Commentary says: To emerge from the preceding four aggregates (*skandhas*) means that within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), one has not yet emerged from this consciousness.
It is like a person walking halfway along a path; if one were to emerge from this consciousness, one would immediately attain Buddhahood.
Now, being currently caught in the midst of generating these false calculations is like becoming deranged midway through the journey.
"Based on and dependent upon delusion.

The commentary states: "Based on" means intimate reliance. This refers to intimately relying upon this delusive confusion, whereby one gives rise to the realization of fulfillment within what is not yet fulfilled.
The commentary states: For instance, those of the two vehicles, such as the śrāvakas, reach only the nirvāṇa of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) as their fulfillment.
All of these belong to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha). Because they employ their minds in a state of mutual interaction, they give rise to this stage.
The commentary states: "Positions" refers to the positions of the sixty-two heterodox views.

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When encountering these [realms] appearing before them, each acts according to their own cherished, previously habitual, and deluded minds.

Next, the cessation of delusion and the stabilization of practice are elucidated. The commentary states: "For example, when those of the two vehicles, the Śrāvakas, proceed toward the principle of the emptiness of persons, these are all objects of their prior attachment and habitual cultivation."
And he rests therein himself.
The Commentary says: He takes this as the place of cessation and repose;
he takes it as the ultimate ground of return and peace.
The commentary states: To take this very life’s emptiness and nirvana as the place of ultimate refuge is merely to reach the "transformed city" at three hundred *yojanas*;

one has not yet arrived at the Precious Place. Only when one proceeds directly to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and becomes a Buddha of Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), constantly experiencing the vast Dharma-bliss, does this truly become the place of ultimate refuge.
To claim for oneself that one has fulfilled unsurpassed *bodhi* constitutes a great falsehood. Such an outsider or demonic being will, when their karmic retribution ends, fall into the Avīci Hell.
Later, it will manifest that their falsehood invited stagnation. The Commentary states: "If such an outsider and the like have committed a great falsehood, they shall undergo [retribution]."
When the retribution for this evil karma is finally exhausted, one subsequently sinks into hell.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not achieve diligence.
