The commentary states: "If they are śrāvakas and the like, they are already satisfied with their own [attainments]; thus they do not achieve the diligence of unsurpassed bodhi."
"You shall not enter hell.
You must maintain this resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata; after my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this Dharma-gate to the final age."
May all sentient beings universally awaken to this meaning, so that they do not allow Māra to cause them to sink into calamity.

May they be protected, comforted, and rescued, with their deviant conditions extinguished, so that their bodies and minds may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From the very beginning of their accomplishment, may they never encounter divergent paths.
"Later Exhortation. The commentary states: "Sui" means to pacify and settle. You all should maintain focus on your minds so that other practitioners do not encounter such demons;
instead, you must ensure their security and offer them compassionate rescue.

In this manner, throughout the kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, countless Tathāgatas, like motes of dust, have awakened their minds by relying upon this Dharma-gate and attained the unsurpassed path.

Next is the general summary of the passage on transcending the ranks, in three parts. First, citing the common vehicle of past Buddhas. The commentary states: An outsider asks, "Is this Dharma-gate spoken by the Buddha for this [present] occasion, or was it spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods? The Sūtra answers: "Such a Dharma-gate" refers to the fifty kinds of demonic activities (*māra-karman*). Previously, in the past ages, there were many such [instances].... Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, how many Tathāgatas have there been within those kalpas? How did this Tathāgata attain the Unsurpassed Way?

It was by means of the opening of this mind that he attained the Unsurpassed Way. The above also concludes the answer to Ānanda’s request upon returning from the place of Matangi, where he invited the World-Honored One, saying:
"I regret that since beginningless time, I have focused solely on extensive learning, yet have not fully perfected the power of the Way."
Upon reaching the initial skillful means, if the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your present six sense faculties will function interchangeably.
Next, the manifestation based on transcendental realization is revealed. The commentary states: "This means that each of the six faculties attains the capacity for mutual exchange; first—"
The faculties give rise to consciousness, which universally perceives all objects.
From within this mutual functioning, one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *kandha-vidyā* (dry wisdom).
The commentary states: "Adamantine" is a metaphor; it signifies that this wisdom is like the vajra held in the hand of Vajrapāṇi.
"Rounding, clarity, and accumulated mind.
The commentary states: "The mind that is perfectly round, concentratedly clear, and subtle is the principle;
within it, transformation and manifestation arise."
The commentary states: This is the wisdom of the very essence that initiates transformations.

It is like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli; in this way, one transcends the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and the four minds of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).
The commentary states: These are the Bodhisattvas of the forty-four minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
This refers to the ten *vajra*-stages practiced by Bodhisattvas.

The commentary further states: These are the ten stages, beginning from the first, the Joyful (*pramuditā*), up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). For these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, each stage is...
This is the adamantine *śuṣka-prajñā* (dry wisdom).

It is the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), perfectly luminous. The commentary states: Following the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), there is the position of Equal Enlightenment; because principle and wisdom are equal, it is called "Equal Enlightenment. One thought-moment...
Because it is provisionally established within a single *kṣaṇa*, it is perfectly integrated, luminous, and enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments. The commentary states:
"This is the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). It is subtly adorned and purely embellished, dwelling in the land of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), like an ocean."
Vast, because it encompasses the qualities of nature;
it perfects Bodhi and returns to non-attainment.
The commentary states: "Attaining through non-attainment."
This is as follows: [It describes] the subtle demonic activities regarding the analytical discernment (*vipaśyanā*) within *śamatha* by the World-Honored Buddhas of the past;

subsequently, it clarifies the text in three parts concerning the certainty of realization through practice. First, it cites the past to demonstrate commonality. The commentary states: "The Buddha further feared..."
Intending to take this as his own realization, he then said: "This is the wisdom of the true awakening and concentrated clarity of the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
it is clearly and analytically expounded."
The realms of Māra appear before you; you are able to recognize them, wash away the defilements of the mind, and do not fall into false views.
This is used to exhort the removal of delusive confusion. The commentary states: Previously it was said that you had not yet recognized [these things];
now, having emerged from the five aggregates and transcended the five turbidities, it is said that you are able to understand, discern, and identify these realms.
The *skandha*-māras are extinguished; the celestial *māras* are shattered. The commentary states:
"The *skandha*-māras are the mental *māras*. When they arise from within the mind, the celestial *māras* attach themselves.
Greatly powerful spirits and deities lose their courage and flee; *chī-mèi* and *wǎng-liǎng* demons no longer manifest."
The commentary states: "To have one's soul and spirit stripped away" means that their souls and spirits are cast off.
Reaching all the way to Bodhi, they lack nothing whatsoever; those of inferior capacity advance, and regarding Great Nirvana, their minds are neither deluded nor distressed.

The subsequent section clarifies the direct advancement toward Bodhi. The commentary states: "Not being deluded means one is not disturbed by Māras; not being distressed means the mind does not engage in false conceptualization.
Alternatively, if one is deluded and does not awaken, or if one is distressed, one will not enter [the path]."

If there are sentient beings of dull faculties in the final age who, later, uphold these true phrases and texts—three in number—the initial section serves as a heading for the subsequent chapters. The commentary states: "That is to say, they are foolish, ignorant, and dull-witted."
"Unfamiliar with dhyāna.
The commentary states: "Dhyāna refers to the wondrous concentration;
[he] does not know how to preach the Dharma."
The commentary states: This means that one lacks wisdom or does not recognize Māra, yet claims that what Māra says is the word of the Buddha, and delights in practicing *samādhi*.
The commentary further states: "Delighting in the practice" refers to the cultivation of *samādhi-samāpatti*, which is an alternative name for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Fearing that you might fall into heterodoxy, I single-mindedly urge you to uphold this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra.
The commentary states: [The Buddha] entrusted Ānanda to focus his mind with single-minded concentration and to exhort all sentient beings to uphold the uṣṇīṣa mantra.
If one is unable to recite it, write it down in the meditation hall or carry it on one's person.

Next, encourage the recitation and transcription of the *Dharmapada* for the Exorcism of Demons (*Chumo*). The annotation states: "The meditation hall (*zendō*) is the hall where one sits in meditation."
"All demons. Commentary:
This refers to the various demon kings at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), by whom [the practitioner] cannot be moved.
The commentary states: "By the power of the mantra, they cannot afflict the practitioners. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice;
as the warmth gradually overcomes it, it will melt away before long."
"You should reverently honor the ultimate cultivation and final instructions left by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

Afterwards, you shall command that these teachings be respectfully circulated. The commentary states: "Fàn" (範) means "fǎ" (法, dharma). After forty-five years [of his ministry], the World-Honored One...
Having finished expounding this sutra, he immediately spoke of nirvana; this was the final teaching he bestowed.
Alternatively, these fifty layers of demonic activities were taught last, and for that reason it is called "the final."
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction and admonition, he prostrated himself in reverent acceptance, memorizing it without loss.

Hereafter, there are two sections: first, the text on the five further elaborations of the five contemplations; second, the text on the initial presentation of doubts and the request for resolution, which has five parts. First, hearing and upholding the sublime intent.

The commentary states: [The Buddha] again elaborates on the five misconceptions for Ānanda’s sake. He sees that the Buddha has taught that all five aggregates (*skandhas*) possess false conceptualization (*vikalpa*):
form is solid, sensation is empty and luminous, perception is pervasive and penetrating, formations are subtle and hidden, and consciousness is like a phantom image.
Since these five all possess false conceptualization, he immediately wonders: "If the colors of the five sense organs and the colors of the five sense objects are insentient, why..."
There is also deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). For this reason, the Buddha repeatedly granted [the disciples] a thorough understanding of these five types of conceptualization.
Within the sutra, there are three questions: first, the question regarding whether form (*rūpa*) is a deluded conceptualization, which I had not heard from the Buddha at that time;

second, the question as to whether the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are eliminated instantaneously or gradually; and third, the question as to what constitutes the boundary (*dhātu*) of the five aggregates. [The Buddha] then provided instruction and guidance.
It is as stated in the preceding text: "This is [the teaching of] the former Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones," and again:

"When the realm of Māra appears before you, [recognize it as] your own consciousness. It further states: "You should reverently honor the ultimate cultivation and progress of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."

In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "As the Buddha has said, among the characteristics of the five aggregates, these five kinds of falsehood constitute the fundamental thinking-mind.
Next, he restated the preceding passage.
"We, in our ordinary state, have not yet received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed exposition.
Thirdly, we have not yet been granted a brief proclamation. The commentary states: "First, regarding the question that form is a false imagination:

we, in our ordinary course, have not seen the Buddha provide such a subtle and meticulous opening and instruction. The intent of the question is simply this: as for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the four [aggregates]..."

The mental factors of the aggregate of form arise from this deluded imagination. For instance, as for the aggregate of form—namely, the forms of the five sense organs, the forms of the five sense objects, and the forms subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana)—these are insentient. Why, then, are they also called deluded imagination?
Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates (*skandhas*), are they eliminated simultaneously, or do they come to an end sequentially?
The fourth section describes the sudden and gradual [attainment] of the limit of the elements (*dhātu-paryanta*). The commentary states: This poses the question:
once the first aggregate has ceased, do the remaining five aggregates vanish all at once, or do they vanish sequentially until the fifth?
Thus there are five layers. To what do they refer as their "boundary" (*dhātu*)?
The commentary states: A boundary possesses four meanings: the meaning of cause, the meaning of nature, the meaning of category, and the meaning of lineage.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion;
I beseech you five times with pity to appear. The commentary states: "Thus Ānanda immediately requested instruction and its proclamation."
For the sake of this great assembly, he clarifies their minds and eyes.
The Commentary states: "Mind" refers to the true mind, which is principle; "eyes" refer to wisdom.
This is done to serve as the future eyes for all sentient beings in the final age.
The commentary states: This refers to this teaching as the eye for illuminating the Way and entering into principle for future generations.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essence is true, wondrously luminous, fundamentally awakened, perfect, and pure."

The subsequent extensive explanation of the preceding passage concerning doubt has two parts. First, the explanation of the term "conception" (*saṃjñā*) has two parts. First, the general presentation of the fundamental characteristics has three parts.
First, the general clarification of the true and the delusive has three parts. First, clarifying that the true is free from defilement. The Commentary states:
"All that above is the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*)."
It does not linger in birth-and-death, nor in the various defilements.
The commentary states: Within reality there is no delusion; it is like clear, still water, wherein there are no further dharmas such as the five aggregates, nor the defilements of karmic dust.
Even up to empty space, all are produced by the arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Next, space arises dependent upon conceptualization. The Commentary states: "This space is the seventh [consciousness] which clings to the eighth consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) as a self;
it transforms and gives rise to this additional layer of dark, dull, and stubborn emptiness."
This is the primordial fundamental enlightenment, the wondrously luminous true essence. Through delusion, it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds.
Later, one investigates how delusion originates from the True. The commentary states: "It is said that this illusory root-source is, from the beginning, the Truth."
Since it is thus, for what reason does delusion arise? It arises because all sentient beings, in a single thought-moment, deviate from Suchness (*tathatā*).

When the aspect of weariness is perceived, there immediately appear the false constructs of form, sensation, perception, and so forth. It is like clear, still water: when stirred by the wind, waves arise;
yet the nature of the water itself is without waves. Just as the true essence is without delusion, there is that upon which these [phenomena] depend.
Regarding the vessel-world and so forth, it is like Yajñadatta, who, being deluded, mistook his own head for its reflection.

Next, the passage concerning the elimination of dualistic attachments has three parts. First is the establishment of the analogy for delusion. The commentary states: "The head is a metaphor for the true mirror within."
This is like being deluded and losing one's original head, mistaking a reflection for the head. It is as all sentient beings lose their fundamental true nature and mistake the false for the true;
yet this falsity originally has no cause.
Next, the four sections describing false conceptualization are presented. First, the description of falsely establishing causes and conditions. The commentary states:
Regarding phenomena that are empty and false, they have no causal basis;
yet, within the midst of deluded thought, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions.
The commentary states: "Regarding the conceptualization of illusory marks... [omitted] ...this is what is clung to by those of the two vehicles within our own school.
Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions refer to them as 'spontaneous' (*svabhāva*)."
Next, the establishment of the deluded perspective is described. The commentary states: To grasp the nature of causes and conditions as being spontaneous is the view of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
That nature of space is likewise truly produced through illusion.
Third, the refutation of emptiness through illusion:
causes and conditions arise spontaneously; all are merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings.
Fourth, the double reproof of the two paths.

Ānanda, when one knows where delusion arises, one can speak of the causes and conditions of delusion. If delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then speaking of the causes and conditions of delusion would be fundamentally nothing at all;
how much more so for those who do not understand this and instead speculate that it is spontaneous?
Later, he rebuked him for speaking falsely. The commentary states: "I say that if you knew how delusion arises, I would grant your claim that it is caused by conditions.
But since delusion is fundamentally unformed, how much more so is it not known through conditions? Yet you instead cling to delusion as being spontaneous."
Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is identical: they are all false imaginings.
Later, he will further reveal that the aggregates share a common cause:
your own body was originally produced from the conceptualization of your parents; had your mind not been conceptualizing, it could not have entered into those conceptualizations to transmit life.

Regarding the perception of form: to say that this body is a material phenomenon (rūpa-dharma) means it cannot transmit life-force (*jīvita*) within the sphere of perception.
This refers to the first seven days of the *kalala* stage when it enters the mother’s womb; this is precisely when the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*) takes up residence in the womb.
"Life-force" (*jīvita*) is the functional capacity of the eighth consciousness to maintain continuity and prevent interruption.

As I have previously stated: when one contemplates the taste of vinegar in the mind, saliva is produced in the mouth; when one contemplates ascending a high place in the mind, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet.
Yet the precipice does not exist, nor has the sour object arrived.

Next, the dual analogy is cited to clarify the category. The commentary states that this refers to the passage in the second scripture, within the refutation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), concerning the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
It says: "It is like a person speaking of sour plums; water flows from their mouth. Or like one thinking of treading upon a precipice;

their feet tingle with a stinging sensation. Since these mouths and feet are both material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), by what cause do they experience such sensations arising from the mind of perception?
"Your essence must not be of the same category as false and illusory phenomena. The commentary states:
"Regarding 'your essence,' if it is certainly said not to be a false and illusory conceptual appearance, then it would be identical to and of the same category as [true] phenomena."
The text states by way of contrast: "Your own substance is precisely this; it belongs to the same category as that which is false and illusory.
How could saliva emerge from speaking of vinegar? The commentary notes:
"This indicates that [saliva] was previously known to belong to the same flow of the false and illusory."
Therefore, you should know that this present physical body of yours is called the first solidified false imagination.
It subsequently forms the initial eye;
it is precisely what is described here as the mind that conceives of being at a high precipice.
Next, "The Empty and Luminous Text," Part Two. First, "The Form Follows the Sour and Astringent. The commentary states: The Buddha is the speaker;
the mind that contemplates loftiness is that which is spoken of.
He can cause your form to truly experience sourness and astringency.
The commentary states: "To 'receive' (vedanā) means to accept or experience. Since it is capable of experiencing bitterness and astringency, it is 'reception.
Arising from the cause of reception, it is able to move the substance of form."
The commentary states: "Because one experiences sourness and astringency as causes, it can cause the physical body to have a sour mouth and numb feet.
Alternatively, what is here described refers back to the preceding text, thereby tracing down to the deluded thoughts [discussed below]."
Now, before you, the two—conformity and benefit, as well as opposition and harm—are actively at work; this is called the second delusive thought of "empty luminosity.
The subsequent summary refers to it by the name "receiving the void. The commentary states: "Conformity brings benefit, while opposition brings harm.
This is the objective realm perceived by the body. Receiving these two realms of conformity and opposition, the two manifest and drive one toward a state of turbulent flow."
"By means of your thoughts and reflections, you cause your physical body to move.
This section has two parts concerning the threefold integration. First, the form follows the movement of thought. The commentary states: "The mind drives the body."
"The body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
The commentary states: "This means that if the body were not of the same lineage as thought, for what reason would it be driven by deluded thoughts?"
Various forms are grasped; the mind gives rise to the apprehension of forms, corresponding with thought. When awake, this is the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams.

The commentary states: "Various" means not one and the same. The mind recollects the objects before it, and the physical body grasps them before it. One has previously known this to be the continuous flow of such thoughts.
Thus, your conceptualizations and the flickering of deluded sentiments are termed the third false discrimination, "Fusion and Pervasion" (Rongtong).

The concluding commentary states: "Fusion" means that the myriad phenomena are contained within the mind; "Pervasion" means that [the mind] extends outward to follow along with all objective conditions.
The principle of transformation does not abide.
Section Four: The Threefold Text on the Obscure and Hidden. First, the description of the subtle transition of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). The Commentary states:

This refers to transformation—the Way in which arising and ceasing pass from non-existence to sudden existence. As for its principle, the *saṃskāra-skandha* arises and ceases moment by moment, changing without ever remaining still.
Furthermore, it shifts and changes subtly with every movement.
The commentary states: "To move constantly is 'motion'; to shift subtly is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha). It migrates in secret, ceasing not for a single moment."
Nails grow long and hair sprouts; vital energy wanes and the face becomes wrinkled. Day and night they alternate with one another, yet there is never any awakening to this.
The Commentary states: "Alternating" refers to the succession of mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*), arising and ceasing in every thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).
"Ānanda, if this [activity-aggregate] were not you, how could its substance undergo transformation?
Next, even if one were to present both [possibilities], the commentary states: it means that if this activity-aggregate were not the delusion of your mind’s arising and ceasing..."
"How can there be such things as the wasting away of vital energy and the appearance of wrinkles?
If this must truly be the case, why do you have no awareness [of it]?

The commentary states: "If one claims that this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the true reality, for what reason does one not perceive the flux of hair growing and nails lengthening?"
Awakening is reality. Now you are not yet awakened;
having known this to be delusion, your various mental formations (saṃskāra) do not rest for even a single moment—this is called the fourth subtle and hidden false imagination.

The subsequent summary of the contemplation on the "mysterious name" (*you-ming*) states: "Mysterious" (*you*) refers to that which is latent, subtle, and difficult to know; "hidden" (*yin*) refers to that which is concealed within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Furthermore, it refers to your own brilliant clarity.
Section Five: The Text on the Non-Entity (Wǎngxiàng). Part One: The Initial Statement and Reprimand; Subsection One: Establishing the Permanence of the Body. The Commentary states:

This refers to that consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha), which constitutes the five and eight consciousnesses. As direct perception (pratyakṣa) facing objects, it does not differentiate between subject and object; therefore, it is called "vital clarity" (jīngmíng).
"Deeply still and unmoving. The commentary states:
"The eighth consciousness is thus subtle in its arising and ceasing; it cannot be seen when one looks at it, appearing as if it were unmoving, and is therefore called 'constant.'"
The commentary states: "The eight consciousnesses are merely constant and lack discernment" is a restatement of the preceding phrase.
Regarding the body, they do not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

Next, the specific functions of the consciousnesses are presented. The commentary states: "Seeing" refers to the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*); "hearing" refers to the auditory and olfactory consciousnesses; "sensing" [refers to...]

This is body-consciousness. It knows. This is tongue-consciousness and mental consciousness; that is to say, these are direct-perception consciousnesses (*pratyakṣa-vijñāna*) which are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective-image portions) of the immediate transformations of the eight consciousnesses.
This refers to the specific portion of the eighth consciousness.
If it were truly essential and authentic, it could not tolerate the practice of delusion.

The subsequent passage clarifies that it cannot tolerate the habitual practice of delusion. The commentary states: "If this were truly the Real, it would not be fitting for there to be the habituation of the breath-like phenomena of delusion."
For what reason did you all, having once beheld a wondrous object in years past, neither remember nor forget it throughout the passing of those years,
yet later, upon suddenly beholding that same object again, recall it with perfect clarity as if nothing had ever been lost?
Third, the passage on "the drawing forth of the entity containing perfuming" consists of two parts. First, the critique regarding the inclusion of remote habituation.

The commentary states: "Fu" means "repetition. This refers to the seeds obtained previously, which fall within the eight consciousnesses; when they encounter an object again, the seeds then give rise to actualized manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
Thus, within this essence that is lucid and unmoving, there is the continuous perfuming from moment to moment; what need is there for calculation?

Later, it is indicated that consciousness is suitable for perfuming. The commentary states: "Because this eighth consciousness, although it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is not a perfumer but only a perfumable object.
From moment to moment, it receives the seeds perfumed by the preceding seven consciousnesses, which then fall into it."
[It is] within [the realm of] calculation and numerical reckoning.
Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the true reality.
This section on the three comparisons of water’s hidden flow has three parts; first, it raises the point that consciousness is not the true reality.
It is like a rapid current of water that appears tranquil at a glance; the rapid flow is not seen, yet it is not that there is no flow.
This is comparable to a hidden, swift current. The commentary states: it is not that there is no arising and ceasing; rather, arising and ceasing are difficult to perceive.
If these were not the fundamental source of perception (*saṃjñā*), how could they receive the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of perception?

The subsequent reference to the habits being unreal means that if these eight consciousnesses were not the root-source of deluded thought (*vikalpa*), it would be illogical for them to receive all habit-energies;
since they now do receive habit-energies, one knows they have always been unreal.
It is not that your six sense organs can interchange their functions through either union or separation;
even with four fingers one may exhaustively investigate, yet the true and the false remain distinct. (Section Two: Textual Analysis).
First, it is raised that the mutual functioning is entirely true. This deluded thought can never be extinguished.
"Later, it reveals that delusion is exhausted. The commentary states: The sutra asks, "When will this consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) be exhausted?
The answer is: "As your six sense-faculties function interchangeably, this deluded thought has no time at which it can be exhausted.
This means that if your six sense-faculties were not manifest and were not closed off by the six sense-objects, then these six sense-faculties would have no time at which they could be dissolved.

To extinguish [the afflictions], one must first attain the mutual functioning of the six sense faculties. Only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood does one transform the eight consciousnesses to realize the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
When this consciousness is transformed, its name changes while its essence remains unchanging.

Therefore, among what you currently see, hear, perceive, and know, there is that which has been habitually practiced; it is a profound clarity within that is formless and void, yet fundamentally original.
This is the fifth inversion: a subtle, refined, and pure ideation.

The subsequent conclusion: The refined contemplation is named *Wangxiang Xuyuan*. "Wang" means non-existence. Being deluded regarding the fundamental, it has no form; deviating from the truth, it appears to exist.
When its source is traced back, it is fundamentally illusory; hence it is called "Empty Origin" (*Xuyuan*). Through inversion, the initial arising begins to condition one another;

through subtlety, the turning of karma becomes manifest. Through refinement, the single Truth merges in profound stillness; through contemplation, one suddenly yearns for perfect luminosity. This is the entangled root of birth and death.
This is the "Lan-hu" (The Barrier). The commentary states: "If one is inverted, then that which first arises is the object-condition.
This means that when the nature first arises as the aspect of clarity, the subtle karma evolves. The two consciousnesses do not speak of the "manifest" (*mian*);

the manifest is the essence of the eight consciousnesses. When it is refined, the One Truth is darkly unified; thus, a portion of the pure part within the eighth consciousness is the ninth consciousness, and therefore it is darkly unified.
[The text] joins. When one suddenly yearns for perfect luminosity (*pariniṣpanna*), then suddenly [the nature of] clarity becomes manifest.
This manifestation of the essence of perfect luminosity is the first arising of thought. The arising of this thought is the root of birth and death; it is most subtle. Above this—
The conclusion answers that all five aggregates (skandhas) consist of false conceptualization.
Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five types of false conceptualization.

Following this, the section on the ultimate limit of the text has two parts. The first part describes the ultimate limit of the five aggregates and has two sub-sections; the first restates the common cause of the five.
The commentary states: These five aggregates all possess the sense of receiving and grasping; therefore, they are called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
They are formed by five kinds of deluded conceptualization: first, the conceptualization of obstructive solidity, up to the fifth, the conceptualization of formless vagueness.

If you now wish to know the shallow and deep nature of the causal realms (*hetu-dhātu*), the subsequent extensive section is divided into ten parts and five chapters. First, regarding the two delusions of form and emptiness: the commentary states that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) all possess causal realms;
that which is shallow is the cause, while that which is deep is the realm. This heading governs what follows.
"Only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form.
The commentary states: "This is because this form is substantial form and emptiness is inert emptiness. This form, characterized by obstruction, is the opposite of emptiness, which is a void space;
therefore, form takes emptiness as its limit. Alternatively, it is said that these are cause and effect, where the cause consists of feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Consciousness. As for the fruit being form, the fruit is deep while the cause is shallow.
Only contact (*sparśa*) and separation (*viyoga*) constitute the limit of feeling (*vedanā*).
Next, regarding contact and separation, it is not stated that they apply to the mental faculty (*manas*). The commentary states: "Feeling takes 'receiving' as its meaning. If there is..."
When there is contact, there is experiencing; if there is separation from contact, there is no experiencing. Contact and separation are the limits of feeling (*vedanā*).
Only recollection and forgetfulness are the limits of perception (*saṃjñā*).
The third is forgetfulness (*muṣita-smṛti*). Forgetfulness is subsumed under delusion (*moha*) because it is identical to the obscuration of consciousness (*saṃjñā-saṃkleśa*).
The commentary states: "Perception (*saṃjñā*) takes up signs as its mode of activity (*ākāra*). If there is recollection, there is the taking up of signs;

since there is no recollection, it is forgetfulness, which is thus the limit of perception. An outsider asks: "Recollection may be considered a derivative of mindfulness (*smṛti*), and mindfulness, by supporting its object, is delusion. But what about forgetfulness?"
This is non-mind. It merges with and becomes one with the true essence; for what reason, then, would it be delusion? Answer: Delusion is likewise the obscuration of consciousness;
both are equally subsumed under "forgetting.
Only cessation and arising constitute the limits of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*).
Fourth, the cessation of arising. There are two kinds of visible cessation of arising: first, the ultimate; second, the phenomenal.

This cessation [involves] the movement of the phenomenal aspect, which exists only as a delusion. The Commentary states: "Because formations (*saṃskāra*) shift and flow, they constitute the aspect of formation.
Since there is formation if there is arising, and no formation if there is cessation, this [cessation] is the limit of formations. An outsider asks:
Question: Is this cessation identical to or different from ultimate cessation? Answer: This cessation is the movement of the phenomenal marks; it exists only as a delusion.
When the turbid enters and merges with the clear, it returns to the limit of consciousness.

The five "tranquil entries" merge with the tranquil. The former refers to the six consciousnesses; the merging refers to the eight sources. The former can be understood as delusion; the latter encompasses both the true and the deluded.
These terms are established from the perspective of birth-and-death and the accumulation of arising; thus they are named "aggregates" (*skandhas*) to manifest the habitual tendencies of delusion.
The commentary states: When the *zhan* (clarity) enters above, the sixth consciousness does not share the same objects as the five [sensory] consciousnesses.

When it merges with the *zhan*, it returns from above to the defiled portion of the eighth consciousness. Thus, if the sixth were present, it would share the same objects as the five; this is the *vijñāna-skandha*.
Now, returning to the substance of the eighth from above, this is the limit of consciousness. The above constitutes the conclusion of these five layers. Proceeding...

What is meant by "dhātu" (elements)? The Commentary states: "The former refers to the six consciousnesses. This sixth consciousness does not share the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses];
it perceives only the mountains and peaks. When combined, they constitute the eight bases. This means that the eighth is the root-source of the preceding consciousnesses.

"The former delusion can be known" means that the sixth consciousness can be known to arise and perish from moment to moment. "The latter penetrates both the real and the delusive" means that the eighth consciousness is defiled...
When divided, they possess distinct characteristics. If the pure portion belongs to the category of wisdom (*jñāna*), the outsider asks:

"Consciousness (*vijñāna*) permeates both the real and the false; as for this 'tranquil entry,' is it real or false? The answer is: "This statement is discussed from the perspective of the side of arising and ceasing and of accumulation and origination. 'Accumulation' means gathering together."

When it arises, it arises. The eighth [consciousness] is beginningless; it arises through accumulation because all seeds, both out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*), arise within it.
Therefore, it is called the "Theory of the Limit of Accumulation" (*saṃcita-pakṣa-vāda*).
These five aggregates fundamentally arise in successive layers.

Second, there is the text for demonstrating their removal and providing encouragement, which has two parts. First, the text for removal has three sections. First, the two gates of cessation. The commentary states:
The root source of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) consists of the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭa-vijñāna*).
Their arising is caused by consciousness.
The commentary states: "As the very first moment of taking birth, one is entrusted within the mother’s womb as *kalala*, a state of impure and defiled contact."
And thus one undergoes conception.
"Cessation proceeds from the removal of form.
The commentary states: "If cessation occurs at the time of non-existence, it first proceeds from the forms of the five sense organs, all of which return to their seeds."
In principle, there is sudden awakening; by means of this awakening, [the hindrances] are eliminated all at once.

Next, both the sudden and gradual approaches are explained together. The commentary states: "If it is the awakening to principle, one awakens to only one aggregate (skandha), while the remaining four aggregates are simultaneously and entirely eliminated."
"Affairs are not eliminated instantaneously; they are exhausted through a gradual sequence.

The Commentary states: This answers the second question. One must gradually bring forth the *rūpa-skandha* (aggregate of form) until the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness), at which point they are finally exhausted.
"I have already shown you the knots in the *kārpāsa* cloth. What is it that you do not understand, that you must inquire about this again?

Later, when you are reproached for your delusion, you shall ask again. The commentary states: This refers to the fifth scripture, "The Doubt Regarding the Identity of Knotting and Untying," which says:
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *kārpāsa* cloth... [up to] the Buddha’s words: 'The six sense faculties are likewise resolved.'"

It is likewise so; this is also the meaning of that [previous] inquiry. You are being questioned: why do you ask again? The preceding [passage] is the summary answer, intended to eliminate [the doubt] all at once or to exhaust it step by step.
You should take this root of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain penetration.

Hereafter, the exhortation has three parts. First, it clarifies that one’s own mind has been opened, so as to be transmitted to all practitioners in the future age of the Dharma-ending period, enabling them to recognize what is false and illusory.
The subsequent preface describes the intent for the circulation of the teaching. The commentary states:

"It causes one to recognize the emptiness and falsity of the five aggregates, to develop a profound weariness with their spontaneous arising, to know that there is nirvana, and not to cling to the three realms."
The commentary states: "To deeply weary of self-arising means that the phenomena of arising and ceasing do not transcend these five aggregates.

Ānanda, suppose there were someone who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never failed."
The fourth period of the teaching’s flourishing further expands the text into four parts. The first clarifies the vast merit of making offerings to the Buddha; this section consists of three parts.
First is the broad exposition on the offering of pearls and jewels. The Commentary states: "In the fourth period, the teaching flourishes and is widely circulated.

Yet, as there is no arising of the teaching's period apart from the dharma itself flowing forth, the World-Honored One extensively explains the comparative measurements and the fruits of transmitting and upholding [the dharma]. The Sūtra says: "Ānanda..."
□ Afterward, suppose there were people filling the ten directions. Up to: "Would they obtain much merit or not, Ānanda?
He answered by comparing the few with the many: "Space is inexhaustible; up to: what limit could it have? It further says: "If, moreover, there were a person..."

The body is endowed with the four requisites; there is nothing it does not experience. Comparing this to previous merit, one who can, with a single thought, uphold this Dharma-gate during the final kalpa—its merit exceeds even that which cannot be reached by analogy, like space, the support of the great void.
As for the seven treasures, such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth: "to hold" means to carry and maintain them; they are offered as the four requisites.
"Regarding food, drink, clothing, and so forth, as well as attending upon and serving the Buddha, their minds do not pass the time in vain—'passing' (du) meaning 'to go beyond.
What do you think? By virtue of these causes and conditions of giving to the Buddha, would this person obtain much merit?"
Next, one examines the abundance of meritorious conditions. The commentary states: "It is said that space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless;
regarding the causes and conditions for serving and making offerings with a mind that never lets them go to waste, one examines the degree to which merit is obtained."
Ahu replied, "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to the Buddha;
even after casting off his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King. How much more so now, when the space before us is already filled with Buddha-lands?"
If one were to bestow precious jewels upon them all, even contemplating this for an entire kalpa would not suffice to reach its limit. How, then, could there be any boundary to such merit?

The subsequent answer states that one who has even slightly felt such inspiration will become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), let alone those with boundless merit. The commentary notes: "Giving seven coins to the Buddha" refers to seven gold coins;
"sacrificing one's body" refers to relinquishing this present retribution-body. Thereafter, one obtains the status of a Wheel-Turning King during an *utkalpa* (increasing eon).
The human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years; they possessed the seven treasures at their disposal, were surrounded by a thousand sons, and governed the transformation of the four continents.
This is an answer using a small number to represent many.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not false.
This is the second section on the accumulation of deep offenses; it is the third textual unit. First, he declares the truth. The commentary states:
"The World-Honored One, wishing first to cite the case of one person who commits the ten evils and the four grave offenses, subsequently transmits the efficacy of the sutra and transforms the hells."
The causes of suffering are transformed into a land of peace and bliss. Fearing that others might not believe this, he first made a solemn vow to them:
"My words are not false; the Buddha speaks only words that are true, words that are real, words that are not deceptive, and words that do not differ from reality."

Furthermore, suppose there is a person whose body has committed the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) and subsequently incurs the transgression of the two roots. The commentary states: "The four grave offenses refer to the four-part precepts (*caturvarga-śīla*) of the Hīnayāna:
sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and false speech."
The ten *pārājika* offenses. The commentary states:
this is translated as "falling. It means that if one commits these offenses, one will fall into undesirable realms in the future.
It is also called "abandonment," meaning that one is cast outside the two assemblies of pure monks. Thus, according to the Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra, first: if one kills oneself...
1. Teaching others to kill, and so forth; 2. If one steals oneself, or teaches others to steal, and so forth; 3.
If one commits sexual misconduct oneself, or teaches others to commit sexual misconduct, and so forth; 4. If one speaks falsehoods oneself, or teaches others to speak falsehoods, and so forth;
5. If one sells alcohol oneself, or teaches others to sell alcohol; 6. If one oneself speaks of the transgressions of laypeople or renunciants, or of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
1. A nun’s transgression; 2. If she instructs another to speak of such a transgression; 3. If she praises herself and disparages others; 4.

If she instructs another to praise themselves and disparage others; 5. If she is herself stingy; 6. If she instructs another to be stingy; 7. If she is herself angry; 8. If she instructs another to be angry; 9. If she herself slanders the Triple Gem.
If one teaches others to slander the Triple Gem,
in a mere instant they shall pass through this world, other worlds, and the Avīci Hell; indeed, they will experience every realm of the ten directions until the very end of the unceasing suffering.
The subsequent passage clarifies the swiftness with which suffering is experienced. The commentary states: "In an instant" refers to the interval between a blink and a breath.
"Avīci" (in Chinese, *wújiàn*) means "without interval," signifying that the various forms of suffering are continuous and uninterrupted.
The phrase "there is none one does not experience" means that there is no part of hell that one does not pass through or traverse completely.
One is able, with a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), to take up this Dharma-gate and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final age.

(Section Three: Manifesting the Flowing Merit; Part Six. First, praising the flowing merit of a single thought-moment. The Commentary states: "A single thought-moment" refers to a minor thought-moment;
a minor thought-moment is non-thought (*amanasikāra*); non-thought is non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which accords with principle (*tattva*). Taking this...

This Dharma gate is this Śūraṅgama Sūtra. In the age of the Final Dharma, it is precisely for this present time that it reveals the teachings to those who have not yet studied them and transmits and upholds this doctrine.
This person’s karmic obstacles of sin should be extinguished upon mere recollection.
Next, long-standing suffering is suddenly and joyfully dissolved. The commentary states:

"The four grave offenses and ten *pārājika* transgressions previously committed should be 'recollected'—that is, by the preceding single thought-moment. A single thought-moment is precisely non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)."
They transform the causes for suffering in the hells they have received into a land of peace and bliss;
they transform the causes of the three difficulties into the fruition of accomplishment. The commentary states:
"Transforming suffering into joy, the merit obtained surpasses that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million, or even a billionfold."
"Fourth, the praise of merit is twofold and inexhaustible. The commentary states: "Regarding the previous giving to others, it was already as vast as the preceding empty space and inexhaustible;

yet the people who fill the Buddha-lands surpass that by a hundredfold without ceasing, surpass it by a thousandfold without ceasing, surpass it by ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million, ten-million, hundred-million, and billionfold—wherein ten-thousand constitutes one *yi* (億)."
Thus it continues until it reaches the point where it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.

The commentary states: "Even if a master mathematician and his disciples were to employ counting sticks for calculation and further resort to metaphors, they would still be unable to encompass that person's merit."
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this vidyā-mantra as I have extensively explained it— exhausting an entire kalpa without reaching the end—
these five praises for upholding it are inconceivable.
Relying on my teachings and practicing the path according to those instructions, one will directly attain Bodhi, and no further demonic activities will arise.
Sixth, praising the realization achieved through reliance on practice.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs...
The four dharmas [are] divided into ten sections. First, the internal assembly is designated:

the *upāsaka*. Next, the householders are listed; the commentary states: "In the language of Tang, this means 'male lay follower' (*upāsaka*). By receiving the three refuges and the five precepts, one attains [this status]. One.
The Upāsikā (laywoman) is divided into two types. One is capable of drawing near to the community of bhikṣus and training in the Buddha’s teachings;
the commentary states that "Upāsikā" is the Tang-language term for "female attendant. She may also draw near to the bhikṣuṇīs and train in the Buddha’s teachings. These are the two [types].
This refers to the lay community.
Throughout all the worlds, these three collectively encompass [them] and dwell therein. The commentary states: "All" universally includes the phenomena of the physical world and their constant flux.
The interval is one hundred [yojanas]. All sentient beings fall within this interval:
devas, humans, asuras, and...
[the term for] "deva" (天) has the meaning of light and the meaning of sovereignty. "Human" (人) means many...
The meaning of "thought and discernment" (*saṃjñā-vitarka*). The five [virtues] are constantly practiced by humans. Regarding the *asuras*, they are explained as before.

As for "and various bodhisattvas from other directions," this lists the great beings (*mahāsattva*) from other directions. The commentary states that "and" (*ji*) carries the sense of inclusion or conjunction. "Various" (*zhu*) means not being one; "other" (*ta*) refers to...
"Method" (*fang*) refers to the method (*fang*); in Sanskrit it is *bodhisattva*, which in the Tang language means "enlightened sentient being.
Regarding the "two vehicles":
the sixth [section] designates the two vehicles within this realm. The commentary states: "śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha."
"Ārya-ṛṣi. "Seven" (sapta) refers to the manifest ṛṣis. "Ārya" means correct; "ṛṣi" means to transcend. It signifies transcending [to dwell] within the mountains.
"Kumāra" means youth.
Eighth is Zhangtongzi (彰童子). The commentary states: "The son of a *kumārabhūta* who does not violate the dust of desire;
he is also a powerful spirit-ghost (*deva-guǐ*) who has first resolved his mind [on enlightenment].
Ninth is Chen Shenguǐ (陳神鬼). The commentary states: "One who has resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind; the destination to which the *po* and *hun* souls of humans return."
He said, "They are ghosts. He said, "They are spirits, for their power is unfathomable through the interplay of yin and yang; thus they are called 'spirits of great power.
Then all the ghosts and spirits were filled with great joy, paid their respects, and departed.
The ten knots were all untied. The commentary states: After the Buddha had preached this sutra, up until the point where they paid homage and departed, [this concludes] the section.
*The Great Buddha-Top Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Ten, Part Two (End).
